docs.title: Lesson 16: Aggregation, GROUP BY and HAVING
docs.text:
Summarising data — counts, totals and per-group filtering

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 4: Structured Query Language · 12 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 7.1 · Murach's MySQL, Ch. 6

Learning Outcomes

  1. Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN correctly, including their treatment of NULL.
  2. Distinguish COUNT(*), COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column).
  3. Write GROUP BY queries and state the single-value rule.
  4. Distinguish WHERE from HAVING precisely.
  5. Combine grouping with joins, including the LEFT JOIN idiom for counting zeros.

docs.title: 16.1 Aggregate Functions
docs.text:
Aggregate function

A function that takes a set of values and returns a single value. Aggregates collapse many rows into one.

Function Returns Works on COUNT(*) Number of rows Any COUNT(col) Number of non-NULL values Any COUNT(DISTINCT col) Number of distinct non-NULL values Any SUM(col) Total Numeric only AVG(col) Arithmetic mean Numeric only MAX(col) Largest Numeric, string, date MIN(col) Smallest Numeric, string, date 
SELECT COUNT(*)          AS TotalCourses,
       SUM(TotalSeats)   AS AllSeats,
       AVG(TotalSeats)   AS MeanSeats,
       MAX(TotalSeats)   AS Largest,
       MIN(TotalSeats)   AS Smallest
FROM   COURSE;
TotalCourses AllSeats MeanSeats Largest Smallest 5 235 47.0000 60 40

With no GROUP BY, the whole table is one group and exactly one row is returned.

docs.title: The three forms of COUNT
docs.text:
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col)

Suppose ADMISSION holds 6 rows, involving 4 distinct students, and a nullable column Grade has 2 NULLs.

Expression Result Counts COUNT(*) 6 Rows — NULLs included COUNT(Rollno) 6 Non-NULL Rollno values (it is NOT NULL, so all) COUNT(DISTINCT Rollno) 4 Distinct students COUNT(Grade) 4 Non-NULL grades only

COUNT(*) is the only aggregate that does not ignore NULLs. Use it when you mean "how many rows", and COUNT(col) when you mean "how many rows have a value here".

docs.title: Aggregates and NULL
docs.text:
All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs entirely. This matters most for AVG:

-- Marks: 80, 90, NULL, NULL
SELECT AVG(Marks) FROM RESULT;                     -- 85 = (80+90)/2
SELECT SUM(Marks)/COUNT(*) FROM RESULT;            -- 42.5 = 170/4
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(Marks,0)) FROM RESULT;         -- 42.5 -- NULL treated as zero

All three are defensible; they answer different questions. AVG(Marks) is the average of the marks that exist; the others treat a missing mark as zero. Decide which you mean, and be explicit.

docs.title: 16.2 GROUP BY
docs.text:
GROUP BY

Partitions the rows into groups that share the same values in the grouping columns, then applies each aggregate function once per group, producing one output row per group.

SELECT   Coursetype, COUNT(*) AS NumCourses, AVG(TotalSeats) AS MeanSeats
FROM     COURSE
GROUP BY Coursetype;
Coursetype NumCourses MeanSeats Fulltime 3 48.3333 Parttime 2 45.0000 
   BEFORE GROUPING (5 rows)          AFTER GROUP BY Coursetype (2 rows)

   CS01  Fulltime  60  --,
   CH01  Fulltime  45  --+-->  group 'Fulltime'  -->  COUNT=3  AVG=48.33
   PH01  Fulltime  40  --'
   MA02  Parttime  50  --,
   EN03  Parttime  40  --+-->  group 'Parttime'  -->  COUNT=2  AVG=45.00

docs.title: The single-value rule
docs.text:
The rule that governs every GROUP BY query

Every column in the SELECT list must either appear in the GROUP BY clause, or be inside an aggregate function.

The reason is arithmetic: a group produces one output row, so every expression in that row must have one value for the group. A grouping column has one value by construction; an aggregate collapses to one value by definition. Any other column has many values in the group, and the DBMS cannot choose among them.

-- INVALID: which of the three Fulltime course names should be shown?
SELECT Coursetype, Cname, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype;

-- VALID
SELECT Coursetype, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype;
SELECT Coursetype, MAX(Cname), COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype;
SELECT Coursetype, Cname, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype, Cname;

A MySQL warning. Older MySQL versions, and installations without ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY in the SQL mode, accept the invalid form and return an arbitrary value from the group — silently wrong. Standard SQL and modern MySQL reject it. Write standard-conforming SQL; do not rely on the permissive behaviour.

docs.title: Grouping by several columns
docs.text:
SELECT   c.Coursetype, YEAR(a.Dateofadmission) AS Yr, COUNT(*) AS Admissions
FROM     ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID = c.SID
GROUP BY c.Coursetype, YEAR(a.Dateofadmission)
ORDER BY c.Coursetype, Yr;

One group per distinct combination of the grouping columns.

docs.title: 16.3 HAVING
docs.text:
HAVING

Filters groups after they are formed, exactly as WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING may reference aggregate functions; WHERE may not.

Syllabus Q8 — course names with more than five students enrolled:

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled
FROM     ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID = c.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5;

WHERE vs HAVING — the definitive comparison

WHERE HAVING Filters Individual rows Groups Evaluated Before GROUP BY (step 2) After GROUP BY (step 4) May use aggregates No Yes May use non-grouped columns Yes No (same single-value rule) Without GROUP BY Normal row filter Treats the whole table as one group Performance Better — reduces rows before grouping Necessary only for aggregate conditions

Rule of thumb: if the condition can be tested on a single row, put it in WHERE. Only conditions on an aggregate belong in HAVING.

Both in one query:

-- Full-time courses (row filter) having more than 5 students (group filter)
SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled
FROM     ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID = c.SID
WHERE    c.Coursetype = 'Fulltime'          -- filter rows first
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5                        -- then filter groups
ORDER BY Enrolled DESC;

Why WHERE first is faster

Putting Coursetype = 'Fulltime' in WHERE discards part-time rows before the grouping work begins — fewer rows to sort or hash into groups.

Writing it as HAVING MAX(c.Coursetype) = 'Fulltime' would group everything first and then throw groups away. Same answer, more work. This is the SQL counterpart of the push selections down rule from Unit 3, Lesson 3.

docs.title: 16.4 The LEFT JOIN Idiom for Counting Zeros
docs.text:
This is the single most important practical pattern in this lesson.

-- WRONG: courses with no students simply vanish
SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled
FROM     COURSE c JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname;

An inner join produces no row for PH01 Physics, so it forms no group and never appears — the report silently understates the course list.

-- RIGHT
SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Enrolled
FROM     COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
ORDER BY Enrolled DESC;
Cname Enrolled Computer Science 2 Mathematics 2 Chemistry 1 English 1 Physics 0

Two details that must both be right

  1. LEFT JOIN keeps every course, padding unmatched ones with NULLs.
  2. COUNT(a.Rollno), not COUNT(*). For PH01 the left join produces one row with all ADMISSION columns NULL. COUNT(*) would count that row and report 1; COUNT(a.Rollno) ignores the NULL and correctly reports 0.

Getting the join right but leaving COUNT(*) is the classic half-correct answer.

Syllabus Q17 — display the vacant seats for each course:

SELECT   c.Cname, c.TotalSeats,
         COUNT(a.Rollno)                  AS Filled,
         c.TotalSeats - COUNT(a.Rollno)   AS Vacant
FROM     COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname, c.TotalSeats
ORDER BY Vacant DESC;

Syllabus Q22 — count courses with more than five students, for each course type:

SELECT   Coursetype, COUNT(*) AS PopularCourses
FROM     ( SELECT   c.SID, c.Coursetype
           FROM     COURSE c JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
           GROUP BY c.SID, c.Coursetype
           HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5 ) AS popular
GROUP BY Coursetype;

Two levels of grouping are needed: the inner query finds which courses qualify, the outer counts them per type. This nested aggregation pattern is common whenever a question aggregates over the result of an aggregation.

Syllabus Q16 — courses where enrolment is only 10 per cent of total seats:

SELECT   c.Cname, c.TotalSeats, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Enrolled
FROM     COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname, c.TotalSeats
HAVING   COUNT(a.Rollno) = c.TotalSeats * 0.10;

docs.title: 16.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Distinguish COUNT(*), COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col) with a worked example. Which ignores NULLs?

A.

  • COUNT(*) counts rows, regardless of content. It is the only aggregate that does not ignore NULLs.
  • COUNT(col) counts rows where col is not NULL.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL values of col.

Take a table RESULT(Rollno, SID, Grade):

Rollno SID Grade X2019 CS01 A X2019 MA02 B X2020 CS01 A Z1188 CH01 NULL Z1188 EN03 NULL Expression Result Reason COUNT(*) 5 Five rows. COUNT(Grade) 3 Two grades are NULL and are ignored. COUNT(DISTINCT Grade) 2 Distinct non-NULL grades are A and B. COUNT(Rollno) 5 Rollno is NOT NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT Rollno) 3 Three distinct students.

Practical significance. "How many students have results?" is COUNT(DISTINCT Rollno) = 3, not COUNT(*) = 5. "How many results have been entered?" is COUNT(Grade) = 3, not COUNT(*) = 5. Choosing the wrong form gives a plausible but wrong number, which is worse than an error.

Solved Question 2

Q. State and justify the single-value rule for GROUP BY. Give an invalid query and three ways to fix it.

A. The rule: every column in the SELECT list must either appear in the GROUP BY clause or be enclosed in an aggregate function.

Justification. GROUP BY produces exactly one output row per group. Every expression in that row must therefore evaluate to exactly one value for the group. A grouping column has one value by construction — that is what defines the group. An aggregate reduces many values to one by definition. Any other column holds several values within the group, and there is no principled way to pick one.

Invalid: 

SELECT Coursetype, Cname, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype;
The Fulltime group contains three different Cname values — Computer Science, Chemistry, Physics — so the query does not specify which to display.

Three fixes, answering three different questions:

  1. Drop the offending column — "how many courses of each type?" 

    SELECT Coursetype, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype;

  2. Aggregate it — "how many, and one representative name?" 

    SELECT Coursetype, MAX(Cname) AS SampleCourse, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype;

  3. Add it to GROUP BY — "how many courses share each (type, name) pair?" This makes the groups finer, so the answer changes. 

    SELECT Coursetype, Cname, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype, Cname;

Caution. MySQL without ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY accepts the invalid query and returns an arbitrary Cname — no error, wrong answer. Always write the standard-conforming form.

Solved Question 3

Q. Distinguish WHERE from HAVING on at least five points. Write one query using both, and explain why the split is as it is.

A. (Comparison table of Section 4.3.) The essential differences: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot reference aggregates; HAVING filters groups after grouping and can.

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled
FROM     ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID = c.SID
WHERE    c.Coursetype = 'Fulltime'
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY Enrolled DESC;

"Among full-time courses, list those with more than five students."

Why the split is as it is. Coursetype = 'Fulltime' is testable on a single row — each admission row, joined to its course, either is or is not full-time. It therefore belongs in WHERE, and putting it there discards part-time rows before the grouping work begins.

COUNT(*) > 5 is not testable on a single row: it is a property of the whole group, which does not exist until GROUP BY has run. It therefore must go in HAVING.

Performance. Moving the Coursetype test into HAVING (as HAVING MAX(c.Coursetype)='Fulltime') would produce the same answer while grouping every row first and then discarding whole groups — strictly more work. This is the SQL form of the push selections down optimisation rule.

Solved Question 4

Q. Write a query listing every course with its enrolment count, including courses with none. Explain both details that must be right.

A.

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Enrolled
FROM     COURSE c
LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
ORDER BY Enrolled DESC, c.Cname;

Detail 1 — the join must be LEFT JOIN. An inner join emits a row only where a match exists. PH01 Physics has no admissions, so an inner join produces no row for it, it forms no group, and it is silently absent from the report. A LEFT JOIN retains every course, padding the ADMISSION columns with NULLs where there is no match.

Detail 2 — the aggregate must be COUNT(a.Rollno), not COUNT(*). After the left join, PH01 contributes exactly one row, whose ADMISSION columns are all NULL. COUNT(*) counts rows and would report 1 — a wrong answer that looks entirely plausible. COUNT(a.Rollno) ignores NULLs and correctly reports 0.

Result:

Cname Enrolled Computer Science 2 Mathematics 2 Chemistry 1 English 1 Physics 0

Grouping by c.SID as well as c.Cname is deliberate: SID is the key, so two courses that happened to share a name would still be separated. Both are in the GROUP BY, satisfying the single-value rule.

Solved Question 5

Q. Write SQL for syllabus practicals 6, 8, 13, 17 and 22.

A.

Q6 — course details with more than N students enrolled, N supplied by the user. 

SET @N = 5;
SELECT   c.*, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Enrolled
FROM     COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID
HAVING   COUNT(a.Rollno) > @N;
A user variable stands in for the input; in an application this becomes a bound parameter (?), which is also the defence against SQL injection.

Q8 — course names in which more than five students have enrolled. 

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled
FROM     ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID = c.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5;
An inner join suffices here: a course with zero students can never satisfy > 5, so nothing is lost by excluding it.

Q13 — course names in which more than 30 students took admission. 

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Admitted
FROM     ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID = c.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
HAVING   COUNT(*) > 30;

Q17 — display the vacant seats for each course. 

SELECT   c.Cname, c.TotalSeats,
         COUNT(a.Rollno)                AS Filled,
         c.TotalSeats - COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Vacant
FROM     COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname, c.TotalSeats
ORDER BY Vacant DESC;
Here the LEFT JOIN is essential: a course with no students has all its seats vacant and must appear, with Vacant = TotalSeats.

Q22 — number of courses with more than five students, per course type. 

SELECT   Coursetype, COUNT(*) AS PopularCourses
FROM   ( SELECT   c.SID, c.Coursetype
         FROM     COURSE c JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
         GROUP BY c.SID, c.Coursetype
         HAVING   COUNT(*) > 5 ) AS popular
GROUP BY Coursetype;
This needs two levels of aggregation: the inner query determines which courses qualify (one row per qualifying course), and the outer counts those rows per type. A single GROUP BY cannot do it, because the two aggregations are at different granularities.

Solved Question 6

Q. AVG(Marks) returns 85 but SUM(Marks)/COUNT(*) returns 42.5 on the same data. Explain, and say which is correct.

A. The data must contain NULLs. Suppose four rows with marks 80, 90, NULL, NULL.

  • AVG(Marks) ignores NULLs: it averages only the two present values, (80+90)/2 = 85.
  • SUM(Marks) also ignores NULLs, giving 170; but COUNT(*) counts rows, giving 4. So 170/4 = 42.5.

The mismatch arises because SUM and COUNT(*) disagree about the denominator: SUM skipped the NULLs, COUNT(*) did not.

Which is correct depends on what the NULLs mean — the three meanings from Unit 2, Lesson 2:

  • If NULL means "the mark has not yet been entered" (unknown-missing), then those students should not influence the class average, and AVG(Marks) = 85 is correct. It is the average of the marks that exist.
  • If NULL means "the student was absent and scores zero", then the missing values are really zeros, and the correct expression states that explicitly: 
    SELECT AVG(COALESCE(Marks,0)) FROM RESULT;   -- 42.5

The lesson. Both numbers are arithmetically right; they answer different questions. Never write SUM(x)/COUNT(*) intending an average — use AVG(x) if NULLs should be excluded, or AVG(COALESCE(x,0)) if they should count as zero. And always report the denominator alongside the average, so the reader can see which convention was used:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS Students, COUNT(Marks) AS Graded, AVG(Marks) AS MeanOfGraded
FROM   RESULT;

docs.title: 16.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Name the five aggregate functions.
  2. Which aggregate does not ignore NULLs?
  3. State the single-value rule.
  4. Give two differences between WHERE and HAVING.
  5. Why is COUNT(*) wrong after a LEFT JOIN when counting matches?
  6. What does a GROUP BY query with no matching rows return?

B. Write the SQL

  1. Total number of students.
  2. Number of distinct courses that have at least one admission.
  3. Average, maximum and minimum seats per course type.
  4. Number of admissions per month of 2019.
  5. Courses with more than two admissions, most popular first.
  6. For each student, the number of courses they are admitted to.
  7. Students admitted to more than one course.
  8. Each society with its member count, including empty societies.
  9. The society with the most members (syllabus Q10).
  10. The two most popular part-time courses (syllabus Q11).
  11. Course types where the average seat count exceeds 45.
  12. For each teacher, the number of courses and total seats they are responsible for.
  13. Percentage of total college seats represented by each course.
  14. Courses that are more than 90 per cent full.

C. Predict and explain

  1. RESULT(Rollno, Marks) has 6 rows with marks 70, 80, NULL, 90, NULL, 60. Give: a. COUNT(*) b. COUNT(Marks) c. SUM(Marks) d. AVG(Marks) e. SUM(Marks)/COUNT(*) f. MAX(Marks) g. COUNT(DISTINCT Marks)
  2. Explain why each is invalid, and correct it: a. SELECT Cname, COUNT(*) FROM COURSE; b. SELECT Coursetype, Cname FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype; c. SELECT Cname FROM COURSE WHERE COUNT(*) > 1; d. SELECT Coursetype, COUNT(*) AS n FROM COURSE GROUP BY Coursetype HAVING n > 1; (consider portability)
  3. A report of courses and enrolments shows 4 courses instead of 5. Diagnose and give two fixes.

D. Analytical

  1. Explain why placing a non-aggregate condition in HAVING rather than WHERE gives the same answer but is slower. Illustrate with row counts.
  2. Write two queries answering "the average number of students per course", one counting empty courses and one not. Explain when each is appropriate.
  3. Explain what MySQL does with an invalid GROUP BY when ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is off, and why this is dangerous.
  4. Design a query producing a single row with: total students, total courses, total admissions, average admissions per student, and the number of students with no admission.
  5. Explain why the syllabus Q11 query ("two most popular part-time courses") could give a misleading answer with ties, and rewrite it to handle them.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. AVG(col) equals SUM(col)/COUNT(*).
  2. HAVING can be used without GROUP BY.
  3. COUNT(DISTINCT col) includes NULL as a distinct value.
  4. Every column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.
  5. WHERE can filter on COUNT(*).
  6. A LEFT JOIN with COUNT(*) correctly reports zero for unmatched rows.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. AVG divides by the number of non-NULL values; COUNT(*) counts all rows. They agree only when the column has no NULLs.
  2. True. Without GROUP BY, the whole table is one group, so HAVING COUNT(*) > 100 is a valid filter on that single group.
  3. False. It counts distinct non-NULL values only.
  4. False. It must appear in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function.
  5. False. WHERE is evaluated before groups exist; aggregate conditions belong in HAVING.
  6. False. COUNT(*) counts the NULL-padded row and reports 1. Use COUNT(<column from the right table>).

Lesson Summary

  • Aggregates collapse a set of values to one. All ignore NULLs except COUNT(*).
  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL values.
  • GROUP BY gives one row per group, so the single-value rule applies: every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot see aggregates; HAVING filters groups after grouping and can. Put a condition in WHERE whenever it is testable on one row.
  • To count zeros, use LEFT JOIN and COUNT(<right-table column>) — both details are required.

docs.title: Lesson 14: ALTER, DROP, Update Behaviours and DML
docs.text:
Changing the schema, and changing the data

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 4: Structured Query Language · 12 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 6.2, 6.4 · Murach's MySQL, Ch. 5, 11

Learning Outcomes

  1. Use ALTER TABLE to add, modify, rename and drop columns and constraints.
  2. Distinguish DROP, DELETE and TRUNCATE precisely.
  3. Write INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in all their forms.
  4. Predict the effect of each referential action on a cascading change.
  5. Avoid the three classic DML disasters.

docs.title: 14.1 ALTER TABLE
docs.text: ALTER TABLE performs schema evolution (Unit 1, Lesson 2) — the operation that program–data independence is designed to make painless.

docs.title: Adding a column
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Mobile CHAR(10) DEFAULT '9999999999';

This is syllabus practical question 23. Every existing row immediately acquires the default value. Without a DEFAULT, existing rows get NULL — which fails if you also specify NOT NULL and the table is non-empty.

ALTER TABLE ENROLLMENT ADD COLUMN FeesPaid VARCHAR(3) DEFAULT 'No'
    CHECK (FeesPaid IN ('Yes','No'));

This is syllabus practical question 19.

Several columns at once:

ALTER TABLE STUDENT
    ADD COLUMN Email   VARCHAR(60),
    ADD COLUMN Address VARCHAR(100);

docs.title: Modifying a column
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY COLUMN Name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL;   -- MySQL
ALTER TABLE STUDENT ALTER COLUMN Name TYPE VARCHAR(60);        -- PostgreSQL

Widening is safe; narrowing is not

VARCHAR(40) → VARCHAR(60) always succeeds. VARCHAR(40) → VARCHAR(20) fails or truncates if any existing value is longer. Always check first:

SELECT MAX(LENGTH(Name)) FROM STUDENT;

docs.title: Renaming
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE COURSE RENAME COLUMN Cname TO CourseName;   -- column
ALTER TABLE COURSE RENAME TO SUBJECT;                   -- table

Renaming is a conceptual schema change and will break any view or application that names the old identifier — the limit of logical data independence (Unit 1, Lesson 3).

docs.title: Dropping a column
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE STUDENT DROP COLUMN Mobile;

This destroys the data in that column irrecoverably. It fails if the column is referenced by a foreign key or used in a constraint.

docs.title: Adding and dropping constraints
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE COURSE ADD CONSTRAINT chk_seats CHECK (TotalSeats > 0);

ALTER TABLE ADMISSION ADD CONSTRAINT fk_adm_course
    FOREIGN KEY (SID) REFERENCES COURSE(SID) ON DELETE RESTRICT;

ALTER TABLE COURSE DROP CONSTRAINT chk_seats;      -- standard
ALTER TABLE COURSE DROP CHECK chk_seats;           -- MySQL
ALTER TABLE ADMISSION DROP FOREIGN KEY fk_adm_course;
ALTER TABLE COURSE DROP PRIMARY KEY;

Adding a constraint validates the existing data first; if any row violates it, the ALTER is rejected and nothing changes. This is why naming constraints at creation time (Lesson 1) pays off — you cannot drop what you cannot name.

docs.title: 14.2 DROP, DELETE and TRUNCATE
docs.text:
The comparison examiners ask for every year

DROP TABLE TRUNCATE TABLE DELETE FROM Category DDL DDL DML Removes Rows and the table definition All rows; keeps the table Rows matching WHERE (all if omitted) WHERE clause No No Yes Speed Fast Very fast — deallocates pages Slow — row by row, logged Rollback Generally no Generally no Yes Fires triggers No No Yes Resets AUTO_INCREMENT n/a Yes No Afterwards Table gone Empty table, structure intact Table with remaining rows 
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ADMISSION;        -- table and data gone
TRUNCATE TABLE ADMISSION;              -- empty, structure kept
DELETE FROM ADMISSION WHERE SID='CS01';-- selective, rollback-able

Drop order. A table referenced by a foreign key cannot be dropped. Drop children before parents:

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ENROLLMENT, ADMISSION;   -- children first
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS SOCIETY, COURSE, STUDENT;-- then parents

docs.title: Form 1 — all columns, in order
docs.text:
INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES ('X2019', 'Ankit Sharma', '2001-03-14');

Fragile: it breaks silently if the column order changes.

docs.title: Form 2 — named columns (always prefer this)
docs.text:
INSERT INTO STUDENT (Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth)
VALUES ('X2020', 'Riya Verma', '2002-05-11');

Robust against column reordering, and lets you omit columns that have defaults or accept NULL.

docs.title: Form 3 — multiple rows
docs.text:
INSERT INTO COURSE (SID, Cname, TotalSeats, Duration, Coursetype, TeacherInCharge)
VALUES ('CS01','Computer Science',60,3,'Fulltime','R. K. Gupta'),
       ('CH01','Chemistry',       45,3,'Fulltime','S. Menon'),
       ('MA02','Mathematics',     50,3,'Parttime','A. Gupta'),
       ('EN03','English',         40,3,'Parttime','P. Das'),
       ('PH01','Physics',         40,3,'Fulltime','V. Rao');

Far faster than five separate statements: one parse, one transaction, one round trip.

docs.title: Form 4 — INSERT ... SELECT
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE PARTTIME_STUDENTS (Rollno VARCHAR(8), Name VARCHAR(40));

INSERT INTO PARTTIME_STUDENTS (Rollno, Name)
SELECT DISTINCT s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime';

Copies the result of a query into a table. The SELECT list must match the target columns in number and domain.

docs.title: Handling duplicates
docs.text:
INSERT IGNORE INTO STUDENT VALUES ('X2019','Duplicate','2001-01-01');  -- skip silently

INSERT INTO STUDENT (Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth)
VALUES ('X2019','Ankit Kumar Sharma','2001-03-14')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE Name = VALUES(Name);                           -- "upsert"

docs.title: 14.4 UPDATE
docs.text:
UPDATE table_name
SET    column1 = expression1, column2 = expression2
WHERE  condition;

Syllabus question 7 — modify a student's name:

UPDATE STUDENT SET Name = 'Ankit Kumar Sharma' WHERE Rollno = 'X2019';

Syllabus question 18 — increase every course's total seats by 10 per cent:

UPDATE COURSE SET TotalSeats = CEIL(TotalSeats * 1.10);

CEIL is used because TotalSeats is an integer and a fractional seat is meaningless; rounding up is the generous interpretation. Note that this statement has no WHERE — deliberately, because every course is to change.

Syllabus question 20 — advance every admission date by one year:

UPDATE ADMISSION SET Dateofadmission = DATE_ADD(Dateofadmission, INTERVAL 1 YEAR);

Conditional update with CASE:

UPDATE COURSE
SET TotalSeats = CASE
        WHEN Coursetype = 'Fulltime' THEN TotalSeats + 10
        WHEN Coursetype = 'Parttime' THEN TotalSeats + 5
        ELSE TotalSeats
    END;

Update driven by another table:

UPDATE COURSE c
SET    c.TotalSeats = c.TotalSeats + 20
WHERE  c.SID IN (SELECT a.SID FROM ADMISSION a
                 GROUP BY a.SID HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);

Disaster 1 — the forgotten WHERE

UPDATE STUDENT SET Name = 'Ankit Kumar Sharma';   -- renames EVERY student

Every row is updated. Three defences:

  1. Run the WHERE as a SELECT first. SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno='X2019'; — check that exactly the intended rows come back.
  2. Wrap it in a transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ...; SELECT ...; -- COMMIT or ROLLBACK
  3. Enable safe-update mode. In MySQL, SET SQL_SAFE_UPDATES = 1; refuses any UPDATE or DELETE that does not restrict on a key.

docs.title: 14.5 DELETE
docs.text:
DELETE FROM ADMISSION WHERE Rollno = 'X2019' AND SID = 'MA02';   -- one row
DELETE FROM ADMISSION WHERE SID = 'EN03';                        -- several
DELETE FROM ADMISSION;                                           -- ALL rows

Delete driven by a subquery:

DELETE FROM ADMISSION
WHERE  SID IN (SELECT SID FROM COURSE WHERE TotalSeats < 30);

Disaster 2 — DELETE without WHERE

DELETE FROM STUDENT; empties the table. Worse, with ON DELETE CASCADE declared, it also empties ADMISSION and ENROLLMENT. One statement, three tables gone. The same three defences apply.

docs.title: 14.6 Update Behaviours — Referential Actions in Practice
docs.text:
Unit 3, Lesson 2 defined the five referential actions. Here is what they actually do.

Setup:

STUDENT:   ('X2019','Ankit Sharma','2001-03-14')
ADMISSION: ('X2019','CS01','2019-07-15'), ('X2019','MA02','2019-08-01')

fk_adm_student : ON DELETE CASCADE  ON UPDATE CASCADE
fk_adm_course  : ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE

Case 1 — delete the student.

DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno = 'X2019';

ON DELETE CASCADE → the student row and both admission rows are deleted. Result: ADMISSION loses two rows.

Case 2 — delete a course that has admissions.

DELETE FROM COURSE WHERE SID = 'CS01';

ON DELETE RESTRICT → rejected. Error: cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails. Nothing changes. To proceed, the admissions must first be removed or transferred.

Case 3 — change a roll number.

UPDATE STUDENT SET Rollno = 'X9019' WHERE Rollno = 'X2019';

ON UPDATE CASCADE → the student row changes and both admission rows are rewritten to X9019. The link is preserved.

Case 4 — the same, but with RESTRICT on update.

The UPDATE would be rejected, because children still reference the old value.

   ON DELETE CASCADE                ON DELETE RESTRICT

   STUDENT                          COURSE
   +--------+                       +------+
   | X2019  |  DELETE               | CS01 |  DELETE
   +---+----+                       +---+--+
       | cascades                       | blocked
       v                                X
   ADMISSION                        ADMISSION
   +--------+------+                +--------+------+
   | X2019  | CS01 | deleted        | X2019  | CS01 | preserved
   | X2019  | MA02 | deleted        +--------+------+
   +--------+------+                     ERROR 1451 raised

Disaster 3 — cascading further than you meant

With ON DELETE CASCADE declared on every foreign key in a ten-table schema, deleting one STUDENT row can propagate through admissions, enrolments, fee receipts, examination results and library issues. One statement, most of the database gone.

Policy: default to RESTRICT. Use CASCADE only where the child is genuinely existence-dependent on the parent (a weak entity, an order line), and never on a table that constitutes an audit trail.

docs.title: 14.7 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Distinguish DROP, DELETE and TRUNCATE on at least six points, with an example of when each is correct.

A. (Table of Section 2.2.) The essential points:

Category. DROP and TRUNCATE are DDL; DELETE is DML. This single fact explains most of the other differences.

What survives. DROP TABLE removes the rows and the table definition — the table ceases to exist. TRUNCATE removes all rows but leaves an empty table with its structure, constraints and privileges intact. DELETE removes only the rows matching WHERE.

Selectivity. Only DELETE accepts a WHERE clause.

Speed and logging. DELETE removes rows one at a time, logging each for rollback — slow on a large table. TRUNCATE deallocates the data pages wholesale, so it is nearly instantaneous regardless of size.

Rollback and triggers. DELETE can be rolled back and fires row-level triggers. TRUNCATE generally cannot be rolled back and fires no triggers — which matters if triggers maintain audit tables.

AUTO_INCREMENT. TRUNCATE resets the counter to 1; DELETE does not.

When each is correct:

  • DELETE FROM ADMISSION WHERE SID='EN03'; — removing selected rows in a live system.
  • TRUNCATE TABLE ADMISSION; — clearing a staging or test table completely before reloading.
  • DROP TABLE ADMISSION; — the table is no longer part of the design.

Solved Question 2

Q. Write SQL for syllabus practicals 7, 18, 19, 20 and 23, explaining each.

A.

Q7 — modify a student's name. 

UPDATE STUDENT SET Name = 'Ankit Kumar Sharma' WHERE Rollno = 'X2019';
The WHERE on the primary key guarantees exactly one row is affected. Omitting it would rename every student.

Q18 — increment total seats of each course by 10 per cent. 

UPDATE COURSE SET TotalSeats = CEIL(TotalSeats * 1.10);
No WHERE, deliberately — every course changes. CEIL is used because TotalSeats is an integer and a fractional seat is meaningless; ROUND would be acceptable if the intent were nearest-integer. Note the CHECK (TotalSeats > 0) constraint is re-validated and still holds.

Q19 — add an enrolment-fees-paid field. 

ALTER TABLE ENROLLMENT
    ADD COLUMN FeesPaid VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'No'
    CHECK (FeesPaid IN ('Yes','No'));
The DEFAULT 'No' is essential: it gives every existing row a valid value, so NOT NULL can be imposed on a non-empty table. The CHECK restricts the domain to the two permitted values.

Q20 — update the date of admission for all courses by one year. 

UPDATE ADMISSION SET Dateofadmission = DATE_ADD(Dateofadmission, INTERVAL 1 YEAR);
DATE_ADD with an INTERVAL handles leap years correctly, which naive arithmetic on a string would not.

Q23 — add a mobile-number column with a default. 

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Mobile CHAR(10) DEFAULT '9999999999';
CHAR(10) rather than VARCHAR(10) because an Indian mobile number is exactly ten digits — a genuinely fixed length. It is stored as a string, not a number, because it is an identifier rather than a quantity: leading zeros must be preserved and no arithmetic is ever performed on it.

Solved Question 3

Q. Given the setup of Section 2.6, state the exact effect of each statement.

a. DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno='X2019'; b. DELETE FROM COURSE WHERE SID='CS01'; c. UPDATE STUDENT SET Rollno='X9019' WHERE Rollno='X2019'; d. UPDATE COURSE SET SID='CS99' WHERE SID='CS01'; e. DELETE FROM ADMISSION WHERE Rollno='X2019'; then DELETE FROM COURSE WHERE SID='CS01';

A.

a. fk_adm_student is ON DELETE CASCADE. The STUDENT row is deleted and both admission rows (CS01, MA02) are deleted automatically. Three rows removed in total by one statement.

b. fk_adm_course is ON DELETE RESTRICT. The admission ('X2019','CS01') still references CS01, so the delete is rejected with a foreign-key error. Nothing changes — neither the course nor the admissions.

c. fk_adm_student is ON UPDATE CASCADE. The student's key changes to X9019, and both admission rows are rewritten to X9019. The relationship is preserved. Note this is possible only because the DBMS temporarily suspends the constraint check during the cascade.

d. fk_adm_course is ON UPDATE CASCADE. The course key becomes CS99, and the admission row ('X2019','CS01') becomes ('X2019','CS99'). Succeeds — the difference from (b) is that update cascades were permitted while delete cascades were not.

e. The first statement deletes both of X2019's admissions, so nothing references CS01 any more. The second then succeeds, because RESTRICT only blocks when a referencing row exists. This is the correct manual procedure that RESTRICT is designed to force upon the administrator — deal with the children explicitly rather than have them silently destroyed.

Solved Question 4

Q. Write INSERT statements to populate STUDENT and COURSE, then copy all part-time students into a new table using INSERT ... SELECT.

A.

INSERT INTO STUDENT (Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth) VALUES
  ('X2019','Ankit Sharma','2001-03-14'),
  ('X2020','Riya Verma',  '2002-05-11'),
  ('Z1188','Sana Iqbal',  '2001-11-02'),
  ('Z2049','Arjun Nair',  '2003-01-25'),
  ('X3001','Aditi Rao',   '2001-07-09');

INSERT INTO COURSE (SID, Cname, TotalSeats, Duration, Coursetype, TeacherInCharge) VALUES
  ('CS01','Computer Science',60,3,'Fulltime','R. K. Gupta'),
  ('CH01','Chemistry',       45,3,'Fulltime','S. Menon'),
  ('MA02','Mathematics',     50,3,'Parttime','A. Gupta'),
  ('EN03','English',         40,3,'Parttime','P. Das'),
  ('PH01','Physics',         40,3,'Fulltime','V. Rao');

CREATE TABLE PARTTIME_STUDENTS (
    Rollno VARCHAR(8) PRIMARY KEY,
    Name   VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO PARTTIME_STUDENTS (Rollno, Name)
SELECT DISTINCT s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime';

Three points. The multi-row form is used because it is one parse and one transaction rather than five, so it is markedly faster. Columns are named explicitly so the statements survive a later column reordering. And DISTINCT is essential in the INSERT ... SELECT: a student admitted to two part-time courses would otherwise produce two rows and violate the primary key of the target table.

Solved Question 5

Q. A junior DBA runs UPDATE STUDENT SET Name='Ankit'; and then DELETE FROM STUDENT;. Describe the damage and give three defences.

A.

Damage from the UPDATE. Every row of STUDENT now has the name 'Ankit'. All original names are gone, and no constraint was violated, so no error was raised. If the statement was auto-committed, the only recovery is a restore from backup.

Damage from the DELETE. Every student row is removed. Because fk_adm_student and fk_enr_student are declared ON DELETE CASCADE, ADMISSION and ENROLLMENT are also emptied. One statement has destroyed three tables. (Had RESTRICT been declared, the delete would have been blocked — an accidental argument for conservative referential actions.)

Three defences:

  1. Run the WHERE clause as a SELECT first. Before any UPDATE or DELETE, execute SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE <condition>; and confirm that exactly the intended rows are returned. This costs seconds and catches almost every such error.

  2. Wrap the statement in an explicit transaction. 

    START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE STUDENT SET Name='Ankit Kumar Sharma' WHERE Rollno='X2019';
SELECT * FROM STUDENT;          -- inspect
ROLLBACK;                        -- or COMMIT if correct
    Nothing is permanent until COMMIT, so a mistake costs nothing.

  3. Enable safe-update mode. SET SQL_SAFE_UPDATES = 1; makes MySQL refuse any UPDATE or DELETE that does not restrict on a key column. MySQL Workbench enables it by default for exactly this reason.

A fourth, organisational defence: grant ordinary users SELECT and INSERT only, reserving UPDATE and DELETE for accounts used deliberately (Lesson 6) — and take regular, tested backups.

Solved Question 6

Q. Why does adding a NOT NULL column to a populated table sometimes fail? Give the failing statement and two fixes.

A. Adding a column gives every existing row a value for it. If no DEFAULT is specified, that value is NULL — which directly contradicts a NOT NULL declaration. The DBMS therefore rejects the statement rather than create rows that violate their own schema.

Fails on a non-empty table: 

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL;
Error: the existing rows would need NULL in a NOT NULL column.

Fix 1 — supply a DEFAULT. Every existing row is filled with it immediately, so no NULL ever exists: 

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'not-supplied';

Fix 2 — add it nullable, populate, then tighten. Preferable when a sensible universal default does not exist, because it forces real values to be supplied: 

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Email VARCHAR(60);                 -- nullable
UPDATE STUDENT SET Email = CONCAT(LOWER(Rollno),'@college.edu');  -- populate
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY COLUMN Email VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL;     -- tighten

The second approach is the standard production pattern, because it separates the schema change from the data migration and lets each be verified independently. Note that the final MODIFY will itself fail if the UPDATE missed any row — which is a useful safety check, not a nuisance.

docs.title: 14.8 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Which sub-language does TRUNCATE belong to, and why?
  2. Can TRUNCATE take a WHERE clause?
  3. Why must child tables be dropped before parent tables?
  4. What happens to existing rows when a column is added without a DEFAULT?
  5. Name three defences against a DELETE with no WHERE.
  6. What does ON UPDATE CASCADE do?

B. Write the SQL

  1. Add a column Email VARCHAR(60) to STUDENT, unique and nullable.
  2. Change Cname to VARCHAR(60).
  3. Rename TeacherInCharge to TIC.
  4. Add a check that Duration is between 1 and 6.
  5. Drop that check.
  6. Add a foreign key from ENROLLMENT.SocID to SOCIETY.SocID with cascade on both actions.
  7. Insert five societies and six enrolments.
  8. Increase TotalSeats by 15 per cent for full-time courses only.
  9. Set FeesPaid to 'Yes' for every student enrolled in the Debating society.
  10. Delete all enrolments in societies with fewer than three members.
  11. Copy every student born in 2001 into a new table SENIOR_STUDENTS.
  12. Advance all enrolment dates by six months.

C. Predict the outcome

  1. With fk_adm_student ON DELETE CASCADE and fk_adm_course ON DELETE RESTRICT, and data as in Section 2.6, state the exact effect of: a. DELETE FROM STUDENT; b. DELETE FROM COURSE; c. TRUNCATE TABLE STUDENT; d. DROP TABLE STUDENT; e. UPDATE COURSE SET SID = CONCAT(SID,'X');
  2. STUDENT has 400 rows, of which 3 have Name longer than 20 characters. What happens on ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY Name VARCHAR(20);? How would you find the problem rows first?
  3. COURSE has a row with TotalSeats = 0. What happens on ALTER TABLE COURSE ADD CONSTRAINT chk CHECK (TotalSeats > 0);? How do you proceed?

D. Analytical

  1. Argue for and against declaring ON DELETE CASCADE on every foreign key. Recommend a policy.
  2. Explain why INSERT ... SELECT into a table with a primary key often needs DISTINCT. Give a concrete failing example.
  3. A table has AUTO_INCREMENT at 500. Compare the state after DELETE FROM t; and after TRUNCATE TABLE t;, and say when each behaviour is desirable.
  4. Write a safe procedure, as a numbered list, for renaming a column that is used by two views and one application.
  5. Explain why ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT validates existing data, and what happens if validation fails.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. DELETE can be rolled back.
  2. TRUNCATE fires delete triggers.
  3. DROP COLUMN can be undone with ADD COLUMN.
  4. ON DELETE SET NULL can be used on a foreign key that is part of the primary key.
  5. UPDATE without WHERE updates one row.
  6. Adding a column to a table with a million rows is instantaneous in all systems.

Answers to Section E

  1. True. It is DML, logged row by row, and participates in the transaction.
  2. False. It does not fire row triggers, because it deallocates pages rather than deleting rows individually — a real hazard if triggers maintain audit tables.
  3. False. ADD COLUMN recreates the column but not its data, which was destroyed.
  4. False. Entity integrity forbids NULL in any part of a primary key.
  5. False. It updates every row in the table.
  6. False. Some systems rewrite the whole table, which can lock it for a long time. Others add the column to the catalog only and are near-instant. Check the specific DBMS and version before altering a large production table.

Lesson Summary

  • ALTER TABLE performs schema evolution: add, modify, rename, drop columns and constraints. Widening is safe; narrowing and dropping destroy data.
  • DROP (table gone), TRUNCATE (rows gone, fast, no rollback, no triggers, resets counters) and DELETE (selective, logged, rollback-able) are three different operations.
  • Prefer named-column INSERT, and the multi-row form for bulk loads. INSERT ... SELECT copies query results — usually needing DISTINCT.
  • Referential actions determine whether a parent change cascades, is blocked, or nulls the children. Default to RESTRICT.
  • The three disasters — UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE, and over-broad CASCADE — are prevented by select first, transaction second, safe-update mode third.

docs.title: Lesson 6: Attributes and Keys
docs.text:
Simple, composite, multivalued, derived — and how entities are identified

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 2: Entity Relationship Modelling · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 3.3

Learning Outcomes

  1. Classify attributes as simple/composite, single-valued/multivalued, stored/derived, key, complex.
  2. Draw each kind in standard Chen notation.
  3. Explain NULL and its three distinct meanings.
  4. Define key attribute, candidate key, primary key and composite key in the ER context.
  5. Choose a sound primary key and justify the choice.

docs.title: 6.1 What an Attribute Is
docs.text:
Attribute

An attribute is a property that describes an entity. Each attribute has a domain — the set of values it may take (also called its value set).

For a particular entity, each attribute has a value. An entity is therefore, formally, a set of (attribute, value) pairs.

For the entity e1 of type STUDENT:

e1 = { (Rollno, 'X2019'), (Name, 'Ankit Sharma'), (Dateofbirth, '2001-03-14') }

In Chen notation an attribute is drawn as an ellipse (oval) joined by a plain line to the rectangle of its entity type.

        (Rollno)      (Name)      (Dateofbirth)
             \           |            /
              \          |           /
               +---------+----------+
               |      STUDENT       |
               +--------------------+

Figure 2.1 — Attributes attached to an entity type.

docs.title: 6.2 The Classification of Attributes
docs.text: There are three independent axes of classification, plus two special cases. Independent means an attribute can be, say, composite and multivalued at the same time.

docs.title: Simple (atomic) vs Composite
docs.text:
Simple / Atomic attribute

An attribute that is not divisible into meaningful smaller parts. Rollno, Age, TotalSeats.

Composite attribute

An attribute that can be divided into smaller sub-parts, each with an independent meaning. The sub-parts may themselves be composite, forming a hierarchy.

Notation: the component ovals hang off the composite oval.

                    (FirstName)  (MiddleName)  (LastName)
                          \           |           /
                           \          |          /
                          ( - - - N a m e - - - )
                                     |
                                     |
                          +----------+---------+
                          |      STUDENT       |
                          +----------+---------+
                                     |
                          ( - - - Address - - - )
                          /     /        \      \
                   (HouseNo) (Street)  (City) (PIN)

Figure 2.2 — Composite attributes Name and Address.

When to make an attribute composite? Only when the application refers to the parts individually. If the college ever sorts students by surname, or posts letters by city, then Name and Address must be composite. If addresses are only ever printed whole, a single simple attribute is correct and simpler.

Rule of thumb

Composite if the parts are referenced separately; simple otherwise. Over-decomposing is as much a design error as under-decomposing.

docs.title: Single-valued vs Multivalued
docs.text:
Single-valued attribute

Has exactly one value for a given entity. Dateofbirth, Rollno.

Multivalued attribute

May have a set of values for the same entity — zero, one, or many. A student may have several phone numbers; a car may have several colours; a person may hold several degrees.

Notation: a double ellipse. Written {PhoneNo} in shorthand.

A multivalued attribute may have lower and upper bounds, e.g. a car has between one and three colours.

              ((PhoneNo))              ((Hobby))
                    \                     /
                     \                   /
                    +-+-----------------+-+
                    |       STUDENT        |
                    +----------------------+

Critical: a multivalued attribute is not representable as a single column in a relation, because relations must be in 1NF (atomic values). Unit 5 gives the mapping rule: every multivalued attribute becomes a separate table.

docs.title: Stored vs Derived
docs.text:
Stored attribute

Its value is physically kept in the database. Dateofbirth.

Derived attribute

Its value is computed from other attributes (or from related entities) and need not be stored. Age is derived from Dateofbirth and today's date; NumberOfStudents for a course is derived by counting related admissions.

Notation: a dashed ellipse.

           (Dateofbirth)          , - - - - .
                  |               (   Age     )     <- dashed = derived
                  |                ` - - - - '
                  |                     |
              +---+---------------------+---+
              |         STUDENT             |
              +-----------------------------+
              Age = today's date - Dateofbirth

Why not store Age? Because it would be wrong within a year. Anything computable from stored data and time should generally be derived, to avoid the update anomalies of Unit 1. The exception is deliberate, controlled redundancy for performance — a stored count maintained by a trigger — which is a physical-design decision, not a conceptual one.

docs.title: Key attributes
docs.text:
Key attribute

An attribute (or a set of attributes) whose value is distinct for each individual entity in the entity set. It provides the uniqueness constraint and is used to identify entities.

Notation: the attribute name is underlined.

An entity type may have more than one key attribute — for example STUDENT might have both Rollno and AadhaarNo, each unique. Each is underlined; each is a candidate key.

A key may be composite: the key is the combination, and no proper subset of it is unique. For a weak entity type there is no key at all, only a partial key — drawn with a dashed underline.

docs.title: Complex attributes
docs.text:
Complex attribute

An attribute formed by arbitrarily nesting composite (grouped with parentheses) and multivalued (grouped with braces) constructions.

A person may have several addresses, and each address has a composite structure with several phones:

{ AddressPhone( {Phone(AreaCode, PhoneNumber)},
                Address(StreetAddress(Number, Street, AptNo),
                        City, State, Zip) ) }

Braces { } mean multivalued; parentheses ( ) mean composite.

docs.title: Summary of notation
docs.text:
Attribute kind Chen notation Shorthand Simple, single-valued Plain ellipse Age Composite Ellipse with child ellipses Name(First, Last) Multivalued Double ellipse {PhoneNo} Derived Dashed ellipse /Age Key Name underlined Rollno Partial key (weak entity) Name dash-underlined Name (dashed) Complex Nested combination {Addr(St, City)} 
   THE COMPLETE PICTURE

        (Rollno)        ( - - Name - - )        ((PhoneNo))
       underlined       /      |      \          double
             |    (First)  (Middle)  (Last)         |
             |         \      |      /              |
             +----------+-----+-----+---------------+
                        |   STUDENT   |
             +----------+-----+-------+-------------+
             |                |                     |
       (Dateofbirth)    , - -Age- - .        ( - Address - )
        stored          ` - - - - - '        /    |    \
                          derived        (City)(Street)(PIN)

Figure 2.3 — All attribute kinds on one entity type.

docs.title: 6.3 NULL Values
docs.text:
NULL

A special marker meaning that a value is absent. It is not zero, and it is not the empty string.

NULL has three distinct meanings, and confusing them is a real source of bugs:

Meaning Sub-case Example Not applicable The attribute does not apply to this entity ApartmentNo for someone living in an independent house Unknown — missing A value exists but is not recorded The student has a date of birth; we simply have not been told it Unknown — not known whether it exists We do not even know whether a value exists We do not know whether a student has a home phone at all

Consequences (developed fully in Unit 4):

  • Any arithmetic involving NULL yields NULL: 5 + NULL is NULL.
  • Any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE: Age > 18 is UNKNOWN when Age is NULL, and so is NULL = NULL.
  • You must therefore test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never with = NULL.
  • Aggregate functions ignore NULLs, except COUNT(*).
  • A primary key can never be NULL (entity integrity, Unit 3).

Design advice

An attribute that is NULL for most entities is a warning sign. It usually means the entity type should be specialised into sub-types (EER, Lesson 4), or that the attribute belongs to a different entity type altogether.

docs.title: 6.4 Keys in the ER Model
docs.text:
The four key terms

Superkey — any set of attributes whose values, taken together, uniquely identify an entity. A superkey may contain redundant attributes.

Candidate key — a minimal superkey: remove any attribute and it stops being unique. An entity type may have several.

Primary key — the candidate key the designer chooses to be the principal means of identification. Exactly one, per entity type. It is the one that becomes PRIMARY KEY on mapping, and it may never be NULL.

Alternate key — a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. It becomes a UNIQUE constraint on mapping.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
STUDENT (Rollno, AadhaarNo, Email, Name, Dateofbirth), where Rollno, AadhaarNo and Email are each unique.

Attribute set Superkey? Candidate key? Why {Rollno} Yes Yes Unique, and minimal (it is a single attribute). {AadhaarNo} Yes Yes Unique and minimal. {Email} Yes Yes Unique and minimal. {Rollno, Name} Yes No Unique, but not minimal — Rollno alone suffices. {Name, Dateofbirth} No No Two students may share both. {Rollno, AadhaarNo} Yes No Not minimal.

So the candidate keys are {Rollno}, {AadhaarNo} and {Email}. Choosing Rollno as primary key makes AadhaarNo and Email alternate keys.

How to choose a primary key

  1. Stable — its value should never need to change. (Email fails: people change email addresses.)
  2. Non-NULL, always available — known at the moment the entity is created. (AadhaarNo may fail: a new student may not have supplied it yet.)
  3. Minimal and short — fewer, smaller attributes make joins and indexes faster.
  4. Simple rather than composite where a good simple candidate exists.
  5. Not privacy-sensitive — using a national identity number as a primary key spreads it into every referencing table.

By these criteria Rollno is the right choice for STUDENT.

Natural vs surrogate keys

A natural key has meaning in the mini-world (Rollno, ISBN). A surrogate key is a system-generated meaningless number (StudentID INT AUTO_INCREMENT).

Surrogates are stable by construction and always available, and never need to change; but they are meaningless to users, and they do not by themselves prevent duplicate real-world entities being inserted twice. Good practice: use a surrogate as primary key and declare the natural key UNIQUE.

docs.title: 6.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Classify the following attributes of an EMPLOYEE entity type, giving the notation for each: Ssn, Name(First, Last), {PhoneNo}, Age, Dateofbirth, Address(House, City, PIN), {Degree}.

A.

Attribute Classification Notation Justification Ssn Simple, single-valued, key, stored Ellipse, name underlined Unique per employee, not divisible. Name(First, Last) Composite, single-valued, stored Ellipse with two child ellipses Divisible into meaningful parts referenced separately (sorting by surname). {PhoneNo} Simple, multivalued, stored Double ellipse An employee may have several phone numbers. Age Simple, single-valued, derived Dashed ellipse Computed from Dateofbirth and the current date; storing it would make it wrong within a year. Dateofbirth Simple, single-valued, stored Plain ellipse The base fact from which Age is derived. Address(House, City, PIN) Composite, single-valued, stored Ellipse with three child ellipses Parts referenced separately (sorting by city, posting by PIN). {Degree} Simple, multivalued, stored Double ellipse An employee may hold BSc, MSc and PhD.

Note that the axes are independent: Name is composite and single-valued; had employees been allowed several names (maiden and married), it would be composite and multivalued, drawn as a double ellipse with children.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish between composite and multivalued attributes. Can an attribute be both? Give an example.

A.

Composite Multivalued Meaning One value, made of parts Several values of the same kind Question it answers "What are the pieces of this value?" "How many values are there?" Notation Ellipse with child ellipses Double ellipse Example Address(House, City, PIN) {PhoneNo} Mapping to relations (Unit 5) Becomes several columns in the same table Becomes a separate table

Yes, an attribute can be both. An employee may have several addresses (home, office, permanent), and each address has parts. This is {Address(House, Street, City, PIN)} — drawn as a double ellipse (multivalued) that has child ellipses (composite).

Such an attribute is a complex attribute. On mapping it produces a separate table EMP_ADDRESS(Ssn, House, Street, City, PIN) whose primary key is Ssn together with enough of the address to be unique.

Solved Question 3

Q. Define superkey, candidate key, primary key and alternate key. For BOOK(ISBN, AccNo, Title, Author, Publisher) — where ISBN identifies the title and AccNo is the library's unique accession number for a physical copy — list all candidate keys and choose a primary key with justification.

A. (Definitions as in Section 2.4.)

Careful reading matters here. ISBN identifies a title, but a library holds several physical copies of the same title, each with a different AccNo. So in a table of physical copies, ISBN is not unique.

  • Superkeys: {AccNo}, {AccNo, ISBN}, {AccNo, Title}, {AccNo, ISBN, Title, Author, Publisher}, and any set containing AccNo.
  • Candidate keys: {AccNo} only — it is the sole minimal superkey.
  • Not keys: {ISBN} (many copies share it), {Title}, {Title, Author} (a library may hold two editions).
  • Primary key: AccNo. It is the only candidate key; it is stable, always available at the moment a copy is accessioned, short and simple.
  • Alternate keys: none.

Design note. The fact that ISBN, Title, Author and Publisher repeat across every copy of the same title is redundancy, and signals that the design should be split into TITLE(ISBN, Title, Author, Publisher) and COPY(AccNo, ISBN). In the split design ISBN is the primary key of TITLE and a foreign key in COPY. This is exactly the reasoning that normalisation formalises in Unit 5.

Solved Question 4

Q. What is a NULL value? Explain its three meanings and state three consequences for query writing.

A. A NULL is a marker indicating the absence of a value. It is not zero, not a blank string, and not the value "unknown" — it is the absence of any value.

Three meanings:

  1. Not applicable. The attribute is meaningless for this entity — ApartmentNo for a student living in an independent house.
  2. Unknown, but exists (missing). The student certainly has a date of birth; the office has not recorded it.
  3. Unknown whether it exists. We do not know whether the student has a landline number at all.

Three consequences:

  1. Comparisons yield UNKNOWN. Age > 18 is neither true nor false when Age is NULL, so such rows are excluded by a WHERE clause. Even NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, which is why WHERE Phone = NULL never matches; you must write WHERE Phone IS NULL.
  2. Arithmetic propagates NULL. Salary + Bonus is NULL whenever Bonus is NULL — so a row with no bonus silently disappears from a total unless handled with COALESCE(Bonus, 0).
  3. Aggregates ignore NULLs. AVG(Marks) averages only the non-NULL marks, so it differs from SUM(Marks)/COUNT(*). Only COUNT(*) counts every row.

Because of these subtleties SQL uses three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), covered in Unit 4.

Solved Question 5

Q. Why should Age be a derived attribute rather than a stored one? Under what circumstance might you store it anyway?

A. Age should be derived because it is a function of a stored fact and the current date: Age = today - Dateofbirth. Storing it creates two problems.

  1. It becomes wrong by the passage of time alone. Every stored age is incorrect on the day after the student's birthday, with no update having occurred. No integrity constraint can detect this, and no application error caused it.
  2. It is redundant. Storing both Dateofbirth and Age means the same information twice, so the two can disagree — the classic update anomaly of Unit 1.

Storing Dateofbirth alone and computing Age on demand (TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, Dateofbirth, CURDATE())) is always correct and never inconsistent.

When you might store it anyway: as a deliberate, controlled redundancy for performance — for instance in a data warehouse holding a nightly snapshot, where ages are recomputed by the load job and queries scanning millions of rows must not evaluate a date function per row. Two conditions must hold: the staleness must be acceptable to the application, and the derived value must be maintained automatically (by a trigger, a scheduled job, or a materialised view) rather than by application code. This is a physical design decision; the conceptual schema still shows Age as derived.

Solved Question 6

Q. Draw the ER fragment for PATIENT with: a unique registration number; a name split into first and last; several phone numbers; date of birth; age; and several addresses, each having city and PIN.

A.

      (RegNo)      ( - - Name - - )       ((PhoneNo))
     underlined     /           \            double
         |     (First)        (Last)            |
         |         \           /                |
         +----------+---------+-----------------+
                    |    PATIENT    |
         +----------+-------+-------+------------+
         |                  |                    |
   (Dateofbirth)      , - -Age- - .      (( - Address - ))
      stored          ` - - - - - '       /            \
                        dashed        (City)          (PIN)
                       = derived      double ellipse WITH children
                                      = multivalued AND composite

Reading of the notation:

  • RegNo — plain ellipse, name underlined: simple, single-valued key attribute.
  • Name — ellipse with two child ellipses First and Last: composite, single-valued.
  • PhoneNo — double ellipse: simple, multivalued.
  • Dateofbirth — plain ellipse: simple, single-valued, stored.
  • Age — dashed ellipse: derived from Dateofbirth.
  • Address — double ellipse with child ellipses City and PIN: multivalued and composite, i.e. a complex attribute.

Shorthand: PATIENT( RegNo , Name(First, Last), {PhoneNo}, Dateofbirth, /Age, {Address(City, PIN)}).

docs.title: 6.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define attribute and domain.
  2. Distinguish simple from composite attributes.
  3. How is a multivalued attribute drawn? Give two examples.
  4. What is a derived attribute? Why is it not stored?
  5. State the three meanings of NULL.
  6. Distinguish candidate key from primary key.
  7. What is an alternate key, and what does it become on mapping?

B. Long answer

  1. Explain all kinds of attributes in the ER model with notation and examples. Show that the classifications are independent by giving an attribute that is both composite and multivalued.
  2. Explain NULL values, their three meanings, and their consequences for comparison, arithmetic and aggregation.
  3. Define superkey, candidate key, primary key and alternate key, and state five criteria for choosing a primary key.
  4. Compare natural and surrogate keys. Recommend a policy and defend it.

C. Application and analytical

  1. For a VEHICLE entity type in an RTO database, classify each attribute and give its notation: registration number, chassis number, owner name (first, middle, last), colours (a vehicle may be two-toned), date of registration, age of the vehicle, engine capacity.
  2. For EMPLOYEE(Ssn, PAN, Email, Name, Dno, Salary) where Ssn, PAN and Email are each unique: a. List five superkeys. b. List all candidate keys. c. Choose a primary key and justify against all five criteria. d. Name the alternate keys and say what they become in SQL.
  3. Draw the ER fragment for a HOTEL with: a unique hotel code; name; address composed of street, city and PIN; several contact numbers; star rating; and the number of rooms currently vacant.
  4. A designer stores TotalMarks alongside Marks1, Marks2 and Marks3. Criticise this. Under what circumstances would it be defensible, and what mechanism would you require?
  5. In a table of employees, ManagerName is NULL for 1 employee and Bonus is NULL for 340 of 400. For each, decide which meaning of NULL applies and whether the design should change.
  6. For each, decide simple or composite, and justify from the application's needs: a. PhoneNumber in a college database that only ever dials the whole number. b. PhoneNumber in a telecom billing system that charges by area code. c. Date in a system that reports by month.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A composite attribute can be multivalued.
  2. NULL is the same as zero for numeric attributes.
  3. A derived attribute is never shown in the ER diagram.
  4. An entity type can have more than one candidate key but only one primary key.
  5. A multivalued attribute maps to a single column in the relational model.
  6. NULL = NULL evaluates to TRUE.
  7. Every superkey is a candidate key.

Answers to Section D

  1. True. The classifications are independent — {Address(City, PIN)} is both, drawn as a double ellipse with children.
  2. False. Zero is a known value; NULL is the absence of a value. 0 + 5 = 5, but NULL + 5 = NULL.
  3. False. It is shown, as a dashed ellipse. It is not stored, which is a different matter.
  4. True. All candidate keys are underlined in the diagram; the designer designates one as primary.
  5. False. It requires a separate table, because relations must be in 1NF with atomic values.
  6. False. It evaluates to UNKNOWN. Use IS NULL.
  7. False. Only minimal superkeys are candidate keys; {Rollno, Name} is a superkey but not a candidate key.

Lesson Summary

  • Attributes are classified on three independent axes — simple/composite, single-valued/multivalued, stored/derived — plus key attributes and complex (nested) attributes.
  • Notation: plain ellipse; children for composite; double ellipse for multivalued; dashed for derived; underline for key; dashed underline for partial key.
  • NULL means not applicable, unknown-missing, or unknown-whether-exists; it makes comparisons UNKNOWN and propagates through arithmetic.
  • Superkey ⊃ candidate key (minimal) → one chosen as primary key, the rest alternate keys.
  • Choose a primary key that is stable, always available, short, simple and not privacy-sensitive.

docs.title: Lesson 22: BCNF and Decomposition
docs.text:
The strongest ordinary normal form, and what it costs

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 5: Database Design · 10 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 14.5, 15.1

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define BCNF and test a relation for it.
  2. Explain exactly when a relation is in 3NF but not BCNF.
  3. Apply the BCNF decomposition algorithm.
  4. Apply the 3NF synthesis algorithm.
  5. State the trade-off: BCNF may sacrifice dependency preservation.

docs.title: 22.1 Boyce-Codd Normal Form
docs.text:
BCNF

A relation R is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that holds in R, X is a superkey of R.

Equivalently: every determinant is a superkey.

Compare the two definitions side by side; the difference is one clause.

3NF (general definition) BCNF For every non-trivial X → A X is a superkey OR A is prime X is a superkey

BCNF is 3NF with the escape clause removed

3NF forgives a dependency whose determinant is not a superkey, provided the dependent attribute is prime. BCNF forgives nothing.

Therefore every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not conversely. BCNF is strictly stronger.

docs.title: When is a relation in 3NF but not BCNF?
docs.text:
The three conditions, all required together

A relation can be in 3NF but not BCNF only if all three hold:

  1. There are two or more candidate keys, and
  2. the candidate keys are composite, and
  3. the candidate keys overlap — they share at least one attribute.

If a relation has only one candidate key, or its keys are single attributes and disjoint, 3NF and BCNF coincide.

This is worth remembering, because it means BCNF violations are relatively rare in practice — most relations that reach 3NF are already in BCNF.

docs.title: The classic example
docs.text:
TEACHING( Student, Subject, Teacher )

Business rules:

  • Each teacher teaches exactly one subject: Teacher → Subject
  • For a given student and subject, there is exactly one teacher: Student, Subject → Teacher

Candidate keys. (Student, Subject)⁺ = {Student, Subject, Teacher} = R. Minimal (neither alone works). Candidate key. (Student, Teacher)⁺ = {Student, Teacher} → (Teacher → Subject) {Student, Teacher, Subject} = R. Minimal. Candidate key.

Two candidate keys, both composite, overlapping on Student — the three conditions are met.

Prime attributes: Student, Subject, Teacher — all of them. Non-prime: none.

In 3NF? Yes. Test each dependency:

  • Student, Subject → Teacher: determinant is a superkey. Passes.
  • Teacher → Subject: determinant is not a superkey (Teacher⁺ = {Teacher, Subject} ≠ R) — but Subject is prime, so the second condition rescues it. Passes.

Since there are no non-prime attributes at all, no 2NF or 3NF violation is even possible.

In BCNF? No. Teacher → Subject has a determinant that is not a superkey, and BCNF has no escape clause.

docs.title: The redundancy BCNF is objecting to
docs.text:
Student Subject Teacher Ankit Database Gupta Riya Database Gupta Sana Database Gupta Ankit Physics Rao

The fact "Gupta teaches Database" is stored three times. All three anomalies follow:

  • Insertion: a newly appointed teacher cannot be recorded until some student is assigned to them (Student is part of every key and cannot be NULL).
  • Deletion: if the three Database students leave, the fact that Gupta teaches Database is lost.
  • Modification: if Gupta switches to Networks, three rows must change together.

So a relation can be in 3NF and still suffer every classic anomaly. That is precisely why BCNF exists.

docs.title: 22.2 The BCNF Decomposition Algorithm
docs.text:
Algorithm

D := { R }
while some relation Q in D is not in BCNF:
    find a non-trivial FD  X -> Y  in Q  where X is NOT a superkey of Q
    replace Q in D by the two relations
        Q1 = ( X ∪ Y )          -- the offending dependency, with X as its key
        Q2 = ( Q − Y )          -- the rest, with X retained as a foreign key
return D

Each step is guaranteed lossless, because the common attribute set is X, and X is the key of Q1 (Lesson 5).

docs.title: Applying it to TEACHING
docs.text:
The violating dependency is Teacher → Subject. So X = {Teacher}, Y = {Subject}.

  • Q1 = (Teacher, Subject) — key Teacher
  • Q2 = (Student, Teacher) — key (Student, Teacher)
TEACHES ( Teacher, Subject )        -- key Teacher
STUDIES ( Student, Teacher )        -- key (Student, Teacher)

Check TEACHES: the only determinant is Teacher, which is its key. BCNF. Check STUDIES: the only key is (Student, Teacher); no smaller determinant exists. BCNF.

Lossless? Common attribute is Teacher; Teacher⁺ = {Teacher, Subject} ⊇ TEACHES, so Teacher is a superkey of TEACHES. Yes, lossless.

The price: a lost dependency

The original dependency Student, Subject → Teacher is no longer enforceable.

Student and Subject now live in different relations, so no constraint on either table can express the rule. Checking it requires joining STUDIES and TEACHES on every insert.

Consequence — the following two rows are individually legal but jointly violate the business rule:

STUDIES TEACHES Ankit Gupta Gupta Database Ankit Sharma Sharma Database

Ankit now has two teachers for Database, which Student, Subject → Teacher forbade. Nothing in the decomposed schema prevents it.

This decomposition is lossless but NOT dependency preserving.

docs.title: 22.3 The Fundamental Trade-off
docs.text:
The theorem to remember

  • A lossless-join decomposition into BCNF relations always exists.
  • A lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF relations always exists.
  • A lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition into BCNF may not exist.

TEACHING is the standard witness for the third statement.

                     lossless?      dependency        redundancy
                                    preserving?       remaining?
   3NF  synthesis      ALWAYS         ALWAYS           possibly some
   BCNF decomposition  ALWAYS         NOT ALWAYS       none (from FDs)

   You may have any two of {BCNF, lossless, dependency preserving},
   but not always all three.  Lossless is never negotiable.

Which should you choose?

Stay in 3NF when the lost dependency matters — when it is a rule the business genuinely needs enforced cheaply, and the residual redundancy is small and controlled.

Go to BCNF when the redundancy is large and the lost dependency is either unimportant or can be enforced in the application or by a trigger.

Never give up losslessness — a lossy decomposition corrupts the data itself, producing spurious tuples on reassembly. The other two properties are trade-offs; this one is a correctness requirement.

In practice most designers stop at 3NF for transactional schemas, because dependency preservation is worth more than the last increment of redundancy, and because (as noted) most 3NF relations happen to be in BCNF anyway.

docs.title: 22.4 The 3NF Synthesis Algorithm
docs.text:
Rather than decomposing top-down, 3NF can be synthesised bottom-up from a minimal cover — and the result is guaranteed to be both lossless and dependency preserving.

Algorithm (3NF synthesis)

  1. Compute a minimal cover G of F (Lesson 2).
  2. For each dependency X → Y in G, create a relation (X ∪ Y). Merge relations whose determinants are identical.
  3. If no relation created so far contains a candidate key of R, add one more relation consisting of any candidate key of R. (This step guarantees losslessness.)
  4. Remove any relation that is a subset of another.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = { A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A }.

Step 1 — minimal cover. Split the right sides: A → B, A → C, CD → E, B → D, E → A. Check for extraneous left attributes in CD → E: is C extraneous? D⁺ = {D}, no. Is D extraneous? C⁺ = {C}, no. Check redundancy: removing any one of the five loses information (verify each with a closure). So the cover is already minimal:

G = { A → B, A → C, CD → E, B → D, E → A }

Step 2 — one relation per dependency, merging equal determinants:

R1 ( A, B, C )      from A → B and A → C merged
R2 ( C, D, E )      from CD → E
R3 ( B, D )         from B → D
R4 ( E, A )         from E → A

Step 3 — does any relation contain a candidate key? The candidate keys are A, E, BC, CD (computed in Lesson 2). R1 contains A; R2 contains CD; R4 contains E. Yes — no extra relation is needed.

Step 4 — subset removal. None is a subset of another.

Result: R1(A,B,C), R2(C,D,E), R3(B,D), R4(E,A) — all in 3NF, the decomposition lossless and dependency preserving by construction.

Step 3 is not optional

Omit it and the decomposition may be lossy. Consider R(A,B,C) with the single dependency A → B. Step 2 gives only R1(A,B); attribute C is lost entirely. Step 3 adds a candidate key relation R2(A,C), restoring both C and losslessness.

docs.title: 22.5 Higher Normal Forms (brief)
docs.text:
Beyond BCNF

4NF removes multivalued dependencies (MVDs). X ↠ Y means that for each value of X there is a set of Y values independent of the other attributes. A relation is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and every non-trivial MVD has a superkey determinant.

Example. EMP(Ename, {Project}, {Dependent}) where projects and dependants are independent. Storing both in one relation forces every combination to be listed — 3 projects × 2 dependants = 6 rows for facts that need 3 + 2 = 5. Split into EMP_PROJECT and EMP_DEPENDENT.

5NF (Project-Join Normal Form) removes join dependencies — cases where a relation must be decomposed into three or more fragments to remove redundancy, though no two-way decomposition suffices.

These are beyond the syllabus for this course, but a complete answer to "list the normal forms" should mention them.

docs.title: 22.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define BCNF. How does it differ from 3NF? Under what conditions can a relation be in 3NF but not BCNF?

A. A relation is in BCNF if for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a superkey.

Difference from 3NF. The general 3NF definition allows X → A when X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF deletes the second alternative. So BCNF is 3NF with the escape clause removed, and is strictly stronger: every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not conversely.

Conditions for 3NF-but-not-BCNF. All three must hold simultaneously:

  1. The relation has two or more candidate keys;
  2. the candidate keys are composite;
  3. the candidate keys overlap (share at least one attribute).

If any fails, 3NF and BCNF coincide. Hence BCNF violations are relatively rare.

Why these conditions? A 3NF-but-not-BCNF violation needs a dependency X → A where X is not a superkey and A is prime. For A to be prime it must lie in some candidate key; for X to be a non-superkey determinant of a key attribute while the relation is still in 3NF, another candidate key must exist and share attributes with the first. TEACHING(Student, Subject, Teacher) with keys (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher) — overlapping on Student — is the canonical instance.

Solved Question 2

Q. Show that TEACHING(Student, Subject, Teacher) with Student,Subject → Teacher and Teacher → Subject is in 3NF but not BCNF. Decompose it and state what is lost.

A.
