Candidate keys. (Student, Subject)⁺ = R and is minimal → candidate key. (Student, Teacher)⁺ = {Student, Teacher} →(Teacher → Subject) = R, minimal → candidate key. Prime: all three attributes. Non-prime: none.

3NF — satisfied. With no non-prime attributes, no 2NF or 3NF violation is possible. Checking each FD by the general definition: Student,Subject → Teacher has a superkey determinant; Teacher → Subject has a non-superkey determinant but Subject is prime, so the second condition applies. In 3NF.

BCNF — violated. Teacher → Subject has determinant Teacher with Teacher⁺ = {Teacher, Subject} ≠ R, so it is not a superkey, and BCNF permits no exception.

The redundancy. "Gupta teaches Database" is repeated once per student of Gupta, giving insertion, deletion and modification anomalies.

Decomposition on the violating dependency X = {Teacher}, Y = {Subject}:

TEACHES ( Teacher, Subject )     key Teacher
STUDIES ( Student, Teacher )     key (Student, Teacher)

Both are in BCNF: each relation's only determinant is its own key.

Lossless? Yes. Common attribute Teacher; Teacher⁺ ⊇ TEACHES, so the common attributes form a superkey of one fragment.

What is lost: the dependency Student, Subject → Teacher. Student and Subject now sit in different relations, so no single-table constraint can enforce it. Two individually legal rows — Ankit/Gupta in STUDIES and Ankit/Sharma in STUDIES, with both teachers teaching Database — jointly break the rule, and nothing detects it. Enforcement would require a join on every insert, or a trigger.

The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving — the standard illustration that BCNF and dependency preservation can be incompatible.

Solved Question 3

Q. State the BCNF decomposition algorithm and apply it to R(A,B,C,D) with AB → CD and D → A.

A. (Algorithm as in Section 4.2.)

Candidate keys. AB⁺ = {A,B} → {A,B,C,D} = R, minimal → candidate key. BD⁺ = {B,D} →(D→A) {A,B,D} →(AB→CD) {A,B,C,D} = R; is it minimal? B⁺ = {B}, D⁺ = {A,D} — neither is R, so BD is a candidate key.

Candidate keys: AB, BD. Prime: A, B, D. Non-prime: C.

3NF? AB → CD — superkey determinant, fine. D → A — D⁺ = {A,D} ≠ R, so not a superkey; but A is prime, so 3NF forgives it. In 3NF.

BCNF? D → A has a non-superkey determinant. Violated.

(Note that this relation satisfies the three conditions: two candidate keys, both composite, overlapping on B.)

Decompose on X = {D}, Y = {A}:

  • Q1 = X ∪ Y = (D, A) — key D
  • Q2 = R − Y = (B, C, D) — the rest, with D retained

Check Q1(D, A): only determinant is D, its key. BCNF. Check Q2(B, C, D): which dependencies hold here? Projecting F onto {B,C,D}: BD⁺ = R, so BD → C holds; nothing smaller determines anything. The only determinant is BD, the key. BCNF.

Lossless? Common attribute D; D⁺ = {A,D} ⊇ Q1. Yes.

Dependency preserving? D → A is checkable in Q1. AB → CD is not checkable — A is in Q1, B and C in Q2, and no fragment contains all of A, B, C, D. Not dependency preserving. Again the characteristic BCNF trade-off.

Solved Question 4

Q. State the 3NF synthesis algorithm and apply it to R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with F = {A → BC, C → DE, E → F, F → A}.

A. (Algorithm as in Section 4.4.)

Step 1 — minimal cover. Split the right sides: A → B, A → C, C → D, C → E, E → F, F → A. Every left side is a single attribute, so none can be extraneous. Test redundancy: removing A → B leaves A⁺ (under the rest) = {A,C,D,E,F} which excludes B, so keep it; similar checks retain all six. The cover is already minimal.

Step 2 — one relation per dependency, merging identical determinants:

R1 ( A, B, C )     from A → B and A → C
R2 ( C, D, E )     from C → D and C → E
R3 ( E, F )        from E → F
R4 ( F, A )        from F → A

Step 3 — does some relation contain a candidate key? Compute the keys. A⁺ = {A,B,C,D,E,F} = R, so A is a candidate key. Likewise C⁺ = {C,D,E,F,A,B} = R, E⁺ = {E,F,A,B,C,D} = R, and F⁺ = R. Candidate keys: A, C, E, F (a cycle of determinants). R1 contains A, so the condition is met — no extra relation needed.

Step 4 — subset removal. None is a subset of another.

Result: R1(A,B,C), R2(C,D,E), R3(E,F), R4(F,A).

Properties, guaranteed by construction: every relation is in 3NF; the decomposition is dependency preserving (each dependency of the cover sits inside one relation); and it is lossless (a relation contains a candidate key).

Are they also in BCNF? R1(A,B,C): the determinants holding here are A (its key) and C, and C⁺ = R ⊇ R1, so C is also a superkey of R1. Both determinants are superkeys — BCNF. Similar checks show the same for the others. Here 3NF synthesis happened to yield BCNF, which is common.

Solved Question 5

Q. State the trade-off between BCNF and dependency preservation. Which property must never be sacrificed, and why?

A. Three properties are wanted from a decomposition: it should be lossless, dependency preserving, and its fragments should be in as high a normal form as possible.

The theorems:

Target Lossless? Dependency preserving? 3NF always achievable always achievable BCNF always achievable not always achievable

TEACHING(Student, Subject, Teacher) is the standard witness for the negative result: any BCNF decomposition loses Student, Subject → Teacher.

Losslessness must never be sacrificed. The reason is a difference in kind, not degree:

  • Losing a dependency costs enforcement: the constraint can still be checked, just more expensively — with a join, a trigger, or application code. The data remains correct, and the correct answer to every query is still obtainable.
  • A lossy decomposition corrupts the data itself. Rejoining the fragments produces spurious tuples — rows that were never in the original relation and assert facts that are simply false. There is no way to tell the genuine rows from the invented ones, and no amount of later care recovers the lost information.

So losslessness is a correctness requirement, while dependency preservation and normal form are engineering trade-offs.

Practical guidance. Decompose to 3NF by synthesis, which gives all three properties whenever they are jointly achievable. Then check whether the result is already in BCNF — usually it is. If it is not, weigh the residual redundancy against the cost of enforcing the lost dependency, and choose deliberately. Most transactional schemas stop at 3NF.

Solved Question 6

Q. Give the sequence of all normal forms with a one-line criterion for each, and state which anomaly each removes.

A.

Normal form Criterion Removes 1NF All attribute values are atomic; no repeating groups, composite or multivalued attributes Non-relational structure; makes querying possible at all 2NF 1NF, and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key Redundancy from attributes belonging to part of a composite key 3NF 2NF, and for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime Redundancy from transitive dependencies — facts about a second entity BCNF Every determinant is a superkey (no exceptions) The remaining redundancy from FDs, where the dependent attribute is prime 4NF BCNF, and every non-trivial multivalued dependency has a superkey determinant Redundancy from independent multivalued facts stored together 5NF / PJNF Every join dependency is implied by the candidate keys Redundancy removable only by decomposing into three or more relations

Each form is strictly stronger than its predecessor: 5NF ⊂ 4NF ⊂ BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF.

The unifying idea is the one from Unit 3, Lesson 1: a relation should describe one kind of thing. Each normal form detects a different way in which a second kind of fact has crept in — via part of a key (2NF), via another non-prime attribute (3NF), via a prime attribute (BCNF), or via an independent multivalued fact (4NF).

For this syllabus, 1NF to BCNF are examinable; 4NF and 5NF should be known by name and criterion.

docs.title: 22.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define BCNF in one sentence.
  2. State the difference between 3NF and BCNF precisely.
  3. Give the three conditions under which a relation can be in 3NF but not BCNF.
  4. Which decomposition target always allows dependency preservation?
  5. Why must losslessness never be sacrificed?
  6. What does step 3 of the 3NF synthesis algorithm guarantee?
  7. What does 4NF remove?

B. Test and decompose

For each: find all candidate keys, determine the highest normal form, and if it is not in BCNF, decompose. State whether your decomposition preserves dependencies.

  1. R(A,B,C) with AB → C, C → A.
  2. R(A,B,C,D) with A → BCD, BC → AD, D → B.
  3. R(A,B,C,D) with AB → C, C → D, D → A.
  4. R(A,B,C,D,E) with AB → CDE, E → AB.
  5. ADDRESS(Street, City, State, PIN) with Street,City,State → PIN and PIN → City,State.
  6. ENROL(Student, Course, Instructor) where each instructor teaches one course, and a student takes each course from one instructor.
  7. SUPPLY(Supplier, Part, City) where each supplier is in one city, and only one supplier of a given part is in a given city.

C. Synthesis

  1. Apply the 3NF synthesis algorithm to R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E, E → A}.
  2. Apply it to R(A,B,C,D,E,G) with F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A, G → A}.
  3. Show, with an example, why omitting step 3 of the synthesis algorithm can produce a lossy decomposition.

D. Analysis

  1. Prove that every BCNF relation is in 3NF.
  2. Prove that a relation with exactly two attributes is always in BCNF.
  3. Prove that a relation with a single candidate key is in BCNF if and only if it is in 3NF.
  4. For TEACHING, construct explicit rows in the decomposed schema that jointly violate Student,Subject → Teacher while each table is individually valid. Then write the SQL query a trigger would need in order to detect the violation.
  5. A designer refuses to go beyond 3NF, saying "BCNF costs a lost dependency". Under what circumstances is this reasoning correct, and under what circumstances is it wrong?
  6. Give a relation in BCNF that still exhibits redundancy. Which normal form addresses it?
  7. Explain why most relations that reach 3NF are already in BCNF, referring to the three conditions.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. Every 3NF relation is in BCNF.
  2. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF.
  3. A lossless BCNF decomposition always exists.
  4. A dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition always exists.
  5. A relation with one candidate key that is in 3NF is in BCNF.
  6. Losing a dependency corrupts the data.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. TEACHING(Student, Subject, Teacher) is the standard counter-example.
  2. True. BCNF's condition implies 3NF's first alternative, so 3NF is automatically satisfied.
  3. True. The decomposition algorithm splits on X → Y into (X ∪ Y) and (R − Y), whose common attributes X form a key of the first — always lossless.
  4. False. This is exactly what TEACHING disproves.
  5. True. With one candidate key the three conditions for a 3NF-but-not-BCNF violation cannot be met, so the two forms coincide.
  6. False. It costs enforcement — the rule needs a join or a trigger — but the stored data remains correct. Only a lossy decomposition corrupts data, by producing spurious tuples.

Lesson Summary

  • BCNF: every determinant is a superkey. It is 3NF with the "or A is prime" escape clause removed, and is strictly stronger.
  • A relation is in 3NF but not BCNF only when it has two or more overlapping composite candidate keys — so BCNF violations are uncommon.
  • The BCNF decomposition algorithm splits on a violating X → Y into (X ∪ Y) and (R − Y); every step is lossless.
  • The 3NF synthesis algorithm builds one relation per dependency of a minimal cover, plus a candidate-key relation if needed — always lossless and dependency preserving.
  • Trade-off: lossless BCNF always exists; lossless and dependency-preserving BCNF may not. Never sacrifice losslessness — it corrupts data, whereas a lost dependency merely costs enforcement.

docs.title: Lesson 2: Characteristics, Data Models, Schemas and Instances
docs.text:
The vocabulary every database designer must own

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 1: Introduction to Database · 5 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture (50 minutes)

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 1.3, 2.1, 2.2

Learning Outcomes

  1. State and explain the four main characteristics of the database approach.
  2. Define a data model and classify models by level of abstraction.
  3. Describe the hierarchical, network, relational, object and semi-structured models, with their pros and cons.
  4. Draw the sharp distinction between a schema and an instance, and between intension and extension.
  5. Explain what a schema evolution is and why it is rare compared with instance change.

docs.title: 2.1 The Four Characteristics of the Database Approach
docs.text: Lesson 1 argued why we need a DBMS. This section states what makes an approach a database approach at all. Elmasri and Navathe identify four defining characteristics.

docs.title: Characteristic 1 — Self-describing nature of a database system
docs.text:
The database contains not only the data but a complete definition of the data, stored in the catalog (also called the data dictionary or metadata).

The catalog stores, for each table: its name, each column's name, data type and size, the constraints, the indexes, the views, the users and their privileges, and often statistics used by the query optimiser.

Why it matters

The DBMS is written once, generically. It learns the shape of your database by reading the catalog at run time. That is why one MySQL installation can serve a college, a bank and a hospital simultaneously.

docs.title: Characteristic 2 — Insulation between programs and data (program–data independence)
docs.text:
In file processing, the record structure is embedded in the program. Adding a column to students.dat means editing and recompiling every program that reads it.

In a DBMS the structure lives in the catalog, so:

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Mobile CHAR(10) DEFAULT '9999999999';

Every existing application continues to run unchanged. This is program–data independence.

The related idea, program–operation independence, applies to object and object-relational databases: an operation is specified by its interface (name and arguments); its implementation can be replaced without touching the callers.

docs.title: Characteristic 3 — Support of multiple views of the data
docs.text:
Different users need different slices of the same database.

  • The admission clerk needs Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth, Course.
  • The society mentor needs Rollno, Name, SocietyName.
  • The Principal needs only counts per course.

A view is a virtual table derived from the base tables. It may not exist physically, yet the user treats it as a table.

CREATE VIEW SocietyRoster AS
SELECT s.Rollno, s.Name, y.Socname
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ENROLLMENT e ON s.Rollno = e.Rollno
JOIN   SOCIETY    y ON e.SocID  = y.SocID;

Views also serve security: grant a user access to the view and they never see the columns you left out.

docs.title: Characteristic 4 — Sharing of data and multi-user transaction processing
docs.text:
A DBMS lets many users access the database concurrently while keeping it correct. The mechanism is the transaction, with its ACID properties (Unit 6). Concurrency control ensures isolation: concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial order.

Applications in which many users update the same data are called OLTP — On-Line Transaction Processing — systems: railway reservation, banking, admissions.

Examination tip

"Characteristics of the database approach" is a standard 5-mark question. Answer with the four headings self-describing, program–data independence, multiple views, sharing and transactions, then one sentence of explanation and one example each.

docs.title: 2.2 Data Models
docs.text:
Data Model

A data model is a collection of concepts that can be used to describe the structure of a database, together with a set of operations for manipulating it and a set of constraints it must obey.

Structure + Operations + Constraints — a data model is all three, not just the pictures.

Structure means the building blocks: in the relational model, relations, tuples and attributes; in the ER model, entities, attributes and relationships.

Operations means the retrieval and update primitives: in the relational model, the operators of relational algebra (Unit 3).

Constraints means the rules the data must satisfy: keys, referential integrity, domain constraints.

docs.title: Classification by level of abstraction
docs.text:
Category Also called Who uses it Concepts Examples High-level / conceptual Semantic model End users, analysts Entity, attribute, relationship ER model, EER model, UML class diagram Representational / implementation Record-based Programmers, DBAs Relation, tuple, record, table Relational model, network, hierarchical Low-level / physical Internal System designers File, block, page, index, pointer B+-tree files, hashed files

A fourth, informal category is the self-describing data model, in which the description of the data is bundled with the data values themselves — XML, JSON, and NoSQL document stores. These are also called semi-structured models.

     REAL WORLD (the mini-world)
            |
            |  requirements analysis
            v
   +--------------------------+
   |  CONCEPTUAL MODEL        |   ER diagram      <-- Unit 2
   |  entity / relationship   |   technology-free
   +------------+-------------+
                |  mapping algorithm               <-- Unit 5
                v
   +--------------------------+
   |  LOGICAL (REPRESENT.)    |   tables          <-- Units 3 and 4
   |  relations / tuples      |   SQL DDL
   +------------+-------------+
                |  physical design
                v
   +--------------------------+
   |  PHYSICAL MODEL          |   files, pages    <-- Unit 6
   |  blocks / indexes        |   B+-trees, hashing
   +--------------------------+

Figure 2.1 — Levels of abstraction, and where each unit of this course sits.

docs.title: The Hierarchical Model (1960s — IBM IMS)
docs.text:
Data is organised as a tree: each record has exactly one parent; the root has none.

                    COLLEGE
                       |
        +--------------+--------------+
        |                             |
    DEPARTMENT                    DEPARTMENT
    (Computer Sc.)                 (Chemistry)
        |                             |
   +----+----+                   +----+----+
   |         |                   |         |
STUDENT   STUDENT             STUDENT   STUDENT

Advantages: simple, fast for queries that follow the tree downward (a parent's children are physically adjacent); enforces one-to-many naturally.

Disadvantages: cannot represent many-to-many relationships without duplicating data; navigation is procedural (the programmer walks pointers); a query "against the grain" of the tree is very slow; structural change is painful.

docs.title: The Network Model (1971 — CODASYL DBTG)
docs.text:
A graph rather than a tree: a record may have many parents. Relationships are called sets and are implemented as owner–member pointer chains.

Advantages: many-to-many relationships are representable; efficient navigation.

Disadvantages: still procedural ("find owner, find next member..."); the programmer must know the physical pointer structure, so there is almost no data independence; very complex to design and change.

docs.title: The Relational Model (E. F. Codd, 1970)
docs.text:
Everything is a relation — a table of rows and columns. There are no pointers visible to the user; relationships are represented by common values (foreign keys).

Codd's key insight

Separate the logical view of data (tables, based on set theory and predicate logic) from its physical storage entirely. Then queries can be declarative — say what you want, not how to get it — and the system is free to choose the access path.

Advantages: simple and uniform; declarative, powerful query language (SQL); strong theoretical foundation (relational algebra, normalisation); excellent data independence.

Disadvantages: performance overhead compared with hand-tuned navigation; awkward for hierarchical or graph-shaped data; the impedance mismatch with object-oriented programming languages.

This is the model the rest of the course is about.

docs.title: The Object-Oriented and Object-Relational Models
docs.text:
The object data model stores objects with identity (OID), attributes, and encapsulated methods, supporting inheritance and complex types. Object-relational systems (PostgreSQL, Oracle) add these features on top of tables.

Advantages: handles complex data (CAD, multimedia, geographic) naturally; no impedance mismatch with OO languages. Disadvantages: more complex; no single standard as universally accepted as SQL.

docs.title: Semi-structured and NoSQL Models
docs.text:
Data carries its own description; different items in the same collection may have different attributes.

{ "Rollno": "X2019", "Name": "Ankit Sharma",
  "Courses": [ {"SID":"CS01","Type":"Fulltime"} ],
  "Societies": ["Debating","Music"] }

Advantages: flexible schema; scales horizontally; natural fit for web data. Disadvantages: weaker consistency guarantees; no universal declarative query language; integrity must often be enforced in the application.

docs.title: Comparison summary
docs.text: Feature Hierarchical Network Relational Object Semi-structured Structure Tree Graph Tables Objects Tree/document Many-to-many No (needs duplication) Yes Yes (via junction table) Yes Yes Access Procedural, pointers Procedural, pointers Declarative (SQL) Method calls / OQL Path expressions Data independence Poor Poor Excellent Good Varies Schema required Yes Yes Yes Yes No Example system IBM IMS IDMS MySQL, Oracle ObjectStore, db4o MongoDB, XML DBs

docs.title: 2.3 Schemas, Instances and Database State
docs.text:
This distinction is examined almost every year. Learn it exactly.

Schema vs Instance

Database schema — the description of the database: the table names, the columns, their types, and the constraints. It is specified during design and changes rarely. Also called the intension of the database. A picture of the schema is a schema diagram; a single description of one table is a schema construct.

Database instance (or database state, or occurrence, or snapshot) — the actual data in the database at a particular moment. It changes every time a row is inserted, deleted or updated. Also called the extension.

An analogy from programming: the schema is the type declaration; the instance is the value of the variable at a moment in time.

struct Student { char rollno[8]; char name[30]; };   /* the SCHEMA  */
struct Student s = {"X2019", "Ankit Sharma"};        /* an INSTANCE */

docs.title: Worked illustration
docs.text:
Schema of COURSE (this never changes during a normal day):

COURSE ( SID       : VARCHAR(6)   PRIMARY KEY,
         Cname     : VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
         TotalSeats: INT          CHECK (TotalSeats > 0),
         Duration  : INT,
         Coursetype: VARCHAR(10)  CHECK (Coursetype IN ('Fulltime','Parttime')),
         TeacherInCharge : VARCHAR(40) )

Instance at 10:00 a.m.:

SID Cname TotalSeats Duration Coursetype TeacherInCharge CS01 Computer Science 60 3 Fulltime R. K. Gupta CH01 Chemistry 45 3 Fulltime S. Menon

Instance at 10:05 a.m., after INSERT INTO COURSE VALUES ('MA02','Mathematics',50,3,'Parttime','A. Gupta');

SID Cname TotalSeats Duration Coursetype TeacherInCharge CS01 Computer Science 60 3 Fulltime R. K. Gupta CH01 Chemistry 45 3 Fulltime S. Menon MA02 Mathematics 50 3 Parttime A. Gupta

The schema did not change; only the instance did.

docs.title: The valid state
docs.text:
Valid state

A database state is valid if it satisfies every constraint in the schema. The DBMS's job on each update is to move the database from one valid state to another valid state; if an update would create an invalid state, it is rejected.

The very first state, when the schema has been created but no data inserted, is the empty state. Loading the initial data gives the initial state.

docs.title: Schema evolution
docs.text:
Changing the schema itself — ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN, dropping a constraint — is called schema evolution. It is rare, is done by the DBA, and is precisely the operation that program–data independence is designed to make painless.

Common student error

Saying "the schema changes when we insert a row". It does not. Inserting, updating and deleting rows change the instance. Only DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) change the schema.

docs.title: 2.4 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define a data model. What are its three components? Classify data models by level of abstraction with one example each.

A. A data model is a collection of concepts for describing the structure of a database, together with the operations for manipulating it and the constraints it must satisfy.

Its three components are:

  1. Structure — the constructs available (relations and tuples in the relational model; entities and relationships in the ER model).
  2. Operations — the retrieval and update primitives (selection, projection and join in relational algebra; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE).
  3. Constraints — rules restricting valid states (primary keys, referential integrity, domain and check constraints).

Classification by abstraction:

Level Example Concepts High-level / conceptual ER model entity, attribute, relationship Representational / implementation Relational model relation, tuple, attribute Low-level / physical B+-tree file organisation block, page, pointer, index

A fourth informal class is the self-describing / semi-structured model (XML, JSON), where the description travels with the data.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish clearly between a database schema and a database instance. Give an example of an operation that changes each.

A.

Schema Instance What it is The description — structure, types, constraints The data actually stored at a moment Other names Intension, metadata Extension, state, snapshot, occurrence Frequency of change Rarely (schema evolution) Constantly Where stored Catalog / data dictionary Data files Changed by DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE Programming analogy Type declaration Value of the variable

Changes the schema: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Mobile CHAR(10); Changes the instance: INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES ('X2020','Riya Verma','2002-05-11');

Note that some DDL statements change both: dropping a column removes it from the schema and discards its data from every row.

Solved Question 3

Q. Why did the relational model displace the hierarchical and network models? Give three reasons.

A.

  1. Declarative querying instead of navigation. In the hierarchical and network models the programmer writes a procedure — "find owner record, get next member, follow pointer" — and must know the physical pointer structure. In the relational model the user writes what is wanted (SELECT ... WHERE ...) and the system's optimiser chooses how. Development time collapses, and unanticipated queries become trivial.

  2. Genuine data independence. Because relationships are expressed by common values rather than stored pointers, the physical storage — indexes, clustering, file organisation — can be changed with no effect on applications. In pointer-based models the pointer structure is the relationship, so reorganising storage breaks programs.

  3. A rigorous mathematical foundation. The relational model rests on set theory and first-order predicate logic. This gave us relational algebra and calculus (so query equivalence and optimisation can be proved), and normalisation theory (so good design can be derived rather than guessed). Neither of the older models had a comparable theory.

Two supplementary reasons often credited: the relational model represents many-to-many relationships naturally with a junction table, whereas the hierarchical model cannot without duplication; and its structural simplicity (everything is a table) made it far easier to learn.

Solved Question 4

Q. Explain the four characteristics of the database approach, illustrating each with the college database.

A.

  1. Self-describing nature. Along with the STUDENT, COURSE and ADMISSION rows, the database stores in its catalog that STUDENT.Rollno is VARCHAR(8) and is the primary key. A query on information_schema.columns retrieves this. The DBMS therefore needs no compiled knowledge of the college.

  2. Insulation between programs and data. Adding Mobile to STUDENT with ALTER TABLE does not require the admission application, the fee application or the library application to be recompiled. In a file system every program that read the record layout would break.

  3. Support of multiple views. The society mentor is given a view exposing only (Rollno, Name, Socname); the accounts clerk gets a view with fee columns but no marks. Each sees a tailored, virtual table over the same base data — which also serves as a security mechanism.

  4. Sharing of data and multi-user transaction processing. Twenty admission counters insert into ADMISSION simultaneously during counselling. The DBMS's concurrency control guarantees that the outcome equals some serial order, so a course with 60 seats never admits 61 students.

Solved Question 5

Q. Consider the schema EMPLOYEE(Eno, Ename, Salary, Dno) with the constraint Salary > 0. State whether each of the following is a schema change or an instance change, and whether the resulting state is valid.

a. INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE VALUES (1,'Asha',25000,10); b. INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE VALUES (2,'Bhanu',-500,10); c. ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE ADD COLUMN DOJ DATE; d. UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET Salary = Salary * 1.1;

A.

Type of change Valid? Reason a Instance Valid 25000 > 0 satisfies the check constraint. b Instance (attempted) Invalid — rejected -500 violates Salary > 0; the DBMS refuses the insert and the state is unchanged. c Schema Valid DDL alters the description; existing rows get NULL for DOJ. d Instance Valid Multiplying a positive salary by 1.1 keeps it positive, so the constraint still holds.

The general principle: the DBMS will only allow a transition from one valid state to another valid state.

Solved Question 6

Q. What is program–data independence? How does the catalog make it possible?

A. Program–data independence is the property that the structure of the stored data can be changed without changing the application programs that access it.

It is possible because the structure is not compiled into the programs; it is stored once, in the DBMS catalog. When an application issues SELECT Name FROM STUDENT, the DBMS at run time consults the catalog to discover where Name sits in the stored record, what its type is, and how to decode it. Change the record layout and the catalog is updated; the next execution of the same unchanged program simply reads the new catalog entry and still works.

In a file-processing system the offset and type of every field is written into the source code of each program, so the same change forces every program to be edited, recompiled and retested.

This is the mechanism behind the two kinds of data independence formalised in Lesson 3: logical and physical data independence.

docs.title: 2.5 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. List the four characteristics of the database approach.
  2. Define data model, and name its three components.
  3. What is the difference between the intension and the extension of a database?
  4. What is a view? Give two reasons for using one.
  5. Which data model cannot represent many-to-many relationships directly, and why?
  6. What is meant by schema evolution?
  7. Define valid state and empty state.

B. Long answer

  1. Explain the four characteristics of the database approach with examples from a hospital database.
  2. Compare the hierarchical, network and relational data models on: structure, handling of many-to-many relationships, query style, and data independence. Present your answer as a table followed by a short verdict.
  3. "A data model is more than a diagram." Justify this statement by explaining structure, operations and constraints for the relational model.
  4. Explain the classification of data models by level of abstraction. At which level does the ER model sit, and at which does the relational model? Why is this separation useful?

C. Application and analytical

  1. For the table SOCIETY(SocID, Socname, Mentor, TotalSeats), write down (i) the schema and (ii) any two consecutive instances differing by one INSERT. Clearly mark what changed.
  2. Classify each of the following as a schema change or an instance change: a. Deleting the row for roll number X2019. b. Making Coursetype accept a third value, 'Weekend'. c. Renaming column Cname to CourseName. d. Increasing every course's TotalSeats by 10 per cent. e. Creating an index on STUDENT.Name.
  3. A shopping website stores products where books have author and ISBN, shoes have size and colour, and phones have RAM and battery. Which data model suits this best, and why? What do you lose by choosing it?
  4. The COURSE table has the constraint CHECK (TotalSeats > 0). The DBA runs UPDATE COURSE SET TotalSeats = TotalSeats - 100; where some courses have 60 seats. Describe exactly what the DBMS does and what the final state is. Which property is being protected?
  5. Design three different views over the college database for three different users, writing the CREATE VIEW statement for each, and state which columns each user is thereby prevented from seeing.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. The catalog is part of the database.
  2. An instance describes the structure of a database.
  3. The network model supports declarative queries.
  4. Views always store data physically.
  5. Semi-structured data models require a schema to be defined before data is loaded.
  6. Program–data independence means programs and data are stored on different disks.

Answers to Section D

  1. True. Metadata is stored inside the database as system tables (information_schema), and is queryable with SQL.
  2. False. The schema describes the structure; the instance is the data at a moment.
  3. False. The network model is navigational and procedural; the programmer follows owner–member pointer chains.
  4. False. A standard view is virtual — its definition is stored, and it is computed on demand. Only a materialised view stores data.
  5. False. They are schema-less or schema-flexible; the description travels with each data item.
  6. False. It means the structure of the data can change without changing the programs, because the structure lives in the catalog rather than in program code.

Lesson Summary

  • The four characteristics: self-describing catalog, program–data independence, multiple views, sharing with transactions.
  • A data model = structure + operations + constraints. Models are conceptual (ER), representational (relational), or physical.
  • The relational model won because it is declarative, value-based (no visible pointers), and mathematically founded.
  • Schema (intension) is the description and changes rarely; instance (extension) is the data and changes constantly. DDL changes the schema; DML changes the instance.
  • The DBMS moves the database only from one valid state to another.

docs.title: Lesson 4: Components, Architectures and Users
docs.text:
Inside the engine, and the people around it

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 1: Introduction to Database · 5 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 1.4, 2.3, 2.5

Learning Outcomes

  1. Name and describe the major functional components of a DBMS.
  2. Distinguish the query processor from the storage manager.
  3. Explain the centralised, client/server, two-tier and three-tier architectures.
  4. Identify every category of database user and state their responsibilities.
  5. Classify the languages and interfaces a DBMS provides.

docs.title: 4.1 Components of a DBMS
docs.text:
A DBMS is not one program; it is a layered collection of cooperating modules. They fall into three groups: the query processor, the storage manager, and the disk structures.

   Naive users   Application    Sophisticated    DBA
   (forms)       programmers    users (SQL)      (DDL)
       |              |              |            |
   +---v---+     +----v----+    +----v----+   +---v----+
   |Applic.|     |Applic.  |    |  Query  |   |  DDL   |
   |interf.|     |programs |    |  tools  |   |interpr.|
   +---+---+     +----+----+    +----+----+   +---+----+
       |              |              |            |
       |         +----v----+         |            |
       |         |Precompi-|         |            |
       |         |ler / API|         |            |
       |         +----+----+         |            |
       +--------------+--------------+            |
                      |                           |
            +---------v----------+                |
            |  DML COMPILER &     |               |
            |  QUERY PARSER       |               |
            +---------+----------+                |
                      |                           |
            +---------v----------+                |
            |  QUERY OPTIMISER    |               |
            +---------+----------+                |
                      |                           |
            +---------v----------+                |
            |  QUERY EVALUATION   |               |
            |  ENGINE             |               |
            +=========+==========+ ============== |======= QUERY PROCESSOR
                      |                           |
            +---------v-----------------+---------v-----+
            |            STORAGE MANAGER                |
            |  +-------------+  +---------------------+ |
            |  | Authorisat. |  | Transaction manager | |
            |  | & integrity |  | (concurrency ctrl,  | |
            |  | manager     |  |  recovery manager)  | |
            |  +-------------+  +---------------------+ |
            |  +-------------+  +---------------------+ |
            |  | File        |  | Buffer manager      | |
            |  | manager     |  |                     | |
            |  +-------------+  +---------------------+ |
            +--------------------+----------------------+
                                 |
       +-------------------------v--------------------------+
       |               D I S K   S T O R A G E               |
       |  data files | data dictionary | indexes | log       |
       |             | (catalog)       |         | statistics|
       +-----------------------------------------------------+

Figure 4.1 — The functional components of a DBMS.

docs.title: The query processor
docs.text:
Component Responsibility DDL interpreter Parses CREATE/ALTER/DROP statements and records the definitions in the catalog. DML compiler / query parser Parses SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, checks syntax, and verifies names and types against the catalog. Query optimiser Chooses the cheapest execution plan among the many equivalent ones — which index to use, which join order, which join algorithm. Uses statistics kept in the catalog. Query evaluation engine Actually executes the chosen plan by calling the storage manager. Embedded DML precompiler Converts DML statements embedded in a host language (C, Java) into procedure calls to the runtime library.

Why an optimiser exists

SQL is declarative: you say what you want, not how. Something must supply the how. For a three-table join there are already many candidate plans; the optimiser estimates the cost of each using catalog statistics (row counts, index selectivity) and picks the cheapest. A good optimiser routinely turns a query that would take minutes into one that takes milliseconds — and it is the direct beneficiary of physical data independence.

docs.title: The storage manager
docs.text:
The storage manager is the interface between the low-level stored data and the queries submitted to the system.

Component Responsibility Authorisation and integrity manager Checks the user's privileges and enforces integrity constraints on every operation. Transaction manager Ensures the database remains in a consistent state despite failures and concurrency; provides COMMIT/ROLLBACK. Contains the concurrency-control manager (locking, serialisability) and the recovery manager (logging, restart recovery). File manager Manages allocation of disk space and the data structures used to represent stored information. Buffer manager Fetches disk blocks into main memory and decides which to keep. The single most important component for performance, because it determines how often a slow disk read must happen.

docs.title: Structures on disk
docs.text:
• Data files — the stored database itself.
  • Data dictionary (catalog) — the metadata: schemas, constraints, users, privileges.
  • Indexes — access structures for fast lookup (Unit 6).
  • Statistics — row counts, value distributions, used by the optimiser.
  • Log — the write-ahead record of every change, used for recovery.

docs.title: Centralised architecture
docs.text:
Everything — DBMS, application, user interface — runs on one machine, a mainframe, with users at "dumb" terminals that only display characters.

Advantages: simple to administer; no network issues. Disadvantages: no scalability; the mainframe is a single point of failure and a bottleneck; expensive.

   Terminal   Terminal   Terminal        (display only)
       \         |         /
        \        |        /
      +--v-------v-------v---+
      |      MAINFRAME       |
      |  UI + Application    |
      |  + DBMS + Data       |
      +----------------------+

docs.title: Client/server architecture
docs.text:
Falling hardware prices made intelligent workstations possible. Function is split between a server that provides a service and clients that consume it.

Two-tier client/server

Tier 1 — Client: the user interface and the application logic run on the user's machine. The client connects to the DBMS through an API such as ODBC or JDBC and sends SQL.

Tier 2 — Server: the DBMS, holding the data and executing the queries.

  +-------------+   +-------------+   +-------------+
  |  CLIENT 1   |   |  CLIENT 2   |   |  CLIENT 3   |
  | UI + logic  |   | UI + logic  |   | UI + logic  |
  +------+------+   +------+------+   +------+------+
         |   SQL over ODBC/JDBC |            |
         +----------+-----------+------------+
                    |
          +---------v----------+
          |    DATABASE SERVER |
          |    DBMS + data     |
          +--------------------+

Advantages: shares the load; clients can be heterogeneous; cheaper than a mainframe. Disadvantages ("fat client" problems): business logic is duplicated on every client, so a rule change means redeploying every client; every client needs a direct database connection and therefore database credentials, which is a security risk; connections do not scale to thousands of users.

Three-tier architecture

Tier 1 — Presentation (client): the browser or thin app. Displays and collects data only.

Tier 2 — Application / business-logic tier (middle tier): the web or application server. Holds all business rules, validates requests, and is the only tier that talks to the database. Also called the web server tier.

Tier 3 — Database tier: the DBMS.

  +----------+  +----------+  +----------+
  | BROWSER  |  | BROWSER  |  | MOBILE   |    TIER 1  presentation
  +-----+----+  +-----+----+  +-----+----+
        |  HTTP / HTTPS |           |
        +-------+-------+-----------+
                |
       +--------v---------+
       | APPLICATION      |                  TIER 2  business logic
       | SERVER           |
       | business rules,  |
       | session, security|
       +--------+---------+
                | SQL (pooled connections)
       +--------v---------+
       | DATABASE SERVER  |                  TIER 3  data
       +------------------+

Advantages: business logic lives in one place, so a rule change is deployed once; clients never hold database credentials, and the middle tier is a security firewall; connection pooling lets thousands of users share a few database connections; each tier scales independently.

Disadvantages: more complex to build and deploy; the extra network hop adds latency.

An n-tier architecture simply subdivides the middle tier further (web server, application server, integration layer).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Centralised Two-tier Three-tier Where is UI? Server Client Client Where is business logic? Server Client (fat) Middle tier Where is data? Server Server Database tier Scalability Poor Moderate High Security Physical only Weak — clients hold DB credentials Strong — middle tier isolates the DB Maintenance Central, easy Hard — redeploy every client Easy — redeploy the middle tier Typical example 1970s mainframe A desktop app with a MySQL connection Any modern web application

docs.title: Actors on the scene (they use the database daily)
docs.text:
Database Administrator (DBA). Responsible for the database system as a whole. Duties:

  • Schema definition and schema evolution.
  • Storage structure and access-method definition (physical design, indexes).
  • Granting and revoking authorisation — deciding who may do what.
  • Routine maintenance: backups, monitoring free space, upgrades.
  • Performance tuning, and acquisition of software and hardware.
  • Liaison with users; enforcement of standards and documentation.

Database Designers. Identify the data to be stored and choose the structures. They interview each user group, reconcile their conflicting requirements, and produce the conceptual schema and then the external schemas. Their work is Units 2 and 5 of this course.

End Users. People who access the database for querying, updating and reports. Four sub-types:

Sub-type Description Casual Occasional users, usually middle or high-level managers, who need different information each time and use a query language or a report generator. Naive / parametric The largest group. They constantly query and update using standard canned transactions through forms and menus — bank tellers, reservation clerks, admission counter staff. They need no knowledge of the database. Sophisticated Engineers, scientists, business analysts. They learn the DBMS facilities thoroughly and write their own complex queries. Stand-alone Maintain a personal database using a ready-made package with a graphical interface (e.g. a personal accounts application).

System Analysts and Application Programmers (Software Engineers). Analysts determine the requirements of naive users and specify the canned transactions; programmers implement, test and document them.

docs.title: Workers behind the scene (they build the DBMS, not the database)
docs.text:
• DBMS system designers and implementers — who write the DBMS software modules of Section 4.1.
  • Tool developers — who build design tools, performance monitors, test-data generators, interfaces.
  • Operators and maintenance personnel — who run and maintain the hardware and software environment.

Frequently confused

The DBA administers a database system that already exists; the database designer decides what that database should contain; the DBMS implementer writes the DBMS software product itself. An examination answer that blurs these loses marks.

docs.title: Languages
docs.text:
Language Full form Purpose Typical statements DDL Data Definition Language Define and modify the schema CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME DML Data Manipulation Language Retrieve and change the data SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE DCL Data Control Language Control access GRANT, REVOKE TCL Transaction Control Language Delimit transactions COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

Two further terms appear in Elmasri and Navathe: SDL (Storage Definition Language) for the internal schema and VDL (View Definition Language) for external schemas. In SQL all of these are folded into one language.

Procedural vs Non-procedural DML

A high-level or non-procedural (declarative) DML — such as SQL — lets you specify what data is wanted in a single statement, leaving the how to the optimiser. It is set-at-a-time: one statement processes many rows.

A low-level or procedural DML — such as embedded record-at-a-time navigation — requires you to specify how to retrieve the data, looping over records one at a time. Relational algebra is procedural in this sense; relational calculus and SQL are declarative.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
• Menu-based and forms-based interfaces, for naive users.
  • Graphical user interfaces, often showing the schema diagrammatically.
  • Natural-language interfaces, which map English-like requests onto queries.
  • Speech input and output, used in enquiry systems.
  • Interfaces for parametric users, with a small set of keystrokes for very high throughput.
  • Interfaces for the DBA, providing privileged commands.
  • APIs / call-level interfaces — ODBC, JDBC, and language connectors such as MySQL Connector/Python. These are covered in Unit 4.

docs.title: 4.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Draw and explain the component modules of a DBMS.

A. (Diagram: reproduce Figure 4.1.) The modules fall into three groups.

Query processor — the DDL interpreter records definitions in the catalog; the DML compiler parses and type-checks queries against the catalog; the query optimiser transforms the query into the cheapest equivalent execution plan using stored statistics; the query evaluation engine executes that plan.

Storage manager — the authorisation and integrity manager checks privileges and constraints; the transaction manager provides atomicity and isolation via its concurrency-control and recovery sub-managers; the file manager allocates disk space and manages the stored data structures; the buffer manager moves blocks between disk and main memory and decides what to keep in memory.

Disk structures — data files, the data dictionary (catalog), indexes, statistics, and the log.

The essential flow: a query enters the query processor, is parsed, optimised and executed; execution issues requests to the storage manager, which checks authorisation, takes locks, and asks the buffer manager for the required pages; results flow back up.

Solved Question 2

Q. Compare two-tier and three-tier client/server architectures. Why is three-tier preferred for web applications?

A. (Table from Section 4.2.3.)

In two-tier, the client holds both the presentation and the business logic and connects directly to the DBMS. In three-tier, the business logic is moved into a middle application-server tier, which alone talks to the database.

Three-tier is preferred for web applications for four reasons:

  1. Security. In two-tier every client holds database credentials and needs a direct route to the database server — impossible to expose safely over the internet. In three-tier the database sits behind the middle tier; a hostile browser never reaches it. The middle tier acts as a firewall.
  2. Maintainability. A change to a business rule is deployed once, on the application server, rather than redeployed to thousands of clients.
  3. Scalability. A database supports a limited number of concurrent connections. The middle tier uses connection pooling so that thousands of web users share a small pool, and additional application servers can be added behind a load balancer.
  4. Thin clients. Users need only a browser, so the system runs on any device with no installation.

The costs are greater architectural complexity and one extra network hop of latency.

Solved Question 3

Q. List the functions of a Database Administrator.

A.

  1. Schema definition — creating the original conceptual schema with DDL.
  2. Storage structure and access-method definition — the internal schema: file organisations, indexes, tablespaces.
  3. Schema and physical organisation modification — schema evolution, and tuning storage as workloads change.
  4. Granting authorisation for data access — CREATE USER, CREATE ROLE, GRANT, REVOKE, so each user reaches only what they should.
  5. Routine maintenance — periodic backups, monitoring disk space, applying patches and upgrades.
  6. Performance monitoring and tuning — watching slow queries, adding or dropping indexes, adjusting buffer sizes.
  7. Ensuring integrity, security and recovery — defining constraints, planning and testing disaster recovery.
  8. Acquisition of software and hardware resources as requirements grow.
  9. Contact with users and enforcement of standards for naming, documentation and design.

Solved Question 4

Q. Classify each of the following users and justify: (a) a bank teller entering deposits; (b) a market analyst writing complex SQL to study sales trends; (c) a person maintaining household accounts in a ready-made package; (d) a manager who occasionally asks for a one-off report; (e) a person who wrote the MySQL optimiser.

A.

Category Justification a Naive / parametric end user Repeatedly executes a small set of canned transactions through a form; needs no knowledge of the database structure. b Sophisticated end user Familiar with the DBMS's facilities and writes complex ad-hoc queries directly, without a programmer's help. c Stand-alone user Maintains a personal database with a ready-made package and a graphical interface. d Casual end user Accesses the database occasionally and needs different information each time, using a query language or report generator. e Worker behind the scene — a DBMS system implementer Builds the DBMS software product, not any particular database.

Solved Question 5

Q. Distinguish DDL, DML, DCL and TCL, giving two statements of each and stating who typically uses it.

A.

Purpose Statements Typical user Level affected DDL Define / change the schema CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE DBA, designer Conceptual (and internal, via storage clauses) DML Retrieve / change the data SELECT, UPDATE End users, application programmers Instance DCL Control access GRANT, REVOKE DBA Authorisation catalog TCL Delimit transactions COMMIT, ROLLBACK Application programmers Transaction boundaries

A further useful distinction is within DML: SQL is a high-level, non-procedural, set-at-a-time DML — you state what you want and the optimiser decides how, and one statement affects many rows. A low-level, procedural, record-at-a-time DML would require you to loop, retrieving one record per call.

Solved Question 6

Q. What is the role of the buffer manager, and why is it critical to performance?

A. The buffer manager is the storage-manager component responsible for moving disk blocks (pages) into a region of main memory called the buffer pool, and for deciding which pages to retain and which to evict when space is needed.

It is critical because of the enormous speed gap between main memory and disk — a memory access takes tens of nanoseconds, a disk access milliseconds, a difference of roughly five orders of magnitude. The number of disk accesses therefore dominates the cost of almost every database operation.

The buffer manager's job is to make the number of physical reads as small as possible. When a query needs a page it first checks the buffer pool; a hit costs nothing extra, a miss costs a disk read. By choosing a good replacement policy (LRU, clock, or policies aware of the access pattern such as sequential scans) and by pinning pages that are in use, the buffer manager raises the hit ratio. A few percentage points of hit ratio can change overall throughput several-fold.

It also cooperates with the recovery manager: under write-ahead logging a dirty page must not be written to disk before the corresponding log record, so the buffer manager must respect the log's ordering constraints before evicting a modified page.

docs.title: 4.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Name the four components of the storage manager.
  2. What does the query optimiser do, and what information does it use?
  3. Define canned transaction, and say which user category uses them.
  4. What is the difference between a DBA and a database designer?
  5. Expand ODBC and JDBC, and say which architectural tier uses them.
  6. Give two examples each of DDL, DML, DCL and TCL statements.
  7. What is stored in the log file, and which component uses it?

B. Long answer

  1. Draw the component diagram of a DBMS and explain the function of each module.
  2. Explain the centralised, two-tier and three-tier architectures with diagrams. Compare them on scalability, security and maintainability.
  3. Describe all the categories of database users, distinguishing actors on the scene from workers behind the scene.
  4. Explain the function of the buffer manager and the transaction manager, and describe how they must cooperate for recovery to work.
  5. Classify database languages and interfaces. Explain the difference between procedural and non-procedural DML with an example of each.

C. Application and analytical

  1. A college wishes to put its admission system online for 5,000 simultaneous applicants. Recommend an architecture, draw it, and justify your choice on security, scalability and maintainability. State one disadvantage of your recommendation.
  2. For each task, name the DBMS component chiefly responsible: a. Deciding to use the index on Cname rather than scanning the table. b. Refusing an INSERT whose SID does not exist in COURSE. c. Undoing a half-finished transfer after a power failure. d. Keeping the most frequently used pages in memory. e. Recording that STUDENT.Rollno is VARCHAR(8). f. Preventing two clerks from booking the same last seat.
  3. A two-tier desktop application is being migrated to three tiers. List the specific changes required, and name three problems the migration solves.
  4. Which user categories exist in a railway reservation system? Name each, and give the actual person and the interface they would use.
  5. Explain why an optimiser is unnecessary in a procedural, record-at-a-time DML but essential in SQL.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. The query optimiser guarantees the fastest possible execution plan.
  2. In three-tier architecture the browser connects directly to the database.
  3. The DBA writes the DBMS software.
  4. GRANT is a DDL statement.
  5. The buffer manager is part of the query processor.
  6. Naive end users must know SQL.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. It chooses the cheapest plan according to its cost estimates, which are based on approximate statistics. A better plan may exist; the optimiser only aims to avoid disastrous ones cheaply.
  2. False. The browser talks to the middle tier over HTTP; only the middle tier issues SQL to the database.
  3. False. The DBA administers a particular database system. DBMS software is written by system implementers — workers behind the scene.
  4. False. GRANT is DCL. (Some textbooks group DCL under a broad definition of DDL; state the standard four-way classification and note the exception.)
  5. False. It is part of the storage manager.
  6. False. They work through forms and menus that invoke canned transactions; they need no knowledge of SQL or of the schema.

Lesson Summary

  • The query processor (DDL interpreter, DML compiler, optimiser, evaluation engine) turns declarative requests into plans; the storage manager (authorisation and integrity, transaction, file, buffer managers) executes them safely against disk.
  • Centralised gave way to two-tier client/server and then to three-tier, which puts business logic in a middle tier for security, maintainability and scalability.
  • Users: DBA, designers, end users (casual, naive, sophisticated, stand-alone), analysts and programmers — plus the workers behind the scene who build the DBMS itself.
  • Languages: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL; SQL is a high-level, non-procedural, set-at-a-time DML.

End of Unit 1. Next: Unit 2, Lesson 1 — Conceptual Data Modelling: Entities and Entity Types.

docs.title: Lesson 5: Conceptual Modelling, Entities and Entity Types
docs.text:
From a requirements document to the first boxes on paper

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 2: Entity Relationship Modelling · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 3.1, 3.2

Learning Outcomes

  1. Explain the motivation for conceptual modelling and where it sits in the design life-cycle.
  2. Define entity, entity type, entity set, and distinguish them rigorously.
  3. Distinguish strong and weak entity types.
  4. Extract candidate entity types from a requirements paragraph.
  5. Avoid the four classic beginner mistakes in choosing entities.

docs.title: 5.1 Why Model Before You Build?
docs.text:
You could start a database project by opening MySQL and typing CREATE TABLE. People do. It is a reliable way to produce a database that has to be thrown away in six months.

The database design life-cycle

  1. Requirements collection and analysis — interview users; write down the data requirements (what must be stored) and the functional requirements (what operations must be supported).
  2. Conceptual design — produce a conceptual schema, technology-free, using a high-level model. This is the ER model. This is Unit 2.
  3. Choice of DBMS — commercial factors, technical factors.
  4. Logical design (data model mapping) — convert the conceptual schema into the data model of the chosen DBMS: ER to relations. This is Unit 5, Lesson 1.
  5. Physical design — file organisations, indexes. Unit 6.
  6. Implementation and tuning — DDL, application programs, monitoring.
   Mini-world
       |
       |  requirements collection & analysis
       v
   Data requirements ---------------------> Functional requirements
       |                                             |
       |  CONCEPTUAL DESIGN  (ER model)              |  functional analysis
       v                                             v
   Conceptual schema  <------ independent of DBMS -----> High-level
       |                                             transaction spec.
       |  LOGICAL DESIGN (mapping)  <-- DBMS chosen here
       v
   Logical (relational) schema
       |
       |  PHYSICAL DESIGN
       v
   Internal schema + application programs

Figure 1.1 — Where conceptual design sits (after Elmasri & Navathe).

docs.title: The three arguments for conceptual modelling
docs.text:
1. It is a communication tool. An ER diagram is understandable by a non-technical user — the college registrar, the hospital administrator — who can then confirm or correct it. CREATE TABLE statements are not. Errors caught at this stage cost minutes; the same error caught after implementation costs weeks.

2. It is implementation-independent. The ER diagram says nothing about MySQL, tables, foreign keys or indexes. The same diagram can be mapped to a relational database, an object database or a document store. The meaning of the enterprise's data outlives any product.

3. It forces the design questions early. Drawing the diagram compels you to ask: Can a student enrol in more than one society? Must every course have a teacher-in-charge? Is a dependant identifiable without its employee? These are business questions, and answering them wrongly produces a database that cannot represent reality.

The ER model

The Entity-Relationship model, introduced by Peter Chen in 1976, describes a mini-world using just three constructs: entities, attributes and relationships. Its diagrammatic form is the ER diagram.

docs.title: 5.2 Entities
docs.text:
Entity

An entity is a thing or object in the mini-world that has an independent existence and can be distinguished from other objects.

Two kinds:

  • Physical (tangible) existence — a particular student, a particular car, a particular book.
  • Conceptual (logical) existence — a particular course, a particular job, a particular society, a university.

Two tests an entity must pass:

  1. Distinguishability. You must be able to tell one from another. Two students with the same name are still two entities.
  2. Relevance. It must matter to this mini-world. A student's favourite colour is real, but if the college has no use for it, it is not part of the model.

docs.title: Entity type, entity set, and the instance/type distinction
docs.text:
This is the same intension/extension distinction met in Unit 1, applied to the ER model. It is examined constantly.

The three terms

Entity type — the definition: a name plus a set of attributes, describing a collection of entities that share the same properties. Written STUDENT. This is the schema or intension, and it is what appears in the diagram.

Entity set (entity collection) — the set of all entities of that type in the database at a given moment. This is the extension, and it changes as data is inserted and deleted.

Entity (entity instance) — one individual member of the entity set: the student with roll number X2019.

   ENTITY TYPE (schema, in the diagram)
   +----------------------------------------+
   |  STUDENT                               |
   |  Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth             |
   +----------------------------------------+
                     |
                     |  at 10:00 a.m. the ENTITY SET is
                     v
   +----------------------------------------+
   |  e1 = ('X2019','Ankit Sharma','2001-03-14')   <- an ENTITY
   |  e2 = ('X2020','Riya Verma','2002-05-11')     <- an ENTITY
   |  e3 = ('Z1188','Sana Iqbal','2001-11-02')     <- an ENTITY
   +----------------------------------------+

Figure 1.2 — Entity type versus entity set versus entity.

By convention the entity type and its entity set are given the same name, and the context tells you which is meant. In a diagram, STUDENT means the type; in the sentence "there are 400 students", it means the set.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
An entity type is drawn as a rectangle containing its name in the singular, in capitals.

        +-----------+           +-----------+
        |  STUDENT  |           |  COURSE   |
        +-----------+           +-----------+

        Strong (regular) entity types: single rectangle.

        +===========+
        ||DEPENDENT||          Weak entity type: double rectangle.
        +===========+

Naming conventions used throughout this course

  • Entity type names: singular, UPPERCASE — STUDENT, not Students.
  • Attribute names: Mixed case — Dateofbirth.
  • Relationship type names: UPPERCASE verb phrases — TAKES_ADMISSION, ENROLS_IN.
  • Relationship names should read sensibly left-to-right: STUDENT TAKES_ADMISSION COURSE.

docs.title: 5.3 Strong and Weak Entity Types
docs.text:
Strong (regular) entity type

An entity type that has a key attribute of its own — a set of attributes whose values uniquely identify each entity, without reference to any other entity type. It has independent existence. Drawn as a single rectangle.

Weak entity type

An entity type that has no key attribute of its own. Its entities are identified only by being related to a specific entity of another type — the identifying (owner) entity type — through an identifying relationship.

  • Drawn as a double rectangle; the identifying relationship as a double diamond.
  • It has a partial key (discriminator): an attribute that distinguishes the weak entities belonging to the same owner. Drawn with a dashed underline.
  • A weak entity type always has total participation in its identifying relationship (double line), and the relationship is 1:N from owner to weak.
  • Existence dependency: delete the owner and the weak entities must go too.

docs.title: The classic example
docs.text:
An employee's dependants. The company records each dependant's name, birth date and relationship. Two different employees may each have a son called Rahul, so Name alone does not identify a dependant. But Name within one employee is unique.

     +------------+        +==========+        +===========+
     |  EMPLOYEE  |========||DEPENDENT_||=======||DEPENDENT ||
     +------------+        ||   OF     ||       +===========+
        Ssn (key)          +==========+          Name (partial key,
                                                 dashed underline)
                                                 Birthdate, Relationship

     Full key of DEPENDENT = Ssn (from owner) + Name (partial key)
     The double lines = total participation: every dependent
     must belong to some employee.

Figure 1.3 — A weak entity type and its identifying relationship.

docs.title: College examples
docs.text:
Situation Strong or weak? Why STUDENT with Rollno Strong Rollno is unique college-wide. COURSE with SID Strong SID is unique. SECTION numbered 1, 2, 3 within a course Weak "Section 1" is meaningless without knowing which course. Owner = COURSE; partial key = SectionNo. ROOM numbered 101 within a building Weak Owner = BUILDING; partial key = RoomNo. EXAM_ATTEMPT numbered 1, 2 within a student-course pair Weak Partial key = AttemptNo.

The most common exam trap

Students declare an entity weak simply because "it depends on" another entity. Dependence is not the test. The test is whether it has a key of its own.

ADMISSION connects a student and a course and cannot exist without both — yet if it is modelled as a relationship it is not an entity at all; and if a SectionNo-style discriminator is not needed, it is not weak either. Conversely, an INVOICE belongs to a CUSTOMER and is meaningless without one, but if InvoiceNo is unique company-wide, INVOICE is strong.

docs.title: 5.4 Identifying Entity Types from Requirements
docs.text:
This is the practical skill the examination tests. There is a reliable procedure.

Procedure

  1. Underline every noun and noun phrase in the requirements document.
  2. Discard nouns that are: synonyms of another noun; outside the mini-world; the name of the system itself; or a mere value rather than a thing.
  3. For each surviving noun ask: does it have properties of its own that we must store? If yes, it is an entity type. If it is a single fact about something else, it is an attribute.
  4. Ask: can there be many of these, and do we need to tell them apart? If yes, entity type.
  5. Ask: does it have a key of its own? No key means a weak entity type — find its owner and its partial key.
  6. Verbs connecting two nouns become candidate relationship types (Lesson 3).

docs.title: Worked extraction — the college mini-world
docs.text:
"The college keeps records of its students: each has a roll number, a name and a date of birth. The college offers several courses; each course has an identifier, a name, a number of total seats, a duration, a course type which is either full-time or part-time, and a teacher-in-charge. A student may take admission in any number of courses, and the date of admission is recorded. The college also has societies, each with an identifier, a name, a mentor and total seats. Students enrol in societies, and the date of enrolment is recorded."

Step 1–2. Nouns surviving the filter: student, roll number, name, date of birth, course, identifier, name, total seats, duration, course type, teacher-in-charge, admission, date of admission, society, mentor, enrolment, date of enrolment. ("College" is the system itself — the whole mini-world — so it is not an entity type here.)

Step 3–5. Classification:

Noun Verdict Reason student Entity type STUDENT Has several properties; many of them; must be distinguished. roll number, name, date of birth Attributes of STUDENT Single facts about a student. course Entity type COURSE Has several properties of its own. identifier, name, total seats, duration, course type, teacher-in-charge Attributes of COURSE Single facts about a course. admission Relationship type TAKES_ADMISSION It is the verb "takes admission" connecting two entity types, not a thing with independent existence. date of admission Attribute of the relationship It is a fact about the pairing, not about the student alone or the course alone. society Entity type SOCIETY Has its own properties. mentor Attribute of SOCIETY A single name here. (See the note below.) enrolment Relationship type ENROLS_IN A verb connecting STUDENT and SOCIETY. date of enrolment Attribute of that relationship A fact about the pairing.

Result: three entity types — STUDENT, COURSE, SOCIETY — all strong.

A judgement call worth discussing

Is TeacherInCharge an attribute of COURSE, or should there be a TEACHER entity type?

  • If all we ever store is the teacher's name, and we never need the teacher's phone number, department or list of courses, then attribute is correct and simpler.
  • If we need the teacher's own properties, or need to ask "which courses does Dr Gupta teach?", then TEACHER should be an entity type related to COURSE.

The requirements decide. In our running college schema, the syllabus stores only a name, so we keep it as an attribute — and we note the limitation. The same reasoning applies to Mentor in SOCIETY.

docs.title: The four classic beginner mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1 — Making an attribute into an entity type

Creating a NAME entity type, or a DATEOFBIRTH entity type. A single-valued fact about something else is an attribute. The test: does it have properties of its own that we must store?

Mistake 2 — Making an entity type into an attribute

Storing Societies as a single text attribute of STUDENT containing "Debating, Music". This makes it impossible to store the society's mentor or total seats, and impossible to query "who is in the Debating society?" without string surgery. If the thing has properties, it is an entity type.

Mistake 3 — Modelling the output rather than the data

Creating a REPORT or MARKSHEET entity type. A report is a view computed from stored data, not a thing in the mini-world. Model what is stored, not what is printed.

Mistake 4 — Confusing type with instance

Drawing three rectangles labelled BSC_CS, BSC_CHEM, BA_ENG. These are three entities — three rows — of one entity type COURSE. If you find yourself drawing a rectangle per data value, you have confused the type with the instance. A useful signal: if adding new data would require redrawing the diagram, the diagram is wrong.

docs.title: 5.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define entity, entity type and entity set. Illustrate with a bank database.

A. An entity is a thing or object in the mini-world with independent existence that can be distinguished from other objects — for example, the particular customer holding account number SB-4471.

An entity type is the definition shared by a collection of such entities: a name together with a set of attributes. CUSTOMER (CustID, Name, Address, Phone) is an entity type. It is the intension, and it is what appears in the ER diagram as a rectangle.

An entity set is the collection of all entities of that type present in the database at a particular moment. It is the extension, and it changes with every insert or delete.

Entity type Entity set Entity Bank example CUSTOMER(CustID, Name, Address) The 12,430 customer records held today ('C1001','Meera Nair','Kochi') Nature Definition / schema Collection / state One instance Changes Rarely Constantly —

By convention both the type and the set carry the same name, and context resolves the ambiguity.

Solved Question 2

Q. What is a weak entity type? State its four characteristics and give two examples with their partial keys.

A. A weak entity type is one that has no key attribute of its own; its entities can be identified only in combination with a related entity of an identifying (owner) entity type, through an identifying relationship.

Four characteristics:

  1. No key of its own. It has instead a partial key (discriminator) that distinguishes weak entities belonging to the same owner. Its full key is the owner's key together with the partial key.
  2. Total participation in the identifying relationship, always. Every weak entity must be related to exactly one owner.
  3. Existence dependency. If the owner entity is deleted, all its weak entities must be deleted too.
  4. Notation: double rectangle for the entity type, double diamond for the identifying relationship, dashed underline for the partial key, double line for total participation. The identifying relationship is 1:N from owner to weak.

Examples:

Weak entity type Owner Identifying relationship Partial key Full key DEPENDENT EMPLOYEE DEPENDENT_OF Name (Ssn, Name) SECTION COURSE HAS_SECTION SectionNo (SID, SectionNo)

In the second example, "Section 1" is meaningless on its own; only "Section 1 of course CS01" identifies a section.

Solved Question 3

Q. Distinguish between a strong and a weak entity type. Is an entity weak merely because it depends on another? Justify.

A.

Strong (regular) Weak Key Has its own key attribute Has only a partial key Identification Self-identifying Needs the owner's key too Existence Independent Existence-dependent on the owner Participation in identifying relationship Not applicable Always total Notation Single rectangle Double rectangle

No — dependence alone does not make an entity weak. The test is identification, not existence or ownership.

Counter-example: an INVOICE cannot exist without a CUSTOMER, and is deleted when the customer's account is purged. Yet if InvoiceNo is allocated uniquely company-wide, INVOICE identifies itself perfectly well and is therefore a strong entity type that merely participates totally in a relationship with CUSTOMER.

Contrast: a hotel ROOM numbered 101 is weak with respect to HOTEL, because room number 101 exists in every hotel and only (HotelID, RoomNo) identifies a room.

So the correct question is always: "Does this entity type have an attribute, or set of attributes, whose value is unique across the whole entity set?" If yes, strong; if no, weak.

Solved Question 4

Q. From the following requirements, identify the entity types, state which are weak, and give the partial key of each weak type.

"A hospital has several wards, each with a ward number, name and capacity. Each ward contains beds, numbered 1 upward within the ward. Patients are admitted, each with a unique hospital registration number, name and age. Doctors have an employee code, name and specialisation."

A.

Candidate noun Verdict Justification hospital Not an entity type here It is the mini-world itself; there is only one, with no properties we store. (If the system covered a chain of hospitals, it would become an entity type.) ward Strong entity type WARD Has properties (WardNo, Name, Capacity); WardNo is unique. bed Weak entity type BED Beds are numbered within a ward, so bed 1 exists in every ward. Owner = WARD; identifying relationship CONTAINS; partial key = BedNo; full key = (WardNo, BedNo). patient Strong entity type PATIENT RegNo is stated to be unique. doctor Strong entity type DOCTOR EmpCode is unique. ward number, name, capacity, registration number, age, employee code, specialisation Attributes Single facts about the entity types above.

BED is drawn as a double rectangle, CONTAINS as a double diamond, BedNo with a dashed underline, and the WARD–CONTAINS line is doubled to show total participation.

Solved Question 5

Q. Why perform conceptual design at all, rather than going straight to CREATE TABLE? Give three reasons.

A.

  1. Communication with users. An ER diagram is comprehensible to the registrar, the doctor or the accountant who actually knows the business.
