They can confirm that a student may take several courses, or correct you when you assume a dependant can belong to two employees. SQL DDL cannot be validated by a non-technical user, so errors of meaning survive into the implementation, where they are orders of magnitude more expensive to fix.

  2. Implementation independence. The conceptual schema captures the meaning of the enterprise's data without committing to MySQL, to tables, or even to the relational model. The choice of DBMS can be deferred, changed, or made differently in different deployments, while the conceptual schema — which reflects the business, not the technology — survives.

  3. It forces the hard questions early, and yields a demonstrably better design. Drawing the diagram compels explicit answers to cardinality and participation questions that CREATE TABLE lets you leave vague. Furthermore, a systematic mapping algorithm (Unit 5) converts a correct ER diagram into a set of relations that is already largely normalised, whereas hand-written tables typically need to be repaired by normalisation afterwards.

A fourth reason worth stating: the diagram is documentation that remains readable years later, when the original designers have left.

Solved Question 6

Q. A student proposes this design: an entity type STUDENT(Rollno, Name, Societies) where Societies holds the text "Debating, Music". Criticise it and give the correct model.

A. The design commits Mistake 2 — turning an entity type into an attribute — and produces four concrete failures.

  1. It violates atomicity. "Debating, Music" packs several values into one field. When mapped to a relation this breaks 1NF (Unit 5).
  2. No properties of a society can be stored. The society's mentor, total seats and identifier have nowhere to live, because a society is not represented as a thing.
  3. Querying becomes string manipulation. "Who is in the Debating society?" requires LIKE '%Debating%', which cannot use an index and wrongly matches a society called "Debating and Elocution".
  4. No integrity. Nothing prevents a typo — "Debatting" — from creating a phantom society, because there is no list of valid societies to reference.

Correct model: SOCIETY is a thing with its own properties, so it is an entity type, and "enrols in" is a many-to-many relationship type carrying its own attribute.

   +-----------+        /-------------\        +-----------+
   |  STUDENT  |-------<   ENROLS_IN   >-------|  SOCIETY  |
   +-----------+   M    \-------------/    N   +-----------+
    Rollno (key)              |                 SocID (key)
    Name                 Dateofenrolment        Socname
    Dateofbirth                                 Mentor
                                                TotalSeats

Dateofenrolment is an attribute of the relationship, because it is a fact about the pairing of a student with a society, not about either one alone. On mapping (Unit 5) this becomes the table ENROLLMENT(Rollno, SocID, Dateofenrolment) with both columns as foreign keys and the pair as the primary key.

docs.title: 5.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Who introduced the ER model, and in which year?
  2. Define entity. Give one example each of physical and conceptual existence.
  3. Distinguish entity type from entity set.
  4. What is a partial key? How is it drawn?
  5. State the four characteristics of a weak entity type.
  6. Why is a weak entity type's participation in its identifying relationship always total?
  7. Name the six phases of the database design life-cycle.

B. Long answer

  1. Explain the database design life-cycle and state precisely where conceptual design fits and what it produces.
  2. Give three arguments for producing an ER diagram before writing DDL.
  3. Distinguish strong and weak entity types with full notation and two examples each. Explain why existence dependency is not the test for weakness.
  4. Describe a systematic procedure for extracting entity types from a requirements document, and apply it to a paragraph of your own choosing.

C. Application and analytical

  1. For each of the following, state whether it should be an entity type, an attribute, or a relationship type, and justify: a. The colour of a car, in a car-showroom database. b. The colour of a car, in a paint-shop database that stocks colours by code and price. c. A student's marks in a subject. d. A book's publisher, where we store the publisher's address. e. A book's number of pages. f. The supervision of one employee by another.
  2. From this description, list all entity types, mark the weak ones with their owners and partial keys: > "An airline operates flights, each with a unique flight number, origin, destination and departure time. A flight has legs numbered 1, 2, 3 within that flight. Passengers, each with a unique passenger ID, book seats. Aircraft have registration numbers and models."
  3. Identify what is wrong with each design and correct it: a. Entity types MONDAY, TUESDAY, WEDNESDAY. b. An entity type PHONE_NUMBER(Number) related to STUDENT, where nothing else about a phone number is stored. c. An entity type FEE_RECEIPT_PRINTOUT. d. EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Name, Child1, Child2, Child3).
  4. A library wants to record, for each copy of a book, a copy number that restarts at 1 for each title. Model BOOK and COPY. Which is weak? What is the full key of a copy? What happens to the copies when a title is withdrawn?
  5. Take the requirements of your college's examination system and extract at least five entity types, marking strong and weak, with justification for each decision.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. Every entity type must have a key attribute.
  2. A weak entity type can have total participation in a non-identifying relationship as well.
  3. The entity set changes when a new row is inserted.
  4. A conceptual schema mentions the chosen DBMS.
  5. DEPENDENT is weak because a dependant cannot exist without an employee.
  6. An entity type is drawn as a diamond.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. A weak entity type has no key of its own — only a partial key. Strong entity types must have a key.
  2. True. A weak entity type may participate in other relationships as well, with any constraints; the total participation requirement applies specifically to its identifying relationship.
  3. True. The entity set is the extension — the set of entities currently present — so an insert changes it. The entity type does not change.
  4. False. The conceptual schema is deliberately implementation-independent; the DBMS is chosen at the next phase.
  5. False, as stated. It is weak because Name alone does not identify a dependant across the whole set — it has no key of its own. Existence dependency is a consequence, not the test.
  6. False. A rectangle. A diamond denotes a relationship type.

Lesson Summary

  • Conceptual design produces a technology-free schema that users can validate; it is the second phase of the design life-cycle.
  • Entity = distinguishable thing; entity type = its definition (intension, the rectangle); entity set = all current entities (extension).
  • Strong entity types have a key of their own; weak entity types have only a partial key and are identified through an owner via an identifying relationship, with total participation and existence dependency.
  • The test for weakness is identification, not dependence.
  • Extract entity types by underlining nouns and asking whether each has properties of its own; avoid the four classic mistakes.

docs.title: Lesson 27: Concurrent Execution and Serialisability
docs.text:
Interference problems, schedules, precedence graphs and locking

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 6: Data Storage and Indexes · 4 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 20.5, 21

Learning Outcomes

  1. Explain why transactions are interleaved rather than run one at a time.
  2. Identify the four concurrency problems: lost update, dirty read, unrepeatable read, phantom.
  3. Define schedule, serial schedule and conflict serialisability.
  4. Test a schedule with a precedence graph.
  5. Explain two-phase locking, deadlock and the SQL isolation levels.

docs.title: 27.1 Why Interleave at All?
docs.text:
Running transactions strictly one after another would make all the concurrency problems disappear — and make the system unusable.

Two reasons for interleaving

1. Throughput and processor utilisation. A transaction spends most of its life waiting for disk (Lesson 1: 10 ms per block access, against nanoseconds of CPU work). While one transaction waits, the processor can execute another. Serial execution would leave the CPU idle almost all the time.

2. Response time and fairness. Without interleaving, a short transaction arriving behind a long one must wait for it to finish entirely. A five-millisecond seat enquiry would queue behind a five-minute report.

The cost of interleaving is interference, and the whole of this lesson is about controlling it.

docs.title: 27.2 The Four Concurrency Problems
docs.text: Throughout, T1 and T2 run concurrently on data items X and Y.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Lost update (write–write)
docs.text:
Two transactions read the same item, both compute from the old value, and one overwrites the other.

   Initially X = 100          (seats available)

   TIME   T1                    T2                   X
   ----   -------------------   ------------------   ---
   t1     read(X)   -> 100                           100
   t2                           read(X)   -> 100     100
   t3     X := X - 10                                100
   t4                           X := X - 20          100
   t5     write(X)  = 90                              90
   t6                           write(X)  = 80        80   <-- T1's update LOST

   Correct answer: 100 - 10 - 20 = 70.  Actual: 80.
   T1's subtraction has vanished because T2 read BEFORE T1 wrote.

This is the two-clerks-and-the-last-seat problem of Unit 1, Lesson 1.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Dirty read (uncommitted dependency, write–read)
docs.text:
One transaction reads a value written by another that later aborts.

   Initially X = 100

   TIME   T1                    T2                   X
   ----   -------------------   ------------------   ---
   t1     read(X)   -> 100                           100
   t2     X := X - 10                                100
   t3     write(X)  = 90                              90
   t4                           read(X)   -> 90       90   <-- reads DIRTY data
   t5                           (uses 90)             90
   t6     **ROLLBACK**                                100  <-- T1 undone
   t7                           commit                100

   T2 committed a decision based on a value that NEVER OFFICIALLY EXISTED.

If T2 has already committed, the damage cannot be undone by rolling T2 back either — this is why aborting T1 may force cascading rollback of every transaction that read its uncommitted data.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Unrepeatable read (read–write)
docs.text:
One transaction reads the same item twice and gets different values, because another transaction modified it in between.

   TIME   T1                          T2                    X
   ----   -------------------------   -------------------   ---
   t1     read(X)   -> 100                                  100
   t2                                 read(X)   -> 100      100
   t3                                 X := X - 50           100
   t4                                 write(X)  = 50         50
   t5                                 commit                 50
   t6     read(X)   -> 50                                    50  <-- DIFFERENT!

   T1 read X twice within one transaction and got two answers.
   Any calculation comparing the two is meaningless.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Phantom read
docs.text:
T1 runs a query twice; the second time, new rows satisfying the condition have appeared.

   TIME   T1                                       T2
   ----   -------------------------------------    ---------------------------
   t1     SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ADMISSION
          WHERE SID='CS01';        -> 40
   t2                                              INSERT INTO ADMISSION
                                                   VALUES ('X9999','CS01',...);
   t3                                              commit
   t4     SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ADMISSION
          WHERE SID='CS01';        -> 41           <-- a PHANTOM row appeared

   Locking the 40 rows T1 read does NOT help -- row 41 did not exist to lock.
   Preventing phantoms requires locking the RANGE or the PREDICATE.

Distinguishing the four — the table examiners want

Problem Conflict type What goes wrong Prevented by Lost update write–write One update silently overwritten Any correct protocol Dirty read write–read Reading data that is later rolled back Read Committed Unrepeatable read read–write Same row read twice, different values Repeatable Read Phantom read–insert Same query run twice, different row set Serializable

Unrepeatable read vs phantom is the pair most often confused. An unrepeatable read concerns an existing row whose value changed; a phantom concerns rows appearing or disappearing from a result set. Row-level locking stops the first; only range or predicate locking stops the second.

docs.title: 27.3 Schedules
docs.text:
Schedule

A schedule (history) S of n transactions is an ordering of all their operations such that, for each transaction, its operations appear in S in the same order as within the transaction. Operations of different transactions may be interleaved.

Serial schedule

A schedule in which the operations of each transaction are executed consecutively, with no interleaving.

Every serial schedule is correct by definition — each transaction sees a consistent database and leaves one. For n transactions there are n! serial schedules, which may give different results; all are considered correct.

Serialisable schedule

A schedule is serialisable if it is equivalent to some serial schedule of the same transactions.

Serialisability is the accepted criterion of correctness for concurrent execution: it delivers the performance of interleaving with the correctness of serial execution.

docs.title: Conflicting operations
docs.text:
Conflict

Two operations conflict if all three hold:

  1. They belong to different transactions;
  2. they access the same data item;
  3. at least one of them is a write.
Pair Conflict? read(X) / read(X) No — neither changes anything read(X) / write(X) Yes write(X) / read(X) Yes write(X) / write(X) Yes write(X) / write(Y) No — different items

Non-conflicting operations may be swapped without changing the result. Conflicting ones may not.

Conflict serialisability

A schedule S is conflict serialisable if it can be transformed into some serial schedule by a sequence of swaps of adjacent non-conflicting operations.

Equivalently — and far easier to test — its precedence graph is acyclic.

docs.title: 27.4 The Precedence Graph Test
docs.text:
Algorithm

  1. Draw one node for each transaction.
  2. Draw a directed edge Ti → Tj whenever an operation of Ti precedes and conflicts with an operation of Tj. Specifically, add Ti → Tj if Ti executes:
    • write(X) before Tj executes read(X), or
    • read(X) before Tj executes write(X), or
    • write(X) before Tj executes write(X).
  3. If the graph has no cycle, the schedule is conflict serialisable, and any topological order of the graph gives an equivalent serial schedule. If it has a cycle, it is not.

docs.title: Worked example 1 — serialisable
docs.text:
S1:  T1: read(X)   T1: write(X)   T2: read(X)   T2: write(X)
     T1: read(Y)   T1: write(Y)   T2: read(Y)   T2: write(Y)

Conflicts: T1:write(X) precedes T2:read(X) → edge T1 → T2. T1:write(Y) precedes T2:read(Y) → also T1 → T2. No conflict runs the other way.

        +----+        +----+
        | T1 |------>| T2 |          no cycle
        +----+        +----+

Acyclic → conflict serialisable, equivalent to the serial order T1, T2.

docs.title: Worked example 2 — not serialisable
docs.text:
S2:  T1: read(X)   T2: read(X)   T2: write(X)   T1: write(X)
  • T1:read(X) precedes T2:write(X) → edge T1 → T2
  • T2:write(X) precedes T1:write(X) → edge T2 → T1
        +----+  ----->  +----+
        | T1 |          | T2 |      CYCLE
        +----+  <-----  +----+

Cyclic → not conflict serialisable. This is exactly the lost update schedule of Section 4.2: T1's write is overwritten.

docs.title: Worked example 3 — three transactions
docs.text:
S3:  T1: read(X)   T2: write(X)   T3: read(X)   T1: write(Y)   T3: write(Y)
  • T1:read(X) before T2:write(X) → T1 → T2
  • T2:write(X) before T3:read(X) → T2 → T3
  • T1:write(Y) before T3:write(Y) → T1 → T3
        +----+ -----> +----+ -----> +----+
        | T1 |        | T2 |        | T3 |
        +--+-+        +----+        +--^-+
           |                           |
           +---------------------------+      no cycle

Acyclic → serialisable, equivalent to the serial order T1, T2, T3 (the unique topological order here).

Conflict serialisability is sufficient, not necessary

Every conflict-serialisable schedule is serialisable, but some serialisable schedules are not conflict serialisable — they happen to produce the right answer for reasons the conflict analysis cannot see (for instance a blind write that overwrites a value nobody used).

The broader notion is view serialisability, which admits more schedules. But testing view serialisability is NP-complete, whereas the precedence graph test is linear-time. Practical systems therefore enforce the stricter, cheaply testable conflict serialisability.

docs.title: Recoverable and cascadeless schedules
docs.text:
Serialisability is not the whole story; a schedule must also behave correctly when a transaction aborts.

Three further classes

Recoverable — a transaction commits only after every transaction whose data it read has committed. Otherwise a committed transaction might depend on an aborted one, which cannot be repaired.

Cascadeless (avoiding cascading rollback) — a transaction reads only data written by committed transactions. This prevents one abort from forcing a chain of rollbacks.

Strict — a transaction neither reads nor writes an item until the transaction that last wrote it has committed or aborted. The strongest and simplest to recover; it makes undo trivial, since the before-image is always the last committed value.

strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable

docs.title: 27.5 Locking and Two-Phase Locking
docs.text:
Testing a schedule after the fact is of no use — the scheduler must prevent non-serialisable schedules as they form. Locking is the standard mechanism.

Lock modes

Shared lock S(X) (read lock) — several transactions may hold it simultaneously; permits reading only.

Exclusive lock X(X) (write lock) — only one transaction may hold it, and no shared lock may coexist; permits reading and writing.

Compatibility matrix:

Requested \ Held None Shared Exclusive Shared grant grant wait Exclusive grant wait wait

Only read–read is compatible, which is precisely the pair that does not conflict.

Two-Phase Locking (2PL)

Every transaction obeys two phases:

Growing (expanding) phase — the transaction may acquire locks but may not release any. Shrinking phase — the transaction may release locks but may not acquire any.

The moment of the first release is the lock point.

Theorem: if every transaction follows 2PL, every resulting schedule is conflict serialisable — and the equivalent serial order is the order of the transactions' lock points.

   locks
   held
     ^
     |        .-----.  <-- LOCK POINT
     |      /         \
     |    /             \
     |  /                 \
     +----------------------------> time
       GROWING     |    SHRINKING
       (acquire    |    (release only)
        only)      |

Variants:

Variant Rule Guarantees Basic 2PL As above Conflict serialisability Conservative (static) 2PL Acquire all locks before starting Serialisability and deadlock-freedom; but requires knowing all items in advance, and reduces concurrency Strict 2PL Hold all exclusive locks until commit or abort Serialisability and strict schedules — no dirty reads, no cascading rollback. The most widely used. Rigorous 2PL Hold all locks until commit or abort Simplest to implement; slightly less concurrency

docs.title: Deadlock
docs.text:
2PL prevents non-serialisable schedules but permits deadlock

   T1: X(A) granted ......................... wants X(B) -- WAITS
   T2: ............... X(B) granted ......... wants X(A) -- WAITS

        +----+  waits for  +----+
        | T1 |------------>| T2 |
        +----+<------------+----+     CYCLE in the wait-for graph
                waits for               = DEADLOCK

Neither can proceed; both wait forever.

Handling deadlock — three approaches:

  1. Detection and recovery. Maintain a wait-for graph; periodically look for a cycle; when one is found, choose a victim transaction and abort it. The usual choice in practice, and what MySQL's InnoDB does.
  2. Prevention. Impose an ordering that makes cycles impossible: acquire locks in a fixed global order, or use timestamp schemes such as wait-die (an older transaction waits, a younger one aborts) and wound-wait (an older transaction forces a younger one to abort).
  3. Timeout. Abort any transaction waiting longer than a threshold. Simple but crude — it aborts transactions that were merely slow.

A related hazard is starvation, where one transaction is repeatedly chosen as the victim and never completes. Fair scheduling — for example, by using transaction age in the victim choice — prevents it.

docs.title: 27.6 SQL Isolation Levels
docs.text:
Full serialisability is expensive. SQL therefore lets an application trade isolation for concurrency, choosing which problems it can tolerate.

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
START TRANSACTION;
   ...
COMMIT;
Isolation level Dirty read Unrepeatable read Phantom READ UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible READ COMMITTED prevented possible possible REPEATABLE READ prevented prevented possible* SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented

* The standard permits phantoms at REPEATABLE READ; MySQL's InnoDB actually prevents them too, using next-key (gap) locking.

Choosing a level

  • READ UNCOMMITTED — almost never justified. Use only for approximate reporting where a small error is acceptable and speed is paramount.
  • READ COMMITTED — the default in Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. A good balance for most applications.
  • REPEATABLE READ — the default in MySQL/InnoDB. Necessary when a transaction reads the same row more than once and must see a stable value.
  • SERIALIZABLE — full correctness, lowest concurrency. Use for financial reconciliation, stock-taking, or anything where a phantom would be unacceptable.

The principle: the lowest level at which the application remains correct, never lower. Do not lower the level to fix a performance problem without proving the resulting anomalies are harmless.

docs.title: 27.7 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Why are transactions interleaved rather than executed serially? Explain the four concurrency problems that result, with a time-line for each.

A. Two reasons for interleaving.

  1. Throughput. A transaction spends most of its life waiting for disk — about 10 ms per block access, against nanoseconds of CPU work. Serial execution would leave the processor idle almost all the time; interleaving lets it run another transaction while the first waits.
  2. Response time. Without interleaving a short transaction queues behind a long one, so a five-millisecond seat enquiry could wait behind a five-minute report.

The four problems (time-lines as in Section 4.2):

Lost update (write–write). Both transactions read X = 100, one subtracts 10 and the other 20, and the second write overwrites the first. The result is 80 instead of 70 — one update has vanished, because T2 read before T1 wrote.

Dirty read (write–read). T1 writes X = 90 and T2 reads it; T1 then rolls back, so X returns to 100. T2 has acted on a value that never officially existed. Worse, if T2 has already committed, rolling it back too is impossible — which is why an abort may force cascading rollback.

Unrepeatable read (read–write). T1 reads X = 100; T2 changes it to 50 and commits; T1 reads X again and gets 50. The same item gave two answers within one transaction, so any calculation comparing them is meaningless.

Phantom read (read–insert). T1 counts admissions to CS01 and gets 40; T2 inserts a new admission and commits; T1 recounts and gets 41. Locking the 40 rows T1 read would not have helped — row 41 did not exist to be locked — so preventing phantoms needs range or predicate locking.

Solved Question 2

Q. Define schedule, serial schedule and conflict serialisability. When do two operations conflict?

A. A schedule S of n transactions is an ordering of all their operations such that each transaction's own operations appear in S in their original relative order. Operations of different transactions may be interleaved.

A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively, with no interleaving. Every serial schedule is correct by definition. For n transactions there are n! of them, which may give different results — all equally acceptable.

A schedule is serialisable if it is equivalent to some serial schedule. This is the accepted criterion of correctness: the performance of interleaving with the correctness of serial execution.

Two operations conflict if all three conditions hold:

  1. they belong to different transactions;
  2. they access the same data item;
  3. at least one is a write.

So read/read never conflicts; read/write, write/read and write/write on the same item always do.

Conflict serialisability. A schedule is conflict serialisable if it can be turned into a serial schedule by repeatedly swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations. Since only non-conflicting swaps are allowed, the result computed is unchanged — which is why the transformation proves equivalence.

The practical test is the precedence graph: draw Ti → Tj whenever an operation of Ti precedes and conflicts with one of Tj; the schedule is conflict serialisable if and only if the graph is acyclic, and any topological order gives an equivalent serial schedule.

Solved Question 3

Q. Test this schedule for conflict serialisability using a precedence graph, and give an equivalent serial schedule if one exists.

S:  r1(X)  r2(X)  w1(X)  r3(Y)  w2(X)  w3(Y)  r1(Y)
(Here r1(X) means T1: read(X).)

A. Examine every pair of conflicting operations, in schedule order.

On item X — operations in order: r1(X), r2(X), w1(X), w2(X).

Earlier Later Conflict? Edge r1(X) r2(X) no (read–read) — r1(X) w2(X) yes (read–write) T1 → T2 r2(X) w1(X) yes (read–write) T2 → T1 w1(X) w2(X) yes (write–write) T1 → T2

On item Y — operations in order: r3(Y), w3(Y), r1(Y).

Earlier Later Conflict? Edge r3(Y) w3(Y) same transaction — w3(Y) r1(Y) yes (write–read) T3 → T1

Precedence graph:

        +----+  ------->  +----+
        | T1 |            | T2 |
        +----+  <-------  +----+          T1 <--> T2 is a CYCLE
           ^
           |
        +--+-+
        | T3 |
        +----+

Edges: T1 → T2, T2 → T1, T3 → T1.

There is a cycle T1 → T2 → T1.

Conclusion: the schedule is NOT conflict serialisable. No equivalent serial schedule exists.

Why intuitively. T2 reads X before T1 writes it, so T2 must come before T1; but T1 writes X before T2 writes it, so T1 must come before T2. The two requirements are contradictory. Concretely, T1's write to X is lost — the lost update problem.

Solved Question 4

Q. Explain two-phase locking. State the theorem, prove informally why it works, and describe the variants.

A. Under two-phase locking, every transaction has two phases:

  • a growing phase, in which it may acquire locks but release none;
  • a shrinking phase, in which it may release locks but acquire none.

The instant of the first release is the transaction's lock point.

Theorem. If every transaction in a schedule follows 2PL, the schedule is conflict serialisable, and the equivalent serial order is the order of the transactions' lock points.

Informal proof. Suppose the precedence graph had a cycle T1 → T2 → ... → Tn → T1. An edge Ti → Tj means Ti performed a conflicting operation on some item before Tj did. Since conflicting operations require incompatible locks, Ti must have released its lock on that item before Tj acquired its own. Releasing puts Ti into its shrinking phase, so Ti's lock point precedes Tj's. Following the cycle round gives lock point of T1 < that of T2 < ... < that of T1 — a contradiction. Hence no cycle exists, and the schedule is conflict serialisable.

Variants:

Variant Rule What it adds Basic 2PL Growing then shrinking Conflict serialisability Conservative (static) Acquire all locks before starting Deadlock-free, but needs all items known in advance and reduces concurrency sharply Strict 2PL Hold all exclusive locks until commit/abort Produces strict schedules: no dirty reads, no cascading rollback. Most widely used. Rigorous 2PL Hold all locks until commit/abort Simplest to implement; the serial order is the commit order

The limitation. 2PL prevents non-serialisable schedules but does not prevent deadlock — two transactions can each hold a lock the other needs. Deadlock must be handled separately, by detection with a wait-for graph, by prevention (wait-die, wound-wait), or by timeout.

Solved Question 5

Q. What is deadlock? Give an example and describe three ways of handling it. What is starvation?

A. Deadlock is a state in which two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so none can proceed. It corresponds to a cycle in the wait-for graph.

Example:

T1:  X(A) granted  .................  requests X(B)  -- WAITS (T2 holds it)
T2:  ............  X(B) granted  ...  requests X(A)  -- WAITS (T1 holds it)

Wait-for graph: T1 → T2 and T2 → T1 — a cycle. Neither transaction can ever proceed.

Three approaches:

1. Detection and recovery. Maintain a wait-for graph with an edge Ti → Tj when Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. Run a cycle-detection algorithm periodically. On finding a cycle, choose a victim and abort it, releasing its locks. Victim selection weighs how long the transaction has run, how many locks it holds, and how many times it has already been aborted. This is what MySQL's InnoDB does. It permits maximum concurrency and pays only when a deadlock actually occurs.

2. Prevention. Make cycles structurally impossible:

  • Ordered acquisition — all transactions request locks in one fixed global order, so no cycle can form.
  • Wait-die — if an older transaction wants a lock held by a younger one it waits; if a younger one wants a lock held by an older one it aborts (dies) and restarts.
  • Wound-wait — the reverse: an older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger holder; a younger one waits. Both timestamp schemes are deadlock-free because waiting always runs in one direction of age.

3. Timeout. Abort any transaction that has waited longer than a threshold. Trivial to implement, but crude: it aborts transactions that were merely slow, and choosing the threshold is guesswork.

Starvation is the situation in which a transaction is repeatedly chosen as the deadlock victim, or repeatedly denied a lock, and so never completes. It is prevented by making the victim-selection and lock-granting policies fair — for example by favouring transactions that have already been aborted several times, or by granting locks first-come-first-served.

Solved Question 6

Q. Describe the four SQL isolation levels and the problems each permits. Which would you choose for (a) a monthly sales report, (b) a seat-booking transaction, (c) an end-of-year financial audit?

A. (Table of Section 4.6.)

READ UNCOMMITTED — permits dirty reads, unrepeatable reads and phantoms. Effectively no isolation; a transaction may read data that is later rolled back.

READ COMMITTED — prevents dirty reads by reading only committed data, but a value may change between two reads within the transaction. Default in Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server.

REPEATABLE READ — additionally guarantees that a row read twice gives the same value. Phantoms are permitted by the standard, though InnoDB prevents them with next-key locking. Default in MySQL.

SERIALIZABLE — full isolation; the outcome is equivalent to some serial execution. Lowest concurrency.

Recommendations:

(a) Monthly sales report. READ COMMITTED. The report reads a large volume of data; SERIALIZABLE would hold locks across the whole run and block the transactional workload. Dirty reads must be excluded — reporting figures from rolled-back transactions is unacceptable — but a small inconsistency between the beginning and end of a long read-only report is tolerable. (If a perfectly consistent snapshot is required, use the DBMS's snapshot-isolation or READ ONLY transaction facility rather than raising the lock level.)

(b) Seat booking. REPEATABLE READ at minimum, and SERIALIZABLE if overbooking must be impossible. The transaction reads the seat count, decides, and writes — the classic lost update pattern. READ COMMITTED would permit two clerks to read the same last seat. In practice the robust idiom is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which takes an exclusive lock at read time and works at any level.

(c) End-of-year financial audit. SERIALIZABLE. The audit must see one consistent instant across many tables; a phantom transaction appearing mid-audit would make the accounts fail to balance, and the cost of a wrong answer far exceeds the cost of reduced concurrency for one overnight run.

The general principle: choose the lowest level at which the application is still correct — and never lower it to fix a performance problem without first proving that the anomalies it admits are genuinely harmless.

docs.title: 27.8 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Give two reasons for interleaving transactions.
  2. Name the four concurrency problems.
  3. Distinguish unrepeatable read from phantom read.
  4. When do two operations conflict?
  5. Define conflict serialisability.
  6. State the two phases of 2PL.
  7. What is a deadlock, and how is it detected?

B. Precedence graphs — test each schedule and give an equivalent serial order if one exists

  1. r1(X) w1(X) r2(X) w2(X)
  2. r1(X) r2(X) w1(X) w2(X)
  3. r1(X) w1(X) r2(X) w2(X) r1(Y) w1(Y)
  4. r1(A) r2(B) w1(A) w2(B) r1(B) w1(B)
  5. r1(X) r2(Y) w1(X) r3(X) w2(Y) w3(X) r1(Y)
  6. w1(A) r2(A) w2(B) r1(B) w1(C) r3(C)

C. Concurrency problems

  1. Construct a time-line demonstrating a lost update on the TotalSeats column, and state what the correct result should have been.
  2. Construct a dirty-read scenario in the college database, and explain why cascading rollback may be needed.
  3. Construct a phantom-read scenario using the ADMISSION table, and explain why row-level locking does not prevent it.
  4. For each of the four problems, state the lowest SQL isolation level that prevents it.

D. Locking

  1. Rewrite the lost-update schedule of question 14 with 2PL locks inserted, and show that the problem disappears.
  2. Show that basic 2PL does not prevent deadlock, by constructing a deadlocked schedule.
  3. Explain why conservative 2PL is deadlock-free, and why it is nevertheless rarely used.
  4. Explain why strict 2PL prevents cascading rollback.
  5. Two transactions repeatedly deadlock and one is always chosen as the victim. Name the problem and give a remedy.

E. Analysis

  1. Explain why conflict serialisability is preferred to view serialisability in practice.
  2. Explain the relationship strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable, giving a schedule in each class but not the next.
  3. Recommend an isolation level for each, with justification: an ATM withdrawal; a "how many seats are left?" display; a payroll run; a search-results page.
  4. Explain why SELECT ... FOR UPDATE solves the lost-update problem at any isolation level.
  5. A developer sets READ UNCOMMITTED to make a slow report faster. Evaluate this decision and suggest alternatives.

F. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. Two read operations on the same item conflict.
  2. Every serial schedule is serialisable.
  3. Every serialisable schedule is conflict serialisable.
  4. 2PL prevents deadlock.
  5. A cycle in the precedence graph means the schedule is not conflict serialisable.
  6. REPEATABLE READ prevents phantoms in the SQL standard.
  7. Strict 2PL prevents cascading rollback.

Answers to Section F

  1. False. Conflict requires at least one write; two reads change nothing and may be swapped freely.
  2. True. A serial schedule is trivially equivalent to itself.
  3. False. The converse holds. Some serialisable schedules (with blind writes) are not conflict serialisable; the broader class is view serialisable, but testing it is NP-complete.
  4. False. It guarantees conflict serialisability but permits deadlock, which needs separate handling.
  5. True. That is exactly the test.
  6. False. The standard permits phantoms at that level; only SERIALIZABLE forbids them. (MySQL's InnoDB happens to prevent them anyway, via next-key locking.)
  7. True. Exclusive locks are held until commit, so no transaction can read uncommitted data, and therefore no abort can cascade.

Lesson Summary

  • Transactions are interleaved for throughput and response time; the price is interference.
  • Four problems: lost update (w–w), dirty read (w–r), unrepeatable read (r–w), phantom (r–insert).
  • Two operations conflict if they are from different transactions, on the same item, with at least one write.
  • A schedule is conflict serialisable iff its precedence graph is acyclic; a topological order gives the equivalent serial schedule.
  • 2PL (growing then shrinking) guarantees conflict serialisability but not freedom from deadlock. Strict 2PL additionally prevents dirty reads and cascading rollback.
  • Deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph, handled by detection, prevention or timeout.
  • SQL isolation levels trade isolation for concurrency: choose the lowest level at which the application remains correct.

End of Unit 6, and of the lecture series. Next: the Laboratory Manual and the Course Handbook.

docs.title: Course Objectives
docs.text: The course introduces students to the fundamentals of database management systems and their architecture. Emphasis is given to the popular relational database system, including data models and data manipulation. Students learn the importance of database structure and its design — both the conceptual approach using the Entity Relationship model and the formal approach using normalisation. The importance of file indexing and the controlled execution of transactions is taught. The course gives students hands-on practice of structured query language in a relational database management system and a glimpse of basic database administration commands.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
On successful completion, students will be able to:

  • Use database management system software to create and manipulate a database.
  • Create conceptual data models using entity relationship diagrams for modelling real-life situations and designing the database schema.
  • Use the concept of functional dependencies to remove redundancy and update anomalies.
  • Apply normalisation theory to obtain a normalised database schema.
  • Write queries using relational algebra, a procedural language.

docs.text:
One schema is used throughout every unit, so that each new idea is applied to data students already know.

   +-------------------+                +-------------------------+
   |      STUDENT      |                |         COURSE          |
   +-------------------+                +-------------------------+
   | PK Rollno         |                | PK SID                  |
   |    Name           |                |    Cname       (UNIQUE) |
   |    Dateofbirth    |                |    TotalSeats  (> 0)    |
   +---------+---------+                |    Duration             |
             |                          |    Coursetype  (F / P)  |
             |                          |    TeacherInCharge      |
             |                          +------------+------------+

             |    | PK,FK Rollno / SID  |
             |    |    Dateofadmission  |

                  | PK,FK Rollno / SocID|        | PK SocID       |

How it threads through the course: Unit 2 derives this from requirements as an ER diagram; Unit 3 states its keys and integrity constraints and queries it in relational algebra; Unit 4 implements and queries it in SQL; Unit 5 maps the ER diagram to exactly these tables and proves them normalised; Unit 6 indexes them and runs transactions over them.

A note on the schema

The syllabus PDF describes this schema in a diagram that did not survive text extraction. The version used here follows the syllabus's stated facts — "Rollno (ADMISSION) and SID (ADMISSION) are foreign keys", "course type may have two values viz. Fulltime and Parttime", "a student may enroll in any number of courses" — together with the attributes implied by the twenty-five prescribed queries. If your class is issued a schema differing in column names, every query transfers unchanged apart from those names.

docs.title: The mistakes that cost the most marks
docs.text:
1. Forgetting DISTINCT after a join that can duplicate rows.
  2. Using COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN when counting matches — it reports 1 instead of 0.
  3. Putting an aggregate condition in WHERE instead of HAVING.
  4. Omitting parentheses when mixing AND with OR.
  5. Not finding all candidate keys before judging the normal form — every 2NF and 3NF test depends on which attributes are prime.
  6. Confusing partial with transitive dependency, and so the wrong normal form.
  7. Claiming an entity is weak because it "depends on" another — the test is identification, not dependence.
  8. Mixing up cardinality and participation, or forgetting that each side is decided separately.
  9. Using ∧ where ∩ is needed in relational algebra, when the two facts are in different tuples.
  10. Writing = NULL instead of IS NULL.
  11. Reversing the (min, max) labels relative to Chen notation.
  12. Forgetting the leading join in the "only" query (Practical 12), so students with no admissions qualify vacuously.

docs.title: Lesson 24: Data Storage and File Organisation
docs.text:
The memory hierarchy, records, blocks and file organisations

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 6: Data Storage and Indexes · 4 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 16

Learning Outcomes

  1. Describe the memory hierarchy and explain why disk access dominates database cost.
  2. Define block, blocking factor and record, and compute them.
  3. Distinguish fixed-length from variable-length records and spanned from unspanned blocking.
  4. Compare heap, sorted and hashed file organisations on each operation.
  5. Choose an organisation for a stated workload.

docs.title: 24.1 The Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
capacity      access time     cost/byte
   +--------------------+
   |  CPU registers     |   ~KB           < 1 ns          highest
   +--------------------+
   |  Cache (L1/L2/L3)  |   MB            1-10 ns
   +--------------------+
   |  Main memory (RAM) |   GB            ~100 ns          PRIMARY
   +====================+  ============================== volatile
   |  Flash / SSD       |   TB            ~100 us          SECONDARY
   +--------------------+                                  non-volatile
   |  Magnetic disk     |   TB            ~10 ms
   +--------------------+
   |  Optical / tape    |   PB            seconds          TERTIARY
   +--------------------+                                  lowest cost

   MAIN MEMORY to DISK is roughly a 100,000-fold jump in access time.
   That single gap dictates almost every design decision in this unit.

Figure 1.1 — The memory hierarchy.

Primary, secondary, tertiary

Primary storage — directly accessible by the CPU: registers, cache, main memory. Fast but volatile (contents lost on power failure) and expensive per byte.

Secondary storage — disks and SSDs. Non-volatile, far larger, far cheaper, and roughly five orders of magnitude slower. The database lives here.

Tertiary storage — tape and optical libraries, used for archives and backups.

Why databases are designed around disk

A main-memory access takes about 100 nanoseconds; a magnetic disk access about 10 milliseconds. The ratio is roughly 100,000 : 1.

If a memory access were one second, a disk access would take over a day.

Consequently the cost of a database operation is measured in block accesses, not in CPU instructions. An algorithm doing twice the computation but half the I/O wins easily. Every structure in this unit — indexes, B+-trees, hashing, the buffer pool — exists to reduce the number of block accesses.

docs.title: Disk geometry and access time
docs.text:
A magnetic disk consists of platters with concentric tracks, divided into sectors; the set of tracks at the same radius across all platters is a cylinder.

Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time

Component What it is Typical Seek time Moving the arm to the right track 3–10 ms — dominant Rotational latency Waiting for the sector to arrive under the head ~4 ms (half a rotation at 7200 rpm) Transfer time Reading the bytes < 1 ms per block

Since seek time dominates, reading blocks that are physically adjacent is far cheaper than reading scattered blocks. This is why clustering related records together matters, and why a sequential scan of a whole file can be faster than an index lookup that touches many scattered blocks.

SSDs have no moving parts, so seek time nearly vanishes and random access is far cheaper. They do not eliminate the memory–storage gap, but they change the balance: index-based random access becomes relatively more attractive.

docs.title: 24.2 Records and Blocks
docs.text:
Definitions

Record — a collection of related field values, corresponding to one tuple.

Block (page) — the unit of transfer between disk and main memory, typically 4 KB or 8 KB. You cannot read a single byte or a single record from disk — you read a whole block.

Blocking factor bfr — the number of records that fit in one block.

bfr = floor( B / R ) where B = block size, R = record size.

Blocks needed for r records: b = ceil( r / bfr ).

docs.title: Worked calculation
docs.text:
A STUDENT file has r = 30,000 records, record size R = 100 bytes, block size B = 1024 bytes.

bfr = floor(1024 / 100) = 10 records per block. b = ceil(30000 / 10) = 3000 blocks.

Unused space per block = 1024 − 10 × 100 = 24 bytes, so about 2.3 per cent is wasted.

Spanned vs unspanned

Unspanned — a record never crosses a block boundary. Simple, and a record is retrieved in one block access, but space is wasted at the end of each block. Required when R > B is impossible.

Spanned — a record may be split across two blocks, with a pointer to the continuation. No wasted space, and necessary when R > B, but a record may need two block accesses.

Fixed-length records are usually unspanned; large variable-length records are usually spanned.

docs.title: Fixed-length and variable-length records
docs.text:
Fixed-length — every record occupies the same number of bytes, so the address of record i is computable arithmetically: start + i × R. Direct access is trivial and deletion can use a simple free list.

Variable-length records arise when a table has VARCHAR fields, optional fields, repeating fields, or several record types in one file. Three techniques identify the field boundaries:

  1. Separator characters between fields;
  2. Length prefixes before each field;
  3. A field-offset table (a directory) at the start of the record — the usual modern choice, since it also gives direct access to any field.

Deletion and fragmentation

Deleting a record leaves a hole. Two strategies:

Deletion marker (tombstone) — a flag byte marks the record as deleted; the space is reused later. Cheap, but the file grows with dead space until reorganised.

Compaction — records are shifted to close the gap. No wasted space, but expensive, and it invalidates any stored record addresses.

Most systems use tombstones plus periodic reorganisation, which is why a table that has had many deletions may need OPTIMIZE TABLE or VACUUM.

docs.title: 24.3 File Organisations
docs.text:
File organisation vs access method

The file organisation is how records are physically arranged on disk. The access method is the set of operations that can be applied to it. One organisation may support several access methods, and the same access method may work over several organisations.

docs.title: Heap (unordered / pile) file
docs.text:
Records are appended at the end of the last block, in no particular order.

Operation Cost Explanation Insert 1–2 block accesses Read the last block, add the record, write it back. Very efficient. Search (any field) b/2 average, b worst A linear search of every block. Delete search + 1 Find the block, mark or remove, rewrite. Leaves dead space. Ordered retrieval must sort the whole file Very expensive.

Use when: the file is small; the workload is insert-heavy; whole-file scans are the normal access pattern (as in bulk loading, or a staging table).

Do the arithmetic

With b = 3000 blocks and 10 ms per block access, a linear search averages 1500 × 10 ms = 15 seconds for one record. This is why indexes exist (Lesson 2).

docs.title: Sorted (sequential) file
docs.text:
Records are kept physically ordered on the value of an ordering field. If that field is also a key, it is the ordering key.

Operation Cost Explanation Search on the ordering field log₂ b Binary search over the blocks. Search on any other field b/2 average No better than a heap — the order does not help. Range query on the ordering field log₂ b + the matching blocks Excellent — matching records are contiguous. Ordered retrieval b, no sort needed The file is already in order. Insert very expensive On average half the file must be shifted to keep the order. Delete search + rewrite Usually a deletion marker.

With b = 3000, a binary search costs log₂ 3000 ≈ 12 block accesses instead of 1500 — a 125-fold improvement, but only for the ordering field.

The insertion problem, and how it is solved

Keeping a file physically sorted on every insert is unaffordable. Real systems use an overflow (transaction) file: new records go into a small unordered overflow area, which is periodically merged with the main file during reorganisation.

Searches must then check both the sorted main file and the overflow area, so performance degrades between reorganisations. This awkwardness is exactly why B+-trees (Lesson 2) displaced sorted files in practice: they keep the logical order while tolerating insertions gracefully.

docs.title: Hashed file
docs.text:
A hash function h maps a field value (the hash field) to a bucket number — a block or small group of blocks.

   h(Rollno) = Rollno mod 5

   'X2019' -> numeric 2019 -> 2019 mod 5 = 4  -> bucket 4
   'X2020' -> 2020 mod 5   = 0                -> bucket 0

   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+
   | bucket 0 |   | bucket 1 |   | bucket 2 |   | bucket 3 |   | bucket 4 |
   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+
   | X2020    |   |          |   | X2017    |   | X2018    |   | X2019    |
   | X2025    |   |          |   |          |   |          |   | X2024    |
   +----+-----+   +----------+   +----------+   +----------+   +----+-----+
        |                                                           |
        v  overflow chain when a bucket fills                       v
   +----------+                                              +----------+
   | X2030    |                                              | X2029    |
   +----------+                                              +----------+
Operation Cost Explanation Equality search on the hash field 1 block access (plus overflow) Compute h, go straight to the bucket. The fastest possible. Range search b — useless A good hash function scatters nearby values, so ranges are meaningless. Search on any other field b/2 Linear scan. Insert 1–2 Compute, write. Ordered retrieval must sort Very expensive.

Collisions and overflow

Two values may hash to the same bucket — a collision. Resolution methods:

  • Open addressing — place the record in the next free bucket.
  • Chaining — keep an overflow chain of extra blocks per bucket. Most common.
  • Multiple hashing — apply a second hash function.

Performance degrades as chains lengthen, so a load factor of about 70–80 per cent is targeted.

Static vs dynamic hashing

Static hashing fixes the number of buckets in advance. If the file grows, chains lengthen and performance collapses; if it shrinks, space is wasted. A full rehash is then needed.

Dynamic hashing — extendible and linear hashing — grows and shrinks the bucket space incrementally, avoiding a total rehash. This is what real systems use.

docs.title: Comparison — the table to memorise
docs.text:
Operation Heap Sorted Hashed Insert best (1–2) worst (shift) good (1–2) Equality search on the key field poor (b/2) good (log₂ b) best (1) Search on a non-key field poor (b/2) poor (b/2) poor (b/2) Range query poor (b) best worst (useless) Ordered retrieval poor (sort) best (free) poor (sort) Delete fair fair good

Choosing — match the organisation to the workload

  • Mostly inserts, rarely searched (a log or audit table) → heap.
  • Frequent exact lookups by a key (WHERE Rollno = 'X2019') → hashed.
  • Frequent range and ordered queries (WHERE Dateofadmission BETWEEN ..., ORDER BY) → sorted, or in practice a B+-tree index (Lesson 2), which gives sorted-file behaviour without the insertion penalty.
  • Mixed workload → a heap file with B+-tree indexes on the queried columns. This is what almost every real DBMS does by default.

docs.title: 24.4 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Describe the memory hierarchy. Why is database performance measured in block accesses rather than instructions?

A. (Diagram: Figure 1.1.) From fastest and smallest to slowest and largest: registers, cache, main memory (all primary, volatile, CPU-addressable); flash/SSD and magnetic disk (secondary, non-volatile, where the database resides); optical and tape (tertiary, for archives).

Why block accesses are the unit of cost. The step from main memory to disk is a jump of roughly five orders of magnitude — about 100 nanoseconds against about 10 milliseconds, a ratio near 100,000:1. Any operation that touches disk is dominated by that cost; the CPU work done in between is negligible by comparison.

Two consequences follow, and they shape the whole unit:

  1. Algorithms are compared by the number of block accesses they require. An algorithm doing more computation but fewer I/Os wins. A linear search of 3000 blocks costs about 15 seconds; a B+-tree lookup of 3 blocks costs 30 milliseconds — a 500-fold difference that no amount of CPU tuning could produce.
  2. Data is transferred a whole block at a time, never a byte or a record. So the design goal is to arrange records so that the ones needed together arrive in the same block — which is what clustering, indexing and the buffer pool all address.

Solved Question 2

Q. A file has 50,000 records of 200 bytes each; the block size is 2048 bytes. Compute the blocking factor and the number of blocks, unspanned. How much space is wasted? Recompute if spanned.

A.

Unspanned. bfr = floor(B / R) = floor(2048 / 200) = floor(10.24) = **10** records per block. b = ceil(r / bfr) = ceil(50000 / 10) = **5000** blocks.

Wasted space per block = 2048 − (10 × 200) = 48 bytes. Total waste = 5000 × 48 = 240,000 bytes ≈ 234 KB, which is 48/2048 = **2.34 per cent**.

Spanned. No space is wasted, so the space needed is exactly the data: total = 50000 × 200 = 10,000,000 bytes; b = ceil(10,000,000 / 2048) = **4883** blocks.

Saving: 117 blocks, about 2.3 per cent.

The trade-off. Spanning saves 2.3 per cent of the space, but a record split across a boundary needs two block accesses instead of one. Given that block accesses are the dominant cost (question 1), sacrificing up to 2× on some retrievals to save 2 per cent of cheap disk is a poor bargain.

Conclusion: for fixed-length records of this size, unspanned is correct. Spanning is justified when records are large relative to the block (so the waste would be substantial) or when R > B, which makes spanning unavoidable.

Solved Question 3

Q. Compare heap, sorted and hashed file organisations on insertion, equality search, range search and ordered retrieval. Recommend one for each of three workloads.

A. (Comparison table of Section 1.3.) Summarising the reasoning behind each entry:

Heap. Insertion is a simple append — read the last block, write it back — so 1–2 accesses. But there is no structure to exploit, so any search is a linear scan averaging b/2 blocks, and ordered retrieval requires sorting the whole file.

Sorted. Because records are physically ordered on the ordering field, a binary search finds a record in log₂ b accesses, ranges are contiguous, and ordered retrieval is free. But maintaining the order on insertion requires shifting on average half the file — prohibitive, which is why real systems use an overflow area and periodic reorganisation.

Hashed. The hash function computes the bucket directly, giving a single block access for an equality search on the hash field — the best possible. But a good hash function deliberately scatters nearby values, so range queries and ordered retrieval are useless.

Recommendations.

Workload Choice Reason An audit log: constant appends, read only in bulk Heap Insertion is optimal and full scans are the access pattern anyway. A lookup table queried only as WHERE Rollno = ? Hashed One block access per lookup; ranges are never needed. A transactions table queried by date ranges and reported in date order Sorted — in practice a B+-tree index Ranges are contiguous and ordering is free; the B+-tree provides this without the insertion penalty.

In practice most tables are heap files with B+-tree indexes on the queried columns, which combines cheap insertion with fast search.

Solved Question 4

Q. Explain hashing, collisions and overflow handling. Why is hashing unsuitable for range queries?

A. In a hashed file, a hash function h maps the value of a chosen hash field to a bucket address. To store or find a record, the system computes h(value) and goes directly to that bucket — one block access, with no search.

A collision occurs when two different field values hash to the same bucket. Collisions are unavoidable: the space of possible key values is far larger than the number of buckets. Three resolution methods:

  1. Open addressing — scan forward to the next free bucket. Simple, but causes clustering that degrades later searches.
  2. Chaining — each bucket has a pointer to an overflow chain of additional blocks. The most common method; searching a bucket means following its chain.
  3. Multiple hashing — apply a second hash function to place the colliding record elsewhere.

Because chain length determines search cost, a load factor of roughly 70–80 per cent is targeted, and dynamic hashing (extendible or linear) is used so the bucket space can grow without a total rehash.

Why range queries fail. A good hash function is designed to distribute values uniformly and unpredictably — that is precisely what avoids collisions. As a direct consequence, values that are close together are scattered to unrelated buckets. Rollno X2019 and X2020 may land in buckets 4 and 0.

So WHERE Rollno BETWEEN 'X2019' AND 'X2050' cannot be answered by visiting a few buckets: the qualifying records could be anywhere, and every bucket must be scanned — cost b, worse than a heap file, since the overflow chains must be followed too.

The same argument rules out ORDER BY and MIN/MAX on the hash field. Hashing is for equality, never for order. Where both are needed, a B+-tree index is the right structure.

Solved Question 5

Q. A file of 3000 blocks is searched for one record. Compute the cost under heap, sorted (on the search field) and hashed organisations, at 10 ms per block access. Comment.

A.

Organisation Block accesses Time Reasoning Heap 1500 average, 3000 worst 15 s average Linear scan; on average half the file is read before the record is found. Sorted on the search field log₂ 3000 ≈ 12 0.12 s Binary search halves the search space each step. Hashed on the search field 1 (plus overflow) 0.01 s The bucket address is computed directly. Sorted or hashed, but searching a different field 1500 average 15 s Neither structure helps for a field it is not organised on.

Comments.

  1. The improvement from heap to sorted is 125-fold; from heap to hashed, 1500-fold. No amount of faster CPU or better code approaches this — the structure of the file is what matters.

  2. The organisation helps only for the field it is built on. A file sorted on Rollno gives no benefit whatever to WHERE Name = 'Ankit Sharma'. Since a file can be physically organised on only one field, all other access paths need indexes (Lesson 2) — which is exactly why indexes exist.

  3. The figures assume magnetic disk. On an SSD each access might cost 0.1 ms, so the heap search falls to 0.15 s — still 15 times worse than the sorted file and 150 times worse than hashing. Faster hardware narrows the absolute gap but not the ratio.

Solved Question 6

Q. Distinguish fixed-length from variable-length records. Give three techniques for identifying field boundaries in variable-length records, and explain how deletion is handled.

A.

Fixed-length records occupy the same number of bytes each. The address of record i is start + i × R, so direct access is a simple calculation, and the blocking factor is a constant. Space is wasted whenever a field is shorter than its allocated width.

Variable-length records arise from VARCHAR fields, optional fields that may be absent, repeating fields, or a file holding several record types. They save space but make the position of the ith record uncomputable, so a directory or index of record positions within each block is normally kept.

Three techniques for field boundaries:

  1. Separator characters — a reserved delimiter (say |) between fields. Simple, but the delimiter must never occur in the data, and finding field k requires scanning from the start.
  2. Length prefixes — each field is preceded by a byte or two giving its length. No reserved character is needed, but again access is sequential within the record.
  3. Field-offset table — a small directory at the head of the record giving the starting offset of each field. Costs a few bytes, but gives direct access to any field without scanning. This is the usual modern choice, and it also represents NULLs cleanly (by an offset equal to the next one).

Deletion. Two strategies:

  • Deletion marker (tombstone) — a flag bit or byte marks the record as deleted, and the space is reused by a later insertion of a record that fits. Cheap and does not invalidate stored addresses, but the file accumulates dead space.
  • Compaction — surviving records are shifted to close the gap. No waste, but expensive and it invalidates any stored record pointers, so indexes would have to be rebuilt.

Real systems use tombstones plus a free-space list, with periodic reorganisation to compact. This is why a heavily-updated table benefits from OPTIMIZE TABLE (MySQL) or VACUUM (PostgreSQL); without it, a table from which most rows have been deleted may still occupy its original space and still be slow to scan.

docs.title: 24.5 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Name the three levels of the storage hierarchy with an example of each.
  2. What is a block, and why is it the unit of transfer?
  3. Define blocking factor and give its formula.
  4. Distinguish spanned from unspanned blocking.
  5. Give the three components of disk access time and say which dominates.
  6. Why is a heap file good for insertion but poor for searching?
  7. Why can a hashed file not answer range queries?

B. Computation

  1. A file has 20,000 records of 150 bytes; the block size is 4096 bytes. Compute bfr, b, and the wasted space per block and in total (unspanned).
  2. Repeat for 1,000,000 records of 512 bytes and a block size of 8192 bytes.
  3. For the file in question 8, compute the average number of block accesses for a search under (a) heap, (b) sorted on the search field, (c) hashed on the search field.
  4. A record is 1500 bytes and the block size is 1024 bytes. What must be done, and why?
  5. A sorted file of 4096 blocks is binary-searched. How many block accesses? How many if the file doubles in size? Comment on the growth rate.

C. Analysis

  1. For each workload, choose a file organisation and justify: a. A web-server access log, appended constantly and analysed monthly in bulk. b. A table of country codes, looked up by exact code, never ranged. c. A table of stock prices queried mostly as WHERE date BETWEEN ... ORDER BY date. d. The ADMISSION table of our college database.
  2. Explain why a sorted file is rarely used in practice despite its good search performance. What replaced it, and why?
  3. A hashed file has a load factor of 95 per cent and searches have become slow. Diagnose the problem and give two remedies.
  4. Explain why an organisation built on one field gives no benefit to queries on another. What is the consequence for database design?
  5. A table has had 90 per cent of its rows deleted, yet full scans are as slow as before. Explain why, and give the remedy.
  6. Compare magnetic disk and SSD on the three components of access time. Which file organisation becomes relatively more attractive on an SSD, and why?

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A single record can be read from disk without reading its whole block.
  2. Rotational latency usually dominates disk access time.
  3. A heap file supports binary search.
  4. A hashed file gives the fastest possible equality search on the hash field.
  5. Spanned records always improve performance.
  6. Ordered retrieval from a sorted file requires a sort.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. The block is the unit of transfer; reading one byte costs a whole block access.
  2. False. Seek time (3–10 ms) usually dominates; rotational latency averages about 4 ms.
  3. False. Binary search requires the records to be ordered; a heap file must be searched linearly.
  4. True. One block access, computed directly — no search at all. Only overflow chains add to it.
  5. False. They save space but may require two block accesses for a record crossing a boundary. Since block accesses dominate cost, unspanned is usually better for small records.
  6. False. The file is already in order, so ordered retrieval is free — one of the sorted file's main advantages.

Lesson Summary

  • The memory–disk gap of about 100,000:1 makes block accesses the unit of database cost.
  • bfr = floor(B/R); b = ceil(r/bfr). Unspanned wastes space but keeps one record in one block; spanned saves space at the cost of a second access.
  • Seek time dominates disk access, so physically adjacent blocks are far cheaper to read.
  • Heap: best insertion, linear search. Sorted: binary search and free ordering, but crippling insertion cost. Hashed: one-access equality search, useless for ranges.
  • Any organisation helps only for the field it is built on — which is why indexes are needed for every other access path.

docs.title: Lesson 8: ER Notation, Weak Entities and Case Studies
docs.text:
Putting it all together — three complete designs, drawn step by step

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 2: Entity Relationship Modelling · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 3.7, 3.8, 4.1–4.4

Learning Outcomes

  1. Reproduce the complete Chen notation from memory.
  2. Draw a full ER diagram for a described mini-world, with all constraints.
  3. Apply a repeatable seven-step design procedure.
  4. Recognise and resolve the standard design traps (fan trap, chasm trap).
  5. Read the EER extensions: specialisation, generalisation, inheritance.

docs.title: 8.2 A Seven-Step Design Procedure
docs.text:
Procedure

  1. Identify entity types. Underline nouns; keep those with properties of their own (Lesson 1).
  2. Identify relationship types. Verbs connecting two entity types.
  3. Attach attributes to entity types and to relationship types (Lesson 2 test).
  4. Determine keys. Underline. Any entity type with no key of its own is weak — find its owner, its identifying relationship, and its partial key.
  5. Determine cardinality ratios, using the two-question method.
  6. Determine participation constraints, side by side.
  7. Review: read the diagram back in English, sentence by sentence, and check every sentence against the requirements.

Step 7 is the one students skip and the one that finds the errors. Read "Every student must be admitted to at least one course, and may be admitted to many" aloud, and ask the registrar whether it is true.

docs.title: 8.3 Case Study 1 — The College Database (our running example)
Requirements
docs.text: The college keeps records of its students: roll number (unique), name, and date of birth. It offers courses, each with an identifier (unique), name, total seats, duration, a course type that is either Fulltime or Parttime, and a teacher-in-charge. A student may take admission in any number of courses, and the date of admission is recorded; every student must be admitted to at least one course, but a newly created course may have no students. The college also runs societies, each with an identifier (unique), name, mentor and total seats. Students enrol in societies and the date of enrolment is recorded; enrolment is optional on both sides.

docs.title: Step-by-step
docs.text:
Steps 1–2. Entity types: STUDENT, COURSE, SOCIETY. Relationship types: TAKES_ADMISSION (student–course), ENROLS_IN (student–society).

Step 3. Attributes as listed; Dateofadmission belongs to TAKES_ADMISSION and Dateofenrolment to ENROLS_IN, because each is determined only by the pair (Lesson 3).

Step 4. Keys: Rollno, SID, SocID. All three entity types are strong.

Step 5. Cardinalities. One student, how many courses? many. One course, how many students? many → M:N. Similarly ENROLS_IN is M:N.

Step 6. Participation. STUDENT in TAKES_ADMISSION: total (stated). COURSE: partial (stated). Both sides of ENROLS_IN: partial.

Step 7. Read back: "Every student is admitted to at least one course and may be admitted to many. A course may have no students, or many. A student may join any number of societies, or none. A society may have no members, or many." This matches the requirements.

docs.title: 8.4 Case Study 2 — The COMPANY Database (the textbook standard)
docs.text: This is Elmasri and Navathe's canonical example, and it appears in examinations year after year because it exercises every notational feature.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: The company is organised into departments. Each department has a unique name, a unique number, and several locations. A department is managed by one employee; the date on which that employee began managing is recorded. Each department controls a number of projects; each project has a unique name, a unique number and a single location. The company stores each employee's social security number (unique), name, address, salary, sex and birth date. Every employee is assigned to exactly one department but may work on several projects, which need not be controlled by the same department; the number of hours per week an employee works on each project is recorded. Each employee has a direct supervisor, who is another employee. Employees have dependants for insurance purposes; for each dependant the first name, sex, birth date and relationship to the employee are recorded. A dependant's first name is unique only within that employee's family.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Element Decision Reasoning DEPARTMENT Strong entity type Two keys: Dname, Dnumber — both underlined; choose Dnumber as primary. Dlocations Multivalued attribute of DEPARTMENT "several locations". Double ellipse. NumberOfEmployees Derived attribute Countable from WORKS_FOR. Dashed ellipse. PROJECT Strong entity type Keys Pname, Pnumber; Plocation is single-valued. EMPLOYEE Strong entity type Key Ssn. Name is composite; Age derived from Bdate. DEPENDENT Weak entity type "unique only within that employee's family" — no key of its own. Owner EMPLOYEE, partial key DependentName. MANAGES 1:1, attribute StartDate One employee manages at most one department; a department has exactly one manager. WORKS_FOR 1:N Employee assigned to exactly one department; department has many employees. CONTROLS 1:N Department controls many projects; a project is controlled by one department. WORKS_ON M:N, attribute Hours Employee works on several projects; a project has several employees. Hours is determined only by the pair. SUPERVISION Recursive 1:N, roles supervisor / supervisee The supervisor is another employee. DEPENDENTS_OF Identifying relationship, 1:N, double diamond Weak entity's identification.

docs.title: 8.5 Case Study 3 — A Hospital Database (with a weak entity)
Requirements

docs.title: 8.6 Design Traps
docs.text: Two classic errors produce diagrams that look right and are wrong. Both arise from careless use of 1:N relationships.

docs.title: The fan trap
docs.text:
Fan trap

Occurs when two or more 1:N relationships fan out from the same entity type, and the path between the outer entity types is therefore ambiguous.

   BAD:
        +----------+  1   /--------\  N  +----------+
        | DIVISION |------< OPERATES>----|  BRANCH  |
        +----+-----+      \--------/     +----------+
             | 1
        /----+----\
       <   HAS      >
        \----+----/
             | N
        +----+-----+
        |  STAFF   |

   Question: which branch does a member of staff work at?
   UNANSWERABLE. Staff hangs off DIVISION, and a division has
   many branches, so the path staff -> division -> branch fans
   out to every branch of the division.

   FIX: re-route the relationship so the path is unambiguous.

        +----------+  1  /--------\  N  +--------+ 1 /-----\ N +-------+
        | DIVISION |-----<OPERATES >----| BRANCH |---< HAS >---| STAFF |
        +----------+     \--------/     +--------+   \-----/   +-------+

   Now: staff -> branch -> division is a single unambiguous path.

docs.title: The chasm trap
docs.text:
Chasm trap

Occurs when a path exists between entity types, but some instances cannot be connected because of a partial participation somewhere along the path.

   +--------+ 1 /-----\ N +-------+ 1 /--------\ N +----------+
   | BRANCH |---< HAS >---| STAFF |---< OVERSEES>---| PROPERTY |
   +--------+   \-----/   +-------+   \--------/    +----------+
                                          ^
                          PARTIAL participation of PROPERTY:
                          a property may not yet be assigned
                          to any member of staff.

   Question: which branch is property PG4 registered at?
   UNANSWERABLE for unassigned properties -- the path is broken
   at the chasm.

   FIX: add the missing direct relationship.

   +--------+ 1  /---------\  N  +----------+
   | BRANCH |----< ADVERTISES>---| PROPERTY |
   +--------+    \---------/     +----------+

How to detect both traps: after drawing, take every pair of entity types that users ask questions about, and check that a single unambiguous, unbroken path connects them. This is Step 7 of the procedure.

docs.title: 8.7 A Glimpse of the EER Model
docs.text:
The basic ER model cannot express "a postgraduate student is a kind of student". The Enhanced (Extended) ER model adds three concepts.

EER concepts

Specialisation — defining a set of subclasses of an entity type (the superclass) on the basis of some distinguishing characteristic. STUDENT specialises into UG_STUDENT and PG_STUDENT.

Generalisation — the reverse process: noticing that CAR and TRUCK share attributes and creating the superclass VEHICLE.

Attribute inheritance — a subclass entity inherits all attributes of its superclass, and participates in all its relationships. PG_STUDENT inherits Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth and adds ThesisTitle, Supervisor.

Notation: a circle with a subset symbol on each line from the circle to the subclass.

                +-------------+
                |   STUDENT   |     superclass
                +------+------+
                       |
                     ( d )        d = DISJOINT  (o = overlapping)
                    /  |  \
                  U    |    U       U = subset symbol
                 /     |     \
        +--------+  +--+---+  +---------+
        |   UG   |  |  PG  |  | DIPLOMA |    subclasses
        +--------+  +------+  +---------+
        ThesisTitle on PG only; all three inherit Rollno,
        Name, Dateofbirth from STUDENT.

Two constraints on a specialisation:

Constraint Values Meaning Notation Disjointness disjoint (d) / overlapping (o) Can an entity belong to more than one subclass? letter in the circle Completeness total / partial Must every superclass entity belong to some subclass? double / single line from superclass to circle

A student is either UG or PG but not both, so the specialisation is disjoint; if every student must be one of the three, it is also total.

Scope note

The syllabus for this course lists the basic ER model. EER is included here so that you recognise the notation if it appears, and because specialisation is the correct answer to the "too many NULLs" design smell of Lesson 2. Examination questions will concentrate on the basic model.

docs.title: 8.8 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Draw a complete ER diagram for the college database and list every business rule it asserts.

A. (Diagram: reproduce Figure 4.1.)

Business rules asserted:

  1. Every student is uniquely identified by Rollno; every course by SID; every society by SocID.
  2. A student may take admission in many courses, and a course may admit many students (M:N).
  3. Every student must be admitted to at least one course (double line on STUDENT).
  4. A course may exist with no students admitted (single line on COURSE) — necessary, since a course must be created before anyone can join it.
  5. For each (student, course) pair a single date of admission is recorded.
  6. A student may enrol in many societies and a society may have many members (M:N).
  7. Enrolment in a society is optional on both sides: a student need join no society, and a new society may have no members.
  8. For each (student, society) pair a single date of enrolment is recorded.
  9. Coursetype is restricted to Fulltime or Parttime — this is a domain constraint which the ER diagram cannot show; it must be recorded in the accompanying documentation and enforced later by a CHECK constraint.

Point 9 illustrates an important limitation: the ER diagram captures structure and cardinality, but not arbitrary business rules.

Solved Question 2

Q. Draw the ER diagram for the COMPANY database, marking all constraints.
