A. (Diagram: reproduce Figure 4.2; constraints as in the (min, max) table of Section 4.4.)

The features that make this the standard examination example:

  • Two candidate keys on DEPARTMENT (Dname, Dnumber) and on PROJECT — both underlined.
  • A multivalued attribute Dlocations (double ellipse).
  • A derived attribute NumberOfEmployees (dashed ellipse).
  • A composite attribute Name(Fname, Minit, Lname) on EMPLOYEE.
  • A 1:1 relationship MANAGES carrying its own attribute StartDate, with DEPARTMENT total (1,1) and EMPLOYEE partial (0,1).
  • Two 1:N relationships, WORKS_FOR and CONTROLS, each with total participation on the N side.
  • An M:N relationship WORKS_ON with the relationship attribute Hours — which cannot be migrated to either entity type.
  • A recursive 1:N relationship SUPERVISION with role names supervisor (0,N) and supervisee (0,1).
  • A weak entity type DEPENDENT (double rectangle) with partial key DependentName (dashed underline), identified through the double-diamond relationship DEPENDENTS_OF, with total participation (double line) on the weak side.

Solved Question 3

Q. What is a fan trap? Give an example and its correction.

A. A fan trap occurs when two or more 1:N relationships radiate ("fan out") from the same entity type, so that the path between two of the outer entity types is ambiguous and a legitimate question cannot be answered.

Example. DIVISION 1:N BRANCH and DIVISION 1:N STAFF. Both BRANCH and STAFF hang off DIVISION. Now ask: "At which branch does staff member S05 work?" We can find S05's division, but that division operates several branches, and nothing in the model says which. The relationships fan out and the answer is indeterminate.

Correction. Restructure so that the path is unique, by re-routing the relationship through the intermediate entity type:

DIVISION --1-- <OPERATES> --N-- BRANCH --1-- <HAS> --N-- STAFF

Now each staff member belongs to exactly one branch, and each branch to exactly one division, so "which branch?" and "which division?" both have unique answers. No information is lost — the division of a staff member is still derivable, by following the path.

Detection. After drawing, list the questions users actually ask, and for each check that a single unambiguous path connects the entity types involved. A fan trap is the case where the path exists but is not unique; the chasm trap is the case where the path exists but is broken by a partial participation.

Solved Question 4

Q. Model this: "A library has books; each book has an ISBN, title and several authors. The library holds several physical copies of each book, numbered 1, 2, 3 within the title. Members borrow copies; the issue date and due date are recorded. A member may borrow many copies over time and a copy may be borrowed by many members over time."

A.

Entity types. BOOK (strong, key ISBN), COPY (weak — copy number restarts at 1 for each title, so owner BOOK, partial key CopyNo, full key (ISBN, CopyNo)), MEMBER (strong, key MemberID).

Attributes. BOOK: ISBN (key), Title, {Author} (multivalued — "several authors"). COPY: CopyNo (partial key), Status. MEMBER: MemberID (key), Name, Address.

Relationships. HAS_COPY — identifying, double diamond, BOOK 1 : COPY N, total on COPY. BORROWS — M:N over time, with relationship attributes IssueDate and DueDate.

    (ISBN)  (Title)   ((Author))
   underlined  |          |
        \      |         /
       +-+-----+--------+-+
       |       BOOK        |
       +---------+---------+
                 || 1
          /======++=======\
         <<    HAS_COPY     >>
          \======++=======/
                 || N  total
          +======++======+
          ||     COPY    ||
          +==============+
           CopyNo (partial key, dashed)
                  |  M
           /------+-------\
          <    BORROWS      >----(IssueDate)
           \------+-------/ \----(DueDate)
                  |  N
          +-------+--------+
          |     MEMBER     |
          +----------------+
           MemberID (key), Name, Address

Note on the M:N choice. BORROWS is M:N because we keep history: the same copy is borrowed by many members over time. If only the current loan were stored, it would be 1:N (a copy is on loan to at most one member) with (0,1) on the copy side.

Note on the key of BORROWS. Since a member may borrow the same copy more than once over the years, the pair (MemberID, ISBN, CopyNo) is not unique; IssueDate must be added to the key. This is a good illustration of why Step 7 — reading the diagram back — matters.

Solved Question 5

Q. Explain specialisation, generalisation and attribute inheritance. When would you specialise an entity type?

A. Specialisation is the process of defining a set of subclasses of an entity type, called the superclass, on the basis of some distinguishing characteristic. From EMPLOYEE one may specialise SECRETARY, ENGINEER and TECHNICIAN by job type. It is a top-down refinement.

Generalisation is the reverse, bottom-up process: recognising that CAR and TRUCK share VehicleID, Price and LicensePlate, and creating the superclass VEHICLE to hold the common attributes.

Attribute inheritance is the property that a subclass entity possesses all the attributes of its superclass in addition to its own, and participates in all the superclass's relationships. An ENGINEER entity has Ssn, Name and Salary inherited from EMPLOYEE, plus EngType of its own; and being an EMPLOYEE, it also participates in WORKS_FOR.

Two constraints apply: disjointness — disjoint (d) if an entity may belong to at most one subclass, overlapping (o) if it may belong to several — and completeness — total (double line) if every superclass entity must belong to some subclass, partial (single line) otherwise.

When to specialise. Three signals:

  1. Certain attributes apply to only some entities of the type — the "too many NULLs" smell. If ThesisTitle is NULL for every undergraduate, specialise.
  2. Some relationships apply to only some entities. If only postgraduates participate in SUPERVISED_BY, specialise.
  3. The subclasses are meaningful to the users and are named in the requirements.

If none of these holds, do not specialise: an unnecessary hierarchy adds joins and complexity for nothing.

Solved Question 6

Q. State four limitations of the ER model.

A.

  1. It cannot express arbitrary business rules. "Coursetype must be Fulltime or Parttime", "a department head must be a professor of that department", "salary must not exceed the manager's salary" — none can be drawn. They must be documented separately and enforced later with CHECK constraints, assertions or triggers.

  2. It has no standard notation. Chen, Crow's Foot, UML and (min,max) all differ, and textbooks disagree on where to write cardinality labels. Diagrams must therefore carry a legend, and answers must state the convention used.

  3. The basic model lacks abstraction mechanisms. It has no specialisation, generalisation, inheritance, categories or aggregation — which is precisely why the EER model was introduced.

  4. Some constraints are inexpressible even in principle. Higher-degree constraints across several relationships, temporal constraints ("a student may not be admitted to two full-time courses simultaneously"), and cycles in recursive relationships cannot be captured.

Two further limitations worth mentioning: there is no operational component — the ER model describes structure but supplies no query language, so it must be mapped to the relational model before data can be manipulated; and large diagrams become unreadable, so practical designs need modularisation into subject-area views.

docs.title: 8.9 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Draw the symbol for each of: weak entity type, identifying relationship, derived attribute, multivalued attribute, total participation, partial key.
  2. State the seven steps of the design procedure.
  3. What is a fan trap? What is a chasm trap?
  4. Define specialisation and generalisation.
  5. What are the two constraints on a specialisation?
  6. Give two limitations of the ER model.

B. Long answer

  1. Explain the complete Chen notation with a diagram illustrating every symbol.
  2. Draw and explain the ER diagram for the COMPANY database, listing every constraint in (min, max) form.
  3. Explain fan and chasm traps with examples and corrections, and describe how to detect them systematically.
  4. Explain specialisation, generalisation, attribute inheritance, and the disjointness and completeness constraints, with a diagram.

C. Design problems — draw the complete ER diagram for each

  1. Airline reservation. Flights have a unique number, origin, destination and departure time. A flight has legs numbered 1, 2, 3 within it. Aircraft have registration numbers and models. Passengers have a unique ID and name, and book seats on flights, with a booking date and seat number. One aircraft is assigned to each flight; an aircraft serves many flights.

  2. Bank. Branches have a unique code, name and address. Customers have a unique ID, name and several phone numbers. Accounts have a unique number, type and balance, and belong to exactly one branch. A customer may hold several accounts and an account may be jointly held. Transactions on an account are numbered 1 upward within that account, and record a date, type and amount. Every account must have at least one holder.

  3. University examination system. Students, courses, examinations, question papers, invigilators and rooms. Decide the entity types yourself, justify each decision, and mark every constraint. Identify at least one weak entity type.

  4. Online shopping. Customers, products, orders, order lines, payments and suppliers. A product may be supplied by several suppliers at different prices. An order contains several products with quantities. State clearly which attributes belong to relationships.

D. Analytical

  1. For the diagram of Figure 4.1, state what would change if: (a) a student were allowed at most one course; (b) every course had to have at least one student; (c) the college began storing each teacher's phone number and department.

  2. A designer draws DEPARTMENT 1 --- <HAS> --- N EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT 1 --- <OWNS> --- N PROJECT, and then asks "which project does employee E works on?". Name the trap, explain why it fails, and give two possible corrections with their different meanings.

  3. In the COMPANY database, argue whether DEPENDENT could be made a strong entity type. What would have to change, and what would be gained and lost?

  4. Convert the entire COMPANY diagram from Chen cardinality labels to (min, max) notation, and verify each pair by reading it aloud in English.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. Every ER diagram maps to exactly one relational schema.
  2. A weak entity type may have a multivalued attribute.
  3. In a specialisation, subclasses inherit relationships as well as attributes.
  4. A fan trap is caused by an M:N relationship.
  5. The ER model can express the rule "salary must be positive".
  6. A double diamond always connects to a double rectangle.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. The mapping algorithm allows choices — for a 1:1 relationship, which side receives the foreign key; whether to merge a subclass into its superclass. Several correct relational schemas may result.
  2. True. Weakness concerns only identification; a weak entity type may have any kind of attribute.
  3. True. A subclass entity is a superclass entity, so it participates in all the superclass's relationships as well as inheriting its attributes.
  4. False. A fan trap arises from two or more 1:N relationships fanning out from the same entity type.
  5. False. Domain and value constraints cannot be drawn; they are documented separately and enforced by CHECK constraints after mapping.
  6. True. A double diamond is an identifying relationship, which by definition identifies a weak entity type, drawn as a double rectangle.

Lesson Summary

  • The Chen notation table is the vocabulary of Unit 2; reproduce it from memory.
  • The seven-step procedure ends with reading the diagram back in English — the step that catches the errors.
  • Three worked case studies: college (M:N with relationship attributes), COMPANY (every feature, including a weak entity, a recursive relationship and a 1:1 with an attribute), and hospital (weak entity plus multivalued attribute).
  • Watch for the fan trap (ambiguous path from fanned-out 1:N relationships) and the chasm trap (path broken by partial participation).
  • EER adds specialisation, generalisation and inheritance, with disjointness and completeness constraints.
  • The ER model cannot express arbitrary business rules; document them separately.

End of Unit 2. Next: Unit 3, Lesson 1 — Update Anomalies and the Relational Data Model.

docs.title: Lesson 19: ER-to-Relational Mapping
docs.text:
The seven-step algorithm, applied end to end

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 5: Database Design · 10 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 9.1

Learning Outcomes

  1. State the seven-step mapping algorithm from memory.
  2. Map strong entities, weak entities, and all three binary relationship types.
  3. Map multivalued attributes and n-ary relationships.
  4. Justify the choice of side for a 1:1 foreign key.
  5. Map a complete ER diagram, producing full SQL DDL.

docs.title: 19.1 Where This Sits
docs.text:
Unit 2 produced an ER diagram — a technology-free description. Unit 3 and 4 described relations and SQL. This lesson is the bridge: a mechanical procedure converting the one into the other.

   ER DIAGRAM  (Unit 2)                RELATIONAL SCHEMA  (Units 3, 4)
   entity types      ------ step 1 ----->  relations
   weak entities     ------ step 2 ----->  relations with composite keys
   1:1 relationships ------ step 3 ----->  a foreign key
   1:N relationships ------ step 4 ----->  a foreign key on the N side
   M:N relationships ------ step 5 ----->  a NEW relation (junction table)
   multivalued attrs ------ step 6 ----->  a NEW relation
   n-ary relationships----- step 7 ----->  a NEW relation

Why the algorithm matters

A schema derived by this algorithm from a correct ER diagram is already close to normalised — usually in 3NF or BCNF. Hand-written tables usually are not, and must be repaired by the normalisation of Lessons 2 to 5.

Good conceptual design is therefore not merely documentation; it is the cheapest route to a good logical design.

docs.title: Step 1 — Regular (strong) entity types
docs.text:
Rule

For each regular entity type E, create a relation R that includes all the simple attributes of E.

  • A composite attribute contributes its simple component attributes as separate columns; the composite name itself does not appear.
  • Choose one key attribute of E as the primary key of R. If the chosen key is composite, the set of its simple attributes together forms the primary key.
  • Other candidate keys become UNIQUE constraints.
  • Multivalued and derived attributes are not included here (steps 6 and "omit" respectively).

EMPLOYEE with Ssn (key), Name(Fname, Minit, Lname) composite, Bdate, Address, Salary, Sex, derived Age, multivalued {Degree}:

EMPLOYEE ( Ssn, Fname, Minit, Lname, Bdate, Address, Salary, Sex )
--         ^^^ primary key
-- Name -> three columns.  Age -> omitted (derived).  {Degree} -> step 6.

docs.title: Step 2 — Weak entity types
docs.text:
Rule

For each weak entity type W with owner E, create a relation R containing all simple attributes of W, plus the primary key of the owner as a foreign key.

The primary key of R is the owner's primary key together with the partial key of W.

Declare ON DELETE CASCADE, because a weak entity is existence-dependent on its owner.

DEPENDENT (partial key DependentName) owned by EMPLOYEE:

DEPENDENT ( Essn, DependentName, Sex, Bdate, Relationship )
--          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ composite primary key
--          Essn is also a FOREIGN KEY to EMPLOYEE(Ssn), ON DELETE CASCADE

If the owner is itself weak, apply step 2 to the owner first — the keys propagate down the chain.

docs.title: Step 3 — Binary 1:1 relationship types
docs.text:
Three approaches; the foreign key approach is almost always correct.

Rule (foreign key approach)

Choose one of the two relations — say S — and include as a foreign key in S the primary key of the other relation T. Add the relationship's own attributes to S as well.

Choose for S the entity type with TOTAL participation. Then the foreign key is never NULL.

EMPLOYEE MANAGES DEPARTMENT, 1:1, with DEPARTMENT total (1,1) and EMPLOYEE partial (0,1), relationship attribute StartDate:

DEPARTMENT ( Dnumber, Dname, MgrSsn, MgrStartDate )
--                           ^^^^^^ FK to EMPLOYEE(Ssn), NOT NULL

Why the total side receives the foreign key

Put MgrSsn in DEPARTMENT: every department has exactly one manager, so the column is never NULL and can be declared NOT NULL.

Put ManagedDept in EMPLOYEE instead: only a handful of employees manage anything, so the column is NULL for almost every row — wasted space, and a design smell suggesting a specialisation is missing.

If both sides are total, the two entity types can be merged into one relation (approach 2). If both are partial, a separate relation (approach 3, as for M:N) avoids the NULLs.

docs.title: Step 4 — Binary 1:N relationship types
docs.text:
Rule

Include in the relation S on the N side a foreign key referencing the primary key of the relation T on the 1 side. Relationship attributes also go to S.

There is no choice here: the foreign key must go on the N side. Each entity on the N side participates in exactly one relationship instance, so it has exactly one value to store.

DEPARTMENT 1:N EMPLOYEE (WORKS_FOR), EMPLOYEE total:

EMPLOYEE ( Ssn, Fname, ..., Dno )
--                          ^^^ FK to DEPARTMENT(Dnumber), NOT NULL

For a recursive 1:N relationship, the foreign key references the same relation:

EMPLOYEE ( Ssn, Fname, ..., Dno, SuperSsn )
--                               ^^^^^^^^ FK to EMPLOYEE(Ssn), NULLable

SuperSsn must allow NULL, because the chief executive has no supervisor.

docs.title: Step 5 — Binary M:N relationship types
docs.text:
Rule

Create a new relation S (a junction, linking or associative table) containing:

  • the primary keys of both participating relations, as foreign keys;
  • all attributes of the relationship.

The primary key of S is the combination of the two foreign keys.

A foreign key approach is impossible here — it would require storing many values in one column, violating 1NF.

EMPLOYEE M:N PROJECT (WORKS_ON) with attribute Hours:

WORKS_ON ( Essn, Pno, Hours )
--         ^^^^^^^^^ composite primary key; both are foreign keys

When the composite key is not enough

The pair (Essn, Pno) is the key only if an employee works on a project once. If the same pair may recur — a member borrowing the same book in different years, a student re-taking a course — a distinguishing attribute must be added to the key, typically a date:

BORROWS ( MemberID, ISBN, IssueDate, DueDate )
--        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ three-part primary key

This is exactly the check that Step 7 of the ER design procedure (read the diagram back in English) is meant to catch.

docs.title: Step 6 — Multivalued attributes
docs.text:
Rule

For each multivalued attribute A, create a new relation R containing:

  • a column for A;
  • the primary key of the owning relation, as a foreign key.

The primary key of R is both together. If A is composite, include its simple components.

Declare ON DELETE CASCADE.

{Dlocations} of DEPARTMENT:

DEPT_LOCATIONS ( Dnumber, Dlocation )
--               ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ composite primary key

This is the 1NF requirement in action (Unit 3, Lesson 1): a set of values cannot occupy a single column.

docs.title: Step 7 — n-ary relationship types
docs.text:
Rule

For each n-ary relationship type (degree > 2), create a new relation S containing the primary keys of all participating relations as foreign keys, plus the relationship's own attributes.

The primary key of S is normally the combination of all the foreign keys — unless a participating entity has cardinality 1, in which case its key may be omitted from the primary key.

SUPPLIER – PART – PROJECT (SUPPLIES) with attribute Quantity:

SUPPLIES ( Sno, Pno, Jno, Quantity )
--         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ three-part primary key

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text: ER construct Maps to Primary key of the result Strong entity type A relation Its own key attribute Weak entity type A relation Owner's key + partial key 1:1 relationship A foreign key in one relation (unchanged) 1:N relationship A foreign key on the N side (unchanged) M:N relationship A new relation Both foreign keys combined Multivalued attribute A new relation Owner's key + the attribute n-ary relationship A new relation All foreign keys combined Composite attribute Its simple components, as columns — Derived attribute Omitted (computed on demand) —

docs.title: 19.3 Worked Mapping 1 — The College Database
docs.text:
Input — the ER diagram of Unit 2, Lesson 4:

STUDENT ( Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth )                       key Rollno
COURSE  ( SID, Cname, TotalSeats, Duration,
          Coursetype, TeacherInCharge )                     key SID
SOCIETY ( SocID, Socname, Mentor, TotalSeats )              key SocID

TAKES_ADMISSION  STUDENT (1,N) -- COURSE  (0,N)   attribute Dateofadmission
ENROLS_IN        STUDENT (0,N) -- SOCIETY (0,N)   attribute Dateofenrollment

Step 1 — three strong entity types give three relations.

Steps 2, 3, 4 — no weak entities, no 1:1, no 1:N relationships. Nothing to do.

Step 5 — two M:N relationships give two new relations:

  • ADMISSION(Rollno, SID, Dateofadmission), primary key (Rollno, SID)
  • ENROLLMENT(Rollno, SocID, Dateofenrollment), primary key (Rollno, SocID)

Steps 6, 7 — no multivalued attributes, no n-ary relationships.

Result:

CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
    Rollno      VARCHAR(8)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name        VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    Dateofbirth DATE
);
CREATE TABLE COURSE (
    SID             VARCHAR(6)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Cname           VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    TotalSeats      INT         NOT NULL CHECK (TotalSeats > 0),
    Duration        INT,
    Coursetype      VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL CHECK (Coursetype IN ('Fulltime','Parttime')),
    TeacherInCharge VARCHAR(40)
);
CREATE TABLE SOCIETY (
    SocID      VARCHAR(6)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Socname    VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    Mentor     VARCHAR(40),
    TotalSeats INT         NOT NULL CHECK (TotalSeats > 0)
);
CREATE TABLE ADMISSION (
    Rollno          VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    SID             VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    Dateofadmission DATE       NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno) ON DELETE CASCADE  ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    FOREIGN KEY (SID)    REFERENCES COURSE(SID)     ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
);
CREATE TABLE ENROLLMENT (
    Rollno           VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    SocID            VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    Dateofenrollment DATE       NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SocID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    FOREIGN KEY (SocID)  REFERENCES SOCIETY(SocID)  ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
);

What the mapping cannot carry across

The total participation of STUDENT in TAKES_ADMISSION — "every student must be admitted to at least one course" — has not been captured. No column or foreign key can express it: the constraint says a row in STUDENT must have a matching row in ADMISSION, which is the reverse direction of a foreign key.

Enforcing it requires a trigger or a deferred assertion. This is a general limitation: total participation on the "1" side of a relationship, and on both sides of an M:N, is not expressible in standard DDL. Always state this explicitly in an examination answer.

docs.title: 19.4 Worked Mapping 2 — The COMPANY Database
docs.text:
The full textbook example, exercising every step.

Step 1 — strong entity types.

EMPLOYEE   ( Ssn, Fname, Minit, Lname, Bdate, Address, Sex, Salary )
DEPARTMENT ( Dnumber, Dname )            -- Dname also UNIQUE (second candidate key)
PROJECT    ( Pnumber, Pname, Plocation ) -- Pname also UNIQUE

Name was composite → three columns. NumberOfEmployees was derived → omitted. {Dlocations} was multivalued → deferred to step 6.

Step 2 — the weak entity type DEPENDENT, owner EMPLOYEE, partial key DependentName:

DEPENDENT ( Essn, DependentName, Sex, Bdate, Relationship )
-- PK (Essn, DependentName);  Essn FK -> EMPLOYEE(Ssn) ON DELETE CASCADE

Step 3 — the 1:1 relationship MANAGES. DEPARTMENT is total (1,1), EMPLOYEE partial (0,1), so the foreign key goes into DEPARTMENT:

DEPARTMENT ( Dnumber, Dname, MgrSsn, MgrStartDate )
-- MgrSsn FK -> EMPLOYEE(Ssn), NOT NULL

Step 4 — the 1:N relationships. Foreign key on the N side each time:

EMPLOYEE ( Ssn, ..., Dno, SuperSsn )
--   Dno      FK -> DEPARTMENT(Dnumber), NOT NULL   (WORKS_FOR, employee total)
--   SuperSsn FK -> EMPLOYEE(Ssn), NULLable         (SUPERVISION, recursive)
PROJECT ( Pnumber, Pname, Plocation, Dnum )
--   Dnum FK -> DEPARTMENT(Dnumber), NOT NULL       (CONTROLS)

Step 5 — the M:N relationship WORKS_ON with attribute Hours:

WORKS_ON ( Essn, Pno, Hours )    -- PK (Essn, Pno); both are foreign keys

Step 6 — the multivalued attribute {Dlocations}:

DEPT_LOCATIONS ( Dnumber, Dlocation )   -- PK both; Dnumber FK, ON DELETE CASCADE

Step 7 — no n-ary relationships.

Final schema — eight relations:

   EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Fname, Minit, Lname, Bdate, Address, Sex, Salary, Dno, SuperSsn)
   DEPARTMENT(Dnumber, Dname, MgrSsn, MgrStartDate)
   DEPT_LOCATIONS(Dnumber, Dlocation)
   PROJECT(Pnumber, Pname, Plocation, Dnum)
   WORKS_ON(Essn, Pno, Hours)
   DEPENDENT(Essn, DependentName, Sex, Bdate, Relationship)

   Foreign keys:
     EMPLOYEE.Dno        -> DEPARTMENT.Dnumber
     EMPLOYEE.SuperSsn   -> EMPLOYEE.Ssn            (recursive, NULLable)
     DEPARTMENT.MgrSsn   -> EMPLOYEE.Ssn
     DEPT_LOCATIONS.Dnumber -> DEPARTMENT.Dnumber
     PROJECT.Dnum        -> DEPARTMENT.Dnumber
     WORKS_ON.Essn       -> EMPLOYEE.Ssn
     WORKS_ON.Pno        -> PROJECT.Pnumber
     DEPENDENT.Essn      -> EMPLOYEE.Ssn

The circular-reference problem

EMPLOYEE.Dno references DEPARTMENT, and DEPARTMENT.MgrSsn references EMPLOYEE. Neither table can be created with both constraints in place, and neither row can be inserted first.

Solutions: create both tables without the foreign keys and add them afterwards with ALTER TABLE; make one of the columns temporarily nullable and update it after both rows exist; or use DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraints in systems that support them.

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE ( Ssn ..., Dno INT );        -- no FK yet
CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT ( Dnumber ..., MgrSsn ... );
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE   ADD FOREIGN KEY (Dno)    REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(Dnumber);
ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT ADD FOREIGN KEY (MgrSsn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn);

docs.title: 19.5 Mapping EER Constructs (brief)
docs.text:
For a specialisation of superclass C into subclasses S1 ... Sm, four options:

Option Relations created Best when A — multiple relations, superclass and subclasses One for C, one per Si holding the key of C plus the subclass's own attributes Any case; works always. Needs a join to see a subclass entity whole. B — multiple relations, subclasses only One per Si holding all attributes (inherited and own) Specialisation is total and disjoint. No join needed; but common attributes are duplicated across relations. C — single relation with one type attribute One relation with all attributes plus a discriminator Specialisation is disjoint; few subclass-specific attributes. Produces NULLs. D — single relation with several Boolean type attributes One relation with one flag per subclass Specialisation is overlapping. Produces the most NULLs.

docs.title: 19.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. State the seven steps of the ER-to-relational mapping algorithm.

A.

Step Construct Action Primary key 1 Regular entity type Create a relation with all simple attributes (composite → components; derived omitted; multivalued deferred) The chosen key attribute 2 Weak entity type Create a relation with its simple attributes plus the owner's primary key as a foreign key, ON DELETE CASCADE Owner's key + partial key 3 Binary 1:1 Put the other relation's key as a foreign key in one of them, together with any relationship attributes Unchanged 4 Binary 1:N Put the 1-side key as a foreign key in the N-side relation Unchanged 5 Binary M:N Create a new relation holding both keys as foreign keys plus the relationship attributes Both foreign keys combined 6 Multivalued attribute Create a new relation holding the attribute and the owner's key Both together 7 n-ary relationship Create a new relation holding all participants' keys plus relationship attributes All the foreign keys

The order matters: steps 1 and 2 create the relations that steps 3 to 7 refer to.

Solved Question 2

Q. Why does an M:N relationship require a new relation while a 1:N does not?

A. Because of how many values must be stored per entity.

In a 1:N relationship each entity on the N side participates in exactly one relationship instance, so it needs to record exactly one related key value. A single foreign-key column holds it perfectly. (The 1 side would need many values, which is why the foreign key must go on the N side, not the 1 side.)

In an M:N relationship both sides may participate many times. A foreign key in EMPLOYEE could hold only one project; a foreign key in PROJECT only one employee. Storing several would mean putting a set of values in one column, which violates atomicity and hence 1NF (Unit 3, Lesson 1).

The only structure that can represent a set of pairs is a relation of pairs — a junction table with one row per relationship instance:

WORKS_ON ( Essn, Pno, Hours )    -- one row per (employee, project) pair

The composite key (Essn, Pno) enforces that each pair occurs once, which is exactly the meaning of the M:N relationship set as a subset of the Cartesian product.

A second, equally decisive reason: an M:N relationship's own attributes (here Hours) belong to the pair, not to either entity (Unit 2, Lesson 3), so they have nowhere else to live.

Solved Question 3

Q. For a 1:1 relationship, which side should receive the foreign key? Justify with the MANAGES example, and state the two alternative approaches.

A. The side with total participation.

In EMPLOYEE (0,1) MANAGES (1,1) DEPARTMENT: every department has exactly one manager, but only a few employees manage anything.

Foreign key in DEPARTMENT — MgrSsn has a value in every row, so it can be declared NOT NULL. No space is wasted and the constraint is enforceable.

Foreign key in EMPLOYEE — ManagedDept would be NULL for almost every employee. This wastes space, makes the column useless as a constraint, and is the classic "too many NULLs" design smell that usually indicates a missing specialisation.

Two alternative approaches:

  1. Merged relation. If both sides have total participation, the two entity types are in one-to-one correspondence and may be combined into a single relation containing all attributes of both. Use with care: it obscures the conceptual distinction, and it becomes wrong if the participation later relaxes.

  2. Cross-reference (relationship) relation. Create a separate relation holding both keys, exactly as for M:N — but with a UNIQUE constraint on each key column to enforce the 1:1 ratio. This is the right choice when both sides are partial, since it stores a row only for pairs that actually exist and avoids NULLs entirely. Its cost is an extra join.

Solved Question 4

Q. Map this ER diagram to relations, giving full DDL:

HOTEL(HotelID, Name, {Phone}); ROOM numbered 1 upward within a hotel, with Type and Rate; GUEST(GuestID, Name); a BOOKS relationship between GUEST and ROOM with CheckIn and CheckOut, where a guest may book many rooms over time and a room is booked by many guests over time.

A.

Step 1 — HOTEL and GUEST are strong. Step 2 — ROOM is weak: room 1 exists in every hotel, so RoomNo alone identifies nothing. Owner HOTEL, partial key RoomNo, full key (HotelID, RoomNo). Step 5 — BOOKS is M:N, so it becomes a new relation. Because a guest may book the same room again later, the pair is not unique and CheckIn must join the key. Step 6 — {Phone} is multivalued, so it becomes a new relation.

CREATE TABLE HOTEL (
    HotelID VARCHAR(6)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE HOTEL_PHONE (                       -- step 6
    HotelID VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    Phone   CHAR(10)   NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (HotelID, Phone),
    FOREIGN KEY (HotelID) REFERENCES HOTEL(HotelID) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE ROOM (                              -- step 2, weak entity
    HotelID VARCHAR(6)   NOT NULL,
    RoomNo  INT          NOT NULL,
    Type    VARCHAR(20),
    Rate    DECIMAL(8,2) CHECK (Rate > 0),
    PRIMARY KEY (HotelID, RoomNo),
    FOREIGN KEY (HotelID) REFERENCES HOTEL(HotelID) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE GUEST (
    GuestID VARCHAR(8)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name    VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE BOOKS (                             -- step 5, M:N
    GuestID  VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    HotelID  VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    RoomNo   INT        NOT NULL,
    CheckIn  DATE       NOT NULL,
    CheckOut DATE       NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (GuestID, HotelID, RoomNo, CheckIn),
    FOREIGN KEY (GuestID)          REFERENCES GUEST(GuestID) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    FOREIGN KEY (HotelID, RoomNo)  REFERENCES ROOM(HotelID, RoomNo) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    CHECK (CheckOut > CheckIn)
);

Three points worth noting. The foreign key in BOOKS is composite — (HotelID, RoomNo) — because the weak entity's key is composite. CheckIn is part of the primary key because the same guest may return to the same room. And ON DELETE RESTRICT protects the booking history, whereas ROOM and HOTEL_PHONE cascade because they are genuinely existence-dependent on the hotel.

Solved Question 5

Q. Which ER constraints cannot be carried into the relational schema by the mapping? How are they enforced?

A. Three kinds.

1. Total participation on the "1" side of a 1:N, and on either side of an M:N. "Every student must be admitted to at least one course" asserts that a STUDENT row must have a matching ADMISSION row. A foreign key enforces the opposite direction — that every ADMISSION has a matching STUDENT. There is no declarative construct for the required direction. Enforcement: a trigger on STUDENT (and on DELETE from ADMISSION), or a deferred assertion in systems that implement them. Some designs instead enforce it in the application layer at the point of admission.

2. Cardinality upper bounds other than 1 and N. "A student may take at most three societies" cannot be expressed by a key or foreign key. Enforcement: a trigger counting the related rows before an insert.

3. Arbitrary business rules and inter-relation constraints. "A department's manager must be an employee of that department", "an employee's salary may not exceed their supervisor's". These span two tables or two rows and are beyond CHECK, which may reference only its own row. Enforcement: triggers, or assertions.

A fourth, subtler loss: role names and much of the diagram's documentary meaning disappear, surviving only as column names. This is one reason the ER diagram should be kept as part of the system's documentation rather than discarded once the tables exist.

Solved Question 6

Q. Explain the circular-reference problem in the COMPANY schema and give two solutions.

A. EMPLOYEE.Dno is a foreign key to DEPARTMENT, and DEPARTMENT.MgrSsn is a foreign key to EMPLOYEE. The dependency is a cycle, which breaks the ordinary rule "create parents before children" — each table is a parent of the other.

The problem appears twice:

  • At creation time. Whichever table is created first refers to one that does not yet exist, so the CREATE TABLE fails.
  • At insertion time. The first employee cannot be inserted without an existing department, and the first department cannot be inserted without an existing manager.

Solution 1 — create the tables without the foreign keys, then add them.

CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE   ( Ssn VARCHAR(9) PRIMARY KEY, ..., Dno INT );
CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT ( Dnumber INT PRIMARY KEY, ..., MgrSsn VARCHAR(9) );
ALTER TABLE EMPLOYEE   ADD CONSTRAINT fk_e_d FOREIGN KEY (Dno)    REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(Dnumber);
ALTER TABLE DEPARTMENT ADD CONSTRAINT fk_d_e FOREIGN KEY (MgrSsn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn);

Solution 2 — make one column nullable and fill it in afterwards. Insert the department with MgrSsn = NULL, insert its employees, then UPDATE DEPARTMENT SET MgrSsn = .... This works because referential integrity permits a NULL foreign key.

INSERT INTO DEPARTMENT VALUES (5, 'Research', NULL, NULL);
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE   VALUES ('123456789', 'John', ..., 5, NULL);
UPDATE DEPARTMENT SET MgrSsn = '123456789', MgrStartDate = '2020-05-22' WHERE Dnumber = 5;

A third solution, where supported, is to declare the constraints DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, so that both inserts occur inside one transaction and the constraints are checked only at COMMIT. Note that solution 2 conflicts with declaring MgrSsn NOT NULL, so the designer must choose between the stricter constraint and the simpler loading procedure.

docs.title: 19.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. State the seven steps of the mapping algorithm.
  2. What happens to a composite attribute? A derived attribute?
  3. What is the primary key of the relation produced from a weak entity type?
  4. On which side of a 1:N relationship does the foreign key go, and why?
  5. Why can an M:N relationship not be mapped with a foreign key?
  6. What is the primary key of the relation produced from a multivalued attribute?
  7. Name one ER constraint that cannot be mapped to DDL.

B. Mapping problems — give full DDL for each

  1. DEPARTMENT(Dno, Dname) 1:N EMPLOYEE(Eno, Ename), employee total.
  2. STUDENT M:N SOCIETY with Dateofenrollment.
  3. PERSON(PID, Name) 1:1 PASSPORT(PassportNo, Expiry), passport total.
  4. COURSE(SID, Cname) with weak entity SECTION numbered within the course, having Room and Timing.
  5. EMPLOYEE with multivalued {Skill} and composite Name(First, Last).
  6. EMPLOYEE recursive 1:N SUPERVISES with roles supervisor / supervisee.
  7. Ternary DOCTOR – PATIENT – DRUG (PRESCRIBES) with Dosage and Date.
  8. The full hospital diagram of Unit 2, Lesson 4 (wards, beds, patients, doctors).
  9. The full airline diagram from Unit 2 exercise 11.

C. Analytical

  1. For the college schema, write the trigger (in pseudocode or SQL) that would enforce the total participation of STUDENT in TAKES_ADMISSION. What events must it fire on?
  2. A designer maps a 1:1 relationship by putting the foreign key on the partial side. 95 per cent of rows are NULL. Explain the cost and give the correct design.
  3. Explain when the merged-relation approach to a 1:1 relationship is correct, and give a case where it would be wrong.
  4. Show that mapping a ternary relationship as three binary relationships loses information, using concrete tuples.
  5. Take the BORROWS example. Explain precisely why (MemberID, ISBN) is an insufficient primary key, and construct the two rows that would collide.
  6. Compare the four EER specialisation mapping options for STUDENT specialised into UG and PG, and recommend one with justification.
  7. Explain why a schema derived by this algorithm is usually already in 3NF. Give an ER diagram whose mapping is not in 3NF, and say what went wrong at the conceptual stage.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A derived attribute becomes a column in the relation.
  2. Every relationship type becomes a relation.
  3. A weak entity's relation has a composite primary key.
  4. The foreign key for a 1:N relationship may be placed on either side.
  5. A multivalued attribute becomes several columns.
  6. Total participation is always enforceable with a NOT NULL foreign key.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. It is omitted and computed on demand; storing it creates redundancy that goes stale.
  2. False. Only M:N and n-ary relationships become relations. 1:1 and 1:N become foreign keys.
  3. True. The owner's primary key together with the partial key.
  4. False. It must go on the N side, where each entity participates exactly once and so has exactly one value to store.
  5. False. It becomes a separate relation — several columns would violate 1NF and fix the number of values in advance.
  6. False. NOT NULL on a foreign key enforces total participation of the child (the N side). Total participation of the parent — "every student must have an admission" — needs a trigger or assertion.

Lesson Summary

  • Seven steps: strong entities → relations; weak entities → relations with owner key + partial key; 1:1 → foreign key on the total side; 1:N → foreign key on the N side; M:N → new relation; multivalued attributes → new relation; n-ary → new relation.
  • Composite attributes become columns; derived attributes are omitted.
  • An M:N junction table's key is both foreign keys — plus a distinguishing attribute if the pair may recur.
  • Total participation on the parent side, cardinality bounds, and cross-table business rules cannot be mapped — they need triggers or assertions.
  • Watch for circular foreign-key references; break them with ALTER TABLE or a nullable column.
  • A schema produced by this algorithm from a good ER diagram is usually already close to 3NF.

docs.title: Lesson 20: Functional Dependencies and Closure
docs.text:
Armstrong's axioms, attribute closure, and minimal cover

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 5: Database Design · 10 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 14.2, 14.3

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define a functional dependency precisely, and identify FDs from a description.
  2. State and apply Armstrong's axioms and the derived rules.
  3. Compute the attribute closure X⁺ mechanically and reliably.
  4. Use X⁺ to test whether X is a superkey, and whether an FD is implied.
  5. Compute a minimal (canonical) cover.

docs.title: 20.1 Functional Dependency
docs.text:
Functional dependency

Let R be a relation schema and X, Y ⊆ R. The functional dependency

X → Y (read "X functionally determines Y", or "Y is functionally dependent on X")

holds if, for any legal relation state of R, whenever two tuples agree on X they must also agree on Y:

for all tuples t1, t2 in r(R): if t1[X] = t2[X] then t1[Y] = t2[Y].

X is the determinant; Y is the dependent.

An FD is a property of the MEANING, not of the data

An FD is a constraint — an assertion about every possible legal state, present and future — derived from the semantics of the mini-world.

You may disprove an FD by finding two tuples in the current data that agree on X and differ on Y. You can never prove one from data alone: today's data may merely happen to satisfy it.

Example. If today no two students share a name, the data satisfies Name → Rollno. But the FD is false, because two students could share a name. Only the mini-world's rules decide.

docs.title: Reading an FD
docs.text: FD English Rollno → Name Each roll number belongs to exactly one student, so it determines the name. SID → Cname, TotalSeats A course id determines its name and seat count. Rollno, SID → Dateofadmission A student-course pair determines one admission date. Name → Rollno False — two students may share a name.

docs.title: Trivial, non-trivial, completely non-trivial
docs.text:
Classification

  • Trivial: X → Y where Y ⊆ X. Always true, carries no information. AB → A.
  • Non-trivial: X → Y where Y ⊄ X (at least one attribute of Y is outside X). AB → BC.
  • Completely non-trivial: X → Y where X ∩ Y = ∅. AB → C.

docs.title: FDs and keys
docs.text:
The link that makes everything work

K is a superkey of R if and only if K → R — that is, K functionally determines every attribute.

K is a candidate key if additionally no proper subset of K determines R.

This is the bridge between the key theory of Unit 3 and the normalisation of Lessons 3 to 5, and it is what makes candidate keys computable rather than guessed.

docs.title: 20.2 Armstrong's Axioms
docs.text:
The three axioms (sound and complete)

Let X, Y, Z be sets of attributes of R.

A1 — Reflexivity. If Y ⊆ X then X → Y. (This generates exactly the trivial dependencies.)

A2 — Augmentation. If X → Y then XZ → YZ, for any Z. (Adding the same attributes to both sides preserves the dependency.)

A3 — Transitivity. If X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.

Sound and complete

Sound — every FD derivable by the axioms is genuinely implied by F; the rules never produce a false dependency.

Complete — every FD implied by F is derivable by the axioms; nothing implied is beyond reach.

Together: the axioms derive exactly the set of implied dependencies — no more and no fewer. This is why F⁺ is well defined.

docs.title: Derived rules (provable from A1–A3, and used constantly)
docs.text:
Rule Statement Proof sketch Union (additivity) If X → Y and X → Z then X → YZ Augment X→Y by X giving X→XY; augment X→Z by Y giving XY→YZ; transitivity. Decomposition (projectivity) If X → YZ then X → Y and X → Z YZ → Y by reflexivity; transitivity with X → YZ. Pseudotransitivity If X → Y and WY → Z then WX → Z Augment X→Y by W giving WX→WY; transitivity with WY→Z. Composition If X → Y and Z → W then XZ → YW Augment each, then combine.

Two rules that do NOT hold

X → YZ does give X → Y (decomposition on the right is valid).

But XY → Z does not give X → Z or Y → Z. Decomposition on the left is invalid.

Counter-example. Rollno, SID → Dateofadmission is true, but Rollno → Dateofadmission is false — a student admitted to two courses has two dates.

Similarly, X → Z and Y → Z do not give XY → Z... they actually do, by augmentation; but the converse (splitting the left) fails. Remember: right sides split, left sides do not.

docs.title: Closure of a set of dependencies
docs.text:
F⁺

The closure F⁺ of a set of dependencies F is the set of all FDs implied by F, obtained by applying Armstrong's axioms until nothing new appears.

F⁺ is usually enormous (exponential in the number of attributes), so it is almost never computed. Instead we compute attribute closure, which answers the questions we actually care about.

docs.title: 20.3 Attribute Closure — the Workhorse
docs.text:
X⁺

The attribute closure X⁺ of a set of attributes X under F is the set of all attributes functionally determined by X:

X⁺ = { A : X → A is in F⁺ }

The algorithm

result := X
repeat
    for each functional dependency  Y -> Z  in F:
        if  Y ⊆ result  and  Z ⊄ result  then
            result := result ∪ Z
until result does not change
return result

Read it as: "start with X; whenever you already have everything on the left of a dependency, you may add everything on its right; repeat until stuck."

docs.title: What X⁺ lets you decide
docs.text: Question Test Is X → Y implied by F? Is Y ⊆ X⁺? Is X a superkey? Is X⁺ = R? Is X a candidate key? X⁺ = R, and for every proper subset X' of X, X'⁺ ≠ R. Are F and G equivalent? Every FD of F follows from G, and vice versa (checked by closures).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = { A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A }.

Compute A⁺:

Step Dependency used Added Result 0 start A {A} 1 A → BC (A ⊆ {A}) B, C {A,B,C} 2 B → D (B ⊆ {A,B,C}) D {A,B,C,D} 3 CD → E (CD ⊆ {A,B,C,D}) E {A,B,C,D,E} 4 E → A — A already present — no change

A⁺ = {A,B,C,D,E} = R, so A is a superkey, and since it is a single attribute it is minimal, so A is a candidate key.

Compute B⁺: start {B}; B → D gives {B,D}; no dependency's left side is now contained in {B,D} (A→BC needs A; CD→E needs C; E→A needs E). So B⁺ = {B,D} — B is not a superkey.

Compute CD⁺: start {C,D}; CD → E gives {C,D,E}; E → A gives {A,C,D,E}; A → BC gives {A,B,C,D,E}. So CD⁺ = R — superkey. Minimal? C⁺ = {C} and D⁺ = {D}, neither is R, so CD is a candidate key.

Compute E⁺: {E} → E→A gives {A,E} → A→BC gives {A,B,C,E} → B→D gives all. E is a candidate key.

Compute BC⁺: {B,C} → B→D gives {B,C,D} → CD→E gives {B,C,D,E} → E→A gives all. Superkey. B⁺={B,D}, C⁺={C} — neither is R, so BC is a candidate key.

Candidate keys of R: A, E, BC, CD.

Checking whether an FD is implied

Is AB → E implied by F? AB⁺ = start {A,B} → A→BC gives {A,B,C} → B→D gives {A,B,C,D} → CD→E gives all. Since E ∈ AB⁺, yes.

Is D → A implied? D⁺ = {D}. A ∉ D⁺, so no.

This single technique replaces any attempt to enumerate F⁺.

docs.title: 20.4 Equivalence and Covers
docs.text:
Cover and equivalence

F covers G if every FD in G can be inferred from F — that is, G ⊆ F⁺.

F and G are equivalent (F ≡ G) if F covers G and G covers F. Equivalent sets impose exactly the same constraints.

To test F ≡ G: for each X → Y in G, compute X⁺ under F and check Y ⊆ X⁺; then repeat in the other direction. There is no need to build either closure of dependencies.

docs.title: Minimal (canonical) cover
docs.text:
Minimal cover

A set F of dependencies is minimal if:

  1. Every dependency has a single attribute on its right-hand side.
  2. No dependency has an extraneous attribute on its left: removing any attribute from X in X → A yields a set no longer equivalent to F.
  3. No dependency is redundant: removing any whole dependency yields a set no longer equivalent to F.

A minimal cover of F is a minimal set equivalent to F. It need not be unique.

The algorithm — the order of the steps matters

Step 1. Split every right-hand side into single attributes. (Valid by the decomposition rule.)

Step 2. For each X → A with |X| > 1, and each attribute B ∈ X: if A ∈ (X − B)⁺ computed under the current set, then B is extraneous — remove it.

Step 3. For each dependency f in the current set: if f is still implied by the set without f, remove f.

Step 1 first, because splitting exposes extraneous attributes; step 2 before step 3, because reducing left sides can make dependencies redundant.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
F = { A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C }

Step 1 — split right sides: A → B, A → C, B → C, A → B (duplicate, drop one), AB → C Current: { A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → C }

Step 2 — extraneous left attributes. Only AB → C has more than one attribute on the left. Is A extraneous? Compute B⁺ under the current set: {B, C}. C ∈ B⁺, so yes — AB → C reduces to B → C, which is already present. Current: { A → B, A → C, B → C }

Step 3 — redundant dependencies.

  • Remove A → B: is B ∈ A⁺ under {A → C, B → C}? A⁺ = {A, C}. No — keep A → B.
  • Remove A → C: is C ∈ A⁺ under {A → B, B → C}? A⁺ = {A, B, C}. Yes — remove it.
  • Remove B → C: is C ∈ B⁺ under {A → B}? B⁺ = {B}. No — keep.

Minimal cover: { A → B, B → C }.

Minimal covers are not unique

For F = { A → B, B → A, A → C, B → C } two different minimal covers exist: { A → B, B → A, A → C } and { A → B, B → A, B → C }.

Both are correct. An examination answer should show the working, which justifies whichever is obtained.

Why minimal covers matter: the 3NF synthesis algorithm (Lesson 5) builds one relation per dependency of a minimal cover. A smaller cover therefore yields a smaller, better schema.

docs.title: 20.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define a functional dependency. Can an FD be proved from a relation state? Justify.

A. For X, Y ⊆ R, the functional dependency X → Y holds if in every legal state of R, any two tuples agreeing on X also agree on Y.

An FD cannot be proved from a relation state; it can only be disproved.

A relation state is a snapshot. An FD is a constraint on all possible states, present and future. Observing that a snapshot satisfies X → Y shows only that no counter-example happens to be present today.

Illustration. In a small college the data may show that no two students share a name:

Rollno Name X2019 Ankit Sharma X2020 Riya Verma

This state satisfies Name → Rollno. But the FD is false, because the mini-world permits two students called Ankit Sharma; admitting one tomorrow would violate it. Declaring it would wrongly reject a legitimate admission.

Disproof, by contrast, is conclusive. Two tuples agreeing on X and differing on Y demonstrate that the constraint does not hold, since a legal state violating it exists.

The practical conclusion: FDs are obtained from the semantics of the mini-world — by asking the users — not by inspecting sample data. Sample data is useful only for catching FDs you asserted wrongly.

Solved Question 2

Q. State Armstrong's axioms. Prove the union and pseudotransitivity rules from them. What is meant by saying the axioms are sound and complete?

A. A1 Reflexivity: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y. A2 Augmentation: if X → Y then XZ → YZ. A3 Transitivity: if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.

Union: given X → Y and X → Z, prove X → YZ.

Step Justification 1. X → Y given 2. X → XY augment (1) with X: XX → YX, and XX = X 3. X → Z given 4. XY → YZ augment (3) with Y 5. X → YZ transitivity of (2) and (4)

Pseudotransitivity: given X → Y and WY → Z, prove WX → Z.

Step Justification 1. X → Y given 2. WX → WY augment (1) with W 3. WY → Z given 4. WX → Z transitivity of (2) and (3)

Soundness means every FD derivable using A1–A3 is genuinely implied by F — the rules never generate a dependency that some legal state violates.

Completeness means every FD implied by F is derivable using A1–A3 — no implied dependency is out of reach.

Together they establish that the axioms generate exactly F⁺, which is what makes F⁺ well defined and makes attribute closure a correct decision procedure for implication.

Solved Question 3

Q. For R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}, compute A⁺, B⁺, CD⁺, AB⁺, and find all candidate keys.

A.

A⁺: {A} →(A→BC) {A,B,C} →(B→D) {A,B,C,D} →(CD→E) {A,B,C,D,E}. A⁺ = R.

B⁺: {B} →(B→D) {B,D}. No further left side is contained. B⁺ = {B,D}.

CD⁺: {C,D} →(CD→E) {C,D,E} →(E→A) {A,C,D,E} →(A→BC) {A,B,C,D,E}. CD⁺ = R.

AB⁺: contains A⁺, so = R (but not minimal, since A alone suffices).

Candidate keys. Test each set: it is a candidate key if its closure is R and no proper subset's closure is R.

Set Closure Superkey? Minimal? Candidate key? A R yes single attribute yes B {B,D} no — no C {C} no — no D {D} no — no E R yes single attribute yes BC R yes B⁺≠R, C⁺≠R yes CD R yes C⁺≠R, D⁺≠R yes AB, AE, … R yes contain A or E no BD, CE, DE {B,D}, R… — E⁺=R so CE, DE contain a key no

Candidate keys: A, E, BC, CD. Prime attributes: A, B, C, D, E — all of them. Non-prime attributes: none. (This is why R turns out to be in 3NF despite B → D violating BCNF — see Lesson 4.)

Solved Question 4

Q. Show that decomposition on the left-hand side is invalid: XY → Z does not imply X → Z. Give a concrete counter-example.

A. The rule fails because X alone may not determine enough to fix Z; the dependency asserts something about the combination.

Counter-example from the college database. The true dependency is

Rollno, SID → Dateofadmission

— a student-course pair has exactly one admission date. Suppose Rollno → Dateofadmission also held. Consider:

Rollno SID Dateofadmission X2019 CS01 2019-07-15 X2019 MA02 2019-08-01

This state is legal: the two tuples differ on (Rollno, SID), so Rollno, SID → Dateofadmission is not violated. But the two tuples agree on Rollno and differ on Dateofadmission, so Rollno → Dateofadmission is violated.

A legal state satisfying the premise while violating the conclusion is exactly a proof that the inference is invalid.

Contrast with the right-hand side, where decomposition is valid: X → YZ implies X → Y, because YZ → Y by reflexivity and transitivity applies. Two tuples agreeing on X must agree on all of YZ, hence in particular on Y.

Mnemonic: right sides split; left sides do not. Getting this backwards is one of the commonest errors in normalisation questions.

Solved Question 5

Q. Compute a minimal cover of F = { AB → C, A → B, B → A, C → AB } over R(A,B,C). Show every step.

A.

Step 1 — single attributes on the right. AB → C, A → B, B → A, C → A, C → B

Step 2 — remove extraneous left attributes. Only AB → C qualifies.

  • Is B extraneous? Compute A⁺ under the current set: {A} →(A→B) {A,B} →(AB→C) {A,B,C}. Since C ∈ A⁺, yes — replace AB → C by A → C.
  • Now the set is { A → C, A → B, B → A, C → A, C → B }. No left side has more than one attribute, so step 2 is complete.

Step 3 — remove redundant dependencies, testing each in turn against the others.

Candidate Test Verdict A → C A⁺ under {A→B, B→A, C→A, C→B} = {A,B}. C ∉ keep A → B A⁺ under {A→C, B→A, C→A, C→B} = {A,C,B}. B ∈ remove B → A B⁺ under {A→C, C→A, C→B} = {B}. A ∉ keep C → A C⁺ under {A→C, B→A, C→B} = {C,B,A}. A ∈ remove C → B C⁺ under {A→C, B→A} = {C}. B ∉ keep

Minimal cover: { A → C, B → A, C → B }.

Verification that it is equivalent to the original: under the cover, A⁺ = {A,C,B} = R, B⁺ = {B,A,C} = R, C⁺ = {C,B,A} = R. So every original dependency — AB → C, A → B, B → A, C → AB — is recovered, and the candidate keys A, B and C are unchanged.

Note the elegant cyclic result A → C → B → A, which correctly captures that all three attributes determine one another.

Solved Question 6

Q. Are F = {A → B, B → C, A → C} and G = {A → B, B → C} equivalent? Prove it.

A. Two sets are equivalent when each covers the other. Test each dependency of one against closures computed under the other.

Does G cover F? For each FD of F, compute the left side's closure under G:

FD of F Closure under G Right side included? A → B A⁺ = {A} →(A→B) {A,B} →(B→C) {A,B,C} B ∈ — yes B → C B⁺ = {B} →(B→C) {B,C} C ∈ — yes A → C A⁺ = {A,B,C} C ∈ — yes

Every FD of F follows from G, so G covers F.

Does F cover G? G ⊆ F literally — both its dependencies appear in F — so trivially yes.

Therefore F ≡ G.

The dependency A → C in F is redundant: it is derivable from A → B and B → C by transitivity. G is in fact a minimal cover of F.

Note on method. It was never necessary to construct F⁺ or G⁺, which would be exponentially large. Testing implication by attribute closure — "is the right side inside the left side's closure?" — is the standard and only practical technique.

docs.title: 20.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define a functional dependency.
  2. Why can an FD not be proved from a relation state?
  3. State Armstrong's axioms.
  4. What does it mean for the axioms to be sound and complete?
  5. Distinguish trivial from completely non-trivial FDs.
  6. State the test for X being a superkey.
  7. What are the three conditions for a set of FDs to be minimal?

B. Computation

  1. For R(A,B,C,D) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}, compute A⁺, B⁺, C⁺, D⁺ and find all candidate keys.
  2. For R(A,B,C,D,E,F) with F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A, F → A}, compute A⁺, F⁺, BC⁺ and find all candidate keys.
  3. For R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A, D → E}, find all candidate keys.
  4. For R(P,Q,R,S,T) with F = {P → QR, RS → T, Q → S, T → P}, find all candidate keys.
  5. Determine whether each is implied by F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E}: a. AC → D b. A → E c. AC → E d. B → E e. ABC → DE
  6. Compute a minimal cover of F = {A → BC, B → C, AB → D, ABC → D}.
  7. Compute a minimal cover of F = {AB → C, C → A, BC → D, ACD → B, D → EG, BE → C, CG → BD, CE → AG}.
  8. Are F = {A → B, AB → C, D → AC, D → E} and G = {A → BC, D → AE} equivalent? Show your working.

C. Proof and analysis

  1. Prove the decomposition rule from Armstrong's axioms.
  2. Prove the composition rule: if X → Y and Z → W then XZ → YW.
  3. Give a counter-example showing X → Z and Y → Z do not imply X → Y.
  4. Explain why F⁺ is not computed in practice, and what is computed instead.
  5. Show that a minimal cover need not be unique, by giving a set with two different minimal covers.
  6. From this description, write down all the FDs: > "Each student has one roll number, name and date of birth. Each course has one identifier, name, seat count and teacher-in-charge. A student may be admitted to several courses; each admission has one date. Each course is taught in one department, and each department has one head."
  7. A colleague asserts Name → Rollno because the current 400 rows satisfy it. Explain, with reference to the definition, why this reasoning is invalid, and describe what evidence would be needed instead.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. X → Y can be verified by examining the current relation state.
  2. Every superkey K satisfies K → R.
  3. AB → C implies A → C.
  4. A → BC implies A → B.
  5. A minimal cover is unique.
  6. Armstrong's axioms are sound but not complete.
  7. If X⁺ = R then X is a candidate key.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. A state can only disprove an FD; an FD constrains all possible states.
  2. True. That is the definition of a superkey in FD terms.
  3. False. Left-side decomposition is invalid. Counter-example: Rollno, SID → Dateofadmission while Rollno → Dateofadmission is false.
  4. True. Right-side decomposition is valid, by reflexivity (BC → B) and transitivity.
  5. False. Different orders of removal can yield different, equally valid minimal covers.
  6. False. They are both sound and complete — they generate exactly F⁺.
  7. False. It makes X a superkey. It is a candidate key only if it is also minimal.

Lesson Summary

  • An FD X → Y constrains every legal state; data can disprove one but never prove one.
  • Armstrong's axioms — reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity — are sound and complete, and yield union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity.
  • Right sides split; left sides do not. X → YZ gives X → Y; XY → Z gives nothing about X → Z.
  • X⁺ is the workhorse: it tests implication (Y ⊆ X⁺), superkeys (X⁺ = R) and candidate keys (superkey + minimal).
  • Two FD sets are equivalent if each covers the other — checked with attribute closures, never by building F⁺.
  • A minimal cover has single-attribute right sides, no extraneous left attributes and no redundant FDs. It need not be unique, and it drives 3NF synthesis.

docs.title: Lesson 25: Indexing
docs.text:
Single-level, multi-level and B+-tree index structures

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 6: Data Storage and Indexes · 4 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 17

Learning Outcomes

  1. Explain the need for indexes and the cost they impose.
  2. Distinguish primary, clustering and secondary indexes.
  3. Distinguish dense from sparse indexes and say which must be which.
  4. Compute the size and search cost of a single-level and a multi-level index.
  5. Describe the structure and advantages of a B+-tree.

docs.title: 25.1 The Need for Indexes
docs.text:
Lesson 1 ended with the decisive limitation: a file can be physically organised on only one field. A STUDENT file sorted on Rollno gives no help whatever to WHERE Name = 'Ankit Sharma', which still costs a linear scan.

Index

An index is an auxiliary access structure on a file, used to speed up the retrieval of records that satisfy a condition on an indexed field. It is stored separately from the data file, and the data file itself is unchanged.

An index entry is a pair <field value, pointer>, where the pointer is a block address or a record address.

Because an index is smaller than the data file — it holds only one field and a pointer, not whole records — searching it costs far fewer block accesses.

The idea is exactly that of a book index: rather than reading every page to find "normalisation", you consult a short alphabetical list at the back and go straight to page 214.

A file may have any number of indexes, on any number of fields. That is how a single physical arrangement can serve many different queries.

Indexes are not free

  • Storage. Each index consumes space, sometimes a substantial fraction of the table.
  • Write cost. Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update every index on the table. A table with eight indexes has slow writes.
  • Maintenance. Indexes fragment and need periodic rebuilding.

So indexes trade write speed and space for read speed. Index the columns that are actually queried, and no others.

docs.title: 25.2 Types of Single-Level Ordered Index
docs.text:
An index file is itself a sorted file of <value, pointer> entries. Three kinds, distinguished by the field they are built on.

The three types

Primary index — built on the ordering key field of a sorted data file. That is, the field is both the physical ordering field and a key (unique). → Sparse: one entry per block, holding that block's anchor record (its first record).

Clustering index — built on the ordering field of a sorted data file where the field is not a key (values repeat). → Sparse: one entry per distinct value, pointing at the first block containing it.

Secondary index — built on a non-ordering field, key or not. The data file may be sorted on something else, or be a heap. → Dense: one entry per record (or per distinct value, with a level of indirection).

The decision tree

   Is the index field the field the FILE IS SORTED ON?
        |                                  |
       YES                                NO
        |                                  |
   Is it unique (a key)?              SECONDARY index
        |            |                (must be DENSE)
       YES          NO
        |            |
   PRIMARY      CLUSTERING
   (sparse)      (sparse)

   A file can have AT MOST ONE primary or clustering index
   (it is sorted on only one field), but ANY NUMBER of secondary indexes.

docs.title: Primary index
docs.text:
INDEX FILE (sparse: one entry per data block)
   +----------+---------+                DATA FILE (sorted on Rollno)
   | Rollno   | pointer |                +-------------------------+
   +----------+---------+                | X2001 Ankit    ...      | block 1
   | X2001    |    ------------------>   | X2002 Riya     ...      |
   | X2011    |    -------------.        | X2003 Sana     ...      |
   | X2021    |    ---------.    \       +-------------------------+
   +----------+---------+     \    `-->  | X2011 Arjun    ...      | block 2
    3 entries for 3 blocks     \         | X2012 Aditi    ...      |
                                \        | X2013 Rahul    ...      |
                                 \       +-------------------------+
                                  `-->   | X2021 Neha     ...      | block 3
                                         | X2022 Vikram   ...      |
                                         +-------------------------+
   The indexed value is the ANCHOR RECORD -- the first record of each block.

Search: binary-search the index for the largest anchor value ≤ the target, follow the pointer, then search within that one block.

docs.title: Clustering index
docs.text:
The ordering field is not unique, so several records share a value.

   INDEX (one entry per DISTINCT value)   DATA FILE (sorted on Coursetype)
   +------------+---------+               +-------------------------+
   | Coursetype | pointer |               | Fulltime  CS01 ...      | block 1
   +------------+---------+               | Fulltime  CH01 ...      |
   | Fulltime   |   --------------->      | Fulltime  PH01 ...      |
   | Parttime   |   ------------.         +-------------------------+
   +------------+---------+      `---->   | Parttime  MA02 ...      | block 2
                                          | Parttime  EN03 ...      |
                                          +-------------------------+
   Points at the FIRST block containing that value; the rest follow.

docs.title: Secondary index
docs.text:
The data file is not sorted on this field, so the index must be dense — every record needs its own entry, because nothing can be inferred about neighbours.

   SECONDARY INDEX on Name (dense, sorted by Name)
   +-----------------+---------+          DATA FILE (sorted on Rollno)
   | Name            | pointer |          +-------------------------+
   +-----------------+---------+          | X2001 Ankit    ...      |
   | Aditi Rao       |  --------------.   | X2002 Riya     ...      |
   | Ankit Sharma    |  ---------.     \  | X2003 Sana     ...      |
   | Arjun Nair      |  ------.   \     \ +-------------------------+
   | Riya Verma      |  ---.   \   \     `| X2011 Arjun    ...      |
   | Sana Iqbal      |  -.  \   \   `-----| X2012 Aditi    ...      |
   +-----------------+---+  |   \         | X2013 Rahul    ...      |
    ONE ENTRY PER RECORD    |    `--------+-------------------------+
    -- must be DENSE                      (order is unrelated to Name)

Why a secondary index must be dense

A sparse index works only because the data file is sorted on the indexed field: knowing where block k starts tells you that every value between anchor k and anchor k+1 is inside block k.

For a non-ordering field that inference is impossible — records with adjacent Name values may be in any blocks at all. So every record needs its own index entry.

Consequences: a secondary index is larger (one entry per record, not per block) and therefore costlier to search and maintain — but it provides an access path that would otherwise not exist at all.

docs.title: Dense and sparse
docs.text:
Dense vs sparse

Dense index — an index entry for every record (or every distinct value) in the data file. Sparse (non-dense) index — an index entry for only some records, typically one per block.

Dense Sparse Entries One per record One per block Size Larger Smaller Search Slightly faster Slightly slower (must then scan within the block) Requires the file to be sorted on the field? No Yes Used by Secondary indexes Primary and clustering indexes Can answer "does this value exist?" without touching the data file Yes No

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Primary Clustering Secondary Index field Ordering key Ordering non-key Non-ordering File sorted on it Yes Yes No Dense or sparse Sparse Sparse Dense Entries One per block One per distinct value One per record How many per file At most one At most one Any number Size Smallest Small Largest

docs.title: 25.3 Index Size and Search Cost
docs.text:
The calculation

Let r = records, R = record size, B = block size, V = index field size, P = pointer size.

Data file: bfr = floor(B/R), b = ceil(r/bfr).

Index: entry size Ri = V + P; index blocking factor bfri = floor(B/Ri). Number of index entries ri = b for a primary index (one per block), or r for a dense secondary index. Index blocks bi = ceil(ri / bfri).

Search cost = ceil(log₂ bi) + 1 — a binary search of the index, then one access to the data block.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
r = 30,000 records, R = 100 bytes, B = 1024 bytes, V = 9 bytes, P = 6 bytes.

Without an index (heap): bfr = 10, b = 3000 blocks. Linear search averages 1500 block accesses.

With a primary index (file sorted on the key):

  • Entry size Ri = 9 + 6 = 15 bytes; bfri = floor(1024/15) = 68 entries per block.
  • Entries ri = b = 3000 (one per data block); bi = ceil(3000/68) = **45** index blocks.
  • Search = ceil(log₂ 45) + 1 = 6 + 1 = **7** block accesses.

Improvement: 1500 → 7, over 200-fold.

(For comparison, a binary search of the sorted data file alone would cost ceil(log₂ 3000) = 12. The index wins because it is 45 blocks rather than 3000.)

With a dense secondary index on a non-ordering field:

  • Entries ri = r = 30,000; bi = ceil(30000/68) = **442** index blocks.
  • Search = ceil(log₂ 442) + 1 = 9 + 1 = **10** block accesses.

Still a 150-fold improvement on the linear scan, though costlier than the primary index because the index is ten times larger.

docs.title: 25.4 Multi-Level Indexes
docs.text:
The index is itself a sorted file, so it can be indexed in turn.

Multi-level index

Treat the index as a data file and build a primary index over it — the second level. Repeat until the top level fits in a single block.

Because each level is a sparse index over the level below, each level shrinks by a factor of fo, the fan-out (the index blocking factor bfri).

Number of levels t = ceil( log_fo (ri) ). Search cost = t + 1 block accesses.

                    +-----------+
   LEVEL 3 (top)    |  1 block  |            <-- fits in one block: stop
                    +-----+-----+
              +-----------+-----------+
              |           |           |
   LEVEL 2  +---+       +---+       +---+     1 block  (45/68 rounded up)
            +-+-+       +-+-+       +-+-+
             ...         ...         ...
   LEVEL 1  [45 blocks: the primary index]
             ...         ...         ...
   DATA     [3000 blocks, sorted]

   Search: 1 (top) + 1 (level 2) + 1 (level 1) + 1 (data) = 4 accesses
   compared with 7 for the single-level index and 1500 for a scan.

docs.title: Worked example continued
docs.text:
The primary index had bi = 45 blocks with fan-out fo = 68.

  • Level 1: 45 blocks (the index itself).
  • Level 2: ceil(45/68) = 1 block — already a single block, so stop.
  • Levels t = 2. Search cost = 2 + 1 = **3** block accesses.

Summary of the whole progression:

Method Block accesses Linear scan of a heap 1500 Binary search of the sorted file 12 Single-level primary index 7 Multi-level index 3

Why the improvement is logarithmic in the fan-out

A binary search halves the search space each step: log₂ n. A multi-level index divides it by the fan-out each step: log_fo n.

With fo = 68, each level does the work of log₂ 68 ≈ 6 binary-search steps. That is the entire advantage of tree-structured indexes, and it is why they are built with high fan-out — which in turn is why internal nodes are kept as small as possible.

docs.title: 25.5 B+-Trees
docs.text:
A static multi-level index suffers the same insertion problem as a sorted file: inserting a record may force the whole index to be reorganised. B-trees and B+-trees are dynamic multi-level indexes that keep themselves balanced.

B+-tree

A balanced tree in which:

  • Internal nodes hold only search keys and tree pointers — no data pointers. They act purely as a directory.
  • Leaf nodes hold all the search key values, each with its data pointer.
  • Leaves are linked together in a chain, in key order.
  • Every leaf is at the same depth — the tree is always balanced.
  • Each node is kept at least half full, guaranteeing the depth bound.
                        +-------------+
   INTERNAL (directory) |   30  |  60 |            keys only, no data pointers
                        +--+---+---+--+
              +------------+   |   +------------+
              |                |                |
        +-----------+   +-------------+   +-----------+
        | 10 | 20    |  | 40 | 50      |  | 70 | 80   |
        +-+--+--+--+-+  +-+--+--+---+--+  +-+--+--+---+
          |     |         |     |            |     |
   LEAVES (all data pointers live here, and leaves are CHAINED)
   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+   +--------+
   |10,20->o|->|30,40->o |->|50,60->o |->|70,80->o |->|90,95->o |
   +---+----+   +---+----+   +---+----+   +---+----+   +---+----+
       |            |            |            |            |
       v            v            v            v            v
                  D A T A    R E C O R D S

   The leaf chain makes a RANGE SCAN a simple sequential walk.

docs.title: B-tree vs B+-tree
docs.text:
B-tree B+-tree Data pointers In every node Leaf nodes only Key duplication A key appears once Keys may appear in internal nodes and leaves Fan-out Lower (nodes carry data pointers too) Higher — so the tree is shallower Leaves linked No Yes Range queries Awkward — requires tree traversal Efficient — walk the leaf chain Search cost Varies; may end early at an internal node Uniform — always reaches a leaf

Why B+-trees won

  1. Higher fan-out, shallower tree. Internal nodes carry only keys and tree pointers, not data pointers, so more entries fit in a block. With fan-out 100, three levels index a million records; four levels index a hundred million. Almost any lookup costs three or four block accesses.

  2. Efficient range queries. WHERE Rollno BETWEEN 'X2019' AND 'X2050' descends to the first matching leaf once, then follows the leaf chain sequentially. A B-tree would have to traverse up and down repeatedly.

  3. Uniform cost. Every search reaches a leaf, so performance is predictable — valuable for the query optimiser's cost estimates.

Consequence: the B+-tree is the default index structure in essentially every relational DBMS, and it is what CREATE INDEX builds unless you ask for something else.

docs.title: Insertion, deletion and balance
docs.text:
Insertion. Find the correct leaf and insert in order. If the leaf overflows, split it into two, and promote the middle key to the parent. If the parent overflows, split it too — the split may propagate to the root, and splitting the root increases the tree's height by one. This is the only way a B+-tree grows, which is why every leaf stays at the same depth.

Deletion. Remove the entry. If the node falls below half full (underflow), borrow an entry from a sibling, or merge with a sibling and remove a key from the parent. Merging may propagate upward and can reduce the height.

The half-full guarantee is what bounds the height at log_(fo/2) n, so performance never degrades however the data arrives.

Practical consequences you can see in SQL

Composite index order matters. An index on (SID, Dateofadmission) is ordered by SID first. It therefore serves WHERE SID = ? and WHERE SID = ? AND Dateofadmission = ?, but not WHERE Dateofadmission = ? alone — a B+-tree searches by leading prefix.

A leading wildcard defeats the index. LIKE 'A%' can descend the tree; LIKE '%Sharma' cannot, because the tree is ordered by prefix.

Functions on the column defeat the index. WHERE YEAR(Dateofbirth) = 2001 must compute the function for every row. This is the sargability rule of Unit 4, Lesson 3, and the B+-tree is the reason for it.

Low-selectivity columns are poor candidates. An index on a two-valued Coursetype narrows the search to half the table; the optimiser will usually prefer a full scan, which reads blocks sequentially and so avoids the seek cost of many scattered index lookups.

CREATE INDEX idx_student_name ON STUDENT(Name);
CREATE INDEX idx_adm_sid_date ON ADMISSION(SID, Dateofadmission);
SHOW INDEX FROM STUDENT;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Name = 'Ankit Sharma';   -- was it used?
DROP INDEX idx_student_name ON STUDENT;

docs.title: 25.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. What is an index? Why is it needed, and what does it cost?

A. An index is an auxiliary access structure, stored separately from the data file, consisting of <field value, pointer> entries sorted on the field value. It speeds up retrieval of records satisfying a condition on the indexed field, without altering the data file.

Why needed. A file can be physically organised on only one field (Lesson 1). A STUDENT file sorted on Rollno gives no benefit whatever to WHERE Name = 'Ankit Sharma', which still costs a linear scan of b/2 blocks. An index provides an additional access path for any other field, and a file may have as many indexes as needed.

An index is fast because it is small: it stores one field and a pointer rather than whole records, so it occupies far fewer blocks and can be searched in far fewer accesses. For the example of Section 2.3, a search falls from 1500 block accesses to 7.

What it costs.
