  1. Storage — sometimes a substantial fraction of the table's own size, especially for dense secondary indexes.
  2. Write penalty — every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update every index on the table. A table with eight indexes performs writes many times more slowly than an unindexed one.
  3. Maintenance — indexes fragment over time and need rebuilding.

So an index trades write speed and space for read speed. The rule is to index columns that appear in WHERE, join conditions and ORDER BY, and are reasonably selective — and to index nothing else.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish primary, clustering and secondary indexes. Why must a secondary index be dense?

A. (Comparison table of Section 2.2.)

Primary index — on the ordering key field of a sorted file: the field is both the physical sort field and unique. Sparse, one entry per block, holding that block's anchor (first) record.

Clustering index — on the ordering field where values are not unique. Sparse, one entry per distinct value, pointing at the first block containing it.

Secondary index — on a non-ordering field. Dense, one entry per record.

A file can have at most one primary or clustering index, because it is physically sorted on only one field; it can have any number of secondary indexes.

Why a secondary index must be dense. A sparse index relies on an inference that only sorting makes valid: if anchor value v_k starts block k and v_{k+1} starts block k+1, then every record with a value between them lies in block k. One entry per block therefore suffices.

For a non-ordering field that inference collapses. Records with adjacent Name values may sit in completely unrelated blocks, since the file's physical order has nothing to do with Name. Knowing where "Ankit Sharma" is tells you nothing about where "Ankit Verma" is. Each record must therefore have its own index entry.

The consequence is that a secondary index has r entries rather than b — typically an order of magnitude more — so it occupies more blocks, costs more accesses to search, and is more expensive to maintain. It is nonetheless worth building, because the alternative is no access path at all.

Solved Question 3

Q. A file has 30,000 records of 100 bytes; block size 1024 bytes; index field 9 bytes; pointer 6 bytes. Compute the cost of a search with no index, with a single-level primary index, and with a multi-level index.

A.

The data file. bfr = floor(1024/100) = 10; b = ceil(30000/10) = 3000 blocks.

(a) No index — heap. Linear search averages b/2 = **1500** block accesses.

(b) Single-level primary index. Entry size Ri = 9 + 6 = 15 bytes. Fan-out fo = bfri = floor(1024/15) = 68 entries per block. A primary index is sparse, one entry per data block: ri = b = 3000 entries. Index blocks bi = ceil(3000/68) = **45**. Search = binary search of the index, then one data access: ceil(log₂ 45) + 1 = 6 + 1 = **7** block accesses.

(c) Multi-level index.

  • Level 1 = the 45-block index.
  • Level 2 = ceil(45/68) = 1 block — a single block, so stop. t = 2 levels. Search = t + 1 = **3** block accesses.

Comparison.

Method Accesses Speed-up vs scan Linear scan 1500 — Binary search of the sorted data file 12 125× Single-level primary index 7 214× Multi-level index 3 500×

Comment. The multi-level index wins because each level divides the search space by the fan-out (68) rather than by 2. One level of a fan-out-68 index does the work of about six binary-search steps. At 10 ms per access, the search falls from 15 seconds to 30 milliseconds.

Solved Question 4

Q. Describe the structure of a B+-tree. How does it differ from a B-tree, and why is it preferred?

A. (Diagram: Section 2.5.) A B+-tree is a balanced multi-level index in which:

  • Internal nodes hold only search keys and tree pointers — they are a pure directory with no data pointers.
  • Leaf nodes hold every search key value together with its data pointer.
  • Leaf nodes are linked in a chain in key order.
  • All leaves are at the same depth, and every node is kept at least half full.

Differences from a B-tree. (Table of Section 2.5.) The essential one: a B-tree stores data pointers in every node, whereas a B+-tree stores them only in leaves.

Why B+-trees are preferred — three reasons.

  1. Higher fan-out, hence a shallower tree. Internal nodes carry no data pointers, so more keys fit in a block. With a fan-out of 100, three levels address a million records and four address a hundred million — so essentially any lookup costs three or four block accesses, regardless of table size.

  2. Efficient range queries. WHERE Rollno BETWEEN 'X2019' AND 'X2050' descends the tree once to the first matching leaf, then follows the leaf chain sequentially. In a B-tree the same query requires repeated traversal up and down the tree, because successive keys are scattered across levels. Range and ORDER BY queries are extremely common, which makes this decisive.

  3. Uniform, predictable cost. Every search reaches a leaf, so every lookup costs the same number of accesses. A B-tree may terminate early at an internal node, making costs variable and harder for the query optimiser to estimate.

Consequently the B+-tree is the default index structure in essentially every relational DBMS.

Solved Question 5

Q. Explain insertion and deletion in a B+-tree, and how balance is maintained.

A.

Insertion.

  1. Descend from the root to the appropriate leaf and insert the key in sorted position.
  2. If the leaf still has room, stop.
  3. If it overflows, split it into two leaves, dividing the entries as evenly as possible, and promote a copy of the middle key to the parent as a separator. (A copy, because in a B+-tree every key must remain present in a leaf.) Relink the leaf chain.
  4. If the parent now overflows, split it too and promote its middle key — this time the key moves up rather than being copied, since internal nodes hold no data.
  5. Splits may propagate to the root. Splitting the root creates a new root and increases the height by one.

This is the only way a B+-tree grows — it grows at the root, not the leaves — which is precisely why every leaf remains at the same depth and the tree stays perfectly balanced without any explicit rebalancing operation.

Deletion. 1. Descend to the leaf and remove the entry. 2. If the node remains at least half full, stop. 3. If it underflows, first try to borrow (redistribute) an entry from an adjacent sibling that has more than the minimum, updating the separator key in the parent. 4. If no sibling can spare one, merge the node with a sibling and remove the now-redundant separator key from the parent. 5. A merge may cause the parent to underflow, propagating upward. If the root is left with a single child, the root is removed and the height decreases by one.

The balance guarantee. Because every node except the root is kept at least half full, a tree of height h with fan-out fo holds at least (fo/2)^h entries. Hence the height is bounded by log_(fo/2) n, and search, insertion and deletion are all O(log n) in the worst case, whatever order the data arrives in — including the sorted order that would degenerate an unbalanced tree into a linked list.

Solved Question 6

Q. Give four practical rules for deciding which columns to index, and explain each in terms of B+-tree structure.

A.

1. Index columns used in WHERE, join conditions and ORDER BY. These are the only places an index can be applied. A join in particular benefits enormously: without an index, each outer row triggers a full scan of the inner table.

2. Prefer highly selective columns. Selectivity is the fraction of rows a typical value matches. An index on Rollno (unique) narrows a search to one row; an index on a two-valued Coursetype narrows it only to half the table. In the latter case the optimiser will usually ignore the index and scan, because reading many scattered blocks via the index costs more seeks than reading the whole file sequentially (Lesson 1: seek time dominates). Indexing a low-selectivity column adds write cost for no read benefit.

3. Put the most selective — or most frequently filtered — column first in a composite index. A B+-tree is ordered by leading prefix. An index on (SID, Dateofadmission) serves WHERE SID = ? and WHERE SID = ? AND Dateofadmission = ?, but is useless for WHERE Dateofadmission = ? alone, since the tree's ordering says nothing about the second column independently of the first.

4. Keep the number of indexes small. Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update every index, and each update may cause node splits or merges that propagate up the tree. A table with eight indexes writes many times more slowly than an unindexed one.

Two corollaries that follow from the same structure:

  • Do not wrap the indexed column in a function. WHERE YEAR(Dateofbirth) = 2001 cannot use the index, because the tree is ordered by Dateofbirth, not by YEAR(Dateofbirth). Rewrite as a range — the sargability rule of Unit 4, Lesson 3.
  • Avoid a leading wildcard. LIKE 'A%' descends the tree by prefix; LIKE '%Sharma' cannot, and forces a full scan.

Finally, primary keys and UNIQUE constraints are indexed automatically — never create a duplicate index on them.

docs.title: 25.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. What is an index, and what does an index entry contain?
  2. Why can a file have at most one primary index but many secondary indexes?
  3. Distinguish dense from sparse indexes.
  4. Why must a secondary index be dense?
  5. What is the fan-out of an index, and why does it matter?
  6. Where are data pointers stored in a B+-tree?
  7. Give two reasons B+-trees are preferred to B-trees.

B. Computation

  1. A file has 100,000 records of 200 bytes; block size 4096 bytes; index field 12 bytes; pointer 8 bytes. Compute: a. bfr and b for the data file. b. The fan-out of the index. c. The size and search cost of a single-level primary index. d. The size and search cost of a dense secondary index. e. The number of levels and search cost of a multi-level index.
  2. Repeat question 8 for 1,000,000 records.
  3. An index has fan-out 100. How many levels are needed for 1000, 10⁶ and 10⁸ entries? What is the search cost in each case?
  4. Compare, in block accesses, a linear scan, a binary search of the sorted file, and a three-level index, for a file of 50,000 blocks.

C. Classification

  1. For each, state whether a primary, clustering or secondary index is appropriate, and whether it will be dense or sparse: a. STUDENT sorted on Rollno, index on Rollno. b. The same file, index on Name. c. COURSE sorted on Coursetype, index on Coursetype. d. ADMISSION as a heap, index on SID. e. EMPLOYEE sorted on Dno, index on Ssn.

D. Analysis

  1. For the college database, decide which indexes you would create, and justify each against the four rules of solved question 6. Which columns would you deliberately leave unindexed, and why?
  2. Explain why WHERE Dateofadmission = '2019-07-15' cannot use an index on (SID, Dateofadmission). What index would serve it?
  3. A developer adds an index to every column of a table and reports that inserts have become ten times slower. Explain, and give a method for deciding which indexes to drop.
  4. Explain why the optimiser may ignore an index on a low-selectivity column, referring to seek time.
  5. Show, step by step, the insertions of the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 into an initially empty B+-tree of order 3 (at most 2 keys per node), drawing the tree after each split.
  6. Explain why a B+-tree grows at the root rather than at the leaves, and why this guarantees balance.
  7. A table is bulk-loaded with 10 million rows. Is it better to create the indexes before or after loading? Justify in terms of node splits.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. An index changes the physical order of the data file.
  2. A primary index is dense.
  3. A file may have several clustering indexes.
  4. Internal nodes of a B+-tree contain data pointers.
  5. A B+-tree's leaves are linked.
  6. An index always speeds up a query.
  7. Creating an index changes the conceptual schema.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. An index is a separate structure; the data file is unchanged. (A clustered table in some systems does reorder data, but that is a different feature.)
  2. False. It is sparse — one entry per block, holding the block's anchor record.
  3. False. At most one, since the file is physically sorted on only one field.
  4. False. Internal nodes hold only keys and tree pointers; all data pointers are in the leaves. That is what gives the high fan-out.
  5. True. The leaf chain is what makes range scans and ORDER BY efficient.
  6. False. On a low-selectivity column the optimiser may correctly prefer a sequential scan; and the index always slows down writes.
  7. False. It is an internal-level change — physical data independence (Unit 1, Lesson 3).

Lesson Summary

  • An index is a separate <value, pointer> structure giving an extra access path; it trades write speed and space for read speed.
  • Primary (ordering key, sparse, one per block), clustering (ordering non-key, sparse, one per value), secondary (non-ordering, must be dense, one per record). At most one primary or clustering index; any number of secondary.
  • Multi-level indexes divide the search space by the fan-out at each level, giving log_fo n rather than log₂ n.
  • B+-trees keep data pointers only in leaves (high fan-out, shallow tree) and chain the leaves (efficient range scans); they stay balanced by splitting at the root.
  • Index selective columns used in WHERE, joins and ORDER BY; respect the leading-prefix rule for composite indexes; keep the column bare in the predicate.

docs.title: Lesson 17: Joins, Subqueries and Set Operations
docs.text:
Combining tables — and queries inside queries

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 4: Structured Query Language · 12 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 6.3, 7.1 · Murach's MySQL, Ch. 4, 7

Learning Outcomes

  1. Write INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and SELF joins, and multi-table joins.
  2. Distinguish non-correlated from correlated subqueries.
  3. Use IN, NOT IN, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, ANY, ALL correctly.
  4. Handle the NOT IN with NULL trap.
  5. Express division ("for all") queries in SQL.
  6. Use UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT, and their MySQL substitutes.

docs.title: The syntax forms
docs.text:
-- Implicit (old style) -- avoid: easy to forget the condition
SELECT s.Name, a.SID FROM STUDENT s, ADMISSION a WHERE s.Rollno = a.Rollno;

-- Explicit (ANSI, preferred) -- join condition cannot be forgotten
SELECT s.Name, a.SID FROM STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno;

-- USING, when the column names match
SELECT s.Name, a.SID FROM STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a USING (Rollno);

-- NATURAL: joins on ALL same-named columns -- risky, avoid
SELECT Name, SID FROM STUDENT NATURAL JOIN ADMISSION;

Always use explicit JOIN ... ON

With the implicit comma form, forgetting the WHERE produces a silent Cartesian product — 5 students × 6 admissions = 30 meaningless rows, with no error. With JOIN ... ON the condition is syntactically required, so the mistake cannot happen. Explicit syntax also separates join conditions from filter conditions, which matters for outer joins (Section 5.1.4).

docs.title: INNER JOIN
docs.text:
Returns only rows with a match on both sides.

SELECT s.Rollno, s.Name, c.Cname, a.Dateofadmission
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
ORDER BY s.Rollno;

Syllabus Q1 — names of students enrolled in any course:

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno;

DISTINCT is required: a student in two courses produces two rows.

Syllabus Q2 — names of students in at least one part-time course:

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime';

docs.title: OUTER JOINs
docs.text:
SELECT s.Name, c.Cname
FROM   STUDENT s
LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
LEFT JOIN COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID;

Every student appears; Arjun Nair shows NULL for Cname.

MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; simulate it:

SELECT s.Name, a.SID FROM STUDENT s LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno=a.Rollno
UNION
SELECT s.Name, a.SID FROM STUDENT s RIGHT JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno=a.Rollno;

docs.title: SELF JOIN
docs.text:
A table joined to itself, using aliases — the SQL form of a recursive relationship (Unit 2, Lesson 3).

-- Pairs of distinct students admitted to the same course
SELECT   a1.Rollno AS Student1, a2.Rollno AS Student2, a1.SID
FROM     ADMISSION a1 JOIN ADMISSION a2 ON a1.SID = a2.SID
WHERE    a1.Rollno < a2.Rollno;

The condition a1.Rollno < a2.Rollno (rather than <>) does two jobs: it excludes a student paired with themselves, and it lists each pair once rather than twice in both orders.

-- Employees and their supervisors
SELECT e.Name AS Employee, s.Name AS Supervisor
FROM   EMPLOYEE e LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE s ON e.SuperSsn = s.Ssn;

The LEFT JOIN keeps the chief executive, who has no supervisor.

docs.title: The outer-join trap: ON vs WHERE
docs.text:
A condition in WHERE silently cancels an outer join

-- WRONG: behaves as an INNER join
SELECT c.Cname, COUNT(a.Rollno)
FROM   COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
WHERE  a.Dateofadmission >= '2019-08-01'
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname;

-- RIGHT: the extra condition belongs in ON
SELECT c.Cname, COUNT(a.Rollno)
FROM   COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a
       ON c.SID = a.SID AND a.Dateofadmission >= '2019-08-01'
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname;

Why. The LEFT JOIN first pads unmatched courses with NULLs. The WHERE clause then tests NULL >= '2019-08-01', which is UNKNOWN, so those rows are discarded — undoing the outer join entirely.

Rule: conditions on the outer (right-hand) table belong in ON; conditions on the preserved (left-hand) table belong in WHERE.

docs.title: 17.2 Subqueries
docs.text:
Subquery (nested query)

A SELECT statement inside another statement. The inner query is the subquery; the enclosing one is the outer query.

Non-correlated: independent of the outer query — evaluated once. Correlated: references a column of the outer query — evaluated once per outer row.

docs.title: Scalar subqueries
docs.text:
Return exactly one value; usable anywhere a value is allowed.

SELECT Cname, TotalSeats FROM COURSE
WHERE  TotalSeats > (SELECT AVG(TotalSeats) FROM COURSE);

SELECT Name, Dateofbirth FROM STUDENT
WHERE  Dateofbirth = (SELECT MAX(Dateofbirth) FROM STUDENT);

docs.title: IN and NOT IN
docs.text:
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE  Rollno IN (SELECT Rollno FROM ADMISSION
                  WHERE SID IN (SELECT SID FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype='Parttime'));

The NOT IN + NULL trap — the most dangerous bug in SQL

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE  Rollno NOT IN (SELECT Rollno FROM ADMISSION);

If any row of the subquery returns NULL, this query returns no rows at all — silently, with no error.

Why. x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) expands to x<>a AND x<>b AND x<>NULL. The last conjunct is UNKNOWN, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so the whole condition can never be TRUE.

Three safe alternatives:

-- 1. Exclude NULLs explicitly
WHERE Rollno NOT IN (SELECT Rollno FROM ADMISSION WHERE Rollno IS NOT NULL)

-- 2. Use NOT EXISTS -- immune to the problem
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno)

-- 3. Use a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
FROM STUDENT s LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno=a.Rollno WHERE a.Rollno IS NULL

Prefer NOT EXISTS. It handles NULLs correctly by construction and is usually at least as fast.

docs.title: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS — correlated subqueries
docs.text:
EXISTS

EXISTS (subquery) is TRUE if the subquery returns at least one row, regardless of its contents. Convention: write SELECT 1, since the values are never examined.

-- Students admitted to at least one course
SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno);

-- Students admitted to no course
SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno);

The reference s.Rollno inside the subquery makes it correlated: it cannot run alone, and is conceptually re-evaluated for each candidate s.

Correlated vs non-correlated

Non-correlated Correlated References the outer query No Yes Evaluated Once Conceptually once per outer row Can run standalone Yes No Typical operators IN, =, > with a scalar EXISTS, NOT EXISTS

Modern optimisers frequently rewrite a correlated subquery into a semi-join or anti-join (Unit 3, Lesson 4), so the "once per row" cost is conceptual rather than actual.

docs.title: ANY / SOME and ALL
docs.text:
SELECT Cname FROM COURSE
WHERE  TotalSeats > ANY (SELECT TotalSeats FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype='Parttime');
-- greater than AT LEAST ONE part-time course, i.e. > the MINIMUM

SELECT Cname FROM COURSE
WHERE  TotalSeats > ALL (SELECT TotalSeats FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype='Parttime');
-- greater than EVERY part-time course, i.e. > the MAXIMUM
Construct Equivalent > ANY (S) > MIN(S) > ALL (S) > MAX(S) < ANY (S) < MAX(S) < ALL (S) < MIN(S) = ANY (S) IN (S) <> ALL (S) NOT IN (S)

Note: > ALL on an empty subquery is vacuously TRUE; > ANY on an empty subquery is FALSE.

docs.title: Subqueries in FROM — derived tables
docs.text:
SELECT Coursetype, AVG(Enrolled) AS MeanEnrolment
FROM ( SELECT c.SID, c.Coursetype, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Enrolled
       FROM   COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
       GROUP BY c.SID, c.Coursetype ) AS per_course
GROUP BY Coursetype;

A derived table must be given an alias. This is the standard way to aggregate over an aggregate.

docs.title: 17.3 Division in SQL — the "for all" queries
docs.text:
SQL has no division operator (Unit 3, Lesson 4). Two idioms.

Query: students admitted to all part-time courses.

docs.title: Method 1 — double NOT EXISTS
docs.text:
The logic: "there is no part-time course for which this student has no admission."

SELECT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (
         SELECT 1 FROM COURSE c
         WHERE  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime'
           AND  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a
                             WHERE  a.Rollno = s.Rollno AND a.SID = c.SID )
       );

Read the double negative carefully — it is the direct translation of "for all", since ∀x P(x) is equivalent to ¬∃x ¬P(x).

docs.title: Method 2 — counting (usually clearer and faster)
docs.text:
The logic: "the number of distinct part-time courses this student has equals the total number of part-time courses."

SELECT   s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM     STUDENT s
JOIN     ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN     COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE    c.Coursetype = 'Parttime'
GROUP BY s.Rollno, s.Name
HAVING   COUNT(DISTINCT c.SID) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype='Parttime');

COUNT(DISTINCT c.SID) rather than COUNT(*) guards against duplicate admission rows inflating the count.

Syllabus Q12 — students admitted to full-time courses only (a related but different pattern — "none of the other kind"):

SELECT DISTINCT s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
WHERE  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a2 JOIN COURSE c2 ON a2.SID = c2.SID
                    WHERE a2.Rollno = s.Rollno AND c2.Coursetype <> 'Fulltime' );

The initial join ensures the student has at least one admission — otherwise a student with no admissions at all would vacuously qualify.

docs.title: 17.4 Set Operations
docs.text:
Operation Meaning MySQL support UNION In either, duplicates removed Yes UNION ALL In either, duplicates kept Yes INTERSECT In both 8.0.31+; else simulate EXCEPT / MINUS In the first, not the second 8.0.31+; else simulate

All require the operands to be union compatible: same number of columns, compatible types (Unit 3, Lesson 3).

Syllabus Q14 — names of all students who took admission to any course, and course names in which at least one student has enrolled:

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name AS Item, 'Student' AS Kind
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
UNION
SELECT DISTINCT c.Cname, 'Course'
FROM   COURSE c JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID;

The literal Kind column makes the combined list interpretable — without it the two sorts of name are indistinguishable.

Simulating INTERSECT in older MySQL:

-- Students in both CS01 and MA02
SELECT DISTINCT a1.Rollno FROM ADMISSION a1
WHERE a1.SID='CS01' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a2
                                WHERE a2.Rollno=a1.Rollno AND a2.SID='MA02');

Simulating EXCEPT:

SELECT DISTINCT a1.Rollno FROM ADMISSION a1
WHERE a1.SID='CS01' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a2
                                    WHERE a2.Rollno=a1.Rollno AND a2.SID='MA02');

UNION vs UNION ALL

UNION removes duplicates, which requires a sort or hash of the combined result — real work on a large query.

UNION ALL does not. If you know the operands are disjoint, always write UNION ALL — it is strictly faster and gives the same answer.

docs.title: 17.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Distinguish correlated from non-correlated subqueries with an example of each. How does each execute?

A. A non-correlated subquery is self-contained: it references nothing from the outer query and can be executed on its own. The DBMS evaluates it once, and uses the resulting value or set for every outer row.

SELECT Cname FROM COURSE
WHERE  TotalSeats > (SELECT AVG(TotalSeats) FROM COURSE);
The inner query returns 47 once; the outer scan then compares each course against 47.

A correlated subquery references a column of the outer query, so it cannot run alone and is conceptually re-evaluated for each outer row.

SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno);
s.Rollno binds to the outer row, so the subquery asks a different question for each student.

Non-correlated Correlated References outer query No Yes Executions (conceptually) 1 1 per outer row Runs standalone Yes No Typical operators =, >, IN EXISTS, NOT EXISTS

In practice the "once per row" cost is conceptual: modern optimisers rewrite a correlated EXISTS into a semi-join and a correlated NOT EXISTS into an anti-join (Unit 3, Lesson 4), evaluating it with a single pass and an index. So EXISTS should not be avoided on performance grounds.

Solved Question 2

Q. Explain the NOT IN with NULL trap. Give a failing example and three fixes, recommending one.

A. x NOT IN (S) is defined as x <> s1 AND x <> s2 AND ... AND x <> sn. If any si is NULL, that conjunct evaluates to UNKNOWN. Since TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN and WHERE retains only TRUE, the condition can never be satisfied — so the query returns zero rows, whatever the data.

There is no error and no warning; the result simply looks like "no such students exist".

Failing example. Suppose ADMISSION is altered so that Rollno is nullable, and one row has Rollno = NULL:

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE  Rollno NOT IN (SELECT Rollno FROM ADMISSION);   -- returns NOTHING

Even though Arjun Nair clearly has no admission, he is not returned.

Three fixes:

  1. Filter the NULLs out of the subquery. 

    WHERE Rollno NOT IN (SELECT Rollno FROM ADMISSION WHERE Rollno IS NOT NULL)
    Correct, but relies on the author remembering the trap every time.

  2. Use NOT EXISTS. 

    SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno);
    EXISTS tests only whether rows exist; a NULL a.Rollno simply fails the equality and contributes nothing. Immune by construction.

  3. Use an anti-join. 

    SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
WHERE a.Rollno IS NULL;
    Also correct, and often the fastest.

Recommendation: NOT EXISTS. It is correct regardless of NULLs, states the intent directly, and optimisers implement it as an anti-join, so it matches the performance of option 3 without the subtlety of reasoning about padded NULLs.

Solved Question 3

Q. Write SQL for syllabus practicals 1, 2, 10, 11, 12 and 14.

A.

Q1 — names of students enrolled in any course. 

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno;

Q2 — names of students enrolled in at least one part-time course. 

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime';

Q10 — the most popular society. 

SELECT   y.Socname, COUNT(*) AS Members
FROM     SOCIETY y JOIN ENROLLMENT e ON y.SocID = e.SocID
GROUP BY y.SocID, y.Socname
HAVING   COUNT(*) = ( SELECT MAX(cnt) FROM
                      (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM ENROLLMENT GROUP BY SocID) t );
Comparing against the maximum rather than using ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 correctly returns all societies that tie for first place.

Q11 — the two most popular part-time courses. 

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(*) AS Enrolled
FROM     COURSE c JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
WHERE    c.Coursetype = 'Parttime'
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname
ORDER BY Enrolled DESC
LIMIT 2;
Note this does cut ties arbitrarily at the boundary; if that is unacceptable, a window function (DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) <= 2) returns all courses in the top two ranks.

Q12 — students admitted to full-time courses only. 

SELECT DISTINCT s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
WHERE  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a2 JOIN COURSE c2 ON a2.SID = c2.SID
                    WHERE a2.Rollno = s.Rollno AND c2.Coursetype <> 'Fulltime' );
The leading join is essential: it requires the student to have at least one admission. Without it, Arjun Nair — who has no admissions at all — would satisfy the NOT EXISTS vacuously and be wrongly returned.

Q14 — names of all students who took admission to any course, and course names in which at least one student enrolled. 

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name AS Item, 'Student' AS Kind
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
UNION
SELECT DISTINCT c.Cname, 'Course'
FROM   COURSE c JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID;
The two SELECTs are union compatible (two columns, both strings). The literal Kind column distinguishes the two sorts of name in the combined list.

Solved Question 4

Q. Express "students admitted to all part-time courses" in two ways. Compare them.

A.

Method 1 — double NOT EXISTS. Direct translation of the logical identity ∀x P(x) ≡ ¬∃x ¬P(x): "there is no part-time course for which this student has no admission."

SELECT s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (
         SELECT 1 FROM COURSE c
         WHERE  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime'
           AND  NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a
                             WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno AND a.SID = c.SID ) );

Method 2 — counting. "The number of distinct part-time courses this student is admitted to equals the total number of part-time courses."

SELECT   s.Rollno, s.Name
FROM     STUDENT s
JOIN     ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN     COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE    c.Coursetype = 'Parttime'
GROUP BY s.Rollno, s.Name
HAVING   COUNT(DISTINCT c.SID) =
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype = 'Parttime');

Comparison.

Double NOT EXISTS Counting Readability Hard — a double negative Easier — states the arithmetic directly Correctness with duplicates Immune Needs COUNT(DISTINCT ...), else duplicate admissions inflate the count Empty divisor (no part-time courses exist) Returns every student, matching the mathematical definition of division Returns no student, since no student has any part-time admission to group Typical performance Anti-join, usually good One grouped pass, usually good

The empty-divisor row is the important difference: the two methods genuinely disagree in that edge case. Method 1 matches the relational-algebra definition (a vacuous "for all" is true); Method 2 matches the more usual practical intent. State which behaviour you want.

Both correctly return no rows on our sample data, since no student is admitted to both MA02 and EN03.

Solved Question 5

Q. Why does adding WHERE a.Dateofadmission >= '2019-08-01' to a LEFT JOIN query turn it into an inner join? Give the fix.

A. A LEFT JOIN executes in two conceptual stages: first it matches rows, then it pads every unmatched left row with NULLs in the right table's columns. Only after that does the WHERE clause run.

For an unmatched course such as PH01, the padded row has a.Dateofadmission = NULL. The condition NULL >= '2019-08-01' evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE retains only rows evaluating to TRUE. So every padded row is discarded — precisely the rows the outer join existed to preserve. The net effect is identical to an inner join.

The fix: move the condition into the ON clause, so it participates in matching rather than in filtering after padding.

SELECT   c.Cname, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS RecentAdmissions
FROM     COURSE c
LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a
       ON c.SID = a.SID AND a.Dateofadmission >= '2019-08-01'
GROUP BY c.SID, c.Cname;

Now a course with no qualifying admission still yields one padded row, and COUNT(a.Rollno) correctly reports 0 for it.

The general rule:

  • Conditions on the preserved (left) table → WHERE. They legitimately remove left rows.
  • Conditions on the optional (right) table → ON. Putting them in WHERE cancels the outer join.
  • The one exception is a deliberate WHERE <right column> IS NULL, which is the anti-join idiom and is meant to keep only the unmatched rows.

Solved Question 6

Q. Compare IN, EXISTS and JOIN for "students admitted to a part-time course". Which is preferable?

A. Three formulations of the same question:

-- 1. IN
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE  Rollno IN (SELECT a.Rollno FROM ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID=c.SID
                  WHERE c.Coursetype='Parttime');

-- 2. EXISTS (correlated)
SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ADMISSION a JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID=c.SID
               WHERE a.Rollno = s.Rollno AND c.Coursetype='Parttime');

-- 3. JOIN
SELECT DISTINCT s.Name FROM STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno=a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID=c.SID
WHERE  c.Coursetype='Parttime';
IN EXISTS JOIN Duplicates None — IN is a membership test None DISTINCT required, else a student in two part-time courses appears twice NULL safety Safe for IN; unsafe for NOT IN Safe both ways Safe Readability Good Good for existence questions Best when columns from both tables are needed Performance Optimised to a semi-join Optimised to a semi-join Fine, but DISTINCT costs a sort or hash

Recommendation.

  • If you need only to test existence and want no columns from the other table, prefer EXISTS: it needs no DISTINCT, and it is NULL-safe in both its positive and negative forms, so the same habit protects you from the NOT IN trap.
  • If you need columns from both tables (say the course name alongside the student name), a JOIN is the natural choice — the duplication is then meaningful data, not an artefact.
  • IN is perfectly good for the positive case and is often the most readable; simply never use NOT IN against a nullable column.

All three are typically compiled to the same semi-join plan, so the choice is one of clarity and correctness rather than speed.

docs.title: 17.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Why is explicit JOIN ... ON preferred to the comma form?
  2. What does EXISTS return, and why write SELECT 1?
  3. State the NOT IN with NULL trap in one sentence.
  4. Give the equivalent of > ANY and > ALL using MIN/MAX.
  5. Why must a derived table have an alias?
  6. When is UNION ALL preferable to UNION?
  7. Which clause should hold a condition on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN?

B. Write the SQL

  1. Students and the societies they belong to, including students in none.
  2. Courses and their teachers, for courses with at least one admission.
  3. Pairs of students in the same society.
  4. Students in both a full-time and a part-time course.
  5. Students in a society but no course.
  6. Courses with more admissions than the average.
  7. The student admitted to the greatest number of courses.
  8. Societies with no members.
  9. Students admitted to every full-time course (both methods).
  10. Students admitted only to part-time courses.
  11. A combined list of all student names and all society mentor names.
  12. Students who share a course with X2019 (excluding X2019).
  13. For each course, its name and the name of the youngest student admitted to it.

C. Predict and explain

  1. ADMISSION has one row with Rollno = NULL. What does SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno NOT IN (SELECT Rollno FROM ADMISSION); return? Why?
  2. Explain the difference in results between: a. FROM COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID=a.SID WHERE a.SID='CS01' b. FROM COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID=a.SID AND a.SID='CS01'
  3. What does SELECT Cname FROM COURSE WHERE TotalSeats > ALL (SELECT TotalSeats FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype='Diploma'); return when no diploma courses exist? Why?

D. Analytical

  1. Explain why the syllabus Q12 query needs the initial join to ADMISSION. Construct the data that breaks it if the join is omitted.
  2. Rewrite three IN subqueries as joins and three as EXISTS, and comment on which reads best in each case.
  3. Explain how an optimiser can turn a correlated NOT EXISTS into an anti-join, and why that matters.
  4. Compare the two division methods on the empty-divisor edge case. Which matches relational algebra? Which matches typical user intent?
  5. Design and write a single query producing, for each course: the name, the enrolment count, the vacant seats, the percentage full, and the name of the earliest-admitted student.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. NOT IN and NOT EXISTS always give the same result.
  2. A correlated subquery can be executed independently.
  3. UNION requires the same column names in both operands.
  4. LEFT JOIN with a WHERE condition on the right table behaves as an inner join.
  5. > ALL (empty set) is FALSE.
  6. EXISTS (SELECT 1 ...) and EXISTS (SELECT * ...) differ in result.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. They differ when the subquery yields NULL: NOT IN returns nothing, NOT EXISTS behaves correctly.
  2. False. It references an outer column and is not a complete query on its own.
  3. False. It requires the same number of columns with compatible types; names may differ, and the result takes the first operand's names.
  4. True in general — the padded NULLs fail the condition and are discarded. The deliberate exception is WHERE <right col> IS NULL, the anti-join idiom.
  5. False. It is vacuously TRUE — there is no counter-example in an empty set. (> ANY (empty) is FALSE.)
  6. False. EXISTS tests only whether a row is produced; the select list is never evaluated. SELECT 1 is a readability convention.

Lesson Summary

  • Prefer explicit JOIN ... ON. Conditions on the right table of an outer join belong in ON, not WHERE.
  • Self-joins need aliases; use < rather than <> to list unordered pairs once.
  • Non-correlated subqueries run once; correlated ones reference the outer row and are optimised into semi-/anti-joins.
  • NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing. Use NOT EXISTS.
  • Division ("for all") is written as double NOT EXISTS or by counting; the two differ on an empty divisor.
  • Set operations need union compatibility; use UNION ALL when the operands are known disjoint.

docs.title: Lesson 10: Keys and Relational Integrity Constraints
docs.text:
Superkeys, candidate keys, foreign keys — and the rules that keep data true

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 3: Relational Data Model · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 5.2, 5.3

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define and compute superkey, candidate key, primary key, alternate key, composite key, foreign key.
  2. Classify constraints as inherent, schema-based or application-based.
  3. State and apply the three schema-based constraints: domain, entity integrity, referential integrity.
  4. Determine which operations violate which constraint, and name the DBMS's options.
  5. Choose the correct referential action (CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION, SET DEFAULT).

docs.title: 10.1 Keys
docs.text: Characteristic 4 of Lesson 1 said a relation cannot contain duplicate tuples. It follows that every relation has a key. This section makes that precise.

docs.title: Superkey
docs.text:
Superkey

A set of attributes SK ⊆ R such that no two distinct tuples in any valid state of R can have the same values for SK.

Formally: for any two distinct tuples t1 and t2 in r(R), t1[SK] ≠ t2[SK].

Because no relation contains duplicates, the set of all attributes is always a superkey. Every relation therefore has at least one.

docs.title: Candidate key
docs.text:
Candidate key

A minimal superkey — a superkey from which no attribute can be removed and still leave a superkey.

Minimality is a property of the set, not of its size: {A, B} is minimal if neither {A} nor {B} alone is a superkey.

Minimal is not the same as smallest

A relation may have candidate keys of different sizes — {Rollno} and {Name, Dateofbirth, Address} could both be candidate keys. Both are minimal (no attribute can be dropped from either). "Minimal" means irreducible, not shortest.

docs.title: Primary key and alternate keys
docs.text:
Primary key

The candidate key chosen by the designer as the principal means of identifying tuples. Exactly one per relation. Its attributes are underlined in the schema notation, and it may never be NULL.

Alternate key

Any candidate key not chosen as the primary key. Declared UNIQUE in SQL.

Composite key

A key consisting of more than one attribute. ADMISSION has the composite primary key (Rollno, SID).

docs.title: A complete worked example
docs.text:
ENROLLMENT( Rollno, SocID, Dateofenrolment, StudentName, Socname )

Business rules: a student enrols in a society at most once; Rollno determines StudentName; SocID determines Socname.

Finding the superkeys. Since a (Rollno, SocID) pair occurs at most once, {Rollno, SocID} is a superkey. Any set containing it is also a superkey:

{Rollno, SocID}
{Rollno, SocID, Dateofenrolment}
{Rollno, SocID, StudentName}
{Rollno, SocID, Socname}
{Rollno, SocID, Dateofenrolment, StudentName}
... and so on, up to all five attributes.

With three remaining attributes there are 2^3 = 8 supersets, so there are 8 superkeys.

Finding the candidate keys. Is {Rollno, SocID} minimal? Remove SocID: {Rollno} is not a superkey, because a student may join several societies. Remove Rollno: {SocID} is not a superkey, because a society has many members. Neither can be dropped, so {Rollno, SocID} is minimal — a candidate key.

Is there any other candidate key? No other set is a superkey without containing both Rollno and SocID.

Result: one candidate key {Rollno, SocID}, which is therefore the primary key (composite). There are no alternate keys.

Procedure for finding candidate keys by inspection

  1. List the attributes and the business rules stating what is unique.
  2. Test each single attribute: is it unique on its own? Each that is, is a candidate key.
  3. Test pairs built from attributes that are not already candidate keys, and so on for larger sets.
  4. Never include a set that already contains a candidate key — it cannot be minimal.
  5. Stop when every attribute has been covered.

A rigorous algorithm using functional dependencies and attribute closure is given in Unit 5, Lesson 3.

docs.title: Foreign key
docs.text:
Foreign key

A set of attributes FK in relation R1 (the referencing or child relation) is a foreign key referencing relation R2 (the referenced or parent relation) if:

  1. The attributes of FK have the same domains as the primary key attributes PK of R2. FK is said to reference R2.
  2. For every tuple t1 in r(R1), either t1[FK] matches the value of t2[PK] for some tuple t2 in r(R2), or t1[FK] is wholly NULL.

In ADMISSION(Rollno, SID, Dateofadmission):

  • Rollno is a foreign key referencing STUDENT(Rollno).
  • SID is a foreign key referencing COURSE(SID).

Foreign keys are how the relational model represents relationships — by matching values, not by pointers. This is the source of its data independence (Unit 1).

     STUDENT (parent)                COURSE (parent)
   +--------+-------------+       +------+-----------------+
   | Rollno | Name        |       | SID  | Cname           |
   +--------+-------------+       +------+-----------------+
   | X2019  | Ankit Sharma|       | CS01 | Computer Science|
   | X2020  | Riya Verma  |       | MA02 | Mathematics     |
   +---+----+-------------+       +---+--+-----------------+
       ^                              ^
       |  referenced by               |  referenced by
       |                              |
   +---+----+------+-----------------+
   | Rollno | SID  | Dateofadmission |     ADMISSION (child)
   +--------+------+-----------------+
   | X2019  | CS01 | 2019-07-15      |  <- valid: both parents exist
   | X2019  | MA02 | 2019-08-01      |  <- valid
   | X9999  | CS01 | 2019-07-20      |  <- INVALID: no student X9999
   +--------+------+-----------------+

Figure 2.1 — Foreign keys link relations by matching values.

Three subtleties about foreign keys

  1. A foreign key may reference its own relation. EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Name, SuperSsn) where SuperSsn references EMPLOYEE(Ssn) — a recursive relationship.
  2. A foreign key may be part of the primary key. In ADMISSION, both Rollno and SID are foreign keys and together form the primary key. When this happens the foreign key cannot be NULL, because primary keys cannot be NULL.
  3. A composite foreign key must be wholly NULL or wholly matching. A partially NULL composite foreign key is not permitted under the standard's MATCH FULL semantics.

docs.title: 10.2 Classification of Constraints
docs.text:
Three categories

1. Inherent model-based (implicit) constraints — built into the definition of the relational model itself, so they need not be declared. Examples: a relation cannot contain duplicate tuples; attribute values must be atomic.

2. Schema-based (explicit) constraints — expressible in the DDL and enforced automatically by the DBMS. These are the three below, plus NOT NULL and CHECK.

3. Application-based (semantic) constraints / business rules — not expressible in the DDL, so they must be enforced by application programs or by triggers and assertions. Example: "a student may not be admitted to two full-time courses simultaneously", or "an employee's salary may not exceed that of their supervisor".

A fourth category is sometimes listed: data dependencies (functional and multivalued dependencies), which are used in normalisation rather than enforced directly. These are Unit 5.

docs.title: Domain constraints
docs.text:
Domain constraint

The value of each attribute A in every tuple must be an atomic value from dom(A).

TotalSeats  INT          CHECK (TotalSeats > 0),
Coursetype  VARCHAR(10)  CHECK (Coursetype IN ('Fulltime','Parttime')),
Dateofbirth DATE         NOT NULL

Domain constraints cover the data type, the length, and any CHECK restriction. NOT NULL is also a domain-level constraint.

docs.title: Key constraints and entity integrity
docs.text:
Key constraint

No two distinct tuples may have the same value for a candidate key. Declared PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE.

Entity integrity constraint

No primary key value may be NULL — not even one attribute of a composite primary key.

Why? Because the primary key is the only means of identifying a tuple. A NULL means "unknown or inapplicable"; a tuple whose identifier is unknown cannot be distinguished from another such tuple, cannot be referenced by a foreign key, and cannot be updated or deleted individually. Permitting NULL primary keys would destroy the identification mechanism on which the whole model rests.

Entity integrity applies only to the primary key

Alternate keys (UNIQUE) may be NULL in SQL — and a UNIQUE column may hold several NULLs in most systems, since NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, so two NULLs are not considered duplicates. Only the primary key is protected by entity integrity.

docs.title: Referential integrity
docs.text:
Referential integrity constraint

A tuple in the referencing relation that refers to another relation must refer to an existing tuple in it.

Formally: for every tuple t1 in r(R1) with foreign key FK, either t1[FK] = t2[PK] for some t2 in r(R2), or t1[FK] is NULL.

Referential integrity is the constraint that prevents dangling references — an admission for a student who does not exist, an order for a customer who was deleted.

Entity integrity vs referential integrity

Entity integrity Referential integrity Concerns The primary key The foreign key Says PK may not be NULL FK must match an existing PK, or be NULL Involves One relation Two relations (or one, if self-referencing) Prevents Unidentifiable tuples Dangling references SQL PRIMARY KEY FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES

docs.title: 10.4 Which Operations Violate Which Constraint
docs.text: This is the classic examination table. Learn it by reasoning, not memorisation: an operation can only violate a constraint by creating something new that must be checked.

docs.title: INSERT
docs.text:
Constraint Can INSERT violate it? How Domain Yes A value outside the domain: TotalSeats = -5. Key Yes A primary key value that already exists. Entity integrity Yes NULL in a primary key attribute. Referential integrity Yes A foreign key value with no matching parent tuple.

INSERT can violate all four.

docs.title: DELETE
docs.text:
Constraint Can DELETE violate it? How Domain No Removing a tuple creates no new value. Key No Removing a tuple cannot create a duplicate. Entity integrity No Removing a tuple cannot create a NULL PK. Referential integrity Yes Deleting a parent tuple that a child still references.

DELETE can violate only referential integrity, and only when deleting from the referenced (parent) relation.

docs.title: UPDATE
docs.text:
Attribute updated Constraints that may be violated An ordinary attribute Domain A primary key attribute Domain, key, entity integrity, and referential integrity (children now dangle) A foreign key attribute Domain, referential integrity

UPDATE is effectively a DELETE followed by an INSERT, so it can violate any constraint.

docs.title: What the DBMS does on violation
docs.text:
Three options, in order of preference:

  1. Reject the operation and return an error. The default, and almost always correct.
  2. Cascade or otherwise propagate the change automatically (Section 2.5).
  3. Inform the user and offer a choice — used by interactive tools, not by the engine.

docs.title: 10.5 Referential Actions
docs.text:
When a parent tuple is deleted or its primary key updated, SQL lets you declare what happens to the children.

CREATE TABLE ADMISSION (
    Rollno          VARCHAR(8),
    SID             VARCHAR(6),
    Dateofadmission DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno)
        ON DELETE CASCADE  ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    FOREIGN KEY (SID)    REFERENCES COURSE(SID)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
);
Action On deleting/updating the parent When to use RESTRICT Reject immediately if any child exists. The default intent. Safest: forces the user to deal with children explicitly. NO ACTION Reject, but the check is deferred to the end of the statement. Standard default. Allows a statement that temporarily breaks and then repairs the reference. CASCADE Delete the children too / update their FK to the new value. When the child is existence-dependent on the parent — a weak entity, an order line, an admission record. Use with care: deletions propagate. SET NULL Set the children's FK to NULL. When the child can meaningfully exist "unassigned" — an employee whose department is dissolved. Impossible if the FK is part of the primary key. SET DEFAULT Set the children's FK to its declared default. Rare; requires the default value to exist in the parent.

Choosing correctly — a worked judgement

ADMISSION.Rollno → STUDENT.Rollno: if a student's record is deleted, their admissions are meaningless. ON DELETE CASCADE is right.

ADMISSION.SID → COURSE.SID: if a course is deleted while students are admitted to it, cascading would silently erase those students' admission history. ON DELETE RESTRICT is right — force the administrator to transfer or explicitly remove the students first.

SET NULL is impossible for both, because Rollno and SID are part of ADMISSION's primary key, and entity integrity forbids NULL there.

ON UPDATE CASCADE is almost always right, because a primary key value changing is a renaming of the same real-world entity, and children should follow. Better still, choose primary keys that never change (Unit 2, Lesson 2).

docs.title: 10.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. For STUDENT(Rollno, AadhaarNo, Email, Name, Dateofbirth) where Rollno, AadhaarNo and Email are each unique, list five superkeys, all candidate keys, choose a primary key, and name the alternate keys.

A.

Superkeys (any set containing at least one unique attribute): {Rollno}, {AadhaarNo}, {Email}, {Rollno, Name}, {AadhaarNo, Email, Dateofbirth} — and many more, including the full attribute set.

Candidate keys — the minimal superkeys: {Rollno}, {AadhaarNo}, {Email}. Each is a single attribute and unique, hence irreducible. {Rollno, Name} is a superkey but not minimal, since {Rollno} alone suffices.

Primary key: Rollno. Justification against the five criteria of Unit 2, Lesson 2:

Criterion Rollno AadhaarNo Email Stable (never changes) Yes Yes No — people change addresses Always available at creation Yes No — may not be supplied yet Usually Short and simple Yes Yes No — long string Not privacy-sensitive Yes No — national identity number Moderately

Rollno wins on every criterion.

Alternate keys: AadhaarNo and Email. In SQL they become UNIQUE constraints:

Rollno    VARCHAR(8)  PRIMARY KEY,
AadhaarNo CHAR(12)    UNIQUE,
Email     VARCHAR(60) UNIQUE

Solved Question 2

Q. Define entity integrity and referential integrity. Why is entity integrity necessary? Give an example of each being violated.

A.

Entity integrity: no attribute of a primary key may be NULL in any tuple.

Why necessary? The primary key is the sole means of identifying a tuple. NULL means "unknown or not applicable". If a primary key could be NULL then: (i) the tuple could not be distinguished from another NULL-keyed tuple, so uniqueness would be unenforceable; (ii) no foreign key could reference it; (iii) it could not be individually updated or deleted, since there would be no way to name it. The identification mechanism on which the entire model rests would collapse.

Violation: INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (NULL, 'Ankit Sharma', '2001-03-14'); — rejected, because Rollno is the primary key.

Referential integrity: every non-NULL foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the referenced relation.

Why necessary? It prevents dangling references — child tuples pointing at parents that do not exist — which would make joins lose rows and reports understate totals.

Violation: INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X9999','CS01','2019-07-20'); when no student X9999 exists — rejected. Equally, DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno='X2019'; while admissions for X2019 remain — rejected under RESTRICT, or cascaded under ON DELETE CASCADE.

Solved Question 3

Q. State which constraints each operation can violate, and justify.

A.

INSERT can violate all four, because it introduces a wholly new tuple, every part of which must be checked: a value may lie outside its domain; the primary key value may duplicate an existing one; a primary key attribute may be NULL; and a foreign key may name a non-existent parent.

DELETE can violate only referential integrity. Removing a tuple creates no new value, so it cannot break a domain constraint; it cannot create a duplicate, so it cannot break a key constraint; and it cannot create a NULL primary key. But deleting a tuple from a parent relation may leave children referencing a row that no longer exists.

UPDATE can violate any of the four, because it is logically a DELETE followed by an INSERT. Specifically:

Attribute updated Possible violations Ordinary attribute Domain only Primary key attribute Domain, key, entity integrity, and referential integrity (children left dangling) Foreign key attribute Domain, referential integrity

On violation the DBMS may reject the operation (the default), propagate the change via a declared referential action, or report and offer options in an interactive tool.

Solved Question 4

Q. Consider STUDENT(Rollno, Name), COURSE(SID, Cname) and ADMISSION(Rollno, SID, Dateofadmission) with the obvious foreign keys. State whether each operation succeeds, and if not, which constraint is violated.

Current data: STUDENT = {(X2019,'Ankit'), (X2020,'Riya')}; COURSE = {(CS01,'CompSci')}; ADMISSION = {(X2019, CS01, 2019-07-15)}.

a. INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X2020','CS01','2019-07-16'); b. INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X2021','CS01','2019-07-17'); c. INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X2019','CS01','2019-08-01'); d. DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno = 'X2020'; e. DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno = 'X2019'; f. UPDATE COURSE SET SID = 'CS02' WHERE SID = 'CS01'; g. INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X2020', NULL, '2019-07-18');

A.

Result Constraint a Succeeds Both parents exist; the pair (X2020, CS01) is new. b Fails Referential integrity — no student X2021 in STUDENT. c Fails Key constraint — the primary key (X2019, CS01) already exists. (Note the date differs, but it is not part of the key.) d Succeeds X2020 has no admissions, so no child dangles. e Depends on the declared action. Under RESTRICT/NO ACTION: fails on referential integrity, because (X2019, CS01) references it. Under ON DELETE CASCADE: succeeds, and the admission row is deleted too. Under SET NULL: fails anyway, because Rollno is part of ADMISSION's primary key and entity integrity forbids NULL there. f Depends. Under ON UPDATE CASCADE: succeeds, and the admission row becomes (X2019,'CS02',...). Under RESTRICT: fails on referential integrity, since the child still references CS01. g Fails Entity integrity — SID is part of ADMISSION's primary key and may not be NULL. (Were SID merely a foreign key and not part of the key, a NULL would be permitted by referential integrity.)

Solved Question 5

Q. Explain the five referential actions. For each foreign key in the college database, choose one and justify.

A. (Definitions as in the table of Section 2.5.)

ADMISSION.Rollno → STUDENT.Rollno

  • ON DELETE CASCADE. An admission record is meaningless without the student; if the student's record is removed, their admissions should go with it. The admission is existence-dependent on the student.
  • ON UPDATE CASCADE. If a roll number is corrected, all admissions must follow the same student.

ADMISSION.SID → COURSE.SID - ON DELETE RESTRICT. Deleting a course while students are admitted to it would silently destroy their admission history. The administrator must first transfer or explicitly remove those students. This is a case where the child carries information the parent's deletion should not be allowed to destroy. - ON UPDATE CASCADE, for the same reason as above.

ENROLLMENT.Rollno → STUDENT.Rollno — ON DELETE CASCADE, same reasoning as admissions.

ENROLLMENT.SocID → SOCIETY.SocID — ON DELETE CASCADE is defensible here: if a society is dissolved, its membership records have no independent meaning. (An institution that wants an audit trail would choose RESTRICT instead. The correct choice is a business decision, and the justification matters more than the answer.)

Why SET NULL is unavailable throughout: in every one of these foreign keys, the referencing column is part of the child's composite primary key, and entity integrity forbids a NULL there.

Solved Question 6

Q. Classify these constraints as inherent, schema-based or application-based, and state how each is enforced.

a. A relation cannot have two identical tuples. b. TotalSeats must be positive. c. Every admission must reference an existing student. d. A student may not be admitted to more than two full-time courses. e. Attribute values must be atomic. f. An employee's salary may not exceed their supervisor's.

A.

Category Enforcement a Inherent (model-based) Follows from a relation being a set; requires no declaration. Note SQL only enforces it if a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE is declared, since SQL tables are multisets. b Schema-based (domain) CHECK (TotalSeats > 0) — enforced automatically by the DBMS. c Schema-based (referential integrity) FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno). d Application-based (semantic / business rule) Not expressible as a simple column or table constraint, because it requires counting related rows in another table. Enforced by a trigger, an assertion (rarely implemented), or application code. e Inherent Part of the definition of the relational model (1NF). The DBMS cannot detect a violation — storing '98111, 98222' in a VARCHAR is a design error, not a runtime error. f Application-based Involves comparing two rows of the same table via a self-join. Requires a trigger.

The general principle: constraints involving one row of one table are schema-based; those spanning multiple rows or multiple tables in a computed way are application-based and need triggers.

docs.title: 10.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define superkey and candidate key. Why is every relation guaranteed to have a superkey?
  2. Distinguish "minimal" from "smallest" for candidate keys.
  3. State the entity integrity constraint and give the reason for it.
  4. State the referential integrity constraint formally.
  5. Can a foreign key be NULL? Under what circumstance can it not?
  6. Name the five referential actions.
  7. Give one example each of an inherent, a schema-based and an application-based constraint.

B. Long answer

  1. Define superkey, candidate key, primary key, alternate key, composite key and foreign key, with an example of each from the college database.
  2. Explain the three schema-based constraints. For each, state the SQL that declares it and one operation that violates it.
  3. Explain which operations can violate which constraints, and justify each entry by reasoning rather than assertion.
  4. Explain the five referential actions with an example of when each is the correct choice.
  5. Distinguish entity integrity from referential integrity in a table of at least five rows of comparison.

C. Application and analytical

  1. For EMPLOYEE(Ssn, PAN, Name, Dno, SuperSsn, Salary) where Ssn and PAN are unique, Dno references DEPARTMENT(Dno) and SuperSsn references EMPLOYEE(Ssn): a. List all candidate keys. b. Identify all foreign keys, including any self-reference. c. Can SuperSsn be NULL? Justify with a business reason. d. Choose referential actions for both foreign keys and justify.
  2. For ORDER_LINE(OrderNo, LineNo, ProductNo, Qty) where line numbers restart at 1 for each order: a. What is the primary key? b. Which attributes are foreign keys? c. Which referential action should OrderNo use, and why? d. Explain why SET NULL is not available for OrderNo.
  3. Given R(A,B,C,D) where A → BCD and B → ACD (both A and B are unique): a. How many superkeys are there? Show the reasoning. b. List all candidate keys.
  4. Determine the result of each operation on the college database and name any constraint violated: a. Adding a course with TotalSeats = 0. b. Adding a second course with SID = 'CS01'. c. Deleting a course that has no admissions. d. Changing a student's Rollno when they have three admissions, with ON UPDATE CASCADE. e. Inserting an enrolment with a SocID that does not exist.
  5. A designer declares ON DELETE CASCADE on every foreign key in a system with ten tables. Describe a scenario in which deleting one row destroys most of the database. What policy would you recommend instead?
  6. Write the complete CREATE TABLE statements for STUDENT, COURSE and ADMISSION including every constraint discussed in this lesson, with justified referential actions.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. Every candidate key is a superkey.
  2. Every superkey is a candidate key.
  3. A relation can have more than one primary key.
  4. A foreign key must always reference a different relation.
  5. A UNIQUE column may contain NULL.
  6. DELETE can violate the domain constraint.
  7. SET NULL is always available as a referential action.
  8. A composite key means the relation has two primary keys.

Answers to Section D

  1. True. A candidate key is by definition a minimal superkey.
  2. False. Only minimal ones are candidate keys; {Rollno, Name} is a superkey but not minimal.
  3. False. Exactly one primary key; the others are alternate keys, declared UNIQUE.
  4. False. It may reference its own relation — a self-reference, as with SuperSsn referencing Ssn.
  5. True. Entity integrity applies only to the primary key. Most systems even permit several NULLs in a UNIQUE column, since NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN.
  6. False. DELETE creates no new value, so it can violate only referential integrity, and only when deleting a parent tuple.
  7. False. It is impossible when the foreign key is part of the child's primary key, since entity integrity forbids a NULL there.
  8. False. A composite key is one key made of several attributes.

Lesson Summary

  • Superkey ⊃ candidate key (minimal superkey) → one chosen as primary key; the rest are alternate keys (UNIQUE).
  • A foreign key links relations by matching values, and may reference its own relation.
  • Constraints are inherent (built into the model), schema-based (CHECK, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL) or application-based (triggers and assertions).
  • Entity integrity: no NULL in a primary key. Referential integrity: every non-NULL foreign key matches an existing primary key.
  • INSERT can violate all four constraints; DELETE only referential integrity; UPDATE any of them.
  • Choose referential actions deliberately: CASCADE for existence-dependent children, RESTRICT where the child holds information worth protecting; SET NULL is unavailable when the foreign key is part of the primary key.

docs.title: Lesson 23: Lossless Join and Dependency Preservation
docs.text:
Lossless join, dependency preservation, and how to test them

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 5: Database Design · 10 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 15.2, 15.3

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define attribute preservation, lossless join and dependency preservation.
  2. Demonstrate spurious tuples from a lossy decomposition.
  3. Apply the binary lossless-join test and justify it.
  4. Apply the chase (tableau) algorithm for a decomposition into three or more relations.
  5. Test a decomposition for dependency preservation.

docs.title: 23.1 The Three Desirable Properties
docs.text:
Decomposition

A decomposition of a relation schema R is a set of relation schemas D = {R1, R2, ..., Rm} obtained by distributing the attributes of R among them.

Property 1 — Attribute preservation

R1 ∪ R2 ∪ ... ∪ Rm = R

Every attribute of R must appear in at least one fragment. Obvious, but worth checking first: a decomposition that quietly drops an attribute has lost information before any join is attempted.

Property 2 — Lossless join (non-additive join)

For every legal state r of R:

π<sub>R1</sub>(r) ⋈ π<sub>R2</sub>(r) ⋈ ... ⋈ π<sub>Rm</sub>(r) = r

Projecting onto the fragments and joining them back must reproduce exactly the original relation — no rows lost and, more importantly, no rows invented.

The name is misleading

"Lossless" suggests tuples might be lost. In fact projecting and rejoining can never lose a tuple — every original tuple always reappears.

The danger is the opposite: extra tuples appear. These are spurious tuples, and they assert facts that were never true. Elmasri and Navathe therefore prefer the name non-additive join property, which is more accurate.

Property 3 — Dependency preservation

Let π<sub>Ri</sub>(F) denote the dependencies of F⁺ involving only attributes of Ri. The decomposition is dependency preserving if

( π<sub>R1</sub>(F) ∪ π<sub>R2</sub>(F) ∪ ... ∪ π<sub>Rm</sub>(F) )⁺ = F⁺

In words: every original constraint can be checked on a single fragment, with no join required.

docs.title: 23.2 Spurious Tuples — the Concrete Danger
docs.text:
Take EMP_PROJ( Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Ename, Pname, Plocation ):

Ssn Pnumber Hours Ename Pname Plocation 111 1 32.5 Smith ProductX Bellaire 111 2 7.5 Smith ProductY Sugarland 222 3 40.0 Narayan ProductZ Houston 333 1 20.0 English ProductX Bellaire

A bad decomposition — split on Plocation, which determines nothing:

EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) and EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation)

EMP_LOCS:

Ename Plocation Smith Bellaire Smith Sugarland Narayan Houston English Bellaire

EMP_PROJ1:

Ssn Pnumber Hours Pname Plocation 111 1 32.5 ProductX Bellaire 111 2 7.5 ProductY Sugarland 222 3 40.0 ProductZ Houston 333 1 20.0 ProductX Bellaire

Now join them back on Plocation:

Ssn Pnumber Hours Pname Plocation Ename Genuine? 111 1 32.5 ProductX Bellaire Smith yes 111 1 32.5 ProductX Bellaire English SPURIOUS 111 2 7.5 ProductY Sugarland Smith yes 222 3 40.0 ProductZ Houston Narayan yes 333 1 20.0 ProductX Bellaire Smith SPURIOUS 333 1 20.0 ProductX Bellaire English yes

Six rows instead of four. Row 2 asserts that employee 111 is named English; row 5 that 333 is named Smith. Both are false.

Why this is worse than a lost dependency

Nothing in the decomposed database is wrong when examined table by table. Both fragments are individually correct and consistent. The corruption appears only when the data is reassembled, and there is no way to distinguish the spurious rows from the genuine ones.

The cause: Plocation is a common attribute that is not a key of either fragment. Joining on a non-key column matches every row to every other row sharing that value.

docs.title: 23.3 Testing for Lossless Join — the Binary Case
docs.text:
The binary test

A decomposition of R into exactly two relations R1 and R2 is lossless if and only if the common attributes form a superkey of at least one fragment:

(R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2

Operationally: compute (R1 ∩ R2)⁺ under F, and check whether it contains all of R1 or all of R2.

Why the test works

The join matches rows of R1 and R2 that agree on the common attributes C = R1 ∩ R2.

If C is a superkey of R2, then each value of C occurs in at most one tuple of R2. So each tuple of R1 finds exactly one partner, the join produces exactly |R1| rows, and no combination can be invented.

If C is a superkey of neither, several tuples on each side may share a C value, and the join forms every cross-combination — precisely the spurious tuples of Section 5.2.

docs.title: Worked tests
docs.text:
Test 1 — the good decomposition. STUDENT(Rollno, Sname, Dno) and DEPARTMENT(Dno, Dname, Dhead), with Rollno → Sname, Dno and Dno → Dname, Dhead.

Common attributes: {Dno}. Dno⁺ = {Dno, Dname, Dhead}, which contains all of DEPARTMENT. So Dno is a superkey of DEPARTMENT. Lossless.

Test 2 — the bad decomposition. R(A,B,C) with A → B and C → B, split into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C).

Common attributes: {B}. B⁺ = {B}, which contains neither R1 = {A,B} nor R2 = {B,C}. Lossy.

Confirm with data. Let r = {(a1,b1,c1), (a2,b1,c2)}:

π<sub>AB</sub>(r) = {(a1,b1), (a2,b1)}; π<sub>BC</sub>(r) = {(b1,c1), (b1,c2)}.

The join on B gives four tuples — (a1,b1,c1), (a1,b1,c2), (a2,b1,c1), (a2,b1,c2) — two of which are spurious.

Test 3 — the BCNF algorithm is always lossless. The algorithm splits Q on a violating X → Y into Q1 = X ∪ Y and Q2 = Q − Y. The common attributes are exactly X, and X is by construction a superkey of Q1 = X ∪ Y (since X → Y and trivially X → X). The condition is therefore satisfied at every step. This is why the algorithm can be applied without checking losslessness each time.

docs.title: 23.4 The Chase (Tableau) Algorithm — Three or More Fragments
docs.text:
The binary test does not generalise. For m ≥ 3 fragments, use the chase.

Algorithm

  1. Build a matrix S with one row per fragment Ri and one column per attribute of R.
  2. Initialise: cell S(i, j) is the distinguished symbol a_j if attribute A_j belongs to Ri; otherwise the non-distinguished symbol b_ij.
  3. Repeat until no change: for each dependency X → Y in F, find rows that agree on all attributes of X. Make them agree on Y too — if one of the rows has an a symbol in a Y column, set the others to that a; otherwise set them all to the same b symbol.
  4. If, at the end, any row consists entirely of a symbols, the decomposition is lossless. Otherwise it is lossy.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = {A → C, B → C, C → D, DE → C, CE → A}, decomposed into R1(A,D), R2(A,B), R3(B,E), R4(C,D,E), R5(A,E).

Initial tableau:

A B C D E R1(A,D) a₁ b₁₂ b₁₃ a₄ b₁₅ R2(A,B) a₁ a₂ b₂₃ b₂₄ b₂₅ R3(B,E) b₃₁ a₂ b₃₃ b₃₄ a₅ R4(C,D,E) b₄₁ b₄₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ R5(A,E) a₁ b₅₂ b₅₃ b₅₄ a₅

Apply A → C. Rows 1, 2 and 5 agree on A (all a₁). Make their C values agree — none is a₃, so set all three to b₁₃.

A B C D E R1 a₁ b₁₂ b₁₃ a₄ b₁₅ R2 a₁ a₂ b₁₃ b₂₄ b₂₅ R3 b₃₁ a₂ b₃₃ b₃₄ a₅ R4 b₄₁ b₄₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ R5 a₁ b₅₂ b₁₃ b₅₄ a₅

Apply B → C. Rows 2 and 3 agree on B (a₂). Set both C values to b₁₃.

Row 3 C becomes b₁₃.

Apply C → D. Rows 1, 2, 3, 5 now share C = b₁₃. Row 1 has D = a₄, a distinguished symbol, so set all of them to a₄.

A B C D E R1 a₁ b₁₂ b₁₃ a₄ b₁₅ R2 a₁ a₂ b₁₃ a₄ b₂₅ R3 b₃₁ a₂ b₁₃ a₄ a₅ R4 b₄₁ b₄₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ R5 a₁ b₅₂ b₁₃ a₄ a₅

Apply DE → C. Rows 3, 4 and 5 agree on D = a₄ and E = a₅. Row 4 has C = a₃, so set rows 3 and 5 to a₃.

A B C D E R3 b₃₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ R5 a₁ b₅₂ a₃ a₄ a₅

Apply CE → A. Rows 3, 4 and 5 agree on C = a₃ and E = a₅. Row 5 has A = a₁, so set rows 3 and 4 to a₁.

A B C D E R1 a₁ b₁₂ b₁₃ a₄ b₁₅ R2 a₁ a₂ b₁₃ a₄ b₂₅ R3 a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ R4 a₁ b₄₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ R5 a₁ b₅₂ a₃ a₄ a₅

Row 3 is now a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ a₅ — all distinguished symbols.

Conclusion: the decomposition is LOSSLESS.

Reading the chase

A row of all a symbols means: whatever legal tuples the fragments contain, the join can always reconstruct a tuple identical to the original on every attribute. The b symbols represent values the fragment does not constrain; the dependencies gradually force them to coincide with the real values.

If the algorithm halts with no complete a-row, the remaining b symbols correspond exactly to the freedom that lets spurious tuples arise.

docs.title: 23.5 Testing Dependency Preservation
docs.text:
Procedure

  1. For each fragment Ri, compute its projected dependencies π<sub>Ri</sub>(F) — every FD X → Y in F⁺ with X ∪ Y ⊆ Ri. In practice: for each subset X of Ri, compute X⁺ under the full F, then intersect with Ri.
  2. Let G be the union of all the projected sets.
  3. For each dependency X → Y in the original F, test whether Y ⊆ X⁺ computed under G.
  4. If every one passes, the decomposition is dependency preserving.

The subtlety in step 3

It is not enough to check whether each original dependency lies inside a single fragment. A dependency may be recoverable from the combination of projected dependencies even though it appears in no fragment.

Example. R(A,B,C) with F = {A → B, B → C}, decomposed into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). The dependency A → C (which is in F⁺) spans both fragments and appears in neither. Yet A⁺ under G = {A → B, B → C} is {A,B,C}, so A → C is preserved. Always run the closure test.

docs.title: Worked test 1 — preserved
docs.text:
R(Rollno, Sname, Dno, Dname) with Rollno → Sname, Dno and Dno → Dname, decomposed into R1(Rollno, Sname, Dno) and R2(Dno, Dname).

  • π<sub>R1</sub>(F) contains Rollno → Sname, Dno.
  • π<sub>R2</sub>(F) contains Dno → Dname.
  • G = {Rollno → Sname, Dno ; Dno → Dname}.

Test each original FD: Rollno⁺ under G = {Rollno, Sname, Dno, Dname} ⊇ {Sname, Dno} ✓. Dno⁺ under G = {Dno, Dname} ⊇ {Dname} ✓.

Dependency preserving.

docs.title: Worked test 2 — not preserved
docs.text:
TEACHING(Student, Subject, Teacher) with Student,Subject → Teacher and Teacher → Subject, decomposed into TEACHES(Teacher, Subject) and STUDIES(Student, Teacher).

  • π<sub>TEACHES</sub>(F) = {Teacher → Subject}.
  • π<sub>STUDIES</sub>(F): compute Student⁺ = {Student}; Teacher⁺ = {Teacher, Subject}, intersected with {Student, Teacher} gives {Teacher} — nothing new. So π<sub>STUDIES</sub>(F) = ∅.
  • G = {Teacher → Subject}.

Test Student, Subject → Teacher: {Student, Subject}⁺ under G = {Student, Subject}. Teacher ∉ it.

Not preserved. This confirms by algorithm what Lesson 4 argued informally.

docs.title: 23.6 Summary of the Whole Unit
docs.text:
REQUIREMENTS
