docs.title: 23.7 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define the lossless-join property. Why is "lossless" a misleading name? Demonstrate spurious tuples.

A. A decomposition of R into R1, ..., Rm has the lossless-join property if, for every legal state r of R,

π<sub>R1</sub>(r) ⋈ ... ⋈ π<sub>Rm</sub>(r) = r

The name is misleading because projecting and rejoining can never lose a tuple — every original tuple always reappears in the join. The actual failure is the reverse: extra tuples are produced. These are spurious tuples, and they assert facts that were never true. Elmasri and Navathe therefore prefer non-additive join property.

Demonstration. R(A,B,C) with A → B and C → B, decomposed into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). Take

r = { (a1, b1, c1), (a2, b1, c2) }

π<sub>R1</sub>(r) = {(a1,b1), (a2,b1)} and π<sub>R2</sub>(r) = {(b1,c1), (b1,c2)}.

Joining on the common attribute B, every row on the left matches every row on the right because all share b1:

A B C Genuine? a1 b1 c1 yes a1 b1 c2 spurious a2 b1 c1 spurious a2 b1 c2 yes

Four tuples instead of two. The cause: the common attribute B is not a superkey of either fragment (B⁺ = {B}), so the join matches many rows to many rows.

Solved Question 2

Q. State the binary lossless-join test and prove why it works. Apply it to two examples.

A. Test. A decomposition of R into exactly two relations R1 and R2 is lossless if and only if

(R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2

— that is, (R1 ∩ R2)⁺ under F contains all of R1 or all of R2.

Why it works. Let C = R1 ∩ R2. The natural join pairs a tuple of π<sub>R1</sub>(r) with a tuple of π<sub>R2</sub>(r) exactly when they agree on C.

Suppose C is a superkey of R2. Then within π<sub>R2</sub>(r) each value of C occurs in at most one tuple. So each tuple of π<sub>R1</sub>(r) has at most one partner, the join yields at most |π<sub>R1</sub>(r)| tuples, and each reconstructs exactly the original tuple it came from. No combination can be invented.

If C is a superkey of neither, then some C value appears in several tuples on both sides, and the join forms every cross-combination — the spurious tuples of question 1.

Example 1 (lossless). STUDENT(Rollno, Sname, Dno) and DEPARTMENT(Dno, Dname, Dhead) with Rollno → Sname, Dno and Dno → Dname, Dhead. Common attribute {Dno}; Dno⁺ = {Dno, Dname, Dhead} ⊇ DEPARTMENT. Lossless.

Example 2 (lossy). R(A,B,C) with A → B, C → B, split into R1(A,B), R2(B,C). Common attribute {B}; B⁺ = {B}, containing neither fragment. Lossy — as the data in question 1 confirms.

Solved Question 3

Q. Apply the chase algorithm to R(A,B,C,D,E) with F = {A → C, B → C, C → D, DE → C, CE → A} decomposed into R1(A,D), R2(A,B), R3(B,E), R4(C,D,E), R5(A,E).

A. (Full working as in Section 5.4.) Summarising the steps:

  1. Build the tableau: a_j where attribute A_j is in Ri, b_ij otherwise.
  2. A → C: rows 1, 2, 5 share a₁, so their C cells all become b₁₃.
  3. B → C: rows 2, 3 share a₂, so row 3's C becomes b₁₃.
  4. C → D: rows 1, 2, 3, 5 now share C = b₁₃; row 1 has D = a₄, so all become a₄.
  5. DE → C: rows 3, 4, 5 share D = a₄, E = a₅; row 4 has C = a₃, so rows 3 and 5 become a₃.
  6. CE → A: rows 3, 4, 5 share C = a₃, E = a₅; row 5 has A = a₁, so rows 3 and 4 become a₁.

Final row 3 = (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, a₅) — all distinguished. The decomposition is LOSSLESS.

Interpretation. A complete a-row means the join can always reconstruct a tuple agreeing with the original on every attribute, whatever legal data the fragments hold. Had the algorithm halted with no such row, the surviving b symbols would mark exactly the attributes the fragments fail to pin down — the freedom that lets spurious tuples appear.

Note. The chase is needed only for three or more fragments; for two the simple binary test suffices, and for a decomposition produced by the BCNF algorithm losslessness is guaranteed by construction.

Solved Question 4

Q. Define dependency preservation and give the test. Show that the BCNF decomposition of TEACHING fails it.

A. A decomposition is dependency preserving if the union of the dependencies projected onto the fragments has the same closure as F:

( π<sub>R1</sub>(F) ∪ ... ∪ π<sub>Rm</sub>(F) )⁺ = F⁺

Practically: every original constraint can be enforced by examining one fragment, with no join.

Test. Compute π<sub>Ri</sub>(F) for each fragment; let G be their union; then for each X → Y in F, check whether Y ⊆ X⁺ computed under G.

Applying it to TEACHING(Student, Subject, Teacher) with F = {Student,Subject → Teacher ; Teacher → Subject}, decomposed into TEACHES(Teacher, Subject) and STUDIES(Student, Teacher):

  • π<sub>TEACHES</sub>(F): within {Teacher, Subject}, we have Teacher⁺ = {Teacher, Subject}, giving Teacher → Subject. (Subject⁺ = {Subject}, nothing.)
  • π<sub>STUDIES</sub>(F): within {Student, Teacher}, Student⁺ = {Student} and Teacher⁺ ∩ {Student,Teacher} = {Teacher}. Nothing is projected.
  • G = { Teacher → Subject }.

Now test the original dependency Student, Subject → Teacher: {Student, Subject}⁺ under G = {Student, Subject}. Teacher is not in it.

The dependency is lost. No constraint on either table can enforce it, because Student and Subject are in different fragments. Enforcement requires joining the two tables on every insert, or a trigger.

Note the contrast with the lossless property, which this same decomposition does satisfy (Teacher⁺ ⊇ TEACHES). It is precisely the standard demonstration that BCNF and dependency preservation can be incompatible.

Solved Question 5

Q. For R(A,B,C,D) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → D} decomposed into R1(A,B), R2(B,C), R3(C,D), test both properties.

A.

Attribute preservation. {A,B} ∪ {B,C} ∪ {C,D} = {A,B,C,D} = R ✓

Lossless join. Three fragments, so use the chase.

Initial tableau:

A B C D R1(A,B) a₁ a₂ b₁₃ b₁₄ R2(B,C) b₂₁ a₂ a₃ b₂₄ R3(C,D) b₃₁ b₃₂ a₃ a₄
  • A → B: only row 1 has a₁; no other row agrees on A. No change.
  • B → C: rows 1 and 2 agree on B = a₂. Row 2 has C = a₃, so row 1's C becomes a₃.
  • C → D: rows 1, 2, 3 now agree on C = a₃. Row 3 has D = a₄, so rows 1 and 2 become a₄.
A B C D R1 a₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ R2 b₂₁ a₂ a₃ a₄ R3 b₃₁ b₃₂ a₃ a₄

Row 1 is all a symbols → LOSSLESS.

(Cross-check by repeated binary tests: R1 ⋈ R2 on {B} — B⁺ = {B,C,D} ⊇ R2 ✓ lossless, giving R12(A,B,C). Then R12 ⋈ R3 on {C} — C⁺ = {C,D} ⊇ R3 ✓ lossless. Same conclusion.)

Dependency preservation. - π<sub>R1</sub>(F) = {A → B} - π<sub>R2</sub>(F) = {B → C} - π<sub>R3</sub>(F) = {C → D} - G = {A → B, B → C, C → D} = F exactly.

Every original dependency is present. Dependency preserving. ✓

Verdict: this decomposition has all three desirable properties, and each fragment is in BCNF (each has a single-attribute determinant that is its own key). It is an ideal decomposition.

Solved Question 6

Q. Rank the three properties in order of importance and justify the ranking.

A.

1. Attribute preservation — an absolute requirement. If an attribute appears in no fragment, the information is simply gone; no join can recover it. A "decomposition" that drops attributes is not a decomposition at all. This is checked first and never traded away.

2. Lossless join — a correctness requirement, never negotiable. A lossy decomposition corrupts the data. Rejoining the fragments yields spurious tuples that assert facts which were never true — and, crucially, they are indistinguishable from genuine rows. Every query over the reassembled data may then return wrong answers, with no way to detect or repair the damage. Note that the individual fragments look perfectly consistent, so the fault is invisible on inspection.

3. Dependency preservation — highly desirable, but a trade-off. Losing a dependency costs enforcement efficiency, not correctness. The constraint can still be enforced — by joining the fragments, by a trigger, or in the application. The stored data remains accurate and every query still returns the right answer; the system merely has to work harder, and the enforcement is easier to get wrong.

The ranking follows from the kind of failure each prevents:

Property If violated Recoverable? Attribute preservation Information is absent No Lossless join Data is silently corrupted No Dependency preservation Constraint checking is expensive Yes — with a join or trigger

This ranking is exactly why the theorem of Lesson 4 matters in the direction it does. A lossless BCNF decomposition always exists, so we never have to choose between BCNF and correctness. A dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition may not exist — and when it does not, the right response is to give up either BCNF (staying at 3NF) or dependency preservation (enforcing the rule another way), but never losslessness.

docs.title: 23.8 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. State the three desirable properties of a decomposition.
  2. Why is "lossless" a misleading name?
  3. What is a spurious tuple?
  4. State the binary lossless-join test.
  5. When must you use the chase algorithm rather than the binary test?
  6. What do the a and b symbols mean in a tableau?
  7. Which property must never be sacrificed, and why?

B. Test these decompositions for lossless join

  1. R(A,B,C), F = {A → B}, into R1(A,B), R2(A,C).
  2. R(A,B,C), F = {A → B}, into R1(A,B), R2(B,C).
  3. R(A,B,C,D), F = {A → B, C → D}, into R1(A,B), R2(C,D).
  4. R(A,B,C,D), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}, into R1(A,B,C), R2(C,D).
  5. R(A,B,C,D,E), F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}, into R1(A,B,C), R2(A,D,E).
  6. R(A,B,C,D,E), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E}, into R1(A,B,C), R2(C,D), R3(D,E) — use the chase.
  7. R(A,B,C,D,E,F), F = {A → BC, B → D, C → E, E → F}, into R1(A,B,C), R2(B,D), R3(C,E), R4(E,F) — use the chase.

C. Test these for dependency preservation

  1. R(A,B,C), F = {A → B, B → C}, into R1(A,B), R2(B,C).
  2. R(A,B,C), F = {A → B, B → C}, into R1(A,C), R2(B,C).
  3. R(A,B,C,D), F = {A → B, C → D}, into R1(A,B), R2(C,D).
  4. R(Student, Subject, Teacher), into R1(Teacher, Subject), R2(Student, Teacher).
  5. R(A,B,C,D), F = {AB → CD, D → A}, into R1(A,D), R2(B,C,D).

D. Analysis

  1. Construct a concrete instance demonstrating the spurious tuples in exercise 9, and count how many extra rows appear.
  2. Prove that the BCNF decomposition algorithm always produces a lossless decomposition.
  3. Explain why "each original FD lies inside some fragment" is sufficient but not necessary for dependency preservation. Give an example where the condition fails but the decomposition is still preserving.
  4. Explain, referring to the ranking of properties, why 3NF synthesis is often preferred to BCNF decomposition in practice.
  5. For the college schema of Unit 5 Lesson 1, verify that no decomposition was needed — that is, show every relation is already in BCNF.
  6. A colleague proposes decomposing ADMISSION(Rollno, SID, Dateofadmission) into (Rollno, SID) and (SID, Dateofadmission). Test both properties and explain the practical consequence.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A lossy decomposition loses tuples.
  2. A lossless decomposition is always dependency preserving.
  3. The binary test works for any number of fragments.
  4. If the common attributes form a superkey of one fragment, the binary decomposition is lossless.
  5. Dependency preservation is more important than losslessness.
  6. Every decomposition produced by the BCNF algorithm is lossless.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. It gains spurious tuples; no original tuple is ever lost. Hence the better name non-additive join.
  2. False. The BCNF decomposition of TEACHING is lossless but loses Student,Subject → Teacher.
  3. False. It applies only to two fragments; for three or more use the chase.
  4. True. That is exactly the condition — each tuple of the other fragment then finds at most one partner.
  5. False. Losslessness is a correctness requirement (a lossy decomposition corrupts data irrecoverably); dependency preservation costs only enforcement efficiency.
  6. True. Each step splits on X → Y into (X ∪ Y) and (R − Y), whose common attributes X form a superkey of the first fragment.

Lesson Summary

  • Three properties: attribute preservation, lossless join, dependency preservation.
  • "Lossless" really means non-additive: the danger is spurious tuples, not missing ones.
  • Binary test: the decomposition is lossless iff (R1 ∩ R2)⁺ contains all of R1 or all of R2.
  • For three or more fragments, use the chase (tableau) algorithm; a row of all a symbols means lossless.
  • Dependency preservation is tested by projecting F onto each fragment and checking that every original FD is recoverable from the union — not merely that each FD sits inside one fragment.
  • Ranking: attribute preservation and losslessness are correctness requirements; dependency preservation is a trade-off.

End of Unit 5. Next: Unit 6, Lesson 1 — Data Storage and File Organisation.

docs.title: Lesson 21: Normal Forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
docs.text:
Removing repeating groups, partial dependencies and transitive dependencies

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 5: Database Design · 10 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 14.3, 14.4

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define prime and non-prime attributes.
  2. Test a relation for 1NF, 2NF and 3NF, and name the exact violating dependency.
  3. Distinguish partial from transitive dependencies.
  4. Decompose a relation to 2NF and then to 3NF.
  5. State both equivalent definitions of 3NF.

docs.title: 21.1 Why Normalise
docs.text:
Unit 3, Lesson 1 showed that a relation storing facts about more than one kind of thing suffers insertion, deletion and modification anomalies. Normalisation is the formal, mechanical procedure for detecting that situation and repairing it.

Normalisation

The process of analysing a relation schema against its functional dependencies to minimise redundancy and eliminate update anomalies, by decomposing it into smaller relations that satisfy progressively stricter conditions called normal forms.

Introduced by E. F. Codd — 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in 1971–72; BCNF with Boyce in 1974.

   1NF   atomic values, no repeating groups
    |
    |  remove PARTIAL dependencies
    v
   2NF   no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key
    |
    |  remove TRANSITIVE dependencies
    v
   3NF   no non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute
    |
    |  remove ALL dependencies whose determinant is not a superkey
    v
   BCNF  every determinant is a superkey        (Lesson 4)

   Each form is STRICTLY STRONGER: every 3NF relation is in 2NF,
   every 2NF relation is in 1NF.

Prime and non-prime — learn this first

An attribute is prime (a key attribute) if it belongs to some candidate key.

An attribute is non-prime if it belongs to no candidate key.

Note "some", not "all". If the candidate keys are {A} and {B,C}, then A, B and C are all prime.

Every 2NF and 3NF test is stated in terms of non-prime attributes, so you must find all candidate keys first. This is why Lesson 2 came before this one.

docs.title: 21.2 First Normal Form (1NF)
docs.text:
1NF

A relation is in 1NF if the domain of every attribute contains only atomic (indivisible) values, and the value of any attribute in a tuple is a single value from that domain.

Equivalently: no composite attributes, no multivalued attributes, no nested relations, no repeating groups.

1NF is not really a normalisation step so much as the definition of a relation (Unit 3, Lesson 1, Characteristic 3). A structure violating it is not a relation at all.

docs.title: Violation and repair
docs.text:
Not in 1NF — a multivalued attribute:

Rollno Name Courses X2019 Ankit Sharma CS01, MA02 X2020 Riya Verma CS01

Three ways to repair, only one of which is correct.

Method 1 — a separate relation (correct). Move the multivalued attribute out, taking the key with it. This is exactly mapping step 6 of Lesson 1.

STUDENT(Rollno, Name) and STUDENT_COURSE(Rollno, SID) with key (Rollno, SID):

Rollno Name X2019 Ankit Sharma X2020 Riya Verma Rollno SID X2019 CS01 X2019 MA02 X2020 CS01

Method 2 — flatten into one relation (poor). Repeat Name on every row and make (Rollno, SID) the key. It is in 1NF but introduces exactly the redundancy that 2NF will then have to remove.

Method 3 — one column per value (wrong). Course1, Course2, Course3. This fixes the maximum number in advance, wastes NULLs, and makes "who takes CS01?" require searching every column. Never do this.

A composite attribute also violates 1NF — technically

Address(House, City, PIN) stored as one field is non-atomic if the parts are used separately. Store them as three columns.

But atomicity is relative to the application. If an address is only ever printed whole and never searched by city, a single VARCHAR is atomic for that application. Codd's point is about what the system must be able to see, not about what a human could subdivide.

docs.title: 21.3 Second Normal Form (2NF)
docs.text:
Full and partial functional dependency

X → Y is a full functional dependency if removing any attribute from X destroys the dependency.

X → Y is a partial functional dependency if some attribute can be removed from X and the dependency still holds — i.e. a proper subset of X already determines Y.

2NF

A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key — equivalently, no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key.

The shortcut every examiner expects you to know

A partial dependency requires a proper subset of a candidate key to determine something. If every candidate key is a single attribute, no proper non-empty subset exists.

A relation whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF. Only look for 2NF violations when there is a composite candidate key.

docs.title: Worked violation
docs.text:
STUDENT_COURSE( Rollno, SID, Sname, Cname, Grade )

FDs: Rollno, SID → Grade; Rollno → Sname; SID → Cname.

Candidate key: (Rollno, SID) — its closure is everything, and neither part alone suffices. Prime: Rollno, SID. Non-prime: Sname, Cname, Grade.

In 1NF? Yes — all values atomic.

In 2NF? No.

  • Rollno → Sname: Rollno is a proper subset of the key, and Sname is non-prime. Partial dependency — violation.
  • SID → Cname: likewise. Violation.
  • Rollno, SID → Grade: full — the whole key is needed. Fine.

The anomalies this predicts (and they are exactly those of Unit 3, Lesson 1): a student's name is repeated once per course; a new course cannot be recorded until a student enrols; deleting the last enrolment loses the course name.

docs.title: Decomposition to 2NF
docs.text:
Procedure

For each partial dependency X → Y (where X is a proper subset of a candidate key):

  1. Create a new relation (X, Y) with X as its primary key.
  2. Remove Y from the original relation, keeping X there as a foreign key.

Merge new relations that share the same X.

  • Rollno → Sname gives STUDENT(Rollno, Sname)
  • SID → Cname gives COURSE(SID, Cname)
  • What remains: ENROLMENT(Rollno, SID, Grade)
Relation Key Check STUDENT(Rollno, Sname) Rollno Single-attribute key → automatically 2NF COURSE(SID, Cname) SID Automatically 2NF ENROLMENT(Rollno, SID, Grade) (Rollno, SID) Grade fully depends on the whole key → 2NF

All three anomalies have gone.

docs.title: 21.4 Third Normal Form (3NF)
docs.text:
Transitive dependency

A transitive dependency on a candidate key K is a chain K → X → A where:

  • X is not a superkey, and
  • A is a non-prime attribute not in X.

The essence: a non-prime attribute is determined by another non-prime attribute rather than directly by a key.

3NF — Codd's original definition

A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key.

3NF — the general (working) definition

A relation is in 3NF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A that holds, at least one of the following is true:

  1. X is a superkey, or
  2. A is a prime attribute.

Condition 1 alone would be BCNF; condition 2 is precisely what 3NF forgives and BCNF does not.

The general definition is easier to apply and handles overlapping candidate keys correctly. Use it.

docs.title: Worked violation
docs.text:
STUDENT( Rollno, Sname, Dno, Dname, Dhead )

FDs: Rollno → Sname, Dno; Dno → Dname, Dhead.

Candidate key: Rollno. Prime: Rollno. Non-prime: Sname, Dno, Dname, Dhead.

In 2NF? Yes — the only candidate key is a single attribute, so no partial dependency is possible.

In 3NF? No. The chain Rollno → Dno → Dname is transitive: Dno is not a superkey (Dno⁺ = {Dno, Dname, Dhead} ≠ R) and Dname is non-prime. By the general definition, Dno → Dname has a non-superkey determinant and a non-prime dependent, failing both conditions.

The anomalies: the department name and head are repeated for every student in the department; a department with no students cannot be recorded; changing a department head requires updating many rows.

docs.title: Decomposition to 3NF
docs.text:
Procedure

For each transitive dependency X → Y where X is not a superkey:

  1. Create a new relation (X, Y) with X as its primary key.
  2. Remove Y from the original relation, keeping X as a foreign key.
  • STUDENT(Rollno, Sname, Dno), key Rollno, Dno a foreign key
  • DEPARTMENT(Dno, Dname, Dhead), key Dno

Both are now in 3NF, and the decomposition is lossless — the common attribute Dno is the key of DEPARTMENT (Lesson 5).

docs.title: 21.5 A Complete Worked Example
docs.text:
INVOICE( InvNo, LineNo, CustID, CustName, CustCity, ProdID, ProdName, UnitPrice, Qty )

FDs: 

InvNo, LineNo → ProdID, Qty
InvNo         → CustID
CustID        → CustName, CustCity
ProdID        → ProdName, UnitPrice

Step 1 — candidate keys. (InvNo, LineNo)⁺ = start {InvNo, LineNo} → ProdID, Qty → CustID → CustName, CustCity → ProdName, UnitPrice = all attributes. So (InvNo, LineNo) is a superkey; neither part alone is (InvNo⁺ lacks LineNo, LineNo⁺ = {LineNo}). Candidate key: (InvNo, LineNo).

Prime: InvNo, LineNo. Non-prime: everything else.

Step 2 — 1NF? Yes.

Step 3 — 2NF? No. InvNo → CustID is a partial dependency: InvNo is a proper subset of the key and CustID is non-prime. Decompose:

INVOICE ( InvNo, CustID )                                        key InvNo
LINE    ( InvNo, LineNo, ProdID, Qty )                           key (InvNo, LineNo)
...but CustName, CustCity, ProdName, UnitPrice must be placed too. They follow their determinants:

INVOICE ( InvNo, CustID, CustName, CustCity )                    key InvNo
LINE    ( InvNo, LineNo, ProdID, Qty, ProdName, UnitPrice )      key (InvNo, LineNo)

Step 4 — 3NF? Neither is in 3NF yet.

  • In INVOICE: CustID → CustName, CustCity — CustID is not a superkey of INVOICE and the dependents are non-prime. Transitive.
  • In LINE: ProdID → ProdName, UnitPrice — same problem.

Decompose both:

CUSTOMER ( CustID, CustName, CustCity )              key CustID
INVOICE  ( InvNo, CustID )                           key InvNo,  FK CustID
PRODUCT  ( ProdID, ProdName, UnitPrice )             key ProdID
LINE     ( InvNo, LineNo, ProdID, Qty )              key (InvNo, LineNo)
                                                     FK InvNo, FK ProdID

Step 5 — verify. Every determinant (CustID, InvNo, ProdID, (InvNo, LineNo)) is the key of its own relation, so each relation is in fact in BCNF, and hence in 3NF.

This is also exactly the schema the ER-to-relational mapping of Lesson 1 would have produced from a correct ER diagram — which is the practical argument for doing the conceptual design properly.

docs.title: 21.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define prime and non-prime attributes. For R(A,B,C,D) with candidate keys {A} and {B,C}, classify every attribute.

A. An attribute is prime if it belongs to at least one candidate key; non-prime if it belongs to none.

The word is some, not all — an attribute in any one candidate key is prime.

Attribute In {A}? In {B,C}? Classification A yes no prime B no yes prime C no yes prime D no no non-prime

Prime: A, B, C. Non-prime: D.

Why it matters: both the 2NF and the 3NF tests are stated entirely in terms of non-prime attributes. Here only D can cause a violation — any dependency whose right side is A, B or C is automatically forgiven by 3NF, however odd its determinant.

This is also why the candidate keys must be computed first: misidentify them and every subsequent normal-form judgement is wrong.

Solved Question 2

Q. Define 2NF. Test STUDENT_COURSE(Rollno, SID, Sname, Cname, Grade) with Rollno,SID → Grade, Rollno → Sname, SID → Cname, and decompose if necessary.

A. A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key — that is, every non-prime attribute is fully dependent on every candidate key.

Candidate key. (Rollno, SID)⁺ = {Rollno, SID} → Grade → Sname → Cname = all. Rollno⁺ = {Rollno, Sname}; SID⁺ = {SID, Cname}. Neither part alone is a superkey, so (Rollno, SID) is the sole candidate key.

Prime: Rollno, SID. Non-prime: Sname, Cname, Grade.

2NF test.

FD Determinant a proper subset of the key? Dependent non-prime? Verdict Rollno, SID → Grade no (it is the whole key) yes full — fine Rollno → Sname yes yes partial — violates 2NF SID → Cname yes yes partial — violates 2NF

Not in 2NF.

Decomposition. One relation per partial dependency, with the remainder keeping the full key:

STUDENT   ( Rollno, Sname )          key Rollno
COURSE    ( SID, Cname )             key SID
ENROLMENT ( Rollno, SID, Grade )     key (Rollno, SID); both columns foreign keys

Verification. STUDENT and COURSE have single-attribute keys, so they are automatically in 2NF (no proper subset exists). In ENROLMENT, Grade depends on the whole key. All three are in 2NF — and in fact in BCNF.

Anomalies removed: a course can now be recorded with no students (insertion); deleting the last enrolment leaves the course intact (deletion); a student's name is stored once (modification).

Solved Question 3

Q. Define 3NF in both forms. Test EMPLOYEE(Eno, Ename, Dno, Dname, Dlocation) with Eno → Ename, Dno and Dno → Dname, Dlocation.

A.

Codd's original definition. In 2NF, and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on any candidate key — no chain K → X → A with X not a superkey and A non-prime.

General definition. For every non-trivial FD X → A: either X is a superkey, or A is prime.

Analysis. Eno⁺ = {Eno, Ename, Dno} → (via Dno) {Eno, Ename, Dno, Dname, Dlocation} = R. So Eno is the only candidate key. Prime: Eno. Non-prime: Ename, Dno, Dname, Dlocation.

1NF: yes. 2NF: yes — the sole candidate key is a single attribute, so no partial dependency can exist.

3NF: no.

  • By the original definition, Eno → Dno → Dname is a transitive chain: Dno is not a superkey (Dno⁺ = {Dno, Dname, Dlocation} ≠ R) and Dname is non-prime.
  • By the general definition, the FD Dno → Dname fails both conditions: Dno is not a superkey, and Dname is not prime.

Decomposition.

EMPLOYEE   ( Eno, Ename, Dno )              key Eno,  Dno a foreign key
DEPARTMENT ( Dno, Dname, Dlocation )        key Dno

Verification. In EMPLOYEE the only determinant is Eno, its key. In DEPARTMENT the only determinant is Dno, its key. Both are in BCNF.

The decomposition is lossless: the common attribute Dno is the primary key of DEPARTMENT, so Dno⁺ contains all of DEPARTMENT (Lesson 5). It is also dependency preserving: Eno → Ename, Dno is checkable within EMPLOYEE and Dno → Dname, Dlocation within DEPARTMENT.

Solved Question 4

Q. Distinguish partial from transitive dependency, with an example of each, and state which normal form removes each.

A.

Partial dependency Transitive dependency Shape X → A where X is a proper subset of a candidate key and A is non-prime K → X → A where X is not a superkey and A is non-prime Determinant Part of a key Not a key at all Requires A composite candidate key Nothing special; occurs with single-attribute keys Removed by 2NF 3NF Example In (Rollno, SID, Sname): Rollno → Sname In (Eno, Dno, Dname): Eno → Dno → Dname

Partial — the attribute belongs with part of the key, so it is repeated once for every value of the rest of the key. Sname is repeated once per course the student takes.

Transitive — the attribute belongs with a different entity that happens to be identified inside this relation. Dname is a fact about a department, repeated once per employee in it.

Both are the same disease in the terms of Unit 3, Lesson 1: the relation stores facts about more than one kind of thing. The cure is the same in both cases — extract the determinant and its dependents into their own relation, leaving the determinant behind as a foreign key.

Note the ordering. A relation with a single-attribute candidate key cannot have a partial dependency, so it is automatically in 2NF and one need only test for 3NF.

Solved Question 5

Q. Normalise ORDER_DETAIL(OrderNo, ProdID, OrderDate, CustID, CustName, ProdName, Price, Qty) to 3NF. Show the FDs, the keys, each violation and the final schema.

A.

FDs from the semantics: 

OrderNo, ProdID → Qty
OrderNo         → OrderDate, CustID
CustID          → CustName
ProdID          → ProdName, Price

Candidate key. (OrderNo, ProdID)⁺ = {OrderNo, ProdID} → Qty → OrderDate, CustID → CustName → ProdName, Price = all attributes. Neither part alone suffices. (OrderNo, ProdID) is the sole candidate key. Prime: OrderNo, ProdID. Non-prime: all the rest.

1NF. Satisfied — all values atomic.

2NF. Violated twice.

  • OrderNo → OrderDate, CustID — proper subset of the key determining non-prime attributes.
  • ProdID → ProdName, Price — likewise.

Decompose: 

ORDERS   ( OrderNo, OrderDate, CustID, CustName )      key OrderNo
PRODUCT  ( ProdID, ProdName, Price )                   key ProdID
LINE     ( OrderNo, ProdID, Qty )                      key (OrderNo, ProdID)

3NF. PRODUCT and LINE are fine — every determinant is the relation's key. But ORDERS still has CustID → CustName, where CustID is not a superkey of ORDERS and CustName is non-prime. Transitive — violated.

Decompose again: 

CUSTOMER ( CustID, CustName )                          key CustID
ORDERS   ( OrderNo, OrderDate, CustID )                key OrderNo, FK CustID

Final schema (all in BCNF, hence 3NF):

CUSTOMER ( CustID, CustName )
PRODUCT  ( ProdID, ProdName, Price )
ORDERS   ( OrderNo, OrderDate, CustID )         FK CustID -> CUSTOMER
LINE     ( OrderNo, ProdID, Qty )               FK OrderNo -> ORDERS, FK ProdID -> PRODUCT

Check: in each relation the only determinant is its own primary key, so every FD has a superkey on the left. Every decomposition step split on a determinant that became the key of the new relation, so each is lossless; and every original FD is checkable within one relation, so the decomposition is dependency preserving.

Solved Question 6

Q. Give a relation that is in 2NF but not 3NF, and one in 1NF but not 2NF. Explain why each fails, and why the general 3NF definition is preferred to Codd's original.

A.

In 1NF but not 2NF. ENROLMENT(Rollno, SID, Sname, Grade) with Rollno, SID → Grade and Rollno → Sname. Candidate key (Rollno, SID); Sname is non-prime. Rollno is a proper subset of the key and determines Sname, so Sname is partially dependent on the key. Values are atomic, so it is in 1NF but fails 2NF.

In 2NF but not 3NF. STUDENT(Rollno, Sname, Dno, Dname) with Rollno → Sname, Dno and Dno → Dname. The sole candidate key Rollno is a single attribute, so no partial dependency is possible and 2NF holds. But Rollno → Dno → Dname is transitive: Dno is not a superkey and Dname is non-prime. Fails 3NF.

Why the general definition is preferred. Codd's original wording — "no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key" — is awkward when candidate keys overlap, because one must trace chains from each key and decide which attributes count as intermediate. The general form is a simple test applied to each dependency independently:

for every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkey or A is prime.

Consider R(A,B,C) with AB → C and C → B. Candidate keys are {A,B} and {A,C}, so all attributes are prime. The general definition immediately gives 3NF: C → B fails the superkey test but B is prime, so the second condition rescues it. Reasoning about transitive chains here is far more error-prone.

The general definition also makes the relationship to BCNF transparent: BCNF is the general 3NF definition with condition 2 deleted.

docs.title: 21.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define prime and non-prime attributes.
  2. State 1NF and give two ways it can be violated.
  3. Define partial functional dependency.
  4. When is a relation automatically in 2NF?
  5. State both definitions of 3NF.
  6. Which normal form removes partial dependencies? Which removes transitive ones?
  7. Why must candidate keys be found before testing 2NF or 3NF?

B. Test and normalise

For each, find all candidate keys, classify the attributes, determine the highest normal form, name every violating dependency, and decompose to 3NF.

  1. R(A,B,C,D) with AB → C, C → D.
  2. R(A,B,C,D,E) with A → BC, C → DE.
  3. R(A,B,C,D) with A → B, B → C, C → D.
  4. STUDENT(Rollno, Name, CourseID, CourseName, TeacherName, TeacherPhone) with the obvious dependencies.
  5. SALES(InvoiceNo, ItemNo, Date, CustID, CustName, ItemName, Rate, Qty).
  6. PROJECT(Eno, Ename, Pno, Pname, Ploc, Hours) with Eno → Ename, Pno → Pname, Ploc, Eno,Pno → Hours.
  7. BOOK(ISBN, Title, AuthorID, AuthorName, PublisherID, PublisherName, PublisherCity).
  8. HOSPITAL(PatientID, PatientName, DoctorID, DoctorName, Speciality, VisitDate, Diagnosis).

C. Analysis

  1. Give a relation in 1NF but not 2NF, and prove it with an instance exhibiting an anomaly.
  2. Give a relation in 2NF but not 3NF, and demonstrate the update anomaly with actual rows.
  3. Explain why Method 3 (Course1, Course2, Course3) is a poor repair for a 1NF violation. Give three specific problems.
  4. Show that a relation with only two attributes is always in 3NF. Is it always in BCNF?
  5. Explain why the general definition of 3NF handles overlapping candidate keys better than Codd's original. Use R(A,B,C) with AB → C, C → B.
  6. For R(A,B,C,D) with AB → CD and D → A, find all candidate keys and determine the highest normal form. (Take care: the keys overlap.)
  7. A relation has candidate keys {A} and {B}, and the dependency A → B. Is it in 3NF? In BCNF? Justify.
  8. "Normalisation always improves a database." Argue both sides, mentioning join cost and denormalisation.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. Every relation in 3NF is in 2NF.
  2. A relation with a single-attribute candidate key is always in 3NF.
  3. A partial dependency can exist when the candidate key is a single attribute.
  4. An attribute in some candidate key is prime.
  5. 1NF prohibits composite attributes.
  6. Removing a transitive dependency requires creating a new relation.
  7. A relation in 2NF has no redundancy.

Answers to Section D

  1. True. The normal forms are strictly nested: 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF.
  2. False. It is automatically in 2NF, but a transitive dependency can still violate 3NF — as in STUDENT(Rollno, Sname, Dno, Dname).
  3. False. A partial dependency needs a proper subset of the key; a single attribute has no non-empty proper subset.
  4. True. That is the definition — membership of some candidate key, not all.
  5. True. A composite attribute is not atomic, so it must be stored as its separate component columns.
  6. True. The determinant and its dependents are extracted into a new relation, with the determinant left behind as a foreign key.
  7. False. 2NF removes only partial dependencies. Transitive dependencies, and hence redundancy, may remain.

Lesson Summary

  • Find all candidate keys first; then classify attributes as prime or non-prime.
  • 1NF: atomic values — no composite, multivalued or repeating groups. Repair with a separate relation, never with Course1, Course2, Course3.
  • 2NF: no partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on a candidate key. Only possible to violate when a key is composite.
  • 3NF: no transitive dependency — or, generally, for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime.
  • Decompose by extracting the offending determinant together with its dependents into a new relation, leaving the determinant as a foreign key.

docs.title: Lesson 1: Purpose of a Database System
docs.text:
Why we abandoned files and invented the DBMS

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 1: Introduction to Database · 5 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture (50 minutes)

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 1 · Silberschatz, Ch. 1

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  1. Define the terms data, information, database, and DBMS precisely.
  2. Explain the classic problems of the file-processing approach.
  3. Justify each problem with a concrete college or bank example.
  4. State how a DBMS solves each problem.
  5. Identify when a DBMS is not the right choice.

docs.title: 1.1 From Data to Database
docs.text:
Definitions

Data — raw, unprocessed facts with no context of their own. 21, "Ankit", 2004-08-19 are data.

Information — data placed in a context so that it answers a question. "Ankit, aged 21, was born on 19-Aug-2004" is information.

Database — a shared, integrated, self-describing collection of logically related data, designed to meet the information needs of an organisation.

DBMS (Database Management System) — a collection of programs that enables users to create, maintain, query and control access to a database. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLite.

Database System — the database + the DBMS + the application programs + the users, taken together.

Unpack the four words in the definition of database; each is a design commitment:

Word What it commits you to Shared Many users and many applications use the same copy of the data, concurrently. Integrated Formerly separate files are merged so that a fact is stored once. Logically related The data describes one mini-world (a college, a bank) — not a random heap. Self-describing The database stores its own structure (the catalog or data dictionary), not just the values.

Mini-world (Universe of Discourse)

The slice of the real world that a database represents. For our course-wide running example the mini-world is a college: its students, the courses they take admission in, the societies they enrol in, and the teachers in charge.

docs.title: The self-describing property — the sharpest difference
docs.text:
A traditional program file, say students.dat, is meaningless on its own. The knowledge that "bytes 0-7 are the roll number, bytes 8-37 are the name" lives inside the C or COBOL program that reads it. Lose the program, lose the data.

A database stores that knowledge inside itself, in the catalog:

-- The catalog is itself queryable data
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_name = 'STUDENT';

+-------------+-----------+-------------+
| column_name | data_type | is_nullable |
+-------------+-----------+-------------+
| Rollno      | varchar   | NO          |
| Name        | varchar   | NO          |
| Dateofbirth | date      | YES         |
+-------------+-----------+-------------+

This is why a DBMS is general-purpose software: it does not need to be recompiled to hold a new kind of data. You describe the new structure; the DBMS reads its own catalog and adapts.

docs.title: 1.2 The File-Processing Approach
docs.text:
Before databases — and still, in badly built systems today — each department wrote its own programs owning its own files.

        FILE-PROCESSING APPROACH  (the "before" picture)

  ADMISSION SECTION            EXAM SECTION              LIBRARY
  +----------------+          +----------------+     +----------------+
  | admission.exe  |          |   result.exe   |     |  library.exe   |
  | (written in C) |          |   (in COBOL)   |     |  (in FoxPro)   |
  +-------+--------+          +-------+--------+     +-------+--------+
          |                           |                      |
          v                           v                      v
  +----------------+          +----------------+     +----------------+
  | students.dat   |          |  marks.dat     |     |  members.dat   |
  | rollno, name,  |          | roll_no, name, |     | mem_id, sname, |
  | dob, course    |          | subj, marks    |     | dob, books     |
  +----------------+          +----------------+     +----------------+
     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
        A student's NAME and DOB are stored THREE times, in three
        different formats, owned by three different programs.

Figure 1.1 — Islands of automation. Each application owns its private files.

docs.title: The classic problems
docs.text:
Problem 1 — Data Redundancy and Inconsistency

Redundancy = the same fact stored in more than one place. Inconsistency = those copies disagree.

Example. Student X2019 is Ankit Sharma in students.dat, in marks.dat, and in members.dat. He gets his name legally corrected to Ankit Kumar Sharma. The admission clerk updates students.dat. Nobody tells the exam section.

Result: the degree certificate prints Ankit Sharma, the library card says Ankit Sharma, the admission register says Ankit Kumar Sharma. The database no longer knows the truth. This is an update anomaly, and it is the single most damaging failure of the file approach.

Redundancy also wastes storage, but inconsistency is the real disease; wasted bytes are only a symptom.

Problem 2 — Difficulty in Accessing Data

File systems answer only the questions their programs were written to answer.

The Principal asks: "Give me the names of students born in 2001 who are enrolled in at least one part-time course." No program does that. Someone must write, compile, test and deploy a new program — a week's work for a one-off question.

In a DBMS this is one statement, answered in milliseconds:

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  YEAR(s.Dateofbirth) = 2001
  AND  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime';

The DBMS provides a general-purpose query language, so unanticipated questions cost nothing.

Problem 3 — Data Isolation

Data is scattered across files in incompatible formats — one CSV, one fixed-width binary, one dBase table, with dates as DD/MM/YY here and YYYYMMDD there. Writing a program that combines them is mostly format-conversion drudgery, not logic.

Problem 4 — Integrity Problems

Business rules — "Total seats must be positive", "course type is only Fulltime or Parttime", "a roll number in ADMISSION must exist in STUDENT" — are buried inside program code in the file approach. Every new program must re-implement every rule, and one programmer who forgets corrupts the data for everybody.

A DBMS lets you declare the rule once, at the data:

CHECK (TotalSeats > 0),
CHECK (Coursetype IN ('Fulltime','Parttime')),
FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno)

The DBMS then enforces it against every access path — SQL prompt, web app, batch job, DBA — with no exceptions.

Problem 5 — Atomicity Problems

A transfer of 5,000 rupees from account A to B is two writes: debit A, credit B. If the machine crashes between them, 5,000 rupees has evaporated.

Atomicity means all-or-nothing: either both writes happen or neither does. File systems have no notion of this; DBMSs implement it with logging and recovery.

Problem 6 — Concurrent Access Anomalies

Two clerks book the last seat of a course at the same instant.

Time Clerk 1 Clerk 2 Vacant in file t1 reads Vacant = 1 1 t2 reads Vacant = 1 1 t3 writes Vacant = 0 0 t4 writes Vacant = 0 0

Two students admitted, one seat consumed. This is a lost update. A DBMS prevents it with concurrency control (Unit 6).

Problem 7 — Security Problems

File permissions are all-or-nothing on the whole file. But a clerk should see a student's address and not their fee-defaulter status. A DBMS grants privileges per table, per column, per operation:

GRANT SELECT (Rollno, Name) ON STUDENT TO 'clerk'@'localhost';

docs.title: 1.3 How the DBMS Answers
docs.text:
DATABASE APPROACH  (the "after" picture)

   Admission App     Exam App      Library App     Ad-hoc SQL
        |                |               |              |
        +--------+-------+-------+-------+------+-------+
                          |
                 +--------v---------+
                 |      D B M S     |   <-- query processor, transaction
                 |  (MySQL/Oracle)  |       manager, security, catalog
                 +--------+---------+
                          |
              +-----------v------------+
              |  ONE SHARED DATABASE   |
              |  STUDENT   COURSE      |
              |  ADMISSION SOCIETY     |
              |  + CATALOG (metadata)  |
              +------------------------+

   Every fact stored ONCE. Every rule enforced ONCE. Every app agrees.

Figure 1.2 — All applications share one integrated, self-describing database.

# File-system problem DBMS facility that removes it 1 Redundancy and inconsistency Integration + normalisation (Unit 5) 2 Difficulty of access SQL — declarative, general-purpose query language (Unit 4) 3 Data isolation One uniform data model + one catalog (Unit 3) 4 Integrity problems Declarative constraints: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, NOT NULL 5 Atomicity Transactions — COMMIT / ROLLBACK, write-ahead log (Unit 6) 6 Concurrency anomalies Concurrency control — locking, serialisable schedules (Unit 6) 7 Security CREATE USER, GRANT, REVOKE, roles, views (Unit 4)

docs.title: 1.4 Advantages of the Database Approach
docs.text:
1. Controlled redundancy. Redundancy is not banned outright — it is controlled. A little is sometimes kept deliberately for performance, but the DBMS then knows about it and keeps copies in step.
  2. Data sharing. Multiple users and applications, concurrently, on one consistent copy.
  3. Enforcement of standards. One naming convention, one date format, one documentation standard, imposed by the DBA.
  4. Improved data integrity and security.
  5. Backup and recovery provided as a service — no application needs to write its own.
  6. Data independence. Change the storage, or even the logical design, without rewriting applications (Lesson 3).
  7. Faster application development. The hard parts — concurrency, recovery, security, indexing — are already written.
  8. Economy of scale. One powerful server for the organisation beats a dozen departmental silos.
  9. Balanced conflicting requirements. The DBA arbitrates centrally between departments.
  10. Availability of up-to-date information. An update is instantly visible to everyone.

docs.title: 1.5 Costs, and When Not to Use a DBMS
docs.text:
Be honest about the trade-offs — this is a favourite examination question.

Costs: high initial cost of software, hardware and DBA salaries; the overhead of generality (a DBMS performs security, concurrency, recovery and integrity checks on every operation, so a single simple read is slower than a raw file read); and a central point of failure.

A DBMS is unnecessary or undesirable when...

  • The database and applications are simple, well-defined and not expected to change.
  • There are stringent real-time requirements that the DBMS overhead would violate (e.g. embedded instrument control).
  • No multi-user access is needed.
  • Embedded systems with very limited storage — a raw file, or a tiny library such as SQLite, is used instead of a server-class DBMS.

docs.title: 1.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Distinguish between data and information with an example from a college database.

A. Data are raw facts recorded without interpretation; information is data processed and placed in context so that it answers a question and supports a decision.

In the college database the row ('X2019', 'Ankit Sharma', '2001-03-14') is data — three values with no stated meaning. Once the schema tells us that the columns are (Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth), and we compute from it that "Ankit Sharma, roll number X2019, is 24 years old and therefore eligible for the senior scholarship", we have information.

The bridge between them is the metadata (the catalog) plus the processing. This is exactly what the self-describing property of a database supplies and a flat file does not.

Solved Question 2

Q. "Redundancy is bad because it wastes disk space." Criticise this statement.

A. The statement is true but trivial, and it identifies the wrong danger. Disk is cheap; correctness is not.

The serious consequence of redundancy is inconsistency. If a student's address is stored in the admission file, the library file and the examination file, then an address change updated in only one of them leaves the organisation with three different answers to the same question, and no way to tell which is right. Reports disagree, letters go to the wrong place, and audits fail.

A second non-space cost is wasted effort and increased error probability: every update must be applied n times, so the chance of a mistake is roughly n times larger, and each application must be coded to remember all n places.

Note further that redundancy is not always wrong: a DBMS may keep a controlled redundant copy (an index, a materialised view, a denormalised summary) precisely because it can then guarantee that all copies stay synchronised. Uncontrolled redundancy is the problem.

Solved Question 3

Q. A college keeps students.dat (admission section) and members.dat (library). Both store a student's name and date of birth. List four distinct problems, and state for each which DBMS feature removes it.

A.

Problem Explanation DBMS remedy Redundancy / inconsistency Name and DOB duplicated; a correction applied to one file only makes them disagree. Integration into a single STUDENT table; normalisation removes duplication. Difficulty of access "List library members who are part-time students" spans two files with no common program. SQL join over STUDENT and MEMBER tables. Data isolation Library uses DD-MM-YY text dates, admission uses a binary date; formats are incompatible. One DATE domain enforced by the DBMS type system. Integrity Nothing stops the library from registering a member who was never admitted. FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno).

(Also acceptable: security — the library clerk can read the whole admission file if given access, whereas a DBMS could grant only SELECT(Rollno, Name).)

Solved Question 4

Q. Show, with a time-line, how two concurrent seat bookings can over-admit a student when files are used. Name the anomaly.

A. Let Vacant = 1 initially.

Time Transaction T1 (Clerk 1) Transaction T2 (Clerk 2) Stored value t1 read(Vacant) returns 1 — 1 t2 — read(Vacant) returns 1 1 t3 test 1 > 0, so admit — 1 t4 — test 1 > 0, so admit 1 t5 Vacant := 1 - 1 = 0; write(0) — 0 t6 — Vacant := 1 - 1 = 0; write(0) 0

Two students have been admitted but Vacant fell by only one. T2's read happened before T1's write, so T1's update was overwritten and lost.

This is the lost update problem. A DBMS prevents it by making the read-modify-write sequence a transaction and serialising conflicting transactions with locks (Unit 6), so the observable result is the same as if T1 ran entirely before T2 — and T2 would then correctly see Vacant = 0 and refuse the admission.

Solved Question 5

Q. Give two situations where using a full DBMS is not justified. Justify each.

A.

  1. A hard real-time embedded controller — e.g. firmware in an anti-lock braking system. Every read must complete within a guaranteed microsecond bound. A DBMS adds query parsing, locking, logging and integrity checking to each access, and cannot give a hard worst-case bound. A fixed, hand-written memory structure is correct here.

  2. A single-user application with a tiny, frozen data structure — e.g. a program storing user preferences in a 2 KB configuration file, used by one person, whose structure will never change. The cost of installing, licensing and administering a DBMS vastly exceeds the benefit, and none of the file-system problems actually bite: there is no sharing, no concurrency, no ad-hoc querying and no redundancy.

(Other valid answers: a device with severe storage limits; a purely archival write-once dataset accessed by one batch program.)

Solved Question 6

Q. Explain the self-describing nature of a database and why it makes a DBMS general-purpose software.

A. A database stores, alongside the user data, a complete description of its own structure — table names, column names, data types, sizes, constraints, views, users and privileges. This description is called the catalog, data dictionary or metadata, and in SQL systems it is itself stored as tables (information_schema) which can be queried with ordinary SQL.

Consequence: the DBMS software contains no knowledge of any particular application. When it is asked to read STUDENT, it first reads the catalog to learn what STUDENT looks like, and then interprets the stored bytes accordingly. The same MySQL binary therefore runs a college database, a bank database and an airline database without a single line being changed or recompiled.

Contrast with file processing, where the record layout is compiled into the application program. There, a new kind of record means new code; and if the program is lost, the file becomes an undecipherable stream of bytes.

docs.title: 1.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer (2 marks each)

  1. Define database and list the four properties implied by the definition.
  2. What is metadata? Where is it stored in a DBMS?
  3. Differentiate between redundancy and inconsistency.
  4. What is meant by a mini-world?
  5. Why is atomicity impossible to guarantee in a plain file system?
  6. Name any three components of a database system.

B. Long answer (5-6 marks each)

  1. Explain the problems of the file-processing approach, giving one college-domain example for each, and state the DBMS feature that solves it.
  2. "A DBMS is not always the right answer." Discuss the costs of the database approach and list four circumstances in which files are preferable.
  3. Explain the self-describing property of databases. How does it differ from the way a C program stores a record layout? Why does this make a DBMS general purpose?
  4. List and explain any eight advantages of the database approach over the file-processing approach.

C. Application and analytical

  1. A hospital keeps three files: patients.dat (Patient section), billing.dat (Accounts), pharmacy.dat (Pharmacy). All three store the patient's name, age and blood group. a. Identify every instance of redundancy. b. Construct a scenario in which the three files disagree about a patient's blood group, and state the possible real-world consequence. c. Redesign the data as an integrated set of tables and say which duplication disappears.
  2. For each requirement below, decide DBMS or plain file, and justify in one sentence: a. Storing the high-score list of a single-player mobile game. b. A university's examination result system for 60,000 students. c. A satellite's attitude-control telemetry buffer. d. An e-commerce site's order and inventory system.
  3. Write, in plain English, three questions about the college mini-world that a file-based system would need a new program for, but that a DBMS answers with one query. Then write the SQL for one of them.
  4. A bank transfers 10,000 rupees from account A to account B. Enumerate every low-level step, then mark the exact points at which a crash would leave the database inconsistent. Which ACID property is at stake?

D. Objective — state True or False with a one-line reason

  1. A DBMS eliminates all redundancy from an organisation's data.
  2. Metadata is stored in the application programs.
  3. The lost-update problem is a consequence of poor security.
  4. A DBMS always performs faster than direct file access for a single record read.
  5. Data isolation refers to keeping different users' data separate for privacy.
  6. Declaring CHECK (TotalSeats > 0) enforces the rule for every application that touches the table.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. It provides controlled redundancy; some is retained deliberately (indexes, materialised views) and kept synchronised.
  2. False. It is stored in the database's own catalog / data dictionary.
  3. False. It is a concurrency-control failure, not a security failure.
  4. False. Generality costs overhead; a raw file read of one known record can be faster. The DBMS wins on flexibility, integrity, sharing and complex queries.
  5. False. Data isolation means data is scattered across files in incompatible formats, making combined access hard.
  6. True. The constraint lives with the data, so every access path — SQL prompt, application, batch job — is checked.

Lesson Summary

  • A database is a shared, integrated, logically related, self-describing collection of data about a mini-world; a DBMS is the general-purpose software that manages it.
  • The file-processing approach fails on redundancy/inconsistency, difficulty of access, data isolation, integrity, atomicity, concurrency and security.
  • The DBMS answers with integration, SQL, a uniform model, declarative constraints, transactions, concurrency control and privileges.
  • The self-describing catalog is what makes a DBMS general purpose.
  • The database approach has real costs; it is not appropriate for simple, single-user, hard-real-time or storage-starved situations.

docs.title: Lesson 15: Querying with SELECT
docs.text:
Filtering, operators, NULLs, functions and ordering

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 4: Structured Query Language · 12 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 6.3 · Murach's MySQL, Ch. 3, 8, 9

Learning Outcomes

  1. Write SELECT with WHERE, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT.
  2. Use comparison, logical, BETWEEN, IN and LIKE operators fluently.
  3. Handle NULL correctly using three-valued logic and IS NULL.
  4. Apply string, numeric and date functions.
  5. State the logical order of evaluation of a SELECT statement.

docs.title: 15.1 The SELECT Statement
docs.text:
SELECT   [DISTINCT] select_list
FROM     table_source
[WHERE   search_condition]
[GROUP BY grouping_columns]
[HAVING  group_condition]
[ORDER BY sort_columns [ASC|DESC]]
[LIMIT   n [OFFSET m]];

The logical order of evaluation

The clauses are written in the order above but evaluated in a different order. This explains almost every puzzling SQL error:

   WRITTEN                    EVALUATED
   1. SELECT                  1. FROM      -- which tables, and join them
   2. FROM                    2. WHERE     -- filter individual ROWS
   3. WHERE                   3. GROUP BY  -- form groups
   4. GROUP BY                4. HAVING    -- filter GROUPS
   5. HAVING                  5. SELECT    -- choose/compute columns
   6. ORDER BY                6. DISTINCT  -- remove duplicate rows
   7. LIMIT                   7. ORDER BY  -- sort the result
                              8. LIMIT     -- take the first n

Two consequences to memorise:

  1. WHERE runs before SELECT, so a column alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE.
  2. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so a column alias can be used in ORDER BY.

docs.title: Basic forms
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM STUDENT;                          -- all columns (avoid in production)
SELECT Rollno, Name FROM STUDENT;               -- projection
SELECT Name AS StudentName FROM STUDENT;        -- alias
SELECT DISTINCT Coursetype FROM COURSE;         -- remove duplicates

SELECT vs relational algebra π

SELECT Coursetype FROM COURSE returns five rows (one per course); the algebra π<sub>Coursetype</sub>(COURSE) returns two.

SQL tables are multisets. π corresponds to SELECT DISTINCT, not to SELECT.

docs.title: Comparison operators
docs.text:
=, <> (or !=), <, <=, >, >=

SELECT * FROM COURSE WHERE TotalSeats > 45;
SELECT * FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype <> 'Fulltime';
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Dateofbirth < '2002-01-01';

docs.title: Logical operators — AND, OR, NOT
docs.text:
NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR. Use parentheses whenever you mix AND and OR.

-- WRONG: reads as Fulltime AND (>50), OR (Parttime)
SELECT * FROM COURSE WHERE Coursetype='Fulltime' AND TotalSeats>50 OR Coursetype='Parttime';

-- RIGHT
SELECT * FROM COURSE
WHERE (Coursetype='Fulltime' OR Coursetype='Parttime') AND TotalSeats > 50;

docs.title: BETWEEN
docs.text:
BETWEEN is inclusive of both endpoints.

SELECT * FROM COURSE WHERE TotalSeats BETWEEN 40 AND 50;   -- 40 and 50 included
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Dateofbirth BETWEEN '2001-01-01' AND '2001-12-31';
SELECT * FROM COURSE WHERE TotalSeats NOT BETWEEN 40 AND 50;

docs.title: IN
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM COURSE WHERE Cname IN ('Computer Science','Chemistry');   -- syllabus Q4
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno NOT IN ('X2019','X2020');

IN is shorthand for a chain of ORs and is far more readable. It also accepts a subquery (Lesson 5).

docs.title: LIKE — pattern matching
docs.text:
Wildcards

Wildcard Matches % Any sequence of characters, including none _ Exactly one character 
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';        -- syllabus Q3: starts with A
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '%Sharma';   -- ends with Sharma
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '%Kumar%';   -- contains Kumar
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '_n%';       -- 'n' is the second letter
SELECT Cname FROM COURSE WHERE TeacherInCharge LIKE '%Gupta%';  -- syllabus Q15

Syllabus Q5 — roll numbers starting with X or Z and ending with 9:

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE (Rollno LIKE 'X%' OR Rollno LIKE 'Z%') AND Rollno LIKE '%9';

The parentheses are essential — without them, AND would bind to the Z% alternative only.

Two cautions about LIKE

  1. A leading % prevents index use. LIKE 'A%' can use an index on Name; LIKE '%Sharma' cannot, and forces a full table scan. Avoid leading wildcards on large tables.
  2. Case sensitivity depends on the collation. With utf8mb4_unicode_ci (ci = case-insensitive), LIKE 'a%' also matches 'Ankit'. Under a _bin or _cs collation it would not. Use UPPER() on both sides if you must be certain.

docs.title: 15.3 NULL and Three-Valued Logic
docs.text:
Three-valued logic

Any comparison involving NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE. SQL therefore has three truth values.

A WHERE clause keeps a row only when its condition is TRUE. Rows evaluating to FALSE or UNKNOWN are discarded.

Truth tables:

AND TRUE FALSE UNKNOWN TRUE TRUE FALSE UNKNOWN FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE UNKNOWN UNKNOWN FALSE UNKNOWN OR TRUE FALSE UNKNOWN TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE UNKNOWN UNKNOWN TRUE UNKNOWN UNKNOWN NOT TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE UNKNOWN UNKNOWN

docs.title: Testing for NULL
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Dateofbirth IS NULL;       -- correct
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Dateofbirth IS NOT NULL;   -- correct
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Dateofbirth = NULL;        -- WRONG: always UNKNOWN, returns nothing

The NULL trap that catches everyone

STUDENT has 400 rows; 40 have a NULL Mobile.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT WHERE Mobile = '9999999999';      -- say 100
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT WHERE Mobile <> '9999999999';     -- 260, NOT 300

The 40 NULL rows satisfy neither condition, because both comparisons yield UNKNOWN. The two counts do not add up to 400. To include them:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT WHERE Mobile <> '9999999999' OR Mobile IS NULL;

docs.title: Handling NULL in expressions
docs.text:
SELECT Name, COALESCE(Mobile, 'Not provided') AS Contact FROM STUDENT;
SELECT Name, IFNULL(Mobile, 'N/A') FROM STUDENT;               -- MySQL
SELECT Salary + COALESCE(Bonus, 0) AS Total FROM EMPLOYEE;     -- avoids NULL total

COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL argument. Without it, Salary + Bonus is NULL whenever Bonus is NULL — so an employee with no bonus silently shows no total at all.

docs.title: 15.4 ORDER BY and LIMIT
docs.text:
SELECT Name, Dateofbirth FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Name;              -- ascending (default)
SELECT Name, Dateofbirth FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Dateofbirth DESC;  -- descending
SELECT * FROM COURSE ORDER BY Coursetype ASC, TotalSeats DESC;    -- two keys
SELECT * FROM COURSE ORDER BY 3 DESC;                             -- by column position

Syllabus Q9 — the youngest student in BSc(P)CS:

SELECT s.Name, s.Dateofbirth
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  c.Cname = 'BSc(P)CS'
ORDER BY s.Dateofbirth DESC
LIMIT 1;

The youngest student is the one with the latest date of birth, hence DESC.

LIMIT 1 and ties

LIMIT 1 returns one row even if several tie for the extreme value. If two students share the latest birth date, one is arbitrarily discarded.

To return all tied rows, compare against the maximum instead:

SELECT s.Name FROM STUDENT s JOIN ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno=a.Rollno
JOIN COURSE c ON a.SID=c.SID
WHERE c.Cname='BSc(P)CS'
  AND s.Dateofbirth = (SELECT MAX(s2.Dateofbirth) FROM STUDENT s2
                       JOIN ADMISSION a2 ON s2.Rollno=a2.Rollno
                       JOIN COURSE c2 ON a2.SID=c2.SID
                       WHERE c2.Cname='BSc(P)CS');

Pagination:

SELECT * FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Rollno LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;   -- rows 21-30

NULL ordering: MySQL sorts NULLs first in ASC; other systems differ. Never assume — state it explicitly if it matters.

docs.title: String functions
docs.text: Function Purpose Example CONCAT(a,b) Join strings CONCAT(Rollno,' - ',Name) UPPER(s) / LOWER(s) Change case UPPER(Name) LENGTH(s) Number of characters LENGTH(Name) > 20 SUBSTRING(s,p,n) Extract n chars from position p SUBSTRING(Rollno,1,1) LEFT(s,n) / RIGHT(s,n) First / last n characters LEFT(Rollno,1) = 'X' TRIM(s) Remove leading/trailing spaces TRIM(Name) REPLACE(s,a,b) Substitute REPLACE(Name,'Kumar','K.') INSTR(s,sub) Position of substring, 0 if absent INSTR(Name,'Gupta') > 0

docs.title: Numeric functions

docs.title: 15.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. State the logical order of evaluation of a SELECT statement. Explain, using it, why a column alias works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE.

A. The evaluation order is:

FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

WHERE is evaluated at step 2, but the SELECT list — where aliases are created — is not evaluated until step 5. When the DBMS processes WHERE, the alias does not yet exist, so it cannot be referenced:

SELECT Name, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR,Dateofbirth,CURDATE()) AS Age
FROM   STUDENT
WHERE  Age > 18;                      -- ERROR: unknown column 'Age'

The remedy is to repeat the expression, or to wrap the query in a derived table:

SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT Name, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR,Dateofbirth,CURDATE()) AS Age FROM STUDENT
) t WHERE t.Age > 18;

ORDER BY is evaluated at step 7, after SELECT, so by then the alias exists and may be used freely:

SELECT Name, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR,Dateofbirth,CURDATE()) AS Age
FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Age DESC;       -- works

The same reasoning explains why HAVING (step 4) can refer to aggregates but WHERE (step 2) cannot: groups do not exist until step 3.

Solved Question 2

Q. Explain three-valued logic. Why does WHERE Mobile <> '9999999999' miss rows? Give two ways to include them.

A. SQL evaluates conditions to TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN, because NULL represents an absent value and nothing can be known about a comparison with it. A WHERE clause retains a row only if its condition is TRUE; rows evaluating to FALSE or UNKNOWN are discarded.

So for a row with Mobile IS NULL, the condition Mobile <> '9999999999' is UNKNOWN, and the row is excluded — even though, intuitively, "the mobile is not that number" seems true of a row with no mobile at all.

The consequence surprises people because the counts do not partition the table:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT;                                -- 400
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT WHERE Mobile =  '9999999999';   -- 100
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT WHERE Mobile <> '9999999999';   -- 260, not 300
The missing 40 are the NULL rows, in neither result.

Two remedies:

  1. Test for NULL explicitly: 

    WHERE Mobile <> '9999999999' OR Mobile IS NULL

  2. Substitute a value before comparing: 

    WHERE COALESCE(Mobile,'') <> '9999999999'
    This is more concise but not sargable — the function on the column prevents index use — so prefer the first form on large tables.

Solved Question 3

Q. Write SQL for syllabus practicals 3, 4, 5, 15, 24 and 25.

A.

Q3 — students' names starting with 'A'. 

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';

Q4 — details of students studying Computer Science or Chemistry. 

SELECT DISTINCT s.*
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  c.Cname IN ('Computer Science','Chemistry');
DISTINCT is needed because a student admitted to both courses would otherwise appear twice.

Q5 — names of students whose roll number starts with 'X' or 'Z' and ends with '9'. 

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE (Rollno LIKE 'X%' OR Rollno LIKE 'Z%') AND Rollno LIKE '%9';
The parentheses are essential. Without them AND binds tighter than OR, so the condition would read "starts with X, or (starts with Z and ends with 9)" — returning every X roll number regardless of its last character.

Q15 — full-time courses whose teacher-in-charge has 'Gupta' in the name. 

SELECT Cname FROM COURSE
WHERE TeacherInCharge LIKE '%Gupta%' AND Coursetype = 'Fulltime';

Q24 — total number of students older than 18. 

SELECT COUNT(*) AS StudentsOver18
FROM   STUDENT
WHERE  TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, Dateofbirth, CURDATE()) > 18;
TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, ...) gives completed years, correctly handling those whose birthday has not yet occurred this year — unlike YEAR(CURDATE()) - YEAR(Dateofbirth), which would be wrong for roughly half the students.

Q25 — students born in 2001 admitted to at least one part-time course. 

SELECT DISTINCT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ADMISSION a ON s.Rollno = a.Rollno
JOIN   COURSE    c ON a.SID    = c.SID
WHERE  s.Dateofbirth >= '2001-01-01' AND s.Dateofbirth < '2002-01-01'
  AND  c.Coursetype = 'Parttime';
The range form is used rather than YEAR(Dateofbirth)=2001 so that an index on Dateofbirth can be used. DISTINCT handles students admitted to two part-time courses.

Solved Question 4

Q. Explain % and _. Write patterns for: names of exactly five letters; roll numbers whose third character is 0; names containing a literal %.

A. % matches any sequence of characters, including the empty sequence. _ matches exactly one character.

Requirement Pattern Names of exactly five characters LIKE '_____' (five underscores) Roll numbers whose third character is 0 LIKE '__0%' Names beginning and ending with 'A' LIKE 'A%A' Names of at least five characters LIKE '_____%'

Matching a literal % requires an escape character, since % is otherwise a wildcard:

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '%\%%';              -- default escape
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '%!%%' ESCAPE '!';   -- explicit escape

The second form is clearer and portable: ESCAPE '!' declares ! as the escape character, so !% means a literal per-cent sign.

A cleaner alternative for "exactly five characters" is WHERE LENGTH(Name) = 5, which states the intent directly — though, being a function on the column, it is not sargable.

Solved Question 5

Q. What is sargability? Rewrite three non-sargable conditions and explain the gain.

A. A condition is sargable (from Search ARGument able) if the optimiser can use an index to satisfy it. The rule is simple: the indexed column must appear bare on one side of the comparison, with no function or arithmetic wrapped around it. Once a function is applied, the DBMS must compute it for every row and therefore scan the whole table.

Non-sargable Sargable rewrite Why it helps WHERE YEAR(Dateofbirth) = 2001 WHERE Dateofbirth >= '2001-01-01' AND Dateofbirth < '2002-01-01' An index on Dateofbirth supports a range scan directly. WHERE UPPER(Name) = 'ANKIT' WHERE Name = 'Ankit' under a case-insensitive collation Removes the per-row function call; the index on Name becomes usable. WHERE TotalSeats * 2 > 100 WHERE TotalSeats > 50 Arithmetic moved to the constant side, which is evaluated once. WHERE Name LIKE '%Sharma' (No general rewrite; consider a reversed-string index or full-text index) A leading wildcard defeats a B+-tree, which searches by prefix.

The gain. On a table of a million rows an index lookup examines perhaps 20 pages, whereas a full scan examines every page. The difference is typically three to four orders of magnitude in I/O, and it is invisible on a five-row practice table — which is exactly why the habit must be formed deliberately rather than discovered.

Note the final row: a leading wildcard cannot be made sargable by rewriting, because a B+-tree index is ordered by prefix (Unit 6, Lesson 2). This is a structural limitation, not a syntax problem.

Solved Question 6

Q. SELECT Name FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Dateofbirth DESC LIMIT 1; is offered as "the youngest student". Criticise it and give a correct version.

A. The query is usually right and silently wrong in two situations.

Problem 1 — ties. If two or more students share the latest date of birth, LIMIT 1 returns exactly one of them, chosen arbitrarily by whatever order the storage engine produced. The result is non-deterministic: the same query may return a different name on a different day, and the user is never told a tie existed.

Problem 2 — NULLs. If Dateofbirth is nullable, the behaviour depends on where the DBMS sorts NULLs. In MySQL, NULLs sort first in ASC and therefore last in DESC, so this particular query is safe; but in a system that sorts NULLs first in DESC, a student with an unknown date of birth would be returned as "the youngest". Relying on unstated NULL-ordering behaviour is not portable.

Correct version — compare against the maximum, and exclude NULLs:

SELECT Name, Dateofbirth
FROM   STUDENT
WHERE  Dateofbirth = (SELECT MAX(Dateofbirth) FROM STUDENT);

MAX ignores NULLs automatically, and the equality test returns every student sharing that date, so ties are reported rather than hidden. This form also states the intent — "the students whose birth date is the greatest" — rather than an ordering trick.

docs.title: 15.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. State the logical order of evaluation of a SELECT statement.
  2. Why can an alias be used in ORDER BY but not WHERE?
  3. What is the difference between SELECT Coursetype and π<sub>Coursetype</sub>?
  4. Is BETWEEN inclusive?
  5. Why does WHERE Mobile = NULL return nothing?
  6. Define sargability.
  7. What does COALESCE do?

B. Write the SQL

  1. All courses ordered by seats, largest first.
  2. Names of students whose name contains 'a' as the second letter.
  3. Courses with 40 to 50 seats inclusive.
  4. Courses that are neither Computer Science nor Chemistry.
  5. Students whose roll number is exactly five characters.
  6. Names of students, in upper case, with their ages.
  7. Courses whose teacher's surname is 'Gupta' (surname = last word).
  8. Students with no recorded date of birth.
  9. Students who either have no mobile number or whose mobile is the default.
  10. The three courses with the fewest seats.
  11. Each course with a label 'Large', 'Medium' or 'Small' by seat count.
  12. Students born in the first half of any year.
  13. Roll numbers and names, concatenated as X2019 - Ankit Sharma.

C. Predict and explain

  1. STUDENT has 100 rows, 10 with NULL Mobile. Give the count returned by: a. WHERE Mobile = '9999999999' (30 rows have this value) b. WHERE Mobile <> '9999999999' c. WHERE Mobile IS NULL d. WHERE NOT (Mobile = '9999999999') e. WHERE Mobile = '9999999999' OR Mobile <> '9999999999'
  2. Explain the difference between the results of: a. WHERE Coursetype='Fulltime' OR Coursetype='Parttime' AND TotalSeats>50 b. WHERE (Coursetype='Fulltime' OR Coursetype='Parttime') AND TotalSeats>50
  3. What is wrong with SELECT Name, YEAR(Dateofbirth) AS BirthYear FROM STUDENT WHERE BirthYear = 2001;? Give two fixes.

D. Analytical

  1. Rewrite each in sargable form and explain the gain: WHERE MONTH(Dateofadmission)=7; WHERE LEFT(Rollno,1)='X'; WHERE TotalSeats/2 > 25.
  2. Explain why SELECT * is discouraged in production code. Give three reasons.
  3. Construct a table of data and two conditions demonstrating that NOT (A AND B) and (NOT A) OR (NOT B) behave identically even with NULLs present.
  4. A report must show "students with no mobile" but returns nothing. Diagnose and fix.
  5. Design a single query listing every course with its seat count and a computed column showing what percentage of the college's total seats it represents.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. BETWEEN 40 AND 50 excludes 40 and 50.
  2. LIKE '%a' can use an index on the column.
  3. NULL = NULL is TRUE.
  4. DISTINCT is applied before ORDER BY.
  5. LIMIT 1 always returns the single correct maximum row.
  6. COUNT(*) and COUNT(Mobile) give the same answer when Mobile has NULLs.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. BETWEEN is inclusive of both endpoints.
  2. False. A leading wildcard defeats a B+-tree index, which searches by prefix; a full scan results.
  3. False. It is UNKNOWN. Use IS NULL.
  4. True. The order is SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY, which is why ORDER BY may only reference columns that survived DISTINCT.
  5. False. It returns one arbitrary row among ties, and its behaviour with NULLs depends on the system's NULL ordering.
  6. False. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(Mobile) counts non-NULL values, so it is smaller whenever NULLs exist.

Lesson Summary

  • Evaluation order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT — hence aliases work in ORDER BY but not in WHERE.
  • SELECT returns a multiset; π corresponds to SELECT DISTINCT.
  • Parenthesise whenever AND and OR are mixed. BETWEEN is inclusive; IN is readable shorthand for OR.
  • NULL makes comparisons UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE — so <> silently omits NULL rows. Use IS NULL and COALESCE.
  • Keep the column bare on one side of a comparison to stay sargable.
  • LIMIT 1 hides ties; compare against MAX/MIN instead.

docs.title: Lesson 11: Relational Algebra I: Unary and Set Operations
docs.text:
Unary operations and set operations

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 3: Relational Data Model · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 8.1, 8.2

Learning Outcomes

  1. Explain what relational algebra is and why the closure property matters.
  2. Apply SELECT (σ), PROJECT (π) and RENAME (ρ) correctly.
  3. Apply the set operations ∪, ∩, −, × and state the union compatibility requirement.
  4. Write nested and sequential expressions, and build query trees.
  5. Predict the exact cardinality and degree of every intermediate result.

docs.title: 11.1 What Relational Algebra Is
docs.text:
Relational algebra

A formal language for the relational model, consisting of a set of operations that take one or two relations as input and produce a new relation as output.

Three properties make it important:

1. It is closed. Every operation returns a relation, so the output of one operation can be the input of the next. This is the closure property, and it is what allows arbitrarily complex expressions to be built.
