2. It is procedural. An expression specifies not only what is wanted but an order of operations — unlike SQL, which is declarative. This is exactly why it matters practically: the DBMS query optimiser translates SQL into relational algebra, then rewrites the algebra into a cheaper but equivalent expression. Understanding algebra is understanding what the optimiser does.

3. It defines the yardstick of expressive power. A query language is called relationally complete if it can express every relational-algebra query. SQL is relationally complete (and more).

Why study it if we have SQL?

Because it is the semantics of SQL. Every SELECT statement is compiled into an algebra expression. Query optimisation, the theory of query equivalence, and the definition of relational completeness are all stated in algebra. It is also far more precise than English for stating exactly what a query means.

docs.title: The operations
docs.text:
Group Operation Symbol Arity Unary SELECT σ (sigma) 1 PROJECT π (pi) 1 RENAME ρ (rho) 1 Set UNION ∪ 2 INTERSECTION ∩ 2 SET DIFFERENCE (MINUS) − 2 CARTESIAN PRODUCT × 2 Join (Lesson 4) JOIN, DIVISION ⋈, ÷ 2

The complete (minimal) set

{ σ, π, ∪, −, × } is a complete set: every other relational-algebra operation can be expressed in terms of these five. For instance R ∩ S = R − (R − S) and R ⋈ S = σ<sub>condition</sub>(R × S).

The other operations exist for convenience and efficiency, not for expressive power.

docs.title: 11.2 The Running Example
docs.text:
Use these three relations throughout.

STUDENT

Rollno Name Dateofbirth X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 X2020 Riya Verma 2002-05-11 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 Z2049 Arjun Nair 2003-01-25 X3001 Aditi Rao 2001-07-09

COURSE

SID Cname TotalSeats Duration Coursetype TeacherInCharge CS01 Computer Science 60 3 Fulltime R. K. Gupta CH01 Chemistry 45 3 Fulltime S. Menon MA02 Mathematics 50 3 Parttime A. Gupta EN03 English 40 3 Parttime P. Das PH01 Physics 40 3 Fulltime V. Rao

ADMISSION

Rollno SID Dateofadmission X2019 CS01 2019-07-15 X2019 MA02 2019-08-01 X2020 CS01 2019-07-16 Z1188 CH01 2019-07-18 Z1188 EN03 2019-08-05 X3001 MA02 2019-07-20

Note that Z2049 Arjun Nair has no admission — this makes several later examples interesting. PH01 Physics has no students.

docs.title: 11.3 SELECT (σ) — choosing rows
docs.text:
SELECT

σ<sub><condition></sub>(R)

Returns the set of tuples of R that satisfy the condition. It is a horizontal partition — it chooses rows.

  • The result has the same degree as R (same attributes).
  • 0 ≤ |σ<sub>c</sub>(R)| ≤ |R|.
  • The condition is a Boolean expression over <attribute> <comparison> <constant-or-attribute>, combined with AND (∧), OR (∨), NOT (¬).
  • Comparison operators: =, ≠, <, ≤, >, ≥.
  • SELECT is commutative: σ<sub>c1</sub>(σ<sub>c2</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c2</sub>(σ<sub>c1</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c1 ∧ c2</sub>(R).

Example 1. All full-time courses.

σ<sub>Coursetype = 'Fulltime'</sub>(COURSE)

SID Cname TotalSeats Duration Coursetype TeacherInCharge CS01 Computer Science 60 3 Fulltime R. K. Gupta CH01 Chemistry 45 3 Fulltime S. Menon PH01 Physics 40 3 Fulltime V. Rao

Degree 6, cardinality 3.

Example 2. Full-time courses with more than 40 seats.

σ<sub>Coursetype = 'Fulltime' ∧ TotalSeats > 40</sub>(COURSE) → CS01, CH01. Cardinality 2.

Example 3. Courses that are part-time or have fewer than 45 seats.

σ<sub>Coursetype = 'Parttime' ∨ TotalSeats < 45</sub>(COURSE) → MA02, EN03, PH01. Cardinality 3.

The commonest error

Writing σ<sub>Cname = 'Computer Science' ∧ Cname = 'Chemistry'</sub>(COURSE) to get both courses. This returns zero tuples: the condition is evaluated one tuple at a time, and no single course is called both things. The correct operator is ∨.

Say it aloud as "for each row, is it true that..." and the error becomes obvious.

docs.title: 11.4 PROJECT (π) — choosing columns
docs.text:
PROJECT

π<sub><attribute list></sub>(R)

Returns a relation containing only the listed attributes, in the listed order, with duplicate tuples removed. It is a vertical partition — it chooses columns.

  • Degree = number of attributes in the list.
  • |π<sub>L</sub>(R)| ≤ |R|, with equality if and only if L contains a superkey of R.
  • PROJECT is not commutative: π<sub>L1</sub>(π<sub>L2</sub>(R)) is valid only if L1 ⊆ L2, and then equals π<sub>L1</sub>(R).

Example 4. Names and types of all courses.

π<sub>Cname, Coursetype</sub>(COURSE)

Cname Coursetype Computer Science Fulltime Chemistry Fulltime Mathematics Parttime English Parttime Physics Fulltime

Degree 2, cardinality 5.

Example 5 — duplicate elimination. π<sub>Coursetype</sub>(COURSE)

Coursetype Fulltime Parttime

Cardinality 2, not 5. PROJECT returns a set, so Fulltime (which occurred three times) appears once.

PROJECT vs SQL SELECT

Relational algebra PROJECT always removes duplicates, because a relation is a set.

SQL's SELECT Coursetype FROM COURSE returns five rows, because SQL tables are multisets. To match the algebra you must write SELECT DISTINCT Coursetype FROM COURSE.

π corresponds to SELECT DISTINCT, not to SELECT. This is a very common examination point.

Example 6 — no duplicates removed. π<sub>SID, Cname</sub>(COURSE) has cardinality 5, because the list contains SID, which is a key. Whenever the projection list contains a superkey, no duplicates can arise.

docs.title: 11.5 RENAME (ρ) — changing names
docs.text:
RENAME

Three forms:

ρ<sub>S</sub>(R) — rename the relation to S, keeping attribute names. ρ<sub>(B1, B2, ..., Bn)</sub>(R) — rename the attributes to B1 ... Bn, keeping the relation name. ρ<sub>S(B1, ..., Bn)</sub>(R) — rename both.

RENAME exists for two essential purposes:

  1. Self-joins and self-products. EMPLOYEE × EMPLOYEE is ambiguous — which Ssn is which? Renaming one copy disambiguates.
  2. Resolving name clashes before a set operation that requires union compatibility.

Example 7. ρ<sub>SUPERVISOR(SupSsn, SupName, SupSalary)</sub>(EMPLOYEE) produces a copy of EMPLOYEE under a new name with new attribute names, usable alongside the original.

docs.title: Sequential notation — the practical alternative
docs.text:
Rather than nesting deeply, name each intermediate result:

FULLTIME     ← σ Coursetype='Fulltime' (COURSE)
BIG_FULLTIME ← σ TotalSeats>40 (FULLTIME)
RESULT       ← π Cname (BIG_FULLTIME)

This is equivalent to π<sub>Cname</sub>(σ<sub>Coursetype='Fulltime' ∧ TotalSeats>40</sub>(COURSE)) and is far easier to read, check and mark. Use it in examinations for any query needing more than two operations.

docs.title: Union compatibility
docs.text:
Union compatibility (type compatibility)

Two relations R(A1,...,An) and S(B1,...,Bm) are union compatible if:

  1. They have the same degree: n = m.
  2. Corresponding attributes have the same domain: dom(Ai) = dom(Bi) for all i.

Attribute names need not match; by convention the result takes the names from the first relation.

∪, ∩ and − all require union compatibility. × does not.

For the examples, let:

  • CS_STUDENTS ← π<sub>Rollno</sub>(σ<sub>SID='CS01'</sub>(ADMISSION)) = {X2019, X2020}
  • MA_STUDENTS ← π<sub>Rollno</sub>(σ<sub>SID='MA02'</sub>(ADMISSION)) = {X2019, X3001}

docs.title: UNION (∪)
docs.text:
UNION

R ∪ S = all tuples that are in R, or in S, or in both. Duplicates are removed.

max(|R|, |S|) ≤ |R ∪ S| ≤ |R| + |S|. Commutative and associative.

Example 8. Students in Computer Science or Mathematics.

CS_STUDENTS ∪ MA_STUDENTS = {X2019, X2020, X3001}. Cardinality 3, not 4 — X2019 appears in both and is counted once.

docs.title: INTERSECTION (∩)
docs.text:
INTERSECTION

R ∩ S = tuples in both. 0 ≤ |R ∩ S| ≤ min(|R|, |S|). Commutative and associative.

Not primitive: R ∩ S = R − (R − S).

Example 9. Students in Computer Science and Mathematics.

CS_STUDENTS ∩ MA_STUDENTS = {X2019}. Cardinality 1.

'and' in English is usually ∩, not ∧

"Students taking CS01 and MA02" cannot be σ<sub>SID='CS01' ∧ SID='MA02'</sub>(ADMISSION), which returns nothing (Section 3.3). The two facts live in different tuples, so they must be combined by intersecting two sets of roll numbers.

Rule: when "and" applies to two facts about the same entity recorded in different rows, use ∩ (or a join). Use ∧ only when both conditions apply to the same row.

docs.title: SET DIFFERENCE (−)
docs.text:
SET DIFFERENCE

R − S = tuples in R that are not in S. Not commutative: R − S ≠ S − R.

0 ≤ |R − S| ≤ |R|.

Example 10. Students in Computer Science but not Mathematics.

CS_STUDENTS − MA_STUDENTS = {X2020}.

MA_STUDENTS − CS_STUDENTS = {X3001} — a different answer, confirming non-commutativity.

Example 11 — the important pattern. Students admitted to no course.

ALL_STUDENTS ← π Rollno (STUDENT)              = {X2019,X2020,Z1188,Z2049,X3001}
ADMITTED     ← π Rollno (ADMISSION)            = {X2019,X2020,Z1188,X3001}
RESULT       ← ALL_STUDENTS − ADMITTED         = {Z2049}

Then π<sub>Name</sub>(STUDENT ⋈ RESULT) gives Arjun Nair.

The universal 'NOT / NONE' pattern

Any query of the form "find X that has no Y" or "...that is not related to..." is answered by set difference:

(all X) − (X that do have Y)

Compute the positive set first, then subtract it from the universe. This pattern appears in almost every examination.

docs.title: CARTESIAN PRODUCT (×)
docs.text:
CARTESIAN PRODUCT (CROSS PRODUCT / CROSS JOIN)

R(A1,...,An) × S(B1,...,Bm) produces a relation Q(A1,...,An,B1,...,Bm) containing every combination of a tuple of R with a tuple of S.

  • Degree = n + m (degrees add).
  • Cardinality = |R| × |S| (cardinalities multiply).
  • Union compatibility is not required.
  • Commutative and associative up to attribute order.

Example 12. STUDENT × COURSE has degree 3 + 6 = 9 and cardinality 5 × 5 = 25.

Most of those 25 rows are meaningless — they pair a student with a course they never took.

× alone is almost never what you want

The Cartesian product is useful only when immediately followed by a SELECT that keeps the meaningful combinations:

σ<sub>STUDENT.Rollno = ADMISSION.Rollno</sub>(STUDENT × ADMISSION)

This combination — product then select — is so common that it is given its own name: the JOIN (Lesson 4). An accidental × without a matching condition is the classic cause of a query that returns millions of rows.

Example 13 — product followed by selection. Names of students admitted to CS01.

T1 ← σ SID='CS01' (ADMISSION)                    2 tuples
T2 ← STUDENT × T1                                5 × 2 = 10 tuples, degree 6
T3 ← σ STUDENT.Rollno = T1.Rollno (T2)           2 tuples
RESULT ← π Name (T3)
Name Ankit Sharma Riya Verma

docs.title: 11.7 Query Trees
docs.text:
Every algebra expression can be drawn as a tree: leaves are base relations, internal nodes are operations, and evaluation proceeds bottom-up. This is exactly the internal representation the optimiser manipulates.

   Query: names of students admitted to 'CS01'

                  π Name
                    |
          σ STUDENT.Rollno = ADMISSION.Rollno
                    |
                    ×
                  /   \
            STUDENT    σ SID='CS01'
                            |
                        ADMISSION

   Read bottom-up: filter ADMISSION, cross with STUDENT,
   keep matching pairs, project the name.

A first optimisation rule

Compare two equivalent expressions:

(a) π<sub>Name</sub>(σ<sub>Rollno=Rollno ∧ SID='CS01'</sub>(STUDENT × ADMISSION)) — the product makes 5 × 6 = 30 tuples, then filters.

(b) π<sub>Name</sub>(σ<sub>Rollno=Rollno</sub>(STUDENT × σ<sub>SID='CS01'</sub>(ADMISSION))) — filter first, so the product makes only 5 × 2 = 10 tuples.

Both give the same answer; (b) does a third of the work. The rule is push selections down the tree, as close to the leaves as possible. This is the single most important heuristic in query optimisation, and it is why the optimiser works in algebra.

docs.title: 11.8 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. What is relational algebra? State the closure property and the complete set of operations. Why is relational algebra important given that we use SQL?

A. Relational algebra is a formal, procedural query language for the relational model, consisting of operations that take one or two relations as input and produce a relation as output.

The closure property states that every operation returns a relation. Because the output is the same kind of object as the input, operations can be composed without limit, which is what makes complex expressions and query trees possible.

The complete (minimal) set is {σ, π, ∪, −, ×}. Every other operation is definable from these — for example R ∩ S = R − (R − S) and R ⋈<sub>c</sub> S = σ<sub>c</sub>(R × S). The additional operations exist for convenience and efficiency, not for expressive power.

Importance despite SQL: relational algebra is the semantics of SQL. A DBMS parses a SQL statement, translates it into an algebra expression, and the query optimiser then rewrites that expression into an equivalent but cheaper one — pushing selections down, reordering joins — before generating an execution plan. Algebra also gives the precise definition of query equivalence, and defines relational completeness, the standard by which a query language's expressive power is measured.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish SELECT from PROJECT. State the exact cardinality relationship of each to its input, and explain when |π<sub>L</sub>(R)| = |R|.

A.

SELECT (σ) PROJECT (π) Chooses Rows (horizontal) Columns (vertical) Notation σ<sub>condition</sub>(R) π<sub>attribute list</sub>(R) Degree of result Same as R Number of attributes listed Cardinality 0 ≤ result ≤ |R| 1 ≤ result ≤ |R| (for non-empty R) Removes duplicates Not applicable — cannot create them Yes, always Commutative with itself Yes No SQL equivalent WHERE clause SELECT DISTINCT column list

When |π<sub>L</sub>(R)| = |R|: exactly when the projection list L contains a superkey of R. A superkey guarantees that no two tuples agree on all of L, so no duplicates can arise and none are removed.

Illustration. π<sub>SID, Cname</sub>(COURSE) has cardinality 5 = |COURSE|, because SID is a key. But π<sub>Coursetype</sub>(COURSE) has cardinality 2, because Coursetype is not a superkey and three Fulltime tuples collapse into one.

Solved Question 3

Q. Write relational algebra for each, using the running example, and give the result.

a. Roll numbers and names of students born in 2001. b. Names of part-time courses with more than 40 seats. c. Distinct course types offered. d. Names of students admitted to CS01. e. Roll numbers of students admitted to CS01 but not MA02. f. Roll numbers of students admitted to no course.

A.

a. π<sub>Rollno, Name</sub>(σ<sub>Dateofbirth ≥ '2001-01-01' ∧ Dateofbirth ≤ '2001-12-31'</sub>(STUDENT))

Rollno Name X2019 Ankit Sharma Z1188 Sana Iqbal X3001 Aditi Rao

b. π<sub>Cname</sub>(σ<sub>Coursetype='Parttime' ∧ TotalSeats>40</sub>(COURSE)) → {Mathematics}. (EN03 English has exactly 40, so it is excluded by the strict >.)

c. π<sub>Coursetype</sub>(COURSE) → {Fulltime, Parttime}. Cardinality 2, because PROJECT removes duplicates.

d. 

T1 ← σ SID='CS01' (ADMISSION)
T2 ← σ STUDENT.Rollno = T1.Rollno (STUDENT × T1)
RESULT ← π Name (T2)
→ {Ankit Sharma, Riya Verma}.

e. 

CS ← π Rollno (σ SID='CS01' (ADMISSION))       = {X2019, X2020}
MA ← π Rollno (σ SID='MA02' (ADMISSION))       = {X2019, X3001}
RESULT ← CS − MA                                = {X2020}
Note that σ<sub>SID='CS01' ∧ SID≠'MA02'</sub> would be wrong — it returns both CS students, since the two facts live in different tuples.

f. 

RESULT ← π Rollno (STUDENT) − π Rollno (ADMISSION)    = {Z2049}
The universal "none" pattern: all X, minus those that do have Y.

Solved Question 4

Q. Define union compatibility. Which operations require it? Given R(A,B) with 5 tuples and S(C,D) with 3 tuples where dom(A)=dom(C) and dom(B)=dom(D), state the degree and the possible range of cardinality of R ∪ S, R ∩ S, R − S and R × S.

A. Two relations are union compatible if they have the same degree and corresponding attributes have the same domains. Attribute names need not agree; the result conventionally takes the names of the first operand.

∪, ∩ and − require union compatibility. × does not — indeed its purpose is to combine relations of different shapes.

Here R and S are union compatible: both have degree 2 with matching domains.

Expression Degree Cardinality range Explanation R ∪ S 2 5 to 8 At least max(5,3)=5 if S ⊆ R; at most 5+3=8 if disjoint. R ∩ S 2 0 to 3 At least 0 if disjoint; at most min(5,3)=3 if S ⊆ R. R − S 2 2 to 5 At most 5 if disjoint; at least 5−3=2 if S ⊆ R. R × S 4 exactly 15 Degrees add (2+2); cardinalities multiply (5×3).

Note that R × S has a fixed cardinality, whereas the set operations depend on how much the relations overlap.

Solved Question 5

Q. Show that σ<sub>c1</sub>(σ<sub>c2</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c1 ∧ c2</sub>(R) and that π is not commutative. Why do these facts matter?

A.

Cascading of SELECT. A tuple t is in σ<sub>c1</sub>(σ<sub>c2</sub>(R)) if and only if t ∈ R, t satisfies c2 (to survive the inner select), and t satisfies c1 (to survive the outer). That is precisely the condition for t to satisfy c1 ∧ c2 while being in R, so the two expressions contain exactly the same tuples. Since conjunction is commutative, the order of the two selects is also immaterial:

σ<sub>c1</sub>(σ<sub>c2</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c2</sub>(σ<sub>c1</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c1 ∧ c2</sub>(R)

PROJECT is not commutative. π<sub>L1</sub>(π<sub>L2</sub>(R)) is even defined only when L1 ⊆ L2, because the inner projection has already discarded every attribute not in L2. When it is defined, it equals π<sub>L1</sub>(R).

Counter-example. π<sub>Name</sub>(π<sub>Rollno</sub>(STUDENT)) is invalid — Name no longer exists after the inner projection — whereas π<sub>Rollno</sub>(π<sub>Rollno, Name</sub>(STUDENT)) is valid and equals π<sub>Rollno</sub>(STUDENT).

Why it matters. These are query-equivalence rules, and the optimiser uses them constantly. Cascading lets a single conjunctive selection be split into several, each of which can then be pushed down the query tree to a different leaf — reducing the size of intermediate results before an expensive product or join. The projection rule lets the optimiser drop unneeded columns early, reducing the width of intermediate tuples. Both directly reduce the amount of data moved and are among the first transformations any optimiser applies.

Solved Question 6

Q. Explain why σ<sub>SID='CS01' ∧ SID='MA02'</sub>(ADMISSION) is wrong for "students in both CS01 and MA02", and give the correct expression.

A. The expression returns the empty relation.

SELECT evaluates its condition one tuple at a time. Each tuple of ADMISSION has exactly one value of SID, so SID='CS01' ∧ SID='MA02' asks for a single value that is simultaneously equal to two different constants — impossible. No tuple can satisfy it.

The error is a category mistake: the English "and" here joins two facts about the same student, and those two facts are recorded in two different tuples. A tuple-at-a-time condition cannot see both at once.

Correct expression — form the two sets of roll numbers and intersect them:

CS ← π Rollno (σ SID='CS01' (ADMISSION))     = {X2019, X2020}
MA ← π Rollno (σ SID='MA02' (ADMISSION))     = {X2019, X3001}
RESULT ← CS ∩ MA                              = {X2019}

Equivalently, using difference alone: CS − (CS − MA).

The general rule. Use ∧ when both conditions describe the same tuple (Coursetype='Fulltime' ∧ TotalSeats>40). Use ∩ (or a self-join) when the conditions describe different tuples relating to the same entity.

docs.title: 11.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Use the running example relations for all computational questions.

A. Short answer

  1. State the closure property and why it matters.
  2. Give the complete set of relational algebra operations.
  3. What is the degree and cardinality of σ<sub>c</sub>(R) relative to R?
  4. When does PROJECT not reduce cardinality?
  5. Define union compatibility. Which operations require it?
  6. Why is RENAME necessary?
  7. Give the cardinality and degree of R × S in terms of those of R and S.

B. Write the relational algebra

  1. Names of all students.
  2. Details of courses with duration 3 and type Parttime.
  3. Roll numbers of students admitted on or after 2019-08-01.
  4. Distinct teachers-in-charge.
  5. Names of courses taught by a teacher whose name contains "Gupta". (State any assumption about string operators.)
  6. Roll numbers of students admitted to both CS01 and MA02.
  7. Roll numbers of students admitted to CS01 or CH01.
  8. Roll numbers of students admitted to CH01 but not CS01.
  9. Names of students not admitted to any course.
  10. Names of students admitted to at least one part-time course.
  11. SIDs of courses with no students admitted.
  12. Names of students born in 2001 who are admitted to MA02.
  13. Roll numbers of students admitted to more than one course. (Hint: you will need a product of ADMISSION with a renamed copy of itself.)

C. Compute the result

  1. For each of questions 8 to 20, give the actual resulting relation from the sample data.
  2. Give the degree and cardinality of: a. STUDENT × COURSE b. STUDENT × ADMISSION c. σ<sub>Coursetype='Fulltime'</sub>(COURSE) × σ<sub>SID='CS01'</sub>(ADMISSION) d. π<sub>Rollno</sub>(ADMISSION) e. π<sub>Rollno, SID</sub>(ADMISSION)
  3. R(A,B) has 8 tuples and S(A,B) has 5. State the minimum and maximum cardinality of R ∪ S, R ∩ S, R − S, S − R and R × S.

D. Analytical

  1. Prove that R ∩ S = R − (R − S), by showing that a tuple is in one side if and only if it is in the other.
  2. Draw the query tree for question 19, then draw an optimised version and explain the improvement, quantifying the number of tuples in the intermediate results in each case.
  3. Explain why π<sub>Name</sub>(σ<sub>SID='CS01'</sub>(STUDENT × ADMISSION)) may give a wrong answer. Correct it.
  4. Is R − (S − T) = (R − S) ∪ (R ∩ T)? Justify with a proof or a counter-example.
  5. Under what conditions is π<sub>L</sub>(σ<sub>c</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c</sub>(π<sub>L</sub>(R))? Give an example where they differ.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. SELECT is commutative.
  2. PROJECT is commutative.
  3. R ∪ S may have more tuples than |R| + |S|.
  4. R − S = S − R when R and S are union compatible.
  5. Cartesian product requires union compatibility.
  6. π in relational algebra corresponds to SQL SELECT without DISTINCT.
  7. σ<sub>A=1 ∧ A=2</sub>(R) is always empty.

Answers to Section E

  1. True. σ<sub>c1</sub>(σ<sub>c2</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c2</sub>(σ<sub>c1</sub>(R)) = σ<sub>c1 ∧ c2</sub>(R).
  2. False. π<sub>L1</sub>(π<sub>L2</sub>(R)) is defined only if L1 ⊆ L2; reversing the order is generally invalid.
  3. False. Duplicates are removed, so |R ∪ S| ≤ |R| + |S|.
  4. False. Difference is not commutative; equality holds only in the special case R = S.
  5. False. Only ∪, ∩ and − require it. Cartesian product exists precisely to combine relations of different shapes.
  6. False. It corresponds to SELECT DISTINCT, because PROJECT always removes duplicates.
  7. True. An attribute has one value per tuple, so it cannot equal two distinct constants at once.

Lesson Summary

  • Relational algebra is procedural and closed; the complete set is {σ, π, ∪, −, ×}.
  • σ chooses rows (same degree, fewer or equal tuples); π chooses columns and always removes duplicates — so it matches SELECT DISTINCT, not SELECT.
  • |π<sub>L</sub>(R)| = |R| exactly when L contains a superkey.
  • ∪, ∩, − require union compatibility; × does not, and multiplies cardinalities while adding degrees.
  • Use ∧ for two conditions on the same tuple; use ∩ for two facts in different tuples.
  • "Find X with no Y" = (all X) − (X with Y).
  • Push selections down the query tree — the first rule of optimisation.

docs.title: Lesson 12: Relational Algebra II: Joins, Division and Aggregation
docs.text:
Joins, outer joins, division and aggregation

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 3: Relational Data Model · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 8.3, 8.4, 8.5

Learning Outcomes

  1. Apply theta join, equijoin and natural join, and state the differences precisely.
  2. Apply left, right and full outer joins, and explain when each is needed.
  3. Apply semi-join and anti-join.
  4. Recognise and solve division (÷) problems — the "for all" queries.
  5. Use aggregate functions and grouping (ℱ).
  6. Compose multi-step queries and reason about intermediate cardinalities.

docs.title: 12.1 The Join Operations
docs.text: Lesson 3 ended with the observation that × followed by σ is the useful combination. That combination is the JOIN.

docs.title: Theta join (⋈<sub>θ</sub>)
docs.text:
Theta join

R ⋈<sub><condition></sub> S = σ<sub><condition></sub>(R × S)

Combines each tuple of R with each tuple of S, keeping only pairs satisfying the condition. The condition may use any comparison operator: =, ≠, <, ≤, >, ≥.

  • Degree = degree(R) + degree(S). All attributes of both are kept.
  • Cardinality: 0 ≤ |R ⋈<sub>θ</sub> S| ≤ |R| × |S|.

Example 1. Pairs of courses where the first has strictly more seats than the second.

COURSE ⋈<sub>TotalSeats > TotalSeats2</sub> ρ<sub>C2(SID2,Cname2,TotalSeats2,...)</sub>(COURSE)

The rename is essential — without it the condition cannot say which TotalSeats is meant.

docs.title: Equijoin
docs.text:
Equijoin

A theta join in which every comparison in the condition is equality (=).

Its defining feature: the result contains two identical columns for each equality — one from each relation.

Example 2. STUDENT ⋈<sub>STUDENT.Rollno = ADMISSION.Rollno</sub> ADMISSION

STUDENT.Rollno Name Dateofbirth ADMISSION.Rollno SID Dateofadmission X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 X2019 CS01 2019-07-15 X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 X2019 MA02 2019-08-01 X2020 Riya Verma 2002-05-11 X2020 CS01 2019-07-16 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 Z1188 CH01 2019-07-18 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 Z1188 EN03 2019-08-05 X3001 Aditi Rao 2001-07-09 X3001 MA02 2019-07-20

Degree 3 + 3 = 6, cardinality 6. Note Rollno appears twice, redundantly — and Z2049 Arjun Nair, having no admission, has disappeared.

docs.title: Natural join (⋈ or *)
docs.text:
Natural join

R ⋈ S

An equijoin on all attributes with the same name in both relations, with the duplicate columns removed — each common attribute appears once.

  • Degree = degree(R) + degree(S) − (number of common attributes).
  • If there are no common attributes, the natural join degenerates to the Cartesian product.

Example 3. STUDENT ⋈ ADMISSION — the common attribute is Rollno.

Rollno Name Dateofbirth SID Dateofadmission X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 CS01 2019-07-15 X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 MA02 2019-08-01 X2020 Riya Verma 2002-05-11 CS01 2019-07-16 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 CH01 2019-07-18 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 EN03 2019-08-05 X3001 Aditi Rao 2001-07-09 MA02 2019-07-20

Degree 3 + 3 − 1 = 5. Rollno appears once.

Example 4 — three-way natural join. STUDENT ⋈ ADMISSION ⋈ COURSE joins on Rollno and then on SID, giving degree 3 + 3 + 6 − 1 − 1 = 10 and cardinality 6.

The danger of natural join

Natural join matches on name, not on meaning. If STUDENT and COURSE both happened to have an attribute called Name, then STUDENT ⋈ COURSE would silently join student names to course names — producing nonsense with no error message.

For this reason many practitioners avoid NATURAL JOIN in production SQL and write the join condition explicitly. Rename first when in doubt.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Theta join Equijoin Natural join Condition Any comparison Equality only Implicit: equality on all same-named attributes Condition written? Yes Yes No Duplicate columns May occur Always occur Removed Degree d(R)+d(S) d(R)+d(S) d(R)+d(S) − #common No matching attributes — — Becomes R × S

docs.title: 12.2 Outer Joins
docs.text:
The joins above are inner joins: unmatched tuples are lost. Arjun Nair vanished from Example 3, and PH01 Physics never appears at all. Outer joins preserve them.

The three outer joins

Left outer join R ⟕ S — every tuple of R appears; where there is no match in S, the S attributes are filled with NULL.

Right outer join R ⟖ S — every tuple of S appears; unmatched R attributes become NULL.

Full outer join R ⟗ S — every tuple of both appears; unmatched attributes on either side become NULL.

Example 5. STUDENT ⟕ ADMISSION — keep every student, matched or not.

Rollno Name Dateofbirth SID Dateofadmission X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 CS01 2019-07-15 X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 MA02 2019-08-01 X2020 Riya Verma 2002-05-11 CS01 2019-07-16 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 CH01 2019-07-18 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 EN03 2019-08-05 Z2049 Arjun Nair 2003-01-25 NULL NULL X3001 Aditi Rao 2001-07-09 MA02 2019-07-20

Cardinality 7 — Arjun Nair is preserved with NULLs.

The outer-join trick for 'find those with none'

Lesson 3 solved "students admitted to no course" with set difference. An outer join gives an alternative:

π<sub>Name</sub>(σ<sub>SID IS NULL</sub>(STUDENT ⟕ ADMISSION)) → {Arjun Nair}

Keep everybody, then keep only the rows where the match failed. In SQL this is the well-known LEFT JOIN ... WHERE ... IS NULL idiom, and it is often faster than NOT IN.

Example 6. Courses with no students: π<sub>Cname</sub>(σ<sub>Rollno IS NULL</sub>(COURSE ⟕ ADMISSION)) → {Physics}.

docs.title: 12.3 Semi-join and Anti-join
docs.text:
Semi-join (⋉)

R ⋉ S = the tuples of R that have at least one matching tuple in S. Only R's attributes are returned, and each qualifying tuple appears once.

R ⋉ S = π<sub>attributes of R</sub>(R ⋈ S)

Anti-join (▷)

R ▷ S = the tuples of R with no matching tuple in S.

R ▷ S = R − (R ⋉ S)

Example 7. STUDENT ⋉ ADMISSION = the four students who have at least one admission — each listed once, even X2019 who has two.

Example 8. STUDENT ▷ ADMISSION = {Arjun Nair} — a third way to express the "no course" query.

These correspond to SQL's EXISTS and NOT EXISTS, and optimisers use them heavily because they avoid producing the wide, duplicated intermediate result that a full join would.

docs.title: 12.4 DIVISION (÷) — the "for all" operation
docs.text:
The hardest operation, and the one examinations love. It answers queries containing "for all", "every" or "all of the".

Division

Let R(Z) and S(X) where X ⊆ Z, and let Y = Z − X (the attributes of R not in S).

R ÷ S is a relation over Y containing every tuple t such that for every tuple s in S, the combined tuple ⟨t, s⟩ appears in R.

In words: the Y-values that are paired with all the X-values in S.

How to spot a division problem

The English contains "all", "every", or "each" applied to a set — for example:

  • Students admitted to all part-time courses.
  • Suppliers who supply every part.
  • Employees who work on all projects controlled by department 5.

If the query says "at least one", it is a join. If it says "all", it is a division.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Query: roll numbers of students admitted to all part-time courses.

Step 1 — the divisor. The set of part-time course IDs:

PT ← π SID (σ Coursetype='Parttime' (COURSE))
SID MA02 EN03

Step 2 — the dividend. The (student, course) pairs:

SC ← π Rollno, SID (ADMISSION)
Rollno SID X2019 CS01 X2019 MA02 X2020 CS01 Z1188 CH01 Z1188 EN03 X3001 MA02

Step 3 — divide. RESULT ← SC ÷ PT

Check each student against both required courses:

Student Has MA02? Has EN03? In result? X2019 yes no no X2020 no no no Z1188 no yes no X3001 yes no no

Result: empty. No student is admitted to both part-time courses. (This is a correct and instructive answer — verify it rather than assuming a non-empty result.)

Second illustration, so the operation is seen to work. Divide by PT2 = {MA02} alone: the answer is {X2019, X3001} — both students admitted to MA02.

docs.title: Division from the basic operations
docs.text:
Division is not primitive. It is defined as:

   R(Z) ÷ S(X),  where Y = Z − X

   T1 ← π Y (R)                     -- every candidate Y value
   T2 ← π Y ( (T1 × S) − R )        -- candidates MISSING some pairing
   RESULT ← T1 − T2                 -- candidates missing NOTHING

Reading the definition. T1 × S builds every pairing that would have to exist. Subtracting R leaves the pairings that are missing. Projecting onto Y names the candidates that are disqualified. Removing them from T1 leaves exactly those paired with everything.

Trace with SC ÷ PT:

T1 = π Rollno (SC) = {X2019, X2020, Z1188, X3001}

T1 × PT = {(X2019,MA02),(X2019,EN03),(X2020,MA02),(X2020,EN03),
           (Z1188,MA02),(Z1188,EN03),(X3001,MA02),(X3001,EN03)}

(T1 × PT) − SC = {(X2019,EN03),(X2020,MA02),(X2020,EN03),
                  (Z1188,MA02),(X3001,EN03)}        -- the missing pairings

T2 = π Rollno(...) = {X2019, X2020, Z1188, X3001}   -- all disqualified

RESULT = T1 − T2 = { }                              -- empty, as computed above

Division and SQL

SQL has no division operator. A division query is written either as a double NOT EXISTS ("there is no required course for which there is no admission") or by counting ("the number of distinct required courses this student has equals the total number of required courses"). Both idioms are shown in Unit 4, Lesson 5.

docs.title: 12.5 Aggregate Functions and Grouping
docs.text:
The operations so far cannot compute a count, sum or average — these produce a single value from a set of tuples, which no set operation does. An extra operator is required.

Aggregate function operation

<sub><grouping attributes></sub> ℱ <sub><function list></sub> (R)

Group the tuples of R by the grouping attributes, then apply each aggregate function to each group. If the grouping list is empty, the whole relation is one group.

Functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN.

Example 9 — no grouping. Total number of admissions.

ℱ<sub>COUNT(Rollno)</sub>(ADMISSION) → a single tuple, 6.

Example 10 — grouping. Number of students admitted to each course.

<sub>SID</sub>ℱ<sub>COUNT(Rollno)</sub>(ADMISSION)

SID COUNT(Rollno) CS01 2 MA02 2 CH01 1 EN03 1

Note that PH01 does not appear — it has no tuples in ADMISSION, so it forms no group. To include it with a count of 0, first take an outer join with COURSE. This is exactly the LEFT JOIN + COUNT idiom of Unit 4.

Example 11 — several functions. <sub>Coursetype</sub>ℱ<sub>COUNT(SID), AVG(TotalSeats), MAX(TotalSeats)</sub>(COURSE)

Coursetype COUNT(SID) AVG(TotalSeats) MAX(TotalSeats) Fulltime 3 48.33 60 Parttime 2 45.00 50

Aggregates and NULL

All aggregate functions ignore NULLs, with one exception: COUNT(*) counts rows, including those that are entirely NULL in the counted column.

So COUNT(*) and COUNT(SomeColumn) differ whenever that column contains NULLs — a distinction that matters constantly after an outer join.

docs.title: 12.6 A Complete Operations Table
docs.text: Operation Symbol Purpose Degree of result Cardinality of result SELECT σ Choose rows same as R 0 … |R| PROJECT π Choose columns, remove duplicates |L| 1 … |R| RENAME ρ Rename relation / attributes same same UNION ∪ Tuples in either same max … |R|+|S| INTERSECTION ∩ Tuples in both same 0 … min DIFFERENCE − Tuples in R not in S same 0 … |R| CARTESIAN PRODUCT × All combinations d(R)+d(S) |R| × |S| THETA JOIN ⋈θ Combine on a condition d(R)+d(S) 0 … |R|×|S| EQUIJOIN ⋈= Combine on equality d(R)+d(S) 0 … |R|×|S| NATURAL JOIN ⋈ Equijoin on same-named attributes, dedup columns d(R)+d(S)−c 0 … |R|×|S| LEFT OUTER JOIN ⟕ Keep all of R d(R)+d(S) ≥ |R| RIGHT OUTER JOIN ⟖ Keep all of S d(R)+d(S) ≥ |S| FULL OUTER JOIN ⟗ Keep all of both d(R)+d(S) ≥ max(|R|,|S|) SEMI-JOIN ⋉ Tuples of R having a match d(R) 0 … |R| ANTI-JOIN ▷ Tuples of R having no match d(R) 0 … |R| DIVISION ÷ "For all" d(R)−d(S) 0 … |π<sub>Y</sub>(R)| AGGREGATE ℱ Group and compute |G| + |F| number of groups

docs.title: 12.7 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Distinguish theta join, equijoin and natural join. Give the degree of each for STUDENT (degree 3) and ADMISSION (degree 3) with one common attribute.

A.

A theta join R ⋈<sub>θ</sub> S = σ<sub>θ</sub>(R × S) combines tuples satisfying any condition θ, which may use any comparison operator.

An equijoin is the special case in which every comparison in θ is equality. Its characteristic consequence is that the result contains two identical columns for each equated pair.

A natural join R ⋈ S is an equijoin on all identically-named attributes, written without an explicit condition, and with the duplicate columns removed.

Theta Equi Natural Condition any operator = only implicit Written explicitly yes yes no Duplicate columns possible always removed Degree here 3+3 = 6 3+3 = 6 3+3−1 = 5

Two cautions. If the relations share no attribute name, the natural join silently becomes the Cartesian product. And because it matches on name rather than meaning, an accidental shared name (say both relations having Name) produces a meaningless join with no error — which is why explicit join conditions are preferred in production code.

Solved Question 2

Q. What is an outer join? Explain the three kinds and give a query that requires each.

A. An inner join discards tuples with no matching partner. An outer join preserves them, padding the missing side with NULLs.

Left outer join R ⟕ S keeps every tuple of R. Query: "List every student with their courses, including students with no admission." STUDENT ⟕ ADMISSION — Arjun Nair appears with NULLs.

Right outer join R ⟖ S keeps every tuple of S. Query: "List every course with its students, including courses with none." ADMISSION ⟖ COURSE — Physics appears with NULLs.

Full outer join R ⟗ S keeps every tuple of both. Query: "List all students and all courses, showing admissions where they exist, and flagging both unadmitted students and empty courses." STUDENT ⟗ ADMISSION combined appropriately — both Arjun Nair and unmatched admissions would be preserved.

Why outer joins matter. They are essential whenever a report must show a zero. An inner join produces no row for a course with no students, so the course silently disappears from the report; a left outer join produces a row with NULL, which COUNT then reports as 0. Note that RIGHT OUTER JOIN is redundant in principle — R ⟖ S equals S ⟕ R — and is provided only for convenience.

Solved Question 3

Q. Define division. Express it using the basic operations. Solve: "roll numbers of students admitted to all full-time courses."

A. Definition. For R(Z) and S(X) with X ⊆ Z and Y = Z − X, the division R ÷ S is the set of Y-tuples t such that for every s ∈ S, the tuple ⟨t, s⟩ is in R.

In terms of the basic operations:

T1     ← π Y (R)
T2     ← π Y ( (T1 × S) − R )
R ÷ S  ← T1 − T2

T1 × S enumerates every pairing that would be required; subtracting R leaves the missing pairings; projecting names the disqualified candidates; removing them leaves those missing nothing.

Solution.

FT ← π SID (σ Coursetype='Fulltime' (COURSE))     = {CS01, CH01, PH01}
SC ← π Rollno, SID (ADMISSION)
RESULT ← SC ÷ FT

Checking each student against all three required courses:

Student CS01 CH01 PH01 Qualifies? X2019 yes no no no X2020 yes no no no Z1188 no yes no no X3001 no no no no

Result: empty. Indeed no student can qualify, since PH01 has no admissions at all — so no student is paired with it, and every candidate is disqualified.

Note on the empty divisor. If the divisor S were empty, the condition "for every s ∈ S" is vacuously true, so R ÷ S would return all of π<sub>Y</sub>(R). This edge case is worth stating in an examination answer.

Solved Question 4

Q. Write relational algebra for each, and give the result from the sample data.

a. Names of students and the names of courses they are admitted to. b. Names of students admitted to a part-time course. c. Names of courses with no students. d. For each course type, the number of courses and the average seats. e. Name of the course with the most students admitted.

A.

a. π<sub>Name, Cname</sub>(STUDENT ⋈ ADMISSION ⋈ COURSE)

Name Cname Ankit Sharma Computer Science Ankit Sharma Mathematics Riya Verma Computer Science Sana Iqbal Chemistry Sana Iqbal English Aditi Rao Mathematics

b. π<sub>Name</sub>(STUDENT ⋈ ADMISSION ⋈ σ<sub>Coursetype='Parttime'</sub>(COURSE)) → {Ankit Sharma, Sana Iqbal, Aditi Rao}.

Note the selection is pushed onto COURSE before the join — the optimisation rule of Lesson 3.

c. π<sub>Cname</sub>(σ<sub>Rollno IS NULL</sub>(COURSE ⟕ ADMISSION)) → {Physics}. Equivalently by difference: π<sub>Cname</sub>(COURSE ⋈ (π<sub>SID</sub>(COURSE) − π<sub>SID</sub>(ADMISSION))).

d. <sub>Coursetype</sub>ℱ<sub>COUNT(SID), AVG(TotalSeats)</sub>(COURSE)

Coursetype COUNT AVG Fulltime 3 48.33 Parttime 2 45.00

e. This needs two steps, because "the maximum" must be computed before it can be matched.

CNT   ← SID ℱ COUNT(Rollno) AS n (ADMISSION)        -- {(CS01,2),(MA02,2),(CH01,1),(EN03,1)}
MAXN  ← ℱ MAX(n) AS m (CNT)                          -- {(2)}
TOP   ← π SID ( CNT ⋈ n = m MAXN )                   -- {CS01, MA02}
RESULT← π Cname (COURSE ⋈ TOP)                       -- {Computer Science, Mathematics}

Two courses tie at 2 students, and both are correctly returned — a reminder that "the maximum" queries must handle ties.

Solved Question 5

Q. Explain semi-join and anti-join, express each using the basic operations, and state why an optimiser prefers them.

A. The semi-join R ⋉ S returns the tuples of R that have at least one match in S, projected back onto R's attributes, with each qualifying tuple appearing once:

R ⋉ S = π<sub>attributes of R</sub>(R ⋈ S)

The anti-join R ▷ S returns the tuples of R with no match:

R ▷ S = R − (R ⋉ S)

Examples. STUDENT ⋉ ADMISSION = the four students with at least one admission — X2019 appears once, though he has two admissions. STUDENT ▷ ADMISSION = {Arjun Nair}.

Why the optimiser prefers them. A full join between STUDENT and ADMISSION produces a result that is both wider (all attributes of both relations) and taller (one row per matching pair, so X2019 is duplicated). If the query only asks which students have an admission, all that extra data is built and then thrown away by a projection.

A semi-join can be evaluated by scanning R and, for each tuple, stopping at the first match in S — no duplication, no wide intermediate tuples. In distributed databases the saving is larger still: only the join column need be shipped across the network, not whole tuples.

These operations correspond directly to SQL's EXISTS and NOT EXISTS, which is why those constructs are often faster than the equivalent IN/NOT IN on large tables.

Solved Question 6

Q. Given R(A,B) with 10 tuples and S(B,C) with 6 tuples, where B is common, state the degree and the possible cardinality range of: R × S, R ⋈ S, R ⟕ S, R ⋉ S. Assume B is a key of S.

A.

Expression Degree Cardinality Reasoning R × S 2 + 2 = 4 exactly 60 Degrees add, cardinalities multiply: 10 × 6. R ⋈ S 2 + 2 − 1 = 3 0 to 10 Since B is a key of S, each tuple of R matches at most one tuple of S. So the join can never exceed |R| = 10, and is 0 if no B value of R occurs in S. R ⟕ S 3 exactly 10 Every tuple of R appears exactly once — matched (at most one partner, since B is a key of S) or padded with NULLs. R ⋉ S 2 0 to 10 Only R's attributes; a subset of R's tuples.

The key insight. Without the assumption that B is a key of S, the natural join could produce up to 10 × 6 = 60 tuples in the worst case (if every R tuple matched every S tuple, which requires all B values equal). Declaring B a key of S caps the join at |R|.

This is precisely the reasoning a query optimiser performs: it uses key and foreign-key constraints from the catalog to estimate intermediate result sizes, and those estimates determine the join order it chooses. Good constraints therefore make for good query plans — another practical reason to declare keys properly.

docs.title: 12.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Use the running relations from Lesson 3.

A. Short answer

  1. Express the theta join in terms of σ and ×.
  2. What is the degree of a natural join of relations of degree 4 and 5 with 2 common attributes?
  3. What happens to a natural join when the relations have no common attribute names?
  4. Distinguish inner join from outer join.
  5. Define semi-join and anti-join.
  6. When does a query require division?
  7. What does R ÷ S return when S is empty?

B. Write the relational algebra

  1. Names of students and their dates of admission.
  2. Names of students admitted to a course taught by a teacher named 'A. Gupta'.
  3. Names and seat counts of all courses, including those with no students.
  4. Names of students admitted to at least two courses.
  5. Names of students admitted to all part-time courses.
  6. Names of students admitted to all courses taught by teachers whose name contains 'Gupta'.
  7. For each student, the number of courses they are admitted to.
  8. For each course, the name and the number of vacant seats.
  9. The name of the course with the fewest students.
  10. Names of students who are admitted to CS01 but to no part-time course.
  11. Pairs of distinct students admitted to the same course. (Take care to avoid listing each pair twice.)
  12. Names of courses in which every admitted student was born in 2001.
  13. Names of teachers who are in charge of both a full-time and a part-time course.

C. Compute

  1. Give the actual result of each of questions 8 to 20 from the sample data.
  2. Give degree and cardinality: a. STUDENT ⋈ ADMISSION ⋈ COURSE b. STUDENT ⟕ ADMISSION c. COURSE ⟕ ADMISSION d. STUDENT ⋉ ADMISSION e. STUDENT ▷ ADMISSION f. π<sub>Rollno,SID</sub>(ADMISSION) ÷ π<sub>SID</sub>(σ<sub>Coursetype='Parttime'</sub>(COURSE))
  3. R(A,B) has 12 tuples, S(B,C) has 4, B is a key of S, and every B value in R occurs in S. Give the exact cardinality of R ⋈ S, R ⟕ S, R ⟖ S and R ⋉ S.

D. Analytical

  1. Prove that R ⟕ S and S ⟖ R produce the same set of tuples (up to attribute order).
  2. Show step by step, with intermediate tables, that the basic-operation definition of division gives the right answer for π<sub>Rollno,SID</sub>(ADMISSION) ÷ {MA02}.
  3. Explain why π<sub>Cname</sub>(σ<sub>Rollno IS NULL</sub>(COURSE ⟕ ADMISSION)) and π<sub>Cname</sub>(COURSE) − π<sub>Cname</sub>(COURSE ⋈ ADMISSION) give the same answer. Which would you expect to be faster, and why?
  4. A student writes <sub>SID</sub>ℱ<sub>COUNT(Rollno)</sub>(COURSE ⟕ ADMISSION) to count students per course including empty courses. Does it give 0 for PH01? Explain carefully, and give the correct expression.
  5. Explain why declaring a foreign key helps the query optimiser estimate join sizes.
  6. Rewrite π<sub>Name</sub>(σ<sub>Coursetype='Parttime'</sub>(STUDENT ⋈ ADMISSION ⋈ COURSE)) in an optimised form and quantify the reduction in intermediate result sizes.

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A natural join always produces fewer tuples than a Cartesian product.
  2. An equijoin removes duplicate columns.
  3. R ⟕ S always has at least |R| tuples.
  4. Division is a primitive operation.
  5. COUNT(*) and COUNT(A) always give the same answer.
  6. A semi-join may return duplicate tuples of R.
  7. R ⋈ S = S ⋈ R.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. If every tuple of R matches every tuple of S on the common attributes, the natural join has |R|×|S| tuples, the same as the product (minus the duplicated columns). It is never more, but it need not be fewer.
  2. False. An equijoin keeps both columns; the natural join removes the duplicate.
  3. True. Every tuple of R appears at least once, padded with NULLs if unmatched — and more than once if it has several partners.
  4. False. It is definable from π, × and −; it exists for convenience.
  5. False. They differ whenever A contains NULLs: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(A) counts non-NULL values.
  6. False. By definition each qualifying tuple of R appears exactly once, however many matches it has.
  7. True as a set of tuples; the attribute order may differ, which is immaterial under the (attribute, value)-pair definition of a tuple.

Lesson Summary

  • Theta join = σ on a product; equijoin = theta join with = only, keeping duplicate columns; natural join = equijoin on same-named attributes, removing them. Degree of natural join = d(R)+d(S) − #common.
  • Outer joins preserve unmatched tuples with NULLs — essential whenever a report must show a zero.
  • Semi-join and anti-join return only R's attributes, without duplication; they correspond to EXISTS and NOT EXISTS.
  • Division answers "for all" queries; it is not primitive, and SQL has no operator for it — use double NOT EXISTS or counting.
  • Aggregation ℱ groups and computes; aggregates ignore NULLs except COUNT(*); empty groups do not appear unless an outer join is used first.

End of Unit 3. Next: Unit 4, Lesson 1 — SQL and Data Definition.

docs.title: Lesson 7: Relationships, Relationship Types and Constraints
docs.text:
Degree, cardinality ratio, participation, roles and recursion

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 2: Entity Relationship Modelling · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 3.4

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define relationship, relationship type and relationship set.
  2. Determine the degree of a relationship type; model recursive relationships with role names.
  3. Apply the two structural constraints: cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and participation (total, partial).
  4. Read and write (min, max) notation, and convert between the two notations.
  5. Decide correctly when an attribute belongs to a relationship rather than to an entity type.

docs.title: 7.1 Relationships
docs.text:
The three terms

Relationship (relationship instance) — an association among entities. One specific fact: student X2019 took admission in course CS01 on 2019-07-15.

Relationship type R among entity types E1, E2, ..., En — the definition of such an association. Drawn as a diamond. This is the intension.

Relationship set — the set of all relationship instances of that type currently in the database. Mathematically it is a subset of the Cartesian product E1 x E2 x ... x En; each instance is an ordered tuple (e1, e2, ..., en). This is the extension.

As with entity types, the type and the set share a name and context disambiguates.

        STUDENT set                          COURSE set
    +---------------+                     +---------------+
    |  s1 (X2019)  o|--------\   /--------|o  c1 (CS01)   |
    |  s2 (X2020)  o|---------\-/---------|o  c2 (CH01)   |
    |  s3 (Z1188)  o|----------X          |o  c3 (MA02)   |
    +---------------+           \_________+---------------+

    Relationship set TAKES_ADMISSION =
        { (s1,c1), (s2,c1), (s2,c2), (s3,c3) }
    -- a SUBSET of STUDENT x COURSE.

Figure 3.1 — A relationship set as a subset of the Cartesian product.

Notation: a diamond joined by plain lines to the participating entity-type rectangles.

     +-----------+       /-----------------\       +-----------+
     |  STUDENT  |-------< TAKES_ADMISSION  >-------|  COURSE   |
     +-----------+       \-----------------/       +-----------+
                                  |
                          (Dateofadmission)

docs.title: 7.2 Degree of a Relationship Type
docs.text:
Degree

The number of participating entity types. (Not the number of entities.)

Degree Name Example 1 Unary / recursive EMPLOYEE SUPERVISES EMPLOYEE 2 Binary STUDENT TAKES_ADMISSION COURSE 3 Ternary SUPPLIER SUPPLIES PART to PROJECT n n-ary rare in practice

Binary relationships are by far the most common and are what the examination concentrates on.

docs.title: Recursive (unary) relationships and role names
docs.text:
The same entity type participates more than once, in different roles.

Role name

A label on the line from an entity type to a relationship diamond, stating the part that entity plays in the relationship. Role names are optional in general but mandatory for recursive relationships, because without them the two lines are indistinguishable.

                      +--------------+
                      |   EMPLOYEE   |
                      +--+--------+--+
              supervisor |        | supervisee
                    (1)  |        |  (N)
                         |        |
                     /---+--------+---\
                    <    SUPERVISES     >
                     \-----------------/

   Read: one employee (as SUPERVISOR) supervises many employees
         (as SUPERVISEE); each employee has at most one supervisor.
   Cardinality 1:N.

Figure 3.2 — A recursive relationship with role names.

Other examples: COURSE IS_PREREQUISITE_OF COURSE (M:N); PERSON IS_MARRIED_TO PERSON (1:1); PART CONTAINS PART in a bill of materials (M:N).

docs.title: Ternary relationships
docs.text:
+-----------+                 +-----------+
          | SUPPLIER  |                 | PROJECT   |
          +-----+-----+                 +-----+-----+
                |                             |
                |      /-------------\        |
                +-----<    SUPPLIES    >------+
                       \------+------/
                              |
                        +-----+-----+       (Quantity)
                        |   PART    |
                        +-----------+

   One instance = (supplier s, part p, project j):
   "supplier s supplies part p to project j".

A ternary relationship is not three binary ones

SUPPLIES(S, P, J) states a genuine three-way fact. Replacing it with CAN_SUPPLY(S,P), USES(P,J) and WORKS_FOR(S,J) loses information: from the three binaries you can infer that s supplies p, that project j uses p, and that s works for j — but not that s supplies p specifically to j. A supplier may supply bolts to project A and nuts to project B; the binaries cannot distinguish that case from supplying both parts to both projects.

Use a ternary relationship when the fact is genuinely irreducible to pairs; otherwise prefer binaries, which are simpler to understand and to map.

docs.title: 7.3 Constraints on Relationship Types
docs.text: Two independent structural constraints apply to every relationship type. Together they are called structural constraints, and getting them right is the substance of ER design.

docs.title: Cardinality ratio (mapping cardinality)
docs.text:
Cardinality ratio

Specifies the maximum number of relationship instances an entity can participate in. For a binary relationship the possibilities are 1:1, 1:N, N:1 and M:N.

  ONE-TO-ONE  (1:1)              A---o          o---1
  Each A relates to at most one B, and each B to at most one A.

      +--------+   1   /--------\   1   +----------+
      | TEACHER|-------<  HEADS   >-----| DEPARTMENT|
      +--------+       \--------/       +----------+
   A teacher heads at most one department; a department has
   at most one head.

  ONE-TO-MANY  (1:N)
      +--------+   1   /----------\   N   +---------+
      | COURSE |-------<  HAS_SEC   >-----| SECTION |
      +--------+       \----------/       +---------+
   One course has many sections; each section belongs to
   exactly one course.

  MANY-TO-MANY  (M:N)
      +--------+   M   /----------------\  N  +--------+
      | STUDENT|-------< TAKES_ADMISSION  >---| COURSE |
      +--------+       \----------------/     +--------+
   A student may take many courses; a course may have
   many students.

Figure 3.3 — The three cardinality ratios for binary relationships.

How to determine the ratio — the two-question method

Always ask two questions, one from each side, and always phrase them with "one ... how many ...?"

For STUDENT – COURSE:

  1. One student can take admission in how many courses? → many (the syllabus says "a student may enrol in any number of courses").
  2. One course can have how many students? → many.

Both "many" → M:N.

For COURSE – SECTION:

  1. One course has how many sections? → many.
  2. One section belongs to how many courses? → exactly one.

One "many", one "one" → 1:N (with the "1" on the COURSE side).

Where to write the label: put 1 or N on the line next to the entity type it describes, meaning "an entity of this type participates this many times". Different textbooks differ; state your convention.

docs.title: Participation constraint (existence dependency)
docs.text:
Participation constraint

Specifies the minimum number of relationship instances an entity may participate in.

Total participation (existence dependency) — every entity of the type must participate in at least one relationship instance. Drawn as a double line. Minimum = 1.

Partial participation — an entity may or may not participate. Drawn as a single line. Minimum = 0.

      +-----------+  M   /----------------\  N   +----------+
      |  STUDENT  |======< TAKES_ADMISSION  >-----|  COURSE  |
      +-----------+      \----------------/      +----------+
        double line                                single line
        = TOTAL participation                      = PARTIAL

   Reading: EVERY student must be admitted to at least one
            course (you cannot be a student otherwise), but a
            course MAY exist with no students yet enrolled.

Figure 3.4 — Total and partial participation on one relationship.

Cardinality and participation are independent

Cardinality is about the maximum ("at most how many?"); participation is about the minimum ("at least one, or possibly none?"). Every relationship type needs both, decided separately for each side. A relationship can be M:N with total participation on one side and partial on the other, as above.

docs.title: The (min, max) notation
docs.text:
An alternative, more precise notation places a pair (min, max) on each line.

(min, max)

For entity type E participating in relationship R, the pair (min, max) means: each entity of E must participate in at least min and at most max relationship instances of R.

  • min = 0 → partial participation.
  • min >= 1 → total participation.
  • max = N (or *) → no upper limit.
  • Necessarily 0 <= min <= max and max >= 1.

The notation trap — the labels swap sides

In Chen (1:N) notation the label describes the entity type it sits next to. In (min, max) notation the pair also sits next to its own entity type — but because it constrains that entity's participation, the resulting picture looks reversed compared with the 1/N labels.

Study this example until it is automatic:

   Chen:      COURSE ---1--- <HAS_SEC> ---N--- SECTION
   (min,max): COURSE --(0,N)-- <HAS_SEC> --(1,1)-- SECTION

   The "1" in Chen sits on COURSE; the "(1,1)" in min-max sits
   on SECTION. Both say the same thing:
      one section belongs to exactly one course.

docs.title: Conversion table
docs.text:
Chen notation Meaning (min, max) on left (min, max) on right A --1-- R --1-- B, both partial 1:1 (0,1) (0,1) A ==1== R --N-- B, A total 1:N (1,1) on A... see below A --M-- R --N-- B, both partial M:N (0,N) (0,N) A ==M== R --N-- B, A total M:N (1,N) (0,N)

Worked: STUDENT ==M== TAKES_ADMISSION --N-- COURSE, student total, course partial.

  • On the STUDENT line: a student participates at least once (total) and possibly many times → (1, N).
  • On the COURSE line: a course may have no students (partial) and possibly many → (0, N).
      +-----------+ (1,N) /----------------\ (0,N) +----------+
      |  STUDENT  |-------< TAKES_ADMISSION  >------|  COURSE  |
      +-----------+       \----------------/       +----------+

Worked: EMPLOYEE MANAGES DEPARTMENT, 1:1, every department must have a manager, but not every employee manages.

  • EMPLOYEE line: an employee manages 0 or 1 departments → (0, 1).
  • DEPARTMENT line: a department has exactly 1 manager → (1, 1).

docs.title: 7.4 Attributes of Relationship Types
docs.text:
Relationship attribute

An attribute that describes the association itself, not either participating entity. Drawn as an ellipse attached to the diamond.

The decisive test

Ask: "Is this fact determined by one entity alone, or only by the combination?"

Dateofadmission is not a property of the student (they have several admission dates, one per course) and not a property of the course (each student joined on a different date). It is determined only by the pair (student, course). Therefore it belongs to the relationship.

   +-----------+  M   /----------------\  N   +----------+
   |  STUDENT  |------< TAKES_ADMISSION  >-----|  COURSE  |
   +-----------+      \-------+--------/       +----------+
                              |
                      (Dateofadmission)   <-- attribute of the
                                              RELATIONSHIP

docs.title: Where a relationship attribute can be moved
docs.text:
Cardinality Can the attribute migrate to an entity type? M:N No. It must stay on the relationship (and becomes a column of the junction table on mapping). 1:N Yes — it can move to the entity type on the N side, since each such entity has exactly one relationship instance. 1:1 Yes — it can move to either side (choose the one with total participation, to avoid NULLs).

Example (1:N). EMPLOYEE WORKS_FOR DEPARTMENT is N:1, with relationship attribute StartDate. Each employee works for exactly one department, so StartDate can equally be an attribute of EMPLOYEE.

Example (M:N). Dateofadmission on the M:N TAKES_ADMISSION cannot move. Putting it on STUDENT would allow only one admission date per student, contradicting the M:N ratio.

docs.title: 7.5 Relationships vs Weak Entities — a comparison
docs.text:
Students confuse the identifying relationship of a weak entity type with an ordinary 1:N relationship. The distinction:

Ordinary 1:N relationship Identifying relationship Notation Single diamond Double diamond Related entity type Strong Weak (double rectangle) Purpose Records an association Supplies the identification of the weak entity Participation of the N side May be partial Always total On mapping Foreign key column Foreign key that is part of the primary key

docs.title: 7.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define relationship type, relationship set and degree. Give one example each of unary, binary and ternary relationships.

A. A relationship type R among entity types E1, ..., En is the definition of an association among entities of those types; it is drawn as a diamond and is the intension.

A relationship set is the set of all current relationship instances of that type. Formally it is a subset of the Cartesian product E1 x E2 x ... x En, each instance being an ordered tuple (e1, ..., en). It is the extension.

The degree of a relationship type is the number of participating entity types.

Degree Name Example One instance means 1 Unary / recursive EMPLOYEE SUPERVISES EMPLOYEE employee a supervises employee b 2 Binary STUDENT TAKES_ADMISSION COURSE student s is admitted to course c 3 Ternary SUPPLIER SUPPLIES PART PROJECT supplier s supplies part p to project j

In a recursive relationship the same entity type participates twice, in different roles, so role names such as supervisor and supervisee must be written on the lines to distinguish them.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish cardinality ratio from participation constraint. Show that they are independent by giving all four combinations for one relationship.

A.

Cardinality ratio Participation constraint Specifies The maximum number of instances The minimum number of instances Question "At most how many?" "At least one, or possibly none?" Values 1:1, 1:N, M:N Total or partial Notation 1, N, M on the line Double line (total) or single line (partial) In (min,max) The max component The min component

They are independent: cardinality fixes the ceiling, participation the floor, and each side of the relationship is decided separately.

Take STUDENT – COURSE, with all four combinations of participation over an M:N ratio:

Case STUDENT side COURSE side Business meaning 1 Partial (0,N) Partial (0,N) A student may be admitted to no course, and a course may have no students. 2 Total (1,N) Partial (0,N) Every student must be admitted to at least one course; a new course may exist with no students. This is our college. 3 Partial (0,N) Total (1,N) A course is only created once someone enrols; a person may be a student without any admission. 4 Total (1,N) Total (1,N) Every student is admitted somewhere and every course has at least one student.

Case 2 is the realistic one, which demonstrates that a single relationship needs both constraints, chosen independently for each side.

Solved Question 3

Q. Determine the cardinality ratio and participation for each, and express in both notations.

a. PERSON – PASSPORT b. DEPARTMENT – EMPLOYEE (works for) c. AUTHOR – BOOK (wrote) d. EMPLOYEE – EMPLOYEE (manages)

A.

a. PERSON – PASSPORT One person holds how many passports? At most one. One passport belongs to how many people? Exactly one. → 1:1. Participation: not every person holds a passport (partial on PERSON); every passport must belong to a person (total on PASSPORT).

   Chen:      PERSON --1-- <HOLDS> ==1== PASSPORT
   (min,max): PERSON (0,1) -- <HOLDS> -- (1,1) PASSPORT

b. DEPARTMENT – EMPLOYEE One department has how many employees? Many. One employee works for how many departments? Exactly one. → 1:N with the 1 on DEPARTMENT. Participation: every employee must belong to a department (total on EMPLOYEE); a newly created department may have no employees yet (partial on DEPARTMENT).

   Chen:      DEPARTMENT --1-- <WORKS_FOR> ==N== EMPLOYEE
   (min,max): DEPARTMENT (0,N) -- <WORKS_FOR> -- (1,1) EMPLOYEE

c. AUTHOR – BOOK One author writes how many books? Many. One book has how many authors? Many. → M:N. Participation: every book must have at least one author (total on BOOK); a person recorded as an author has written at least one book (total on AUTHOR).

   Chen:      AUTHOR ==M== <WROTE> ==N== BOOK
   (min,max): AUTHOR (1,N) -- <WROTE> -- (1,N) BOOK

d. EMPLOYEE – EMPLOYEE (manages) — recursive, so role names are required. One manager manages how many employees? Many. One employee has how many managers? At most one. → 1:N. Participation: not every employee is a manager (partial in the manager role); the chief executive has no manager, so participation in the subordinate role is also partial.

   Chen:      EMPLOYEE --1(manager)-- <MANAGES> --N(subordinate)-- EMPLOYEE
   (min,max): manager role (0,N) ; subordinate role (0,1)

Solved Question 4

Q. Where should Dateofadmission be placed, and why? What would go wrong if it were made an attribute of STUDENT? Of COURSE?

A. It belongs to the relationship type TAKES_ADMISSION, drawn as an ellipse attached to the diamond.

Test: is the fact determined by one entity alone, or only by the combination? A student admitted to three courses has three admission dates, so the date is not a function of the student. A course with 60 students was joined on many different dates, so it is not a function of the course. It is determined only by the pair (student, course), which is precisely the definition of a relationship attribute.

If made an attribute of STUDENT: each student could store only one admission date, so a student admitted to Computer Science in July and to a part-time Mathematics course in September could not record both. This silently contradicts the M:N cardinality, and forces either data loss or a repeating group that violates 1NF.

If made an attribute of COURSE: each course could store only one admission date for all its students — meaningless, since students join on different dates. Recording the correct date for even two students becomes impossible.

General rule. On an M:N relationship the attribute cannot be migrated to either entity type. On a 1:N relationship it may be migrated to the entity type on the N side (each such entity participates exactly once); on a 1:1 relationship it may be migrated to either side, preferably the one with total participation to avoid NULLs.

On mapping (Unit 5) the M:N relationship becomes ADMISSION(Rollno, SID, Dateofadmission) with primary key (Rollno, SID) — and the relationship attribute becomes an ordinary column of that table.

Solved Question 5

Q. What is a recursive relationship? Why are role names essential? Model "a course may have several prerequisite courses".

A. A recursive (unary) relationship is one in which the same entity type participates more than once, each time in a different role.

Role names are essential because the two lines run between the same rectangle and the same diamond, so they are otherwise indistinguishable. Without labels, EMPLOYEE — SUPERVISES — EMPLOYEE does not say which end is the supervisor; the diagram becomes ambiguous, and the cardinality labels cannot be interpreted. Role names also become the column names on mapping, so they carry through to the implementation.

Prerequisites. One course may have how many prerequisites? Many (a course can require several). One course may be a prerequisite for how many courses? Many. → M:N. Participation is partial on both sides: an introductory course has no prerequisites, and an advanced course is a prerequisite for nothing.

                      +--------------+
                      |    COURSE    |
                      +--+--------+--+
       (0,N) has_prereq |        | is_prereq_for (0,N)
                        |        |
                    /---+--------+---\
                   <   PREREQUISITE    >
                    \-----------------/

On mapping this M:N recursive relationship yields a table with two foreign keys to the same table, both named after the roles:

CREATE TABLE PREREQUISITE (
    CourseID   VARCHAR(6),
    PrereqID   VARCHAR(6),
    PRIMARY KEY (CourseID, PrereqID),
    FOREIGN KEY (CourseID) REFERENCES COURSE(SID),
    FOREIGN KEY (PrereqID) REFERENCES COURSE(SID),
    CHECK (CourseID <> PrereqID)
);

The CHECK prevents a course being its own prerequisite. (Detecting longer cycles requires a recursive query, which is beyond a table constraint.)

Solved Question 6

Q. Explain why a ternary relationship cannot in general be replaced by three binary relationships. Illustrate.

A. Because a ternary relationship records an irreducible three-way fact, whereas three binaries record only three separate two-way facts, and the pairwise facts do not determine the triples.

Consider SUPPLIES(Supplier, Part, Project) with these instances:

Supplier Part Project S1 Bolt P1 S1 Nut P2

Now decompose into three binaries:

  • CAN_SUPPLY(Supplier, Part) = {(S1, Bolt), (S1, Nut)}
  • USES(Part, Project) = {(Bolt, P1), (Nut, P2)}
  • WORKS_FOR(Supplier, Project) = {(S1, P1), (S1, P2)}

Reconstructing by joining the three binaries yields four triples, not two:

Supplier Part Project Real? S1 Bolt P1 yes S1 Bolt P2 spurious S1 Nut P1 spurious S1 Nut P2 yes

The two spurious tuples are indistinguishable from the genuine ones, so information has been lost: the decomposition is not lossless. The binaries can say "S1 can supply bolts", "P1 uses bolts" and "S1 works for P1", but they cannot say "S1 supplies bolts specifically to P1".

When decomposition is safe: if the business rule happens to be that a supplier supplies a given part to every project that uses it, then the ternary fact is genuinely determined by the pairs, and three binaries lose nothing. The general rule: use a ternary relationship when the association is genuinely three-way; prefer binaries otherwise, since they are simpler to read, to constrain and to map.

docs.title: 7.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define relationship type and relationship set.
  2. What is the degree of a relationship type? Give an example of degree 3.
  3. What is a role name? When is it compulsory?
  4. Define cardinality ratio and list the possibilities for a binary relationship.
  5. How is total participation drawn? What does it mean?
  6. In (min, max) notation, what does (1, N) mean?
  7. Where is a relationship attribute drawn?

B. Long answer

  1. Explain the structural constraints on a binary relationship type. Show with examples that cardinality and participation are independent.
  2. Explain (min, max) notation and convert three examples between it and Chen notation, explaining the apparent reversal of labels.
  3. What is a recursive relationship? Explain with two examples of different cardinality, showing role names, and describe how each maps to tables.
  4. When does an attribute belong to a relationship rather than to an entity type? State the test, and explain for which cardinalities the attribute may be migrated.
  5. Explain why a ternary relationship is not in general equivalent to three binary relationships, with a numeric illustration.

C. Application and analytical

  1. Determine cardinality and participation, and express in both notations: a. CUSTOMER – ACCOUNT in a bank where joint accounts are allowed. b. PATIENT – BED in a hospital at a given moment. c. DRIVER – LICENCE. d. STUDENT – SOCIETY in our college. e. EMPLOYEE – PROJECT where an employee may work on several projects. f. MOTHER – CHILD.
  2. For the college database, draw the fragment for STUDENT, COURSE and TAKES_ADMISSION, with correct cardinality, participation and the relationship attribute. State every business rule your diagram asserts, in English.
  3. A university insists that every department must have exactly one head, that a head must be a professor of that department, and that a professor may head at most one department. Draw this and give the (min, max) pairs. Which constraint cannot be captured in the ER diagram at all?
  4. Model a ternary relationship for "a doctor prescribes a drug to a patient on a date". Then argue whether it could be decomposed into binaries.
  5. For each, state whether the attribute belongs to an entity type or a relationship, and justify: a. Salary in EMPLOYEE – WORKS_FOR – DEPARTMENT (N:1). b. HoursPerWeek in EMPLOYEE – WORKS_ON – PROJECT (M:N). c. Dateofenrolment in STUDENT – ENROLS_IN – SOCIETY (M:N). d. Grade in STUDENT – TAKES – EXAM (M:N).
  6. A designer draws STUDENT ==M== TAKES_ADMISSION ==N== COURSE (both total). What business rule does this assert? Is it realistic for a college? What practical problem arises when the first course of a new session is created?

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. The degree of a relationship is the number of entity instances participating.
  2. A relationship set is a subset of a Cartesian product.
  3. In a 1:N relationship the attribute of the relationship can always be moved to the 1 side.
  4. Total participation is drawn as a double diamond.
  5. (0, 1) indicates total participation.
  6. Role names are compulsory for all relationships.
  7. A weak entity type's participation in its identifying relationship is always total.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. It is the number of participating entity types.
  2. True. Each instance is a tuple (e1, ..., en) drawn from E1 x ... x En.
  3. False. It moves to the N side, where each entity participates exactly once. Moving it to the 1 side would allow only one value for many relationship instances.
  4. False. Total participation is a double line. A double diamond is an identifying relationship.
  5. False. min = 0 means partial. Total requires min >= 1.
  6. False. They are optional in general, but compulsory for recursive relationships, where the lines are otherwise indistinguishable.
  7. True. Every weak entity must be related to exactly one owner in order to be identified at all.

Lesson Summary

  • A relationship set is a subset of the Cartesian product of the participating entity sets; its degree is the number of participating entity types.
  • Recursive relationships need role names.
  • Cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) sets the maximum; participation (total = double line, partial = single) sets the minimum. They are independent and are decided per side.
  • (min, max) notation combines both; the pair sits on its own entity's line, which makes it look reversed relative to Chen labels.
  • A relationship attribute is one determined only by the combination of entities. It cannot be migrated on an M:N relationship; it may be migrated to the N side of a 1:N.
  • A ternary relationship is generally not decomposable into three binaries without losing information.

docs.title: Lesson 13: SQL: Data Definition and Constraints
docs.text:
Creating databases and tables, data types, and table constraints

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 4: Structured Query Language · 12 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 2 lectures

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 6.1, 6.2 · Murach's MySQL, Ch. 10, 11

Learning Outcomes

  1. State the history and sub-languages of SQL (DDL, DML, DCL, TCL).
  2. Choose appropriate data types for numeric, string, date and boolean data.
  3. Write CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE with all constraint clauses.
  4. Distinguish column-level from table-level constraints and know when each is required.
  5. Build the complete college schema used throughout the practical component.

docs.title: 13.1 SQL — Origins and Structure
docs.text:
SQL

Structured Query Language — the standard language of relational databases. Developed at IBM's San Jose Research Laboratory in the early 1970s as SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) for the System R prototype, based on Codd's relational model. Standardised by ANSI in 1986 and by ISO in 1987; major revisions followed as SQL-89, SQL-92, SQL:1999, SQL:2003, and onward.

SQL is declarative: you state what you want, and the optimiser decides how (Unit 1, Lesson 4). It is also relationally complete — everything expressible in relational algebra is expressible in SQL.

docs.title: The sub-languages
docs.text:
Sub-language Purpose Statements DDL — Data Definition Define and change the schema CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME DML — Data Manipulation Retrieve and change data SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE DCL — Data Control Control access GRANT, REVOKE TCL — Transaction Control Delimit transactions COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

This lesson covers DDL. DML is Lessons 2 to 5; DCL and TCL are Lesson 6.

Terminology: SQL vs the relational model

Relational model SQL Relation Table Tuple Row Attribute Column Relation is a set Table is a multiset (bag) — duplicates possible

The bag semantics is the single most important difference, and it is why DISTINCT exists.

docs.title: 13.2 Data Types
docs.text: Choosing the right type is a design decision, not a formality: it is the domain constraint of Unit 3 in practice.

docs.title: Numeric
docs.text:
Type Range / meaning Use for TINYINT −128 to 127 (or 0–255 unsigned) Small counters, flags SMALLINT ±32,767 Seat counts, ages INT / INTEGER ±2.1 billion Most integer data BIGINT ±9.2 × 1018 Large IDs, counters DECIMAL(p,s) / NUMERIC(p,s) Exact decimal: p total digits, s after the point Money, marks, any exact fraction FLOAT, DOUBLE Approximate binary floating point Scientific measurements

Never use FLOAT for money

FLOAT and DOUBLE are binary approximations. The decimal value 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so 0.1 + 0.2 may not equal 0.3, and a sum of a thousand payments can drift by rupees.

Use DECIMAL(10,2) for currency. It stores the digits exactly and arithmetic is exact.

docs.title: String
docs.text:
Type Meaning Notes CHAR(n) Fixed length, space-padded to n Use when every value is the same length: CHAR(10) for a mobile number, CHAR(12) for Aadhaar VARCHAR(n) Variable length, up to n The default choice for names, addresses TEXT Long text, no length limit given Descriptions, comments; cannot be fully indexed ENUM('a','b') One of a listed set (MySQL) Alternative to a CHECK constraint

CHAR vs VARCHAR
