CHAR(40) storing 'Ankit' occupies 40 characters (padded with spaces); VARCHAR(40) occupies about 6 (5 + a length byte).

Use CHAR only when the length really is fixed — the padding then costs nothing and lookups are marginally faster because rows are fixed-width. Use VARCHAR for everything else.

docs.title: Date and time
docs.text:
Type Format Example DATE YYYY-MM-DD 2019-07-15 TIME HH:MM:SS 14:30:00 DATETIME YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS 2019-07-15 14:30:00 TIMESTAMP As DATETIME, but timezone-aware and auto-updating Audit columns YEAR YYYY 2019

Always store dates in a date type, never as a string. A VARCHAR date cannot be compared or sorted chronologically, cannot use date functions, and permits '31-02-2019'.

docs.title: Boolean and other
docs.text: BOOLEAN (in MySQL a synonym for TINYINT(1), where 0 is false and non-zero is true); BLOB for binary data; JSON in modern versions.

docs.title: 13.3 CREATE DATABASE
docs.text:
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS college
    CHARACTER SET utf8mb4
    COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;

USE college;
  • IF NOT EXISTS prevents an error if it is already there — useful in scripts run repeatedly.
  • CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 supports the full range of Unicode, including Indic scripts and emoji. Prefer it always.
  • COLLATE fixes the sorting and comparison rules; _ci means case-insensitive.

Related statements: SHOW DATABASES;, DROP DATABASE college;, SHOW TABLES;, DESCRIBE STUDENT;.

docs.title: General form
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE table_name (
    column_name  data_type  [column constraints],
    ...
    [table constraints]
);

docs.title: The five constraint types
docs.text:
Constraint Meaning Level NOT NULL The column may not hold NULL Column only UNIQUE No two rows may share this value Either PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE and NOT NULL; the identifier Either FOREIGN KEY Must match a primary key elsewhere, or be NULL Table (mostly) CHECK An arbitrary Boolean condition Either DEFAULT Value used when none is supplied Column only

Column-level vs table-level

A column-level constraint is written immediately after the column definition and applies to that one column:

Rollno VARCHAR(8) PRIMARY KEY

A table-level constraint is written as a separate item after all columns, and must be used when the constraint involves more than one column:

PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID)

Table-level constraints may also be named, which makes them far easier to drop or diagnose later:

CONSTRAINT chk_seats CHECK (TotalSeats > 0)

docs.title: Building the college schema, step by step
docs.text:
Table 1 — STUDENT (no dependencies, so create it first).

CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
    Rollno      VARCHAR(8)   NOT NULL,
    Name        VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    Dateofbirth DATE,
    CONSTRAINT pk_student PRIMARY KEY (Rollno)
);

Table 2 — COURSE.

CREATE TABLE COURSE (
    SID             VARCHAR(6)   NOT NULL,
    Cname           VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    TotalSeats      INT          NOT NULL,
    Duration        INT,
    Coursetype      VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL,
    TeacherInCharge VARCHAR(40),
    CONSTRAINT pk_course      PRIMARY KEY (SID),
    CONSTRAINT uq_cname       UNIQUE (Cname),
    CONSTRAINT chk_seats      CHECK (TotalSeats > 0),
    CONSTRAINT chk_duration   CHECK (Duration BETWEEN 1 AND 6),
    CONSTRAINT chk_ctype      CHECK (Coursetype IN ('Fulltime','Parttime'))
);

Note each constraint encodes a business rule stated in the requirements — this is where the rules that the ER diagram could not draw (Unit 2, Lesson 4) finally get enforced.

Table 3 — ADMISSION (depends on both, so create it last).

CREATE TABLE ADMISSION (
    Rollno          VARCHAR(8)  NOT NULL,
    SID             VARCHAR(6)  NOT NULL,
    Dateofadmission DATE        NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_admission PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID),
    CONSTRAINT fk_adm_student FOREIGN KEY (Rollno)
        REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno) ON DELETE CASCADE  ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_adm_course  FOREIGN KEY (SID)
        REFERENCES COURSE(SID)     ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
);

Three points:

  • The composite primary key (Rollno, SID) must be table-level, and it enforces the business rule "a student may be admitted to a given course only once".
  • ON DELETE CASCADE on Rollno and ON DELETE RESTRICT on SID — the reasoning is in Unit 3, Lesson 2.
  • Order matters: a foreign key cannot reference a table that does not yet exist.

Tables 4 and 5 — the society schema.

CREATE TABLE SOCIETY (
    SocID      VARCHAR(6)   NOT NULL,
    Socname    VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    Mentor     VARCHAR(40),
    TotalSeats INT          NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_society  PRIMARY KEY (SocID),
    CONSTRAINT uq_socname  UNIQUE (Socname),
    CONSTRAINT chk_socseats CHECK (TotalSeats > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE ENROLLMENT (
    Rollno           VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    SocID            VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    Dateofenrollment DATE       NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_enrollment PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SocID),
    CONSTRAINT fk_enr_student FOREIGN KEY (Rollno)
        REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_enr_society FOREIGN KEY (SocID)
        REFERENCES SOCIETY(SocID)  ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
);

   THE COLLEGE SCHEMA

   +-------------------+                    +-------------------------+
   |      STUDENT      |                    |         COURSE          |
   +-------------------+                    +-------------------------+
   | PK Rollno         |                    | PK SID                  |
   |    Name           |                    |    Cname       (UNIQUE) |
   |    Dateofbirth    |                    |    TotalSeats  (>0)     |
   +---------+---------+                    |    Duration             |
             |                              |    Coursetype  (F/P)    |
             |                              |    TeacherInCharge      |
             |                              +------------+------------+
             |                                           |
             |     +-------------------------+           |
             +-----+       ADMISSION         +-----------+
             |     +-------------------------+
             |     | PK,FK Rollno            |
             |     | PK,FK SID               |
             |     |       Dateofadmission   |
             |     +-------------------------+
             |
             |     +-------------------------+           +----------------+
             +-----+       ENROLLMENT        +-----------+    SOCIETY     |
                   +-------------------------+           +----------------+
                   | PK,FK Rollno            |           | PK SocID       |
                   | PK,FK SocID             |           |    Socname     |
                   |       Dateofenrollment  |           |    Mentor      |
                   +-------------------------+           |    TotalSeats  |
                                                         +----------------+

Figure 1.1 — The college schema used throughout the practical component.

docs.title: 13.5 AUTO_INCREMENT and Surrogate Keys
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE FEE_RECEIPT (
    ReceiptNo INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    Rollno    VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    Amount    DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (Amount > 0),
    PaidOn    DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE),
    FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno)
);

AUTO_INCREMENT generates the next integer automatically — a surrogate key (Unit 2, Lesson 2). Use it when no good natural key exists, and declare the natural key UNIQUE alongside.

docs.title: 13.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Classify SQL statements into its sub-languages, giving two examples of each and stating who uses them.

A.

Sub-language Purpose Examples Typical user What it changes DDL Define/alter the schema CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE DBA, designer The schema (catalog) DML Retrieve/change data SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE End users, programmers The instance DCL Control access GRANT, REVOKE DBA Privileges in the catalog TCL Delimit transactions COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT Programmers Transaction boundaries

Two notes worth adding. TRUNCATE is classified as DDL even though it removes rows, because it deallocates the table's storage rather than deleting row by row, and (in most systems) cannot be rolled back. And some textbooks fold DCL into a broad definition of DDL; state the four-way classification and mention the variation.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish CHAR from VARCHAR, and DECIMAL from FLOAT. When would you use each?

A.

CHAR(n) vs VARCHAR(n)

CHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) Storage Always exactly n characters, space-padded Actual length plus 1–2 length bytes 'Ankit' in a size-40 column 40 characters ~6 bytes Rows Fixed width — marginally faster to scan Variable width Use for Genuinely fixed-length codes: CHAR(10) mobile, CHAR(12) Aadhaar, CHAR(1) sex Everything variable: names, addresses, titles

DECIMAL(p,s) vs FLOAT/DOUBLE

DECIMAL(p,s) FLOAT / DOUBLE Representation Exact decimal Approximate binary 0.1 + 0.2 Exactly 0.3 May be 0.30000000000000004 Use for Money, marks, fees, any exact fraction Scientific measurements, where a tiny relative error is acceptable and range matters more

The decisive argument: a currency column summed over a million rows in FLOAT accumulates rounding error, and an account can fail to balance. DECIMAL(10,2) stores the digits themselves, so arithmetic is exact. Never store money in a floating-point type.

Solved Question 3

Q. Write the CREATE TABLE statement for ADMISSION, explaining every clause.

A.

CREATE TABLE ADMISSION (
    Rollno          VARCHAR(8) NOT NULL,
    SID             VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    Dateofadmission DATE       NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_admission PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID),
    CONSTRAINT fk_adm_student FOREIGN KEY (Rollno)
        REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno) ON DELETE CASCADE  ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_adm_course  FOREIGN KEY (SID)
        REFERENCES COURSE(SID)     ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE
);
Clause Purpose VARCHAR(8) / VARCHAR(6) Domains matching the referenced primary keys exactly — a foreign key must have the same domain as the key it references. NOT NULL on all three The first two are part of the primary key, so entity integrity requires it; the third is a business rule. PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID) A composite key, so it must be table-level. Encodes the rule "a student may be admitted to a given course only once", and enforces entity integrity on both columns. FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT Referential integrity: no admission for a non-existent student. ON DELETE CASCADE (student) An admission is meaningless without the student, so deleting the student removes their admissions. ON DELETE RESTRICT (course) Deleting a course with admitted students would destroy their history, so it is forbidden until they are transferred or removed. ON UPDATE CASCADE (both) A changed key value is a renaming of the same entity, and children should follow. CONSTRAINT <name> Naming makes constraints easy to drop (ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT pk_admission) and produces readable error messages.

Creation order matters: STUDENT and COURSE must exist first, since a foreign key cannot reference a non-existent table.

Solved Question 4

Q. Distinguish column-level from table-level constraints. Give a constraint that must be table-level and one that cannot be.

A. A column-level constraint is written inline after a column's data type and applies to that single column. A table-level constraint is written as a separate element after all column definitions and may reference several columns.

Must be table-level: any constraint spanning more than one column.

PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID)                     -- composite key
CHECK (Dateofadmission >= Dateofbirth)        -- relates two columns
UNIQUE (Cname, Coursetype)                    -- composite uniqueness

A composite primary key cannot be expressed column-by-column: writing PRIMARY KEY after both Rollno and SID would attempt to declare two primary keys, which is an error.

Cannot be table-level: NOT NULL and DEFAULT. Both are properties of a single column's storage rather than relations among columns, and SQL provides no table-level syntax for them.

Name   VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
Mobile CHAR(10) DEFAULT '9999999999'

Either level: single-column PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY. Prefer the table level with a name for anything you may later need to drop or diagnose, since an unnamed constraint receives a system-generated name that differs between systems.

Solved Question 5

Q. Write DDL for a LIBRARY database: BOOK(ISBN, Title, Publisher, Price), MEMBER(MemberID, Name, Email, JoinDate), ISSUE(ISBN, MemberID, IssueDate, DueDate, Returned). Include every sensible constraint.

A.

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS library
    CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE library;

CREATE TABLE BOOK (
    ISBN      CHAR(13)      NOT NULL,
    Title     VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL,
    Publisher VARCHAR(60),
    Price     DECIMAL(8,2)  NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT pk_book    PRIMARY KEY (ISBN),
    CONSTRAINT chk_price  CHECK (Price > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE MEMBER (
    MemberID INT AUTO_INCREMENT,
    Name     VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    Email    VARCHAR(60)  NOT NULL,
    JoinDate DATE         NOT NULL DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE),
    CONSTRAINT pk_member PRIMARY KEY (MemberID),
    CONSTRAINT uq_email  UNIQUE (Email)
);

CREATE TABLE ISSUE (
    ISBN      CHAR(13)  NOT NULL,
    MemberID  INT       NOT NULL,
    IssueDate DATE      NOT NULL,
    DueDate   DATE      NOT NULL,
    Returned  BOOLEAN   NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    CONSTRAINT pk_issue PRIMARY KEY (ISBN, MemberID, IssueDate),
    CONSTRAINT fk_iss_book   FOREIGN KEY (ISBN)
        REFERENCES BOOK(ISBN)     ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT fk_iss_member FOREIGN KEY (MemberID)
        REFERENCES MEMBER(MemberID) ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
    CONSTRAINT chk_dates CHECK (DueDate > IssueDate)
);

Design decisions worth stating:

  • ISBN is CHAR(13) because an ISBN-13 is exactly 13 characters — a genuinely fixed length.
  • MemberID is a surrogate key with AUTO_INCREMENT, because no stable natural key exists; Email is declared UNIQUE as the natural alternate key.
  • Price uses DECIMAL(8,2), never FLOAT.
  • ISSUE's primary key includes IssueDate, because the same member may borrow the same book again later — without the date, the second loan would violate the key.
  • ON DELETE RESTRICT on both foreign keys: an issue record is an audit trail, and deleting a book or a member must not silently erase the borrowing history.
  • CHECK (DueDate > IssueDate) is a table-level constraint because it relates two columns.

Solved Question 6

Q. What is AUTO_INCREMENT? When should a surrogate key be preferred to a natural key, and what should accompany it?

A. AUTO_INCREMENT (MySQL; SERIAL in PostgreSQL, IDENTITY in SQL Server) instructs the DBMS to generate the next integer automatically whenever a row is inserted without a value for that column. It is the standard way of creating a surrogate key — a system-generated, meaningless identifier.

Prefer a surrogate key when:

  1. No natural candidate key is stable. Email addresses, phone numbers and names all change; a primary key that changes forces cascading updates through every referencing table.
  2. No natural key is always available at insertion time. A patient arriving unconscious has no recorded identity document, yet must be admitted immediately.
  3. The only natural key is long or composite. A four-column composite key is copied into every child table, bloating indexes and slowing joins.
  4. The natural key is privacy-sensitive. Using a national identity number as a primary key propagates it into every referencing table and every index.

Prefer a natural key when one exists that is stable, short, always available and non-sensitive — Rollno for STUDENT, ISBN for a book title. A natural key is meaningful to users and often removes the need for a join.

What must accompany a surrogate key: a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key. A surrogate guarantees that every row is distinct, but not that every real-world entity appears only once — without UNIQUE (Email), the same person can be inserted twice with two different MemberIDs, and the surrogate happily calls them different members.

docs.title: 13.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. What does SQL stand for, and what was it originally called?
  2. Name the four sub-languages of SQL with two statements each.
  3. Why should money never be stored in FLOAT?
  4. Distinguish CHAR(10) from VARCHAR(10).
  5. Name two constraints that cannot be written at table level.
  6. Why must STUDENT be created before ADMISSION?
  7. What is the advantage of naming a constraint?

B. Write the SQL

  1. Create a database hospital with UTF-8 support and select it.
  2. Create WARD(WardNo, Name, Capacity) where capacity is between 1 and 100.
  3. Create PATIENT(RegNo, Name, Dateofbirth, BloodGroup) where blood group is one of the eight valid values and RegNo is auto-generated.
  4. Create DOCTOR(EmpCode, Name, Specialisation, Salary) with salary positive and stored exactly.
  5. Create TREATS(EmpCode, RegNo, FirstConsult, Fee) with the appropriate composite key, both foreign keys, sensible referential actions, and a check that the fee is not negative.
  6. Create the complete college schema (all five tables) from scratch, in the correct order.
  7. Create EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Name, Salary, SuperSsn, Dno) where SuperSsn references the same table.

C. Analytical

  1. For each column below, choose a data type and justify: a. A student's roll number, always one letter plus four digits. b. A course fee in rupees and paise. c. A student's photograph. d. The date and time an exam starts. e. Whether a fee has been paid. f. A 500-word course description. g. A mobile number.
  2. Explain what happens, and why, for each: a. CREATE TABLE ADMISSION before STUDENT exists. b. Two PRIMARY KEY clauses on the same table. c. A FOREIGN KEY whose column is VARCHAR(20) referencing a VARCHAR(8) primary key. d. CHECK (TotalSeats > 0) when a row with TotalSeats = 0 already exists.
  3. A designer writes Coursetype VARCHAR(10) with no CHECK. List three specific ways the data can become corrupt, and give two different SQL mechanisms to prevent it.
  4. Compare ENUM('Fulltime','Parttime') with VARCHAR(10) CHECK (Coursetype IN (...)). Give one advantage of each.
  5. Write the DDL for a schema of your own design for a canteen (items, orders, order lines, payments), with full justification of every key and constraint.

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. TRUNCATE is a DML statement.
  2. A table may have several UNIQUE constraints.
  3. A CHECK constraint may reference a column of another table.
  4. PRIMARY KEY implies NOT NULL.
  5. VARCHAR(40) always occupies 40 bytes.
  6. A foreign key must have the same data type as the key it references.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. It is DDL — it deallocates the table's storage rather than deleting rows individually, and generally cannot be rolled back.
  2. True. Only the primary key is limited to one; any number of alternate keys may be declared UNIQUE.
  3. False. A CHECK may reference only columns of its own row. Cross-table rules need a trigger or an assertion.
  4. True. By the entity integrity constraint, a primary key may never be NULL, so NOT NULL is implied.
  5. False. It occupies the actual length plus 1–2 length bytes. CHAR(40) occupies 40.
  6. True in effect — it must have the same domain; most systems reject a mismatched type or length outright.

Lesson Summary

  • SQL comprises DDL, DML, DCL, TCL; this lesson covered DDL.
  • Choose types deliberately: DECIMAL for money (never FLOAT), VARCHAR unless the length is genuinely fixed, real DATE types for dates.
  • CREATE TABLE carries the constraints that enforce the business rules the ER diagram could not draw: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT.
  • Constraints spanning several columns must be table-level; NOT NULL and DEFAULT must be column-level. Name your constraints.
  • Create parent tables before child tables.
  • Use AUTO_INCREMENT surrogate keys when no stable natural key exists — and always add UNIQUE on the natural key alongside.

docs.title: Lesson 3: Three-Schema Architecture and Data Independence
docs.text:
Three levels, two mappings, two independences

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 1: Introduction to Database · 5 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture (50 minutes)

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 2.2 · ANSI/SPARC 1975

Learning Outcomes

  1. Draw and label the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture.
  2. Describe the internal, conceptual and external levels, and say what each contains.
  3. Explain the two mappings and the cost of maintaining them.
  4. Define logical and physical data independence and distinguish them with examples.
  5. Explain why logical data independence is harder to achieve than physical.

docs.title: 3.1 The Problem the Architecture Solves
docs.text:
Lesson 2 established program–data independence as a goal. The three-schema architecture, proposed by the ANSI/SPARC study group in 1975, is the design that achieves it.

The idea is to separate the user's view of the data from the way the data is physically stored, and to insert a stable layer between them. Three levels of description, therefore, rather than one.

          END USERS
     clerk       mentor       principal
       |            |             |
   +---v----+  +----v---+  +------v-----+
   | EXTERNAL  |EXTERNAL |  | EXTERNAL   |   <---- EXTERNAL / VIEW LEVEL
   | SCHEMA 1  |SCHEMA 2 |  | SCHEMA 3   |         (many; one per user group)
   +---+----+  +----+---+  +------+-----+
       |            |             |
       +----- external/conceptual mapping ------+
                    |
        +-----------v-------------+
        |   CONCEPTUAL SCHEMA     |             <---- CONCEPTUAL / LOGICAL LEVEL
        |  all entities, all      |                   (exactly ONE)
        |  attributes, all        |
        |  relationships,         |
        |  all constraints        |
        +-----------+-------------+
                    |
        +---- conceptual/internal mapping ----+
                    |
        +-----------v-------------+
        |   INTERNAL SCHEMA       |             <---- INTERNAL / PHYSICAL LEVEL
        |  file organisation,     |                   (exactly ONE)
        |  indexes, page size,    |
        |  compression, ordering  |
        +-----------+-------------+
                    |
        +-----------v-------------+
        |   STORED DATABASE       |
        |   (disk blocks)         |
        +-------------------------+

Figure 3.1 — The ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture.

docs.title: Internal level (physical level)
docs.text:
What it describes: how the data is physically stored.

The internal schema, written in a physical data definition language, specifies:

  • the file organisation of each table — heap, sorted, hashed (Unit 6);
  • which indexes exist and of what kind (B+-tree, hash);
  • the record format — field order, sizes, encoding;
  • compression and encryption used;
  • physical placement and clustering of related records.

Illustrative internal schema:

STORED_STUDENT
    LENGTH = 48 bytes
    ORGANISATION = B+-tree clustered on Rollno
    PREFIX  : type = BYTE(1),   offset = 0
    Rollno  : type = BYTE(8),   offset = 1,  INDEX rollno_idx
    Name    : type = BYTE(30),  offset = 9
    Dob     : type = DATE(4),   offset = 39, INDEX dob_idx
    COMPRESSION = prefix

Note there is exactly one internal schema.

Careful

The internal level is not the physical device level. Deciding which disk sector a page lands on is the operating system's business, below the DBMS. The internal schema describes structures — files, pages, indexes — not hardware.

docs.title: Conceptual level (logical level)
docs.text:
What it describes: what data is stored and what relationships exist among it — for the whole community of users — while hiding all physical detail.

The conceptual schema specifies entities, attributes, data types, relationships, user operations and constraints. It says nothing about indexes, file organisation or storage.

CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
    Rollno      VARCHAR(8)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name        VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    Dateofbirth DATE
);
CREATE TABLE COURSE (
    SID        VARCHAR(6)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Cname      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    TotalSeats INT         CHECK (TotalSeats > 0),
    Coursetype VARCHAR(10) CHECK (Coursetype IN ('Fulltime','Parttime'))
);
CREATE TABLE ADMISSION (
    Rollno         VARCHAR(8),
    SID            VARCHAR(6),
    Dateofadmission DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (Rollno, SID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Rollno) REFERENCES STUDENT(Rollno),
    FOREIGN KEY (SID)    REFERENCES COURSE(SID)
);

There is exactly one conceptual schema. It is the stable centre of the architecture — the single agreed description of the enterprise's data.

docs.title: External level (view level)
docs.text:
What it describes: the part of the database that a particular user group sees, in the form most convenient to them. Everything else is hidden.

There are many external schemas — one per user group. An external schema may:

  • expose a subset of tables and a subset of columns;
  • rename things to suit the user's vocabulary;
  • present derived data that is not stored at all (e.g. Age computed from Dateofbirth);
  • restructure — join several tables so the user sees one.
-- External schema for the Society Mentor
CREATE VIEW MentorView AS
SELECT s.Rollno, s.Name AS StudentName, y.Socname AS Society
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ENROLLMENT e ON s.Rollno = e.Rollno
JOIN   SOCIETY    y ON e.SocID  = y.SocID;

-- External schema for the Principal (aggregated, no personal data at all)
CREATE VIEW CourseLoad AS
SELECT c.Cname, COUNT(a.Rollno) AS Enrolled, c.TotalSeats
FROM   COURSE c LEFT JOIN ADMISSION a ON c.SID = a.SID
GROUP  BY c.SID, c.Cname, c.TotalSeats;

The mentor cannot see Dateofbirth; the Principal cannot see any individual student. The view is simultaneously a convenience and a security boundary.

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text: Internal Conceptual External Question answered How is it stored? What is stored? What does this user see? How many One One Many Written by DBA / system designer DBA with the enterprise DBA per user group Contains Files, indexes, record formats Tables, types, relationships, constraints Views Hides Nothing below it All physical detail Everything the user need not see DBMS artefact Storage engine settings, indexes Base tables (CREATE TABLE) Views (CREATE VIEW)

docs.title: 3.3 The Two Mappings
docs.text:
The three levels are only descriptions. Something must translate a request stated at one level into a request at the level below. That is the job of the two mappings, maintained by the DBMS.

External/conceptual mapping — relates each external schema to the conceptual schema. It tells the DBMS that the mentor's StudentName is the conceptual STUDENT.Name, and that MentorView is a join of three conceptual tables.

Conceptual/internal mapping — relates the conceptual schema to the internal schema. It tells the DBMS that conceptual column STUDENT.Rollno occupies bytes 1–8 of the stored record in the B+-tree-organised file, and that an index rollno_idx may be used.

Query processing across the levels

A user submits SELECT StudentName FROM MentorView WHERE Society = 'Debating';

  1. The DBMS uses the external/conceptual mapping to rewrite the query against base tables STUDENT, ENROLLMENT, SOCIETY.
  2. The optimiser uses the conceptual/internal mapping to choose access paths — "use soc_idx on SOCIETY.Socname, then the clustered index on Rollno".
  3. The storage engine reads the pages.
  4. The result travels back up, being reshaped at each level, until the user receives exactly the columns their external schema promised.

This is called mapping or, when it happens in the reverse direction for results, transformation.

The cost of the architecture

Every query pays for two levels of translation. That is a real overhead. Most commercial DBMSs therefore do not implement the three levels as three literally separate schema files; they support the effect of the architecture (base tables, views, storage parameters and indexes) while blending the levels internally for speed.

docs.title: 3.4 Data Independence
docs.text:
Data Independence

The capacity to change the schema at one level of a database system without having to change the schema at the next higher level. Only the mapping between the two levels is changed; everything above is untouched.

docs.title: Physical data independence
docs.text:
Physical data independence

The capacity to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema — and therefore without changing the external schemas or the application programs.

Changes that should be invisible upwards:

  • Creating or dropping an index. CREATE INDEX idx_name ON STUDENT(Name); makes queries faster and changes nothing about what data exists.
  • Reorganising a file from heap to sorted, or to hashed on Rollno.
  • Moving the database to a faster disk, or splitting it across several disks.
  • Changing the page size, or enabling compression.

After any of these, SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Rollno='X2019'; returns exactly the same answer, and no application is recompiled. Only the conceptual/internal mapping is revised.

Physical data independence is generally achieved well by modern DBMSs, because there is a clean, well-understood boundary: the conceptual level was defined from the outset to exclude all storage detail.

docs.title: Logical data independence
docs.text:
Logical data independence

The capacity to change the conceptual schema without changing the external schemas — and therefore without changing the application programs.

Changes that can be absorbed:

  • Adding a column. ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD COLUMN Mobile CHAR(10); — existing views that list columns explicitly are unaffected.
  • Adding a new table or a new relationship that existing users do not use.
  • Splitting a table by normalisation. Suppose STUDENT(Rollno, Name, Dob, Deptname, Deptphone) is decomposed into STUDENT(Rollno, Name, Dob, Dno) and DEPT(Dno, Deptname, Deptphone). Applications that expected the wide table need not change: redefine their external schema as a join view with the original name and columns.
-- Absorbing a decomposition; the old application still sees the old shape
CREATE VIEW STUDENT_OLD AS
SELECT s.Rollno, s.Name, s.Dob, d.Deptname, d.Deptphone
FROM   STUDENT s JOIN DEPT d ON s.Dno = d.Dno;
  • Removing a column or table that no external schema uses.

Changes that cannot be absorbed:

  • Removing a column that a view actually exposes. If Dateofbirth is deleted from the conceptual schema, no mapping can conjure it back for a view that publishes it. The information is simply gone.
  • Narrowing a domain so that data the view promised no longer fits.

Why logical data independence is harder

  1. Applications are written directly against the logical structure — they name tables and columns. Physical structures (indexes, page sizes) are never named by an application, so hiding them is easy.
  2. A change to the conceptual schema may destroy information rather than merely relocate it. A physical change never destroys information; it only moves or reorganises it.
  3. Views are not fully updatable. Even if a view can reproduce the old read shape after a decomposition, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE through a multi-table join view is restricted or forbidden by most DBMSs, so write-path applications may still break.

Hence: physical data independence is generally achievable; logical data independence is only partially achievable.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Physical data independence Logical data independence Insulates Conceptual level from internal level External level from conceptual level Uses which mapping Conceptual/internal External/conceptual Example change Add an index; switch to a hashed file Add a column; split a table by normalisation Difficulty Easier — generally achieved Harder — only partially achieved Why Applications never name physical structures Applications name tables and columns directly

docs.title: 3.5 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Explain the three-schema architecture with a neat diagram. Why are three levels needed rather than two?

A. (Diagram: reproduce Figure 3.1.)

Internal level — described by the internal schema; specifies the physical storage structures: file organisation, indexes, record layout, compression. There is one internal schema.

Conceptual level — described by the conceptual schema; specifies all entities, attributes, relationships, data types and constraints for the whole community of users, hiding all physical detail. There is one conceptual schema.

External level — described by many external schemas (views); each shows one user group the part of the database relevant to it, possibly renamed, restructured or derived, and hides the rest.

Two mappings connect the levels: external/conceptual and conceptual/internal. The DBMS uses them to translate a user request down to storage operations and the result back up.

Why three rather than two? With only "user view" and "storage" there would be a single mapping, so any storage change would ripple straight into user views. The conceptual level is inserted as a stable buffer: it is the one agreed, technology-free description of the enterprise's data. Physical changes stop at the conceptual level (physical data independence), and user-specific concerns stop at the external level (logical data independence). Additionally the conceptual level provides a single place to state constraints once for everybody, and lets many differing views coexist over one consistent design.

Solved Question 2

Q. Distinguish between logical and physical data independence. Which is harder to achieve, and why?

A. See the comparison table in Section 3.4.3 for the core distinction.

Physical data independence insulates the conceptual schema from changes to the internal schema. Building an index on STUDENT.Name speeds queries up but changes no table, no column and no application.

Logical data independence insulates external schemas from changes to the conceptual schema. Adding a Mobile column to STUDENT should not disturb a view that lists only Rollno and Name.

Logical data independence is harder, for three reasons:

  1. Applications refer to logical objects by name — they say SELECT Name FROM STUDENT. They never refer to a B+-tree or a page size, so physical structures can be swapped freely beneath them.
  2. A conceptual change can remove information. Dropping Dateofbirth cannot be hidden from a view that shows Dateofbirth; a physical change never destroys information.
  3. Even when a view can restore the old read shape (for instance after a normalising decomposition), updates through join views are restricted, so applications that write may still fail.

In practice DBMSs achieve physical data independence well, and logical data independence only partially.

Solved Question 3

Q. For each change, state which level it affects, which mapping must be revised, and which kind of data independence (if any) protects the applications.

a. Building a hash index on COURSE.Cname. b. Adding Mobile to STUDENT. c. Decomposing STUDENT into STUDENT and DEPT. d. Dropping Dateofbirth, which the admission view displays. e. Migrating the database from one disk to a RAID array.

A.

Level changed Mapping revised Independence Applications safe? a Internal Conceptual/internal Physical Yes — queries return the same answers, only faster. b Conceptual External/conceptual Logical Yes — views that name columns explicitly are unaffected. (A view using SELECT * may change shape, which is one reason SELECT * is discouraged in view definitions.) c Conceptual External/conceptual Logical Mostly — define a join view with the old name and columns, and readers are unaffected. Applications that update the old wide shape may break, since join views are not generally updatable. d Conceptual Cannot be repaired Logical independence fails No — the information no longer exists; no mapping can recreate it. e Internal (indeed below it) Conceptual/internal Physical Yes — completely invisible above the internal level.

Solved Question 4

Q. Trace the processing of the query SELECT StudentName FROM MentorView WHERE Society = 'Debating'; through the three levels.

A.

  1. External level. The user's request is expressed against MentorView, which their external schema defines as columns (Rollno, StudentName, Society).

  2. External/conceptual mapping. The DBMS looks up the view definition in the catalog and rewrites the query against conceptual base tables. StudentName is resolved to STUDENT.Name, Society to SOCIETY.Socname:

SELECT s.Name
FROM   STUDENT s
JOIN   ENROLLMENT e ON s.Rollno = e.Rollno
JOIN   SOCIETY    y ON e.SocID  = y.SocID
WHERE  y.Socname = 'Debating';

  1. Conceptual level. Constraints and privileges are checked: does this user hold SELECT on the view? Are the joins over declared foreign keys?

  2. Conceptual/internal mapping. The optimiser consults the internal schema for available access paths and statistics, and chooses a plan — for example, use the index on SOCIETY.Socname to find SocID, probe the index on ENROLLMENT.SocID, then look up STUDENT rows by the clustered index on Rollno.

  3. Internal level. The storage engine reads the relevant disk pages into the buffer pool and extracts the byte ranges holding Name.

  4. Result travels back up, being transformed at each mapping, and the user receives a single column labelled StudentName — the shape their external schema promised, with no knowledge of the three underlying tables or of any index.

Solved Question 5

Q. Why do most commercial DBMSs not implement the three-schema architecture literally?

A. Because of performance and pragmatism.

The architecture is a reference model: it describes a clean separation of concerns, not a mandatory implementation. Implementing it literally would mean that every single query is parsed and translated twice — once through the external/conceptual mapping and once through the conceptual/internal mapping — and that each result is transformed twice on the way back. For high-throughput OLTP workloads that overhead is unacceptable.

Real systems therefore support the effect without the literal structure. In MySQL or Oracle:

  • the conceptual schema appears as the set of base tables created with CREATE TABLE;
  • the external schemas appear as views and per-user privileges;
  • the internal schema appears as storage-engine choices, tablespaces, indexes and physical parameters — specified as clauses of the same DDL rather than in a separate schema language.

The optimiser flattens views into the base query and compiles a single execution plan, so the two translations collapse into one pass. Users still get logical and physical data independence; they simply do not pay for two literal levels of indirection.

docs.title: 3.6 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Who proposed the three-schema architecture, and in what year?
  2. How many internal, conceptual and external schemas can a database have?
  3. Name the two mappings and say what each connects.
  4. Define physical data independence in one sentence.
  5. Give one example of a change that logical data independence cannot absorb.
  6. At which level are constraints such as PRIMARY KEY specified?

B. Long answer

  1. Explain the three-schema architecture with a labelled diagram. Describe the contents of each schema and the purpose of each mapping.
  2. Define logical and physical data independence. Compare them in a table and explain, with three arguments, why logical independence is the harder of the two.
  3. "The conceptual level is the stable centre of the architecture." Explain and justify this statement.
  4. Describe how a query is processed through the three levels, from submission to result.

C. Application and analytical

  1. For a BANK database with tables CUSTOMER, ACCOUNT, TRANSACTION, write: a. two sentences of the conceptual schema; b. two different external schemas (as CREATE VIEW statements) — one for a teller and one for an auditor; c. three plausible entries of the internal schema.
  2. Classify each change as internal, conceptual or external, and state whether applications break: a. Adding a CHECK constraint to TotalSeats. b. Increasing the buffer pool size. c. Granting a new user access to an existing view. d. Renaming column Cname to CourseName. e. Rebuilding a fragmented index. f. Merging two tables into one.
  3. A company normalises EMPLOYEE(Eno, Ename, Dno, Dname, Dlocation) into EMPLOYEE(Eno, Ename, Dno) and DEPARTMENT(Dno, Dname, Dlocation). Write the view that preserves the old external schema. Then explain precisely which operations on that view will still fail, and why.
  4. Argue for or against: "With modern hardware, physical data independence no longer matters."
  5. A hospital DBA wants to encrypt the Diagnosis column at rest. Which level does this change? Which independence protects the applications? What could still go wrong?

D. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A database can have several conceptual schemas.
  2. Views belong to the internal level.
  3. Adding an index changes the conceptual schema.
  4. Logical data independence is easier to achieve than physical.
  5. The internal schema describes which disk sector each record occupies.
  6. Mappings are stored in the catalog.

Answers to Section D

  1. False. Exactly one — it is the single agreed description of the whole enterprise's data.
  2. False. Views are the external level.
  3. False. An index is an internal-level structure; the conceptual schema is unchanged. This is precisely physical data independence.
  4. False. It is harder, because applications name logical objects directly and conceptual changes can destroy information.
  5. False. Sector allocation is the operating system's concern. The internal schema describes files, records, indexes and access structures.
  6. True. The catalog stores view definitions (external/conceptual) and storage/column layout information (conceptual/internal).

Lesson Summary

  • Three levels: internal (how it is stored, one), conceptual (what is stored, one), external (what a user sees, many).
  • Two mappings: external/conceptual and conceptual/internal, maintained by the DBMS in the catalog.
  • Physical data independence: change the internal schema without touching the conceptual schema. Generally achieved.
  • Logical data independence: change the conceptual schema without touching external schemas. Only partially achieved — because applications name logical objects, conceptual changes can destroy information, and join views are not fully updatable.
  • Commercial systems realise the effect of the architecture without literally implementing three separate schema layers, for performance reasons.

docs.title: Lesson 26: Transactions and ACID Properties
docs.text:
All-or-nothing units of work, and how the DBMS guarantees them

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 6: Data Storage and Indexes · 4 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 20

Learning Outcomes

  1. Define a transaction and its primitive operations.
  2. State and explain the four ACID properties, and name the component responsible for each.
  3. Draw and explain the transaction state diagram.
  4. Explain write-ahead logging and how it delivers atomicity and durability.
  5. Classify the kinds of failure a DBMS must survive.

docs.title: 26.1 What a Transaction Is
docs.text:
Transaction

A transaction is a logical unit of database processing — an indivisible sequence of operations that takes the database from one consistent state to another.

It is indivisible in the strict sense: either all its operations take effect, or none does.

The canonical example is a bank transfer of ₹5,000 from account A to account B:

T:  read(A)
    A := A - 5000
    write(A)
    read(B)
    B := B + 5000
    write(B)

These six steps are one logical action — "transfer money" — even though they touch two accounts. If the system crashes after write(A) but before write(B), ₹5,000 has vanished. The transaction concept exists to make that impossible.

docs.title: The primitive operations
docs.text:
Operation Meaning read_item(X) Read database item X into a program variable. Involves finding the block, reading it into a buffer if not already there, and copying the value. write_item(X) Write the program variable's value back into item X in the buffer. The buffer block is written to disk later. BEGIN_TRANSACTION Mark the start. COMMIT Signal successful completion; all changes are to be made permanent. ROLLBACK / ABORT Signal failure; all changes must be undone.

The gap between write and disk

write_item(X) writes to the buffer, not to disk. The buffer manager (Unit 1, Lesson 4) decides later when to flush the block.

This is the source of both problems that recovery must solve: a committed transaction's changes may not yet be on disk when the system crashes (needing redo), and an uncommitted transaction's changes may already have been flushed (needing undo).

docs.title: 26.2 The ACID Properties
docs.text:
ACID

A — Atomicity. A transaction is an indivisible unit: either all its operations are reflected in the database, or none are. Guaranteed by the recovery manager.

C — Consistency preservation. A transaction executed alone on a consistent database leaves it consistent — every integrity constraint still holds. Guaranteed jointly by the programmer (who writes a correct transaction) and the DBMS (which enforces declared constraints).

I — Isolation. A transaction's updates must not be visible to other transactions until it commits; concurrent execution must yield the same result as some serial execution. Guaranteed by the concurrency-control manager.

D — Durability (permanence). Once a transaction commits, its changes survive any subsequent failure. Guaranteed by the recovery manager, via the log.

docs.title: Each property, with its failure mode
docs.text:
Atomicity. Without it, a crash between the debit and the credit destroys ₹5,000. The recovery manager guarantees it by undoing the partial work of any transaction that had not committed at the time of the crash.

Consistency. The transfer preserves the rule "total money is unchanged". Note this is not something the DBMS can infer — it enforces the constraints you declare (CHECK, FOREIGN KEY), but the logic of a correct transfer is the programmer's responsibility. A transaction that debits without crediting is atomic, isolated and durable, and still wrong.

Isolation. Without it, concurrent transactions interfere. Two clerks reading the same "last seat" both see it free and both admit a student — the lost update of Unit 1, Lesson 1. Isolation makes the outcome equal to some serial order.

Durability. Once the user is told "transfer complete", the money must stay transferred even if the power fails one millisecond later. The log record is forced to disk before the commit is acknowledged, so the change can be redone on restart.

Which component provides which

Property Responsible component Mechanism Atomicity Recovery manager Undo using the log Consistency Programmer + integrity subsystem Correct transaction logic + declared constraints Isolation Concurrency-control manager Locking, serialisable schedules (Lesson 4) Durability Recovery manager Redo using the write-ahead log

This table is a standard examination question. Note that atomicity and durability are two sides of the same mechanism — the log — and that consistency is the only one the DBMS cannot deliver by itself.

docs.title: 26.3 Transaction States
docs.text:
BEGIN
                          |
                          v
                    +------------+   read/write operations
              +-----|   ACTIVE   |<--------+
              |     +-----+------+         |
              |           |  last operation executed
     failure  |           v
              |   +----------------------+
              |   | PARTIALLY COMMITTED  |    changes still in buffers;
              |   +------+--------+------+    log records being forced
              |          |        |
              |   commit |        | failure (e.g. cannot force the log)
              |          v        |
              |   +------------+  |
              |   | COMMITTED  |  |     changes are PERMANENT
              |   +-----+------+  |
              |         |         |
              v         |         v
       +------------+   |   +------------+
       |   FAILED   |<--+---|   FAILED   |
       +-----+------+       +-----+------+
             |  roll back (UNDO all changes)
             v
       +------------+
       |  ABORTED   |----> restart the transaction, or kill it
       +-----+------+
             |
             v
        TERMINATED <----- also reached from COMMITTED

Figure 3.1 — The transaction state diagram.

State Meaning Active The initial state; the transaction is executing its operations. Partially committed The final operation has executed, but the changes may still be only in buffers. The log records must be forced to disk before the commit can be confirmed. Committed Successful completion recorded permanently. The changes can never now be undone. Failed Normal execution can no longer proceed — a constraint violation, a deadlock, a hardware error, or an explicit ROLLBACK. Aborted The transaction has been rolled back and the database restored to its state before the transaction began. Terminated The transaction has left the system, whether committed or aborted.

Why 'partially committed' exists as a separate state

It marks the window in which the transaction has finished computing but its effects are not yet durable — the log records are still being written.

A crash in this window means the transaction must be rolled back, even though it executed every operation successfully, because it was never promised to the user. Only after the commit log record is safely on disk does the transaction become committed, and only then is the "transaction complete" message sent.

Once committed, a transaction can never be undone. The only remedy for a mistaken committed transaction is a compensating transaction — a new transaction that reverses its effect.

docs.title: Kinds of failure
docs.text:
Category Examples Data lost Transaction failure Logical error, constraint violation, deadlock, explicit ROLLBACK, bad input None — one transaction is undone System crash Power failure, operating-system crash, main-memory failure Volatile storage (buffers) lost; disk intact Media failure Disk head crash, disk controller failure Non-volatile storage lost

Transaction and system failures are handled by the log. Media failure is handled by backups plus the archived log.

docs.title: The system log
docs.text:
Log (journal)

A sequential file on stable storage recording every change made by every transaction, so that the changes can be undone or redone.

Log record types:

Record Meaning [start_transaction, T] T has begun. [write_item, T, X, old_value, new_value] T changed X; both values are recorded. [read_item, T, X] T read X (optional; needed only for some protocols). [commit, T] T completed successfully. [abort, T] T was rolled back. [checkpoint] All buffers were flushed at this point.

Recording both the old and the new value is what makes the log usable in both directions: the old value supports UNDO, the new value supports REDO.

docs.title: Write-Ahead Logging
docs.text:
The WAL protocol — two rules

Rule 1 (for undo). The log record for a change must be forced to disk before the changed data block is written to disk. Otherwise: a crash could leave a modified block on disk with no log record of its old value, so the change could never be undone.

Rule 2 (for redo). All log records for a transaction, including its commit record, must be forced to disk before the transaction is reported as committed. Otherwise: a crash could lose a change the user was told had succeeded, so it could never be redone.

   TIME ---->

   T:  write(A)         write(B)        COMMIT
        |                 |                |
        v                 v                v
   LOG: [T,A,old,new]  [T,B,old,new]   [commit,T]
        |                 |                |
        +--- forced to disk BEFORE --------+  the data blocks are written
                                              and BEFORE the user is told
                                              "committed"

   Only after [commit,T] is safely on disk may the DBMS answer "done".

docs.title: Recovery after a crash
docs.text:
On restart the recovery manager scans the log from the last checkpoint:

  1. Build an undo list of transactions with a start_transaction record but no commit record, and a redo list of those with a commit record.
  2. UNDO — traverse the log backwards, restoring the old_value for every write by a transaction on the undo list.
  3. REDO — traverse the log forwards, applying the new_value for every write by a transaction on the redo list.

The result: every committed transaction's effects are present, and no uncommitted transaction's effects remain. That is precisely atomicity and durability delivered together.

Checkpoints

Periodically the DBMS suspends new transactions briefly, flushes all modified buffers to disk, and writes a [checkpoint] record to the log.

Recovery then needs to examine the log only from the last checkpoint onward, rather than from the beginning of time. Transactions that committed before the checkpoint need no redo, since their changes are known to be on disk.

docs.title: 26.5 Transactions in SQL
docs.text:
START TRANSACTION;                       -- or BEGIN

UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'A';
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'B';

-- verify before committing
SELECT AccNo, Balance FROM ACCOUNT WHERE AccNo IN ('A','B');

COMMIT;        -- make permanent
-- ROLLBACK;   -- or undo everything

Savepoints allow partial rollback:

START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES ('X9001','Test Student','2003-01-01');
SAVEPOINT after_student;
INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X9001','BADSID','2019-07-15');   -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_student;    -- undo only the admission
COMMIT;                                  -- the student insert survives

Autocommit

By default MySQL runs in autocommit mode: every individual statement is its own transaction, committed immediately. So

UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'A';
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'B';

is two separate transactions, and a crash between them loses the money — exactly the atomicity failure we set out to prevent.

START TRANSACTION suspends autocommit until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Use it whenever two or more statements must succeed or fail together. (SET autocommit = 0; changes the default for the session.)

Note also that DDL statements cause an implicit commit in MySQL: running CREATE TABLE inside a transaction silently commits everything before it.

docs.title: 26.6 Solved Questions
docs.text:
Solved Question 1

Q. Define a transaction. Explain the four ACID properties with the bank-transfer example, naming the component responsible for each.

A. A transaction is a logical unit of database processing — an indivisible sequence of operations taking the database from one consistent state to another.

Consider transferring ₹5,000 from account A to account B: read(A); A := A − 5000; write(A); read(B); B := B + 5000; write(B)

Atomicity — all or nothing. If the system crashes after write(A) but before write(B), ₹5,000 has vanished. Atomicity guarantees that such a partial execution is undone entirely on restart. Component: the recovery manager, using the old values in the log.

Consistency preservation. The rule "total money across all accounts is unchanged" holds before and after. The transaction may violate it momentarily — between the two writes the total is ₹5,000 short — but that intermediate state is never visible to anyone else (which is isolation's job) and never final (atomicity's job). Component: the programmer, who must write a transfer that debits and credits equal amounts, together with the integrity subsystem, which enforces declared constraints such as CHECK (Balance >= 0).

Isolation. If another transaction computed the bank's total assets while ours sat between the two writes, it would report ₹5,000 too little. Isolation ensures concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial order. Component: the concurrency-control manager.

Durability. Once the customer is told "transfer complete", the money must stay transferred even if the power fails immediately afterwards. Component: the recovery manager, which forces the commit log record to disk before acknowledging, so the change can be redone.

Note that consistency is the only property the DBMS cannot supply by itself — a transaction that debits without crediting satisfies A, I and D perfectly and is still wrong.

Solved Question 2

Q. Draw the transaction state diagram and explain each state. Why is "partially committed" a separate state?

A. (Diagram: Figure 3.1.)

Active — the initial state; the transaction is executing its reads and writes.

Partially committed — the last operation has executed, but the changes may still be in volatile buffers and the log records may not yet be on disk.

Committed — successful completion has been recorded permanently. The changes can never now be undone.

Failed — normal execution cannot proceed: a constraint violation, a deadlock victim, a hardware error, or an explicit ROLLBACK.

Aborted — the transaction has been rolled back and the database restored to its pre-transaction state. The transaction may then be restarted or killed.

Terminated — the transaction has left the system, from either committed or aborted.

Why "partially committed" is separate. It marks the interval in which the transaction has finished computing but its effects are not yet durable. Two things are still pending: dirty buffer blocks may not have reached disk, and the [commit, T] log record may not yet be forced.

If the system crashes in this window, the transaction must be rolled back — even though every operation succeeded — because it was never promised to the user, and the write-ahead rule may not yet have been satisfied. The transition to committed occurs only when the commit log record is safely on stable storage; only then is the user told "done".

Without this state the model could not express the difference between "finished executing" and "guaranteed permanent" — which is exactly the distinction durability depends on.

Solved Question 3

Q. What is a log? What does a write_item log record contain, and why? State the write-ahead logging protocol and explain what each rule prevents.

A. The log (journal) is a sequential file on stable storage recording every change made by every transaction, so that changes can be undone or redone after a failure.

A write_item record is [write_item, T, X, old_value, new_value]. It records both values because the log must serve two opposite purposes:

  • the old value allows UNDO — restoring X when T did not commit;
  • the new value allows REDO — reapplying T's change when T did commit but the data block had not reached disk.

The write-ahead logging protocol — two rules.

Rule 1 (undo rule). The log record describing a change must be forced to disk before the corresponding data block is written to disk. Prevents: a crash leaving a modified block on disk with no record of its old value. The change could then never be undone, breaking atomicity.

Rule 2 (redo rule). All of a transaction's log records, including [commit, T], must be forced to disk before the transaction is reported committed. Prevents: a crash losing a change the user was told had succeeded. Without the log record there is nothing to redo, breaking durability.

Recovery. On restart, scan the log from the last checkpoint; build the undo list (started but not committed) and the redo list (committed). Traverse backwards restoring old values for the undo list, then forwards applying new values for the redo list. The outcome is exactly atomicity and durability: every committed effect present, no uncommitted effect remaining.

Solved Question 4

Q. Classify the kinds of failure a DBMS must survive, and state how each is handled.

A.

1. Transaction failure (local). One transaction cannot complete: a logical error (division by zero, bad input), a constraint violation, a deadlock in which it is chosen as the victim, or an explicit ROLLBACK. Effect: only that transaction is affected; the database and other transactions are untouched. Handling: the recovery manager undoes the transaction's writes using the old values in the log, restoring the pre-transaction state. The transaction may then be restarted.

2. System crash (soft failure). Power failure, operating-system crash, or main-memory failure. Effect: the contents of volatile storage — the buffer pool — are lost. Disk contents survive. Some committed changes may not yet have been flushed; some uncommitted changes may already have been. Handling: restart recovery from the log. Scan from the last checkpoint, undo every transaction without a commit record, redo every transaction with one.

3. Media failure (hard failure). A disk head crash or controller failure destroys part of the non-volatile storage. Effect: the database itself is damaged; the log alone cannot help, since it may be on the failed device. Handling: restore the most recent backup (dump), then redo all committed transactions from the archived log kept on separate media. This is why backups and the log must be stored on different devices, and why backups must be tested.

A fourth category sometimes listed: concurrency-control enforcement — the scheduler aborts a transaction to preserve serialisability or break a deadlock. This is really a form of transaction failure, and it is handled identically.

The general principle: the DBMS assumes disk is reliable and memory is not (categories 1–2, handled by the log); when even that assumption fails (category 3), it falls back on redundancy held elsewhere.

Solved Question 5

Q. What is a checkpoint? Why is it needed? Describe what happens at one.

A. A checkpoint is a point at which the DBMS guarantees that all modified buffer blocks have been written to disk, recorded by a [checkpoint] entry in the log.

Why needed. Without checkpoints, recovery after a crash would require scanning the log from the very beginning, because the recovery manager could not know which committed changes had already reached disk. For a system running for months this is impossible — recovery would take longer than the outage it was repairing. It would also mean redoing millions of changes already safely on disk.

What happens at a checkpoint:

  1. Suspend the start of new transactions (and briefly suspend execution of active ones).
  2. Force all log records currently in main memory to disk.
  3. Write all modified (dirty) buffer blocks to disk.
  4. Write a [checkpoint] record — usually listing the currently active transactions — to the log, and force it to disk.
  5. Resume normal execution.

Effect on recovery. The recovery manager scans the log backwards only as far as the last checkpoint. Any transaction that committed before the checkpoint needs no redo, because step 3 guarantees its changes are on disk. Only transactions active at or after the checkpoint need attention.

The trade-off. Checkpoints cost a brief pause and a burst of disk writes. Frequent checkpoints make recovery fast but slow normal operation; infrequent ones do the reverse. Real systems use fuzzy checkpointing, which avoids suspending transactions by recording the set of dirty pages rather than flushing them all synchronously.

Solved Question 6

Q. Explain autocommit and why it is dangerous for a multi-statement operation. Show the correct SQL for a transfer, and explain savepoints.

A. In autocommit mode — the default in MySQL — every individual statement is its own transaction, committed immediately on completion.

Why this is dangerous. A logical operation spanning several statements is then not atomic:

UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'A';   -- committed
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'B';   -- separate txn

These are two transactions. If the second fails — a constraint violation, a crash, a lost connection — the first has already committed and cannot be undone. ₹5,000 has been destroyed, and the database is in a state no single constraint can detect as wrong. This is precisely the atomicity failure the transaction concept exists to prevent.

Correct form:

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'A';
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 5000 WHERE AccNo = 'B';
COMMIT;                     -- both, or (on ROLLBACK) neither

START TRANSACTION suspends autocommit until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so the two updates become one atomic unit.

Savepoints mark an intermediate point to which a transaction may be partially rolled back, without abandoning the whole transaction:

START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES ('X9001','Test Student','2003-01-01');
SAVEPOINT after_student;
INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X9001','BADSID','2019-07-15');   -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_student;     -- undo only the admission
INSERT INTO ADMISSION VALUES ('X9001','CS01','2019-07-15');     -- retry
COMMIT;                                   -- the student insert survives

Savepoints are useful for long transactions in which one step may fail recoverably. A caution specific to MySQL: DDL statements such as CREATE TABLE cause an implicit commit, silently ending the transaction and committing everything before them — so never mix DDL into a transaction you intend to be able to roll back.

docs.title: 26.7 Exercises
docs.text:
A. Short answer

  1. Define a transaction.
  2. List the ACID properties and the component responsible for each.
  3. Name the six transaction states.
  4. What does a write_item log record contain, and why both values?
  5. State the two rules of write-ahead logging.
  6. What is a checkpoint, and why is it needed?
  7. What is autocommit?

B. Long answer

  1. Explain the four ACID properties with the bank-transfer example. Which cannot be guaranteed by the DBMS alone, and why?
  2. Draw and explain the transaction state diagram, justifying the existence of the "partially committed" state.
  3. Explain the write-ahead logging protocol. State precisely what each rule prevents and which ACID property it protects.
  4. Classify the kinds of failure and state how each is handled.
  5. Describe the recovery procedure after a system crash, explaining the undo and redo lists.

C. Application

  1. Write the SQL for transferring ₹10,000 from account A to B as a single atomic transaction, including a check that A has sufficient balance.
  2. Write a transaction that admits a student to a course and increments an enrolment counter, so that both succeed or neither does.
  3. Given this log after a crash, determine which transactions must be undone and which redone: 
    [start, T1]
[write, T1, A, 100, 150]
[start, T2]
[write, T2, B, 200, 250]
[commit, T1]
[start, T3]
[write, T3, C, 300, 350]
[write, T2, D, 400, 450]
[commit, T3]
<<< CRASH >>>
  4. Repeat question 15 assuming a [checkpoint] record appeared immediately after [commit, T1]. Which log records must now be examined?
  5. A student runs two UPDATE statements in MySQL without START TRANSACTION, and the connection drops between them. Describe the resulting state and how it could have been prevented.
  6. Explain what a compensating transaction is, and why it is the only remedy for a mistaken committed transaction.

D. Analysis

  1. Explain why atomicity and durability are described as "two sides of the same mechanism".
  2. Argue whether the following are transactions, and state the ACID property most at risk in each: a. Booking a railway ticket. b. Running a monthly report. c. Adding a column to a table. d. Transferring a student between two courses.
  3. Explain why a committed transaction can never be undone, and what this implies for application design.
  4. Explain the trade-off in checkpoint frequency.
  5. Why must the backup and the archived log be stored on different devices?

E. Objective — True or False with reason

  1. A transaction always changes the database.
  2. Consistency is guaranteed entirely by the DBMS.
  3. A committed transaction can be rolled back.
  4. The log records only new values.
  5. Checkpoints are needed for atomicity.
  6. In autocommit mode, two UPDATE statements form one transaction.
  7. Durability protects against media failure.

Answers to Section E

  1. False. A read-only transaction (a report) changes nothing but is still a transaction, needing isolation and consistency.
  2. False. The DBMS enforces declared constraints; the logic of a correct transaction is the programmer's responsibility.
  3. False. Never. The only remedy is a compensating transaction that reverses its effect.
  4. False. It records both old and new values — old for undo, new for redo.
  5. False. They are a performance optimisation, bounding how much log must be scanned. Atomicity comes from the log itself.
  6. False. Each statement is its own transaction, committed immediately — which is exactly the danger.
  7. Partly. Durability guarantees committed changes survive system failure via the log. Surviving media failure additionally requires backups plus an archived log on separate media.

Lesson Summary

  • A transaction is an indivisible logical unit taking the database from one consistent state to another.
  • ACID: Atomicity (recovery manager, undo), Consistency (programmer + constraints), Isolation (concurrency control), Durability (recovery manager, redo).
  • States: active → partially committed → committed, or active → failed → aborted. "Partially committed" is the window before durability is guaranteed.
  • The log records old and new values. WAL: log before data; commit record before acknowledging.
  • Recovery = undo the uncommitted, redo the committed, scanning from the last checkpoint.
  • Autocommit makes each statement its own transaction — use START TRANSACTION whenever several statements must be atomic.

docs.title: Lesson 9: Update Anomalies and the Relational Data Model
docs.text:
Why bad tables hurt, and what a relation formally is

About this lesson

Course: Database Management Systems (DSC11 / DSC05 / GE3a)

Unit 3: Relational Data Model · 7 Lecture Hours

Lesson duration: 1 lecture

Reading: Elmasri & Navathe, Ch. 5.1, 14.1

Learning Outcomes

  1. Identify insertion, deletion and modification anomalies in a badly designed table.
  2. Explain that anomalies are caused by storing facts about two things in one relation.
  3. State the formal definition of a relation, and the terms domain, tuple, attribute, degree, cardinality.
  4. Explain the four characteristics of relations, and why order does not matter.
  5. Distinguish relation schema from relation state (instance).

docs.title: 9.1 Update Anomalies — the Motivation
docs.text:
Unit 1 said redundancy causes inconsistency. This lesson makes that precise, because update anomalies are the reason normalisation exists (Unit 5).

Consider a college that stores everything in one table.

The bad design

STUDENT_COURSE( Rollno, Sname, Dateofbirth, SID, Cname, TotalSeats, TeacherInCharge, Dateofadmission )

Rollno Sname Dateofbirth SID Cname TotalSeats TeacherInCharge Dateofadmission X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 CS01 Computer Science 60 R. K. Gupta 2019-07-15 X2019 Ankit Sharma 2001-03-14 MA02 Mathematics 50 A. Gupta 2019-08-01 X2020 Riya Verma 2002-05-11 CS01 Computer Science 60 R. K. Gupta 2019-07-16 Z1188 Sana Iqbal 2001-11-02 CS01 Computer Science 60 R. K. Gupta 2019-07-18

Look at the redundancy: "Computer Science has 60 seats and is taught by R. K. Gupta" is stored three times; "Ankit Sharma was born on 2001-03-14" is stored twice.

Three kinds of failure follow directly.

docs.title: Insertion anomaly
docs.text:
Insertion anomaly

You cannot record a fact because some unrelated information is missing.

The college creates a new course, PH01 Physics, 40 seats, teacher-in-charge Dr Rao. No student has enrolled yet.

Try to insert it:

INSERT INTO STUDENT_COURSE
VALUES (NULL, NULL, NULL, 'PH01', 'Physics', 40, 'Dr Rao', NULL);

Rollno is part of the primary key (Rollno, SID), and a primary key may not be NULL (entity integrity, Lesson 2). The insert is rejected. The college cannot record a course until a student joins it — an absurd restriction created purely by the design.

The symmetric case: a student who has been admitted but not yet assigned a course cannot be recorded either.

docs.title: Deletion anomaly
docs.text:
Deletion anomaly

Deleting a row destroys facts you wanted to keep, as a side effect.

X2020 Riya Verma and Z1188 Sana Iqbal withdraw, then X2019 Ankit Sharma drops Computer Science. All rows mentioning CS01 disappear.

Result: the college has lost the facts that a course CS01 called Computer Science exists, has 60 seats, and is taught by R. K. Gupta. Deleting an enrolment silently destroyed a course.

docs.title: Modification (update) anomaly
docs.text:
Modification anomaly

A single logical change requires many physical updates, and if any is missed the database becomes inconsistent.

R. K. Gupta is replaced by Dr S. Iyer as teacher-in-charge of Computer Science. That is one real-world fact, but it appears in three rows. If a program updates only the row it happens to be looking at:

Rollno SID Cname TeacherInCharge X2019 CS01 Computer Science Dr S. Iyer X2020 CS01 Computer Science R. K. Gupta Z1188 CS01 Computer Science R. K. Gupta

The database now asserts that one course has two different teachers-in-charge. It is inconsistent, and there is no way to tell which value is right.

The single sentence that explains all three

Anomalies arise because the relation stores facts about more than one kind of thing. STUDENT_COURSE mixes facts about students, facts about courses, and facts about admissions. A fact about a course should be stored once, in a place that exists independently of any student.

docs.title: The cure
docs.text:
Split into one relation per kind of thing — exactly what the ER diagram of Unit 2 already told us:

STUDENT   ( Rollno, Sname, Dateofbirth )
COURSE    ( SID, Cname, TotalSeats, TeacherInCharge )
ADMISSION ( Rollno, SID, Dateofadmission )
Anomaly Now? Insert a course with no students Fine — insert into COURSE alone. Delete the last enrolment in CS01 Fine — the COURSE row survives. Change the teacher-in-charge Fine — exactly one row is updated.

Fourth anomaly: spurious tuples

Splitting badly is also possible. If tables are decomposed along the wrong attributes, joining them back produces spurious tuples — rows that were never in the original data. Unit 5, Lesson 5 shows how to guarantee a lossless-join decomposition, which is the formal statement of "split correctly".

docs.title: 9.2 The Relational Model — Formal Definitions
docs.text: Proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970 in "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks". Its power comes from being founded on set theory.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Domain

A domain D is a set of atomic values — indivisible with respect to the model. A domain has a name, a data type and a format.

Domain name Description Data type / format Roll_numbers Roll numbers of students VARCHAR(8), pattern letter + 4 digits Names Personal names VARCHAR(40) Dates Calendar dates DATE, YYYY-MM-DD Seat_counts Seats in a course INT, 1 to 500 Course_types Type of course {'Fulltime', 'Parttime'}

Note that Course_types is an enumerated domain of exactly two values, and that giving a domain a name and a meaning is more than giving it a data type: Roll_numbers and Society_codes might both be VARCHAR(8), but comparing them is meaningless.

docs.title: Relation schema
docs.text:
Relation schema

A relation schema R, written R(A1, A2, ..., An), consists of a relation name R and a list of attributes A1 ... An. Each attribute Ai is the name of a role played by some domain D in R; that domain is called the domain of Ai, written dom(Ai).

The degree (arity) of a relation is n, the number of attributes.

STUDENT ( Rollno, Name, Dateofbirth )        degree 3

dom(Rollno)      = Roll_numbers
dom(Name)        = Names
dom(Dateofbirth) = Dates

'Role played by a domain' — why the wording matters

Two different attributes may draw on the same domain while meaning different things. In FLIGHT(Origin, Destination) both attributes have the domain City_names, but Origin and Destination are different roles. The attribute name records the role; the domain records the permitted values.

docs.title: Relation state (instance)
docs.text:
Relation state

A relation state (or relation instance, or simply relation) r of the schema R(A1, ..., An), written r(R), is a set of n-tuples:

r = { t1, t2, ..., tm }

Each tuple t is an ordered list of n values t = <v1, v2, ..., vn>, where each vi is an element of dom(Ai) or the special value NULL.

Formally: r(R) is a subset of the Cartesian product of the domains:

r(R) ⊆ dom(A1) × dom(A2) × ... × dom(An)

The number of tuples m is the cardinality of the relation.

Degree vs cardinality

Degree = number of attributes (columns) — a property of the schema, and fixed. Cardinality = number of tuples (rows) — a property of the state, and changing constantly.

docs.title: The correspondence of terms
docs.text: Formal (relational theory) Informal (tables) Physical (files) Relation Table File Tuple Row Record Attribute Column Field Domain Set of legal column values Data type Degree Number of columns Number of fields Cardinality Number of rows Number of records Relation schema Table definition File layout / header Relation state Table contents File contents

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Schema: COURSE(SID, Cname, TotalSeats, Coursetype), degree 4.

State r(COURSE):

SID Cname TotalSeats Coursetype CS01 Computer Science 60 Fulltime CH01 Chemistry 45 Fulltime MA02 Mathematics 50 Parttime

Cardinality = 3.

As a set of tuples:

r(COURSE) = { <'CS01','Computer Science',60,'Fulltime'>,
              <'CH01','Chemistry',       45,'Fulltime'>,
              <'MA02','Mathematics',     50,'Parttime'> }

Tuple access. t[Cname] denotes the value of attribute Cname in tuple t. If t is the first tuple, t[Cname] = 'Computer Science' and t[SID, Coursetype] = <'CS01','Fulltime'>.

docs.title: 9.3 The Four Characteristics of Relations
docs.text: These follow from the definition "a relation is a set of tuples", and each is examinable.

docs.title: Characteristic 1 — Ordering of tuples is immaterial
docs.text:
A relation is a set, and a set has no order. These two are the same relation:

SID Cname CS01 Computer Science CH01 Chemistry SID Cname CH01 Chemistry CS01 Computer Science
